event_model_payload.headline: Part 4: The Alert That Could Never Fire
event_model_payload.summary:
Since the first week of this project, observability/prometheus/alerts.yml has contained this:

- alert: PDSCircuitOpen
  expr: pybreaker_state{name="pds"} == 1

It is a correct rule. The circuit breaker in front of the Personal Demographics Service opens after five consecutive failures, the pipeline carries on with the demographics from the message, and somebody should be told.

No service has ever exported pybreaker_state. The rule has been watching a series that does not exist, which looks exactly like a healthy system.

The problem

Monitoring has a particular failure mode: you cannot tell the difference between nothing being wrong and nothing being watched. A dashboard with no red on it means one of those two things, and it does not say which.

In this pipeline, that matters more than usual, because the failures I care about mostly return 200. A patient written without an NHS number to match on is a successful request. A date of birth that failed to parse is a successful request. The breaker opening and the pipeline silently dropping to unenriched demographics is a whole shift of successful requests.

So this week I went looking for the things the pipeline does that nobody would ever find out about.

What the pipeline could not see

The breaker opens, and nothing says so

I started the transform service, sent a message, and scraped /metrics. Twenty-eight metric families, and pybreaker_state is not among them. Nothing with breaker or circuit in the name at all.

Then I drove the breaker open, which takes five failures:

breaker before      : closed | failures: 0
breaker after       : open   | failures: 5
pybreaker_state now : False

The breaker is open. The pipeline has stopped enriching. The alert cannot fire, and there is no other signal anywhere.

pybreaker makes this easy to fix. It has a CircuitBreakerListener with a state_change hook, which is called on every transition, so there is nothing to poll:

class _BreakerStateExporter(pybreaker.CircuitBreakerListener):
    def state_change(self, cb, old_state, new_state) -> None:
        BREAKER_STATE.labels(name=cb.name).set(
            _BREAKER_STATE_VALUES.get(getattr(new_state, "name", None), 0)
        )

That getattr(new_state, "name", None) is the second version. My first read new_state.state, which does not exist in pybreaker 1.2.0. The state objects carry a name instead, holding the string closed, open or half-open.

The failure mode of getting that wrong is the thing this whole article is about. getattr with a default does not raise. The lookup misses, falls back to 0, and the gauge sits there reading closed while the breaker is open. I would have shipped a fix for an unfireable alert that left it unfireable, and the metric would have existed, which is worse, because now the dashboard has a panel on it.

The test caught it.

Fields that fail to map leave no trace

Part 3 was about nine mapping defects. The reason all nine survived is in this article: only a whole-message parse failure goes to the dead-letter folder. A single field that fails to map is simply absent from the resource, and the message returns 200.

I sent a message with an unparseable date of birth:

message with an unparseable date of birth -> HTTP 200
birthDate in the resource : False
hl7_dlq_total moved?      : no
any metric for a lost field: none

The mapper now reports what it dropped, and transform turns that into
hl7_field_dropped_total{segment,field,reason}. The mapper itself stays free of Prometheus imports: it reports, the service counts. Known gaps like PID-11 and PV1-19 come through as not_mapped, so they are visible without being alarming, and unparseable_date is the one with an alert on it.

Alert rules are code that only runs during an incident

Which is the actual reason this sat here for weeks. Nothing in the build ever executed that rule.

Prometheus ships a unit test framework for alerting rules, and it took about twenty minutes to use. You give it synthetic series and assert which alerts fire and when:

- interval: 1m
  name: PDSCircuitOpen fires once the breaker is open
  input_series:
    - series: 'pybreaker_state{name="pds"}'
      values: "0x5 1x10"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 4m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []
    - eval_time: 9m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts:
        - exp_labels: { severity: warning, team: interop, name: pds }

There are nine cases now. The one I would keep if I could only keep one is this:

- name: with no series exported the rule is silent, which was the bug
  input_series:
    - series: 'up{job="transform"}'
      values: "1x20"
  alert_rule_test:
    - eval_time: 15m
      alertname: PDSCircuitOpen
      exp_alerts: []

That is the repo as it actually stood. The rule is right, there is nothing for it to read, and the test documents that this is indistinguishable from health.

promtool check rules and promtool test rules now run as a CI job, so the rules are exercised on every pull request rather than during the first outage.

Watching it fire, rather than trusting the test

A promtool test proves the expression is right. It does not prove the pipeline produces the series under real conditions, so the last step was to break the thing on purpose:

make break-pds

That stops pds-client, sends eight messages two seconds apart, and prints the gauge after each one. Every message returns 200 throughout, which is the whole point: enrichment has stopped, the stored demographics are now whatever arrived in the message, and the front door is reporting success.

The first time I ran it against the real stack, the gauge read 0 after all eight messages. The breaker never opened.

The fix that still could not fire

The unit test for the gauge passed because it drove the breaker with an
ordinary function. The real PDS call is async, and I had wrapped it with pybreaker's decorator:

@pds_breaker
async def _call() -> dict | None:
    ...

pybreaker's only async support is for Tornado, and its README does not mention asyncio at all. On an async def function, the decorator calls it, gets a coroutine object back, and records a success. The request fails later, when the coroutine is awaited, outside the breaker. The running service had logged 16 PDS failures, and the breaker had counted none of them.

The fix is pybreaker's calling() context manager, which wraps the awaited block itself:

async def _call() -> dict | None:
    with pds_breaker.calling(), PDS_LATENCY.labels(outcome="success").time():
        resp = await http.get(...)

There is now a test that goes through the real async path with PDS failing. It fails against the old code.

It's the same shape as the getattr bug, one layer further down. The rule was right, the gauge was right, the listener was right, and the breaker they all depended on was never told anything had gone wrong. Every layer had a test and every test passed.

With the fix in, the breaker opens on the fifth message, and PDSCircuitOpen goes to Firing once the rule's two minutes have passed.

I had also worried that for: 2m could never be satisfied, because the
breaker's reset_timeout is 30 seconds and I expected the state to bounce between open and half-open. My first check of that went through the same synchronous test path, so it measured nothing real. In the running stack, the gauge held flat at 1 for twelve minutes, until I brought PDS back. pybreaker only moves to half-open when a call arrives after the timeout, and that trial call closes or reopens it in the same moment, so a ten-second scrape never sees it.

There is a second script for the other failure path, and writing it corrected something in my own plan for this article. The plan said to "stop the transform service mid-burst and show the DLQ". That does not work. The dead-letter folder is written by transform, so stopping transform means nothing writes to it at all: ingest logs the failure and answers 200 with forwarded: false. To fill the dead-letter folder you have to break what transform writes to, which is HAPI FHIR. make break-fhir does that.

Its first real run found one more. Every dead-letter write failed with
PermissionError. The service runs as an unprivileged user, and the Docker volume mounted over its dead-letter folder belonged to root, because the image never created that folder. So the messages the folder exists to keep were the ones being lost. The image now creates the folder, owned by the service user, and Docker copies it into a new volume when the volume is first created.

The panels, which I nearly forgot

Four new metrics and, for most of a day, no way to see any of them. The Grafana dashboard had six panels, and not one showed the breaker state, the dropped fields, the invalid NHS numbers or the write identity.

That is a fairly pointed thing to nearly ship in an article about not being able to see things. The series existed, and the alerts worked, and the place people actually look had not changed at all. There are ten panels now.

The one a reader found

Kevin Mayfield, who does health integration and data architecture for a living, read Part 3 and pointed out something I had not considered at all.

I had just shipped a fix that keys patient identity on the NHS number, as a conditional update. He pointed out that his trust is near the Scottish border, and that a Scottish CHI number sometimes arrives in the NHS Number field. More than that: a patient's NHS number can change when they move between the Scottish and English NHS.

Which means the identity key I had just built the whole write path around is not stable.

I tested it. Same patient, same hospital number, two messages with different NHS numbers:

message 1 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|1111111111
message 2 request : PUT Patient?identifier=...nhs-number|9000000009
same target?      : False
local MRN in both : L12345, L12345

Two records. The hospital number is identical in both messages and is simply not looked at. Nothing counts it, nothing alerts on it, and the FHIR server returns 200 twice.

That led somewhere I should have gone in Part 3. If the NHS number is the identity key, is it ever validated?

9000000009   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1111111111   checksum valid: True   accepted: True
1234567890   checksum valid: False  accepted: True

No. An NHS number carries a Modulus 11 check digit, and the NHS Data Dictionary is unambiguous about it: "The check digit is validated using the Modulus 11 algorithm, and the use of this algorithm is mandatory." Multiply the first nine digits by 10 down to 2, sum, take the remainder modulo 11, and subtract from 11. A result of 11 means a check digit of 0, and "If the result is 10 then the NHS NUMBER is invalid and not used".

I was not running it. 1234567890 was being accepted as an NHS number and used to match a patient.

This is also a partial answer to Kevin's CHI point, which is why it is worth doing beyond tidiness. A CHI number is also ten digits, and it will not satisfy the NHS check digit. So a sending system supplying CHI numbers in the NHS Number field now shows up as a rate on nhs_number_invalid_total rather than as silently mismatched patients.

An identifier that fails the check is still kept on the resource, because the sender sent it and dropping it loses information. It is just never used to look a patient up or to match an existing record. A wrong identity is worse than no identity.

Writes with nothing to match on are now counted as patient_write_total{identity="none"}, and there is an alert when that passes a tenth of writes.

What none of this catches

The thing Kevin actually described is not a metric problem.

Counting writes with no identity tells you when matching is degrading. It does not tell you that the same person has arrived twice under two different NHS numbers, because from inside a single message that looks completely normal. Both messages are valid, both have good check digits, both write successfully.

Catching that needs a matching step, which is what he does:

I have a scoring system based on identifier, date of birth, gender, name and postcode. I weight MRN and NHS the highest, then DOB.

A demographic query first, then a weighted score across several fields, rather than trusting one identifier. He also raised the fetus and baby case, where a newborn may not have its own NHS number yet, which breaks identifier-first matching in a different direction.

That is a substantial piece of work, and it is not in this week's change. What this week does is make the conditions that feed it visible, so when the matching goes in there is something to measure it against.

Worth stealing

Test your alert rules. They are the only code in the repo that runs exclusively during an incident, which makes them the least exercised and the most load-bearing. promtool test rules exists and takes an afternoon to adopt.

Assert the series exists, not just that the rule is right. My rule was correct the whole time. The failure was one level below it, and no amount of reviewing the expression would have found it.

Watch for silent fallbacks in monitoring code: getattr with a default, or a synchronous decorator around an async function. Both fail by doing nothing, in the thing that is supposed to tell you about silent failures. My gauge read zero for the same reason the alert read quiet.

Count the successes you are unsure about. Error rates are the easy half. patient_write_total{identity="none"} counts requests that returned 200 and did something I would rather they had not.

Export the metric and add the panel in the same change. I had the series, the alert and the rule test before I noticed the dashboard still showed the same six panels it had in week one. A metric nobody has a graph for is halfway back to where this started.

Where AI helps here, and where it doesn't

I built this project with Claude Code. This week I had it write the metrics, the promtool tests and the break scripts, then made it prove each one against the running stack, not the code.

Writing the listener, the metrics and the promtool cases was quick. The useful part was the step before: starting the service, scraping /metrics and reading the list of what was actually there, rather than reading the alert file and the service code and believing they lined up. They had not lined up for weeks, and both halves looked correct on their own.

It also wrote the async decorator bug, and the first timing check that went through the same synchronous path. Both were caught the same way, by running the real stack and reading what it did.

Four weeks in, the pattern is stable enough to state plainly. Every finding in this series has come from running the thing, and the two most valuable have come from people who read it and knew more than I did about the domain. Neither of those is a code review.

What I'd do differently

I would have written the alert rule tests at the same time as the alert rules, in the first week. Not because the rules were wrong, but because writing the test is what forces you to produce the series, and producing the series is what I had skipped.

I would also have written the break scripts first. make break-pds is about thirty lines, and it is the only thing here that tests the whole chain, from a stopped container through to a rule evaluating in Prometheus. Everything else in this article tests one layer and assumes the next one. I would also have run it before tagging this part, not after.

And I would have remembered that fixing the code does not fix the data it already wrote. The demo database held 996 copies of the same test patient from before Part 3's conditional update. The conditional update then refused, correctly, to pick one, with the 412 the FHIR spec requires. I reset the demo database. A trust can't, and that is where the matching work Kevin described begins.

Sources

  • NHS Data Dictionary: NHS NUMBER, including the Modulus 11 check
  • Prometheus: unit testing rules
  • Prometheus: alerting rules
  • pybreaker on PyPI
  • pybreaker README: the calling() context manager and Tornado-only async support
  • FHIR R4: conditional update, including the 412 on multiple matches
  • Docker: populating a volume from a container
  • prometheus_client for Python
  • The code for this article, tag part-4

Next

Part 5, on 11 November, is security and compliance, which has a backlog of its own: two documents in this repo describe a DataClass tag applied by a Terraform block that is commented out.

Which of your alert rules has never fired, and do you know whether that is good news?

This is a personal project. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by NHS England or any NHS organisation. It uses the public PDS FHIR sandbox and synthetic test data only. Views are my own.

event_model_payload.headline: Adrianzhi Kuan Ong（王志寬）︱人工智能與日本股市同時升溫：新一輪結構性行情正在形成？
event_model_payload.summary:
2023年上半年，全球市場出現了兩個讓我非常關注的變化。
一個在美國——人工智能迅速成為科技行業最重要的投資主題之一，AI、半導體、算力和數據相關公司受到資本追捧。
另一個在日本——沉寂多年的日本股市重新吸引全球資金，企業治理、資本效率和估值修復成為新的市場焦點。


表面上，這是兩個完全不同的故事。
一個交易未來，一個重新發現價值。
但它們背後存在同一個邏輯：當舊的投資環境發生變化，資本就會重新尋找增長和定價機會。
日本真正改變的，不只是日元
2015年至2019年，我長期參與日本及亞洲市場的量化投資組合管理。
那段經歷讓我看到一個很有意思的現象：
優秀的企業，與優秀的投資，並不是同一個概念。
日本擁有汽車、機器人、精密製造、半導體材料等領域的大量優秀企業，但長期以來，資本效率、企業治理和股東回報限制了部分公司的估值。
今年日本股市上漲，日元疲弱只是其中一個因素。
我更關注的是企業治理正在發生的變化——越來越多公司開始重新審視資本成本、資本回報率和市場估值。
很多日本企業並不是2023年突然變好了。
真正發生變化的是：
市場開始用新的方式給它們定價。
這正是量化投資長期研究的問題之一：不僅要尋找好公司，還要判斷市場已經為「好」支付了多少價格。
另一邊，AI正在讓市場交易「未來」
如果說日本代表價值重估，那麼美國AI熱潮交易的則是未來增長。
我經歷過2000年前後的互聯網泡沫，因此對今天的AI行情既關注，也保持謹慎。
互聯網最終改變了世界，但這並不意味著當年所有互聯網股票都是好投資。
AI同樣如此。
一項技術擁有巨大未來，與所有相關資產都值得以任何價格買入，是兩件完全不同的事情。
但相比AI股票能夠上漲多少，我現在更感興趣的是：
人工智能本身，會不會改變投資行業？
金融市場真正缺少的，已經不是數據
今天市場每天產生的信息已經遠遠超過一個投資團隊能夠人工處理的範圍。
價格、成交量、財報、宏觀數據、企業公告、新聞、央行講話、社交媒體、另類數據……
真正的問題早已不是「有沒有數據」。
而是：
我們能不能足夠快地理解數據之間的關係。
傳統量化模型非常擅長處理價格、估值、盈利、波動率等結構化數據。
但市場中還有大量非結構化信息。
一份央行聲明措辭的變化、一家公司管理層語氣的改變、一條供應鏈新聞，都可能同時影響多個資產。
過去，這些信息主要依靠分析師閱讀和判斷。
而人工智能讓我開始認真思考一個新的可能：
如果機器不僅能夠計算數字，還能夠理解語言，會發生什麼？
下一代量化投資，可能從「計算」走向「理解」
過去十多年，量化投資的典型流程是：
數據 → 因子 → 信號 → 投資組合 → 風險控制 → 交易執行。
未來，這條鏈條可能增加一個非常重要的環節：
信息理解。
機器先閱讀新聞、公告和宏觀信息，把非結構化內容轉換成可以分析的數據，再與價格、成交量、利率、匯率和歷史市場行為建立聯繫。
這意味著機器可能不再只是幫助投資者「算得更快」。
而是開始幫助我們看得更廣、理解得更快。
但我並不認為AI的價值是準確預測明天哪隻股票上漲。
真正有價值的AI投資體系，應該把：
信息採集 → 信息理解 → 信號識別 → 組合構建 → 風險控制 → 交易執行
連接成一個完整系統。
回顧自己的職業經歷，我經歷了傳統基本面研究走向量化和系統化投資。
現在，我越來越感覺第三個階段可能正在出現：
人工智能與量化投資的結合。
它最終能走多遠，現在沒有人知道。
但有一個方向值得持續研究：
讓機器幫助我們更快理解市場，再用系統化的方法，把這種理解轉化為投資決策。
這可能比預測下一隻「AI概念股」，更加值得關注。
—— Adrianzhi Kuan Ong（王志寬）

event_model_payload.headline: I Built a Scraper That Turns 1,000 Book Listings Into a Clean Excel Report — Here's How
event_model_payload.summary:
Most "learn web scraping" tutorials stop at printing a few titles to the terminal. That never felt like a finished tool to me, so I built one that goes all the way: scrape a catalogue, clean the data, and hand over a formatted Excel report someone could actually use.

The stack is plain Python: requests, BeautifulSoup, pandas, and openpyxl. No frameworks, no paid APIs. The target is books.toscrape.com, a site built specifically for practising scraping — so everything here is on a public practice page, not a real store.

What you end up with

Running two scripts produces:

  • data/books_raw.csv — the raw scrape, one row per book
  • data/books_clean.csv — the same data, cleaned
  • data/books_clean.xlsx — a formatted Excel report: bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, and sensible column widths

The full run collects 1,000 books, and the cleaned report's average price comes out at £35.07.

Step 0: Setup 

pip install requests beautifulsoup4 pandas openpyxl

Three files: scraper.py (collect), clean_export.py (clean + export), and a data/ folder for the outputs.

Step 1: Scrape every page, not just the first one

A catalogue scraper that only reads page 1 is a demo, not a tool. The real job is walking the pagination until there is no "next" link left. The core loop does exactly that:

def scrape(max_pages=None):
    all_books = []
    page = 1
    while True:
        url = CATALOGUE_URL.format(page)
        response = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=20)
        response.raise_for_status()
        response.encoding = "utf-8"
        books, has_next = parse_page(response.text, url)
        all_books.extend(books)
        if not has_next:
            break
        page += 1
        if max_pages and page > max_pages:
            break
        time.sleep(0.2)  # be polite to the server
    return all_books

Each page is parsed with one function that pulls five fields out of every book card:

def parse_page(html, page_url):
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    books = []
    for article in soup.select("article.product_pod"):
        title = article.h3.a["title"].strip()
        price_text = article.select_one("p.price_color").get_text(strip=True)
        rating_word = article.select_one("p.star-rating")["class"][1]
        availability = article.select_one("p.instock").get_text(strip=True)
        rel_url = article.h3.a["href"]
        books.append({
            "title": title,
            "price": price_text,
            "rating": rating_word,
            "availability": availability,
            "url": urljoin(page_url, rel_url),
        })
    has_next = soup.select_one("li.next a") is not None
    return books, has_next

Three details worth calling out, because each one bit me or would have:

  1. The £ encoding gotcha. This site doesn't declare its charset, so requests guesses Latin-1 and corrupts the £ sign. The pages are actually UTF-8, so one line — response.encoding = "utf-8" — fixes it before parsing. If your scraped prices ever look like Â£51.77, this is almost certainly why.
  2. Be polite. A 0.2 second sleep between pages and an honest User-Agent (python-automation-toolkit/1.0 (learning project)) cost nothing and keep you from hammering someone else's server. Scraping fast is not a skill; scraping without getting blocked is.
  3. Relative URLs. Book links on the page are relative, so urljoin(page_url, rel_url) turns them into full URLs you can actually click later.

Run it with python scraper.py (or --pages 5 for a quick test run), and you get data/books_raw.csv with 1,000 rows.

Step 2: Clean the data before anyone sees it

Raw scraped data is never report-ready. Prices are strings with currency symbols (£51.77), ratings are words (Three), and availability is a sentence fragment. The cleaning step turns all of that into typed, analysable data:

RATING_MAP = {"One": 1, "Two": 2, "Three": 3, "Four": 4, "Five": 5}

def clean(df):
    df = df.copy()
    # "£51.77" -> 51.77 (drop anything that is not a digit or a dot)
    df["price"] = df["price"].astype(str).str.replace(r"[^0-9.]", "", regex=True)
    df["price"] = pd.to_numeric(df["price"], errors="coerce")
    df = df.dropna(subset=["price"])
    # "Three" -> 3
    df["rating"] = df["rating"].map(RATING_MAP)
    # "In stock" -> True, anything else -> False
    df["in_stock"] = df["availability"].str.contains("In stock", na=False)
    df = df.drop(columns=["availability"])
    df = df.drop_duplicates(subset=["title", "url"])
    return df

The pattern here is worth stealing for any scrape: strip, convert with errors="coerce" (bad values become NaN instead of crashing the run), drop the rows that didn't convert, and drop duplicates on a sensible key — here, title + URL.

Step 3: Export an Excel file a human would enjoy opening

A CSV is fine for machines. If a person is going to read the report, formatting matters — and it's only a few lines with openpyxl:

def write_excel(df, path):
    with pd.ExcelWriter(path, engine="openpyxl") as writer:
        df.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Books", index=False)
        sheet = writer.sheets["Books"]
        for cell in sheet[1]:
            cell.font = Font(bold=True)
        sheet.auto_filter.ref = sheet.dimensions
        sheet.freeze_panes = "A2"
        widths = {"title": 55, "price": 10, "rating": 10,
                  "in_stock": 10, "url": 60}
        for idx, col in enumerate(df.columns, start=1):
            sheet.column_dimensions[get_column_letter(idx)].width = (
                widths.get(col, 20)
            )

Bold headers, filters, a frozen top row, columns wide enough for the content. That's the difference between "here's a file" and "here's a report."

python clean_export.py also prints a short summary: book count, average price, how many are in stock, and the rating mix.

The result

Output Contents
books_raw.csv 1,000 books, raw strings
books_clean.csv 1,000 books, typed and deduplicated
books_clean.xlsx Same data, formatted and filterable

Average price across the catalogue: £35.07.

Three lessons I'd pass on

  1. Scrape practice sites to learn. Real sites have terms of service, rate limits, and anti-bot measures. Learn the mechanics on a site built for it, and only scrape public pages with permission when real data is involved.
  2. The pipeline is the project. Scraping is the easy third. Cleaning and presenting the data is where a script becomes a tool someone would pay for.
  3. Small, polite, honest scripts beat clever ones. A 0.2 second delay and a real User-Agent never got anyone blocked; pretending to be a browser did.

The full code is in my Python Automation Toolkit project, and the same scrape → clean → report pattern works for any tabular listing: products, jobs, or prices. Next, I'll write about the other half of the toolkit — a file organiser that tidies a messy downloads folder without ever deleting anything by default.

Malik Ali Hassan — .NET & full-stack developer, final-year Software Engineering student. I build Python automation, AI assistants, and web apps.

event_model_payload.headline: Reverting Git Won’t Undo Your Database Migration
event_model_payload.summary:
A release introduces an application bug. You revert the deployment configuration, and the previous container image starts successfully.

But requests still fail.

The application has returned to its previous version. The database has not.

For stateful applications, a deployment rollback and a recovery plan cover different things.

A simple column rename can break rollback

Consider an application that reads this column:

SELECT customer_name FROM orders;

A new release renames it:

ALTER TABLE orders
RENAME COLUMN customer_name TO billing_name;

The new application expects billing_name. The previous application expects customer_name.

If the release fails after the migration, deploying the previous image leaves it querying a column that no longer exists.

The same compatibility problem can appear during a rolling deployment, while old and new application instances run together.

This is an illustrative example. The locking and operational impact of schema changes depend on the database engine and workload.

Separate schema evolution into stages

The expand, migrate, contract pattern spreads a breaking change across compatible steps. GitLab documents this approach for changes that must work across application versions. GitLab's compatibility guide

For this example, a staged approach could look like:

1. Expand

Introduce the new column while keeping the existing one.

Old application instances can continue using the original schema.

Adding a column still needs operational review: defaults, constraints, table size and database behavior can affect deployment safety.

2. Migrate

Introduce application behavior that supports the transition.

Define how both representations stay consistent while older instances remain active. A one-time backfill is insufficient if ongoing writes can immediately make the columns disagree.

Backfill existing records in controlled batches where appropriate. Make progress observable and retries safe.

Check completeness and consistency before switching reads.

3. Contract

Remove the old representation only after its consumers have stopped using it and the intended rollback window has closed.

Consumers may include background workers, reports, integrations and scheduled jobs—not just web application instances.

Once the old column is removed, an older application version may no longer be a valid recovery target.

Keep GitOps reconciliation in the recovery plan

A manual change to a running Deployment can conflict with the desired state maintained by a GitOps controller.

Decide how recovery changes the authoritative configuration, and how reconciliation behaves during the incident.

Also distinguish a Git revert from the deployment tool's rollback operation. They are separate mechanisms with their own behavior and constraints. Check the documentation for your deployed version, such as Argo CD's automated sync policy.

Neither operation inherently reverses database writes or external side effects.

Test the previous application against the migrated database

A useful compatibility test is:

Create representative starting data
    → Apply the proposed migration
    → Run the previous application version
    → Exercise important reads and writes
    → Run the new application version
    → Verify transition behavior

For a rolling release, also test the period when both versions operate concurrently.

A successful migration command proves that the database accepted the change. It does not prove application compatibility.

Write down where rollback stops being safe

Before release, answer:

  • Which application versions support the resulting schema?
  • Can migration jobs resume safely after interruption?
  • What happens to writes made during the transition?
  • At what step does recovery require a forward fix?
  • If restoration is necessary, what happens to data written since the backup?

The recovery target is a compatible application-and-data state.

How does your team define the rollback window for releases that change the database?

event_model_payload.headline: RagLeap Physical: A Simulation-First Safety Bridge for AI Agents
event_model_payload.summary:
What should happen when an AI agent proposes an action that affects a physical-system simulation?

At RagLeap, we're exploring a controlled workflow:

AI proposes → Human approves → Safety limits are checked → Simulator verifies

RagLeap Physical is an open-source, pre-alpha Python project built around this idea.

🔗 GitHub: https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

What it does

RagLeap Physical provides a simulation-first bridge between AI agents and physical-system simulators.

The project includes:

  • Safety envelopes
  • Exact-proposal approval
  • Dry runs
  • Runtime monitoring
  • Stop functionality
  • Audit logs
  • AI-facing tools
  • MCP server
  • Optional MuJoCo adapters
  • Workspace limits
  • Runnable simulation demos

The focus is not unrestricted AI control. It is controlled, observable interaction.

Release journey

v0.0.1 — Core bridge

The first release introduced the safety bridge, exact-proposal approval, runtime monitoring, audit logs, MCP tools, MuJoCo adapters, workspace limits, and simulation examples.

v0.0.2 — Operator console

The second release added a human operator console.

A named person can review pending proposals, approve the exact digest, apply the action, and stop.

The console is loopback-only, uses one token per person, and is not an AI tool.

v0.0.3 — Two-link workspace demo

The latest release adds:

examples/two_link_workspace_demo.py

The demo shows a two-link arm with one accepted workspace move and one refused move.

It also includes package metadata improvements and a fix for request handling in the operator console and MCP server.

Install 

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

Optional extras:

pip install "ragleap-physical[mujoco]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[test]"
pip install "ragleap-physical[interop]"

Testing

The v0.0.3 release reports:

  • 255 tests passed with MuJoCo and the MCP SDK installed in Colab
  • GitHub CI on Python 3.10, 3.11, and 3.12

The Windows refusal-fix behavior is not yet verified.

Important limitations

This is pre-alpha and simulation-only.

It does not control real hardware. No real-robot or real-machine validation, safety certification, or regulatory compliance is claimed.

MuJoCo results are repeatable within one installed environment only. The wear-study and machine-tool numbers are invented.

Contribute

We welcome feedback and contributions from developers working on AI agents, simulation, robotics, MCP, and safety engineering.

Explore the package:

https://github.com/ragleap/ragleap-core/tree/main/packages/ragleap-physical

Install:

pip install ragleap-physical==0.0.3

AI proposes. Humans approve. The system verifies.

event_model_payload.headline: Ask HN: Advice on local efficient analogical retrieval?
event_model_payload.summary:
So.. I've been running my own archive of conversations, voice recordings, documents, and etc for AI agents (mostly Claude Code) for past 6 month.

Currently, when i ask or it answers something it runs hook that checks previous conversations, lists up potential related conversations.

The intention is not only to retreive relative memories, but also to be able to connect 2 or more conversations that looks irrelevant but extract some kind of pattern or insight from it. In other words, I want my model to partially go off on a tangent, in a good way...

For example; Let's say I bring up topic on investing on OKLO as a potential 10x company. So I say I will keep it small but don't cut loss, only buy more from time to time. I want model to be able to bring up the memory that I also regularly buy things from my few favorite small restuarants just to keep them alive. Maybe connect those 2, and be able to tell that in perspective, I may have a consistant view on spending money. I even have few conversations on that exact topic as well. It just doesn't use similar keywords.

I feel like maybe the obstacle is that model can't come up with the direction that the conversation could develop to a broader(or deeper) topic on my philosophy on capital? I'm not sure.

These are the list I've tried: 1. Personalized PageRank 2. Hebbian edge reinforcement(between opened conversation) 3. character n-gram TF-IDF similarity 4.contrastive embedding trained on my conversation 5. query expansion over a word co-occurrence graph 6. matching on shared verbs 7. serendipity slot 8. simple agentic search 9. abstracting each message into a domain-free sentence 10. keword search + LLM judgement 11. BGE-M3

All these can't quite achieve to the point I describe. It certainly works well getting related memory.

The search should be fast, light, because reading the history itself takes time, so can't really afford long search time on top of that. I run this on multi device, so it should be portable friendly.

Any advice or idea on this approach? public version of the repo: https://github.com/milez770/madeleine

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50361973

Points: 1

event_model_payload.headline: Git Branches Explained: How to Create, Switch, Merge and Delete Branches
event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

A Git branch is a lightweight pointer to a line of commits that lets you work on a new feature, a bug fix or a wild experiment without touching your main, working code. You create a branch, switch to it, commit your changes there, and when everything works you merge it back into main. If the idea fails, you delete the branch and main never knew it existed. This guide covers creating, switching, merging and deleting branches, with real commands you can try today.

What Is a Git Branch?

Think of your project history as a road made of commits. Each commit is a saved snapshot of your files. A branch is a movable signpost on that road. When you commit, your current branch's signpost moves forward to the new commit. The default branch is usually called main, and it holds the stable version you would show to the world.

When you create a branch, Git does not copy your project folder, which surprises many beginners. It simply adds a new signpost pointing at the same commit. That is why Git branches are fast and cheap. You can have ten branches for ten ideas, and your disk will barely notice.

If Git is new on your machine, start with our guide on how to install Git on Windows, Mac and Linux, then follow along here in your terminal.

How to Create a Branch

There are two jobs here: creating a branch, and moving onto it. Plain git branch only creates it. It does not switch you to it, and this tiny detail causes a classic beginner moment: you write code happily, then discover all your commits landed on main. Oops.

# List local branches
git branch

# Create a branch called feature-login
git branch feature-login

# Create AND switch in one step (modern way)
git switch -c feature-login

# Older command, still seen in tutorials
git checkout -b feature-login

Both git switch -c and git checkout -b do the same thing: create the branch and move you onto it. The switch command is newer and clearer, because checkout does several jobs. The official git branch command reference lists every option, but the small set here is what most developers use daily. Choose short, clear names like fix-header-bug. Your future self will thank you.

How to Switch Between Branches

Switching means moving to another signpost, so your files change to match that branch's latest commit. Git updates your folder for you, almost like changing the channel, except the channel is your own code at a different stage.

# Switch to an existing branch
git switch main

# Older way, same result
git checkout main

# Jump back to previous branch
git switch -

One warning that saves real pain: commit or stash unfinished work before you switch. If unsaved changes clash with the other branch, Git will either carry them along or refuse to switch. A quick git status first is a healthy habit, like checking your pockets before leaving the house.

The official Git website, git-scm.com, home of the free Git book and command reference.

How to Merge a Branch

Merging means combining work from one branch into another, usually bringing a finished feature into main. The routine is always the same: switch to the receiving branch, then run git merge with the other branch's name.

# Move to the receiving branch
git switch main

# Bring the feature into main
git merge feature-login

Git merges in two common ways. A fast-forward merge happens when main has not moved since you branched off. Git simply slides the main signpost forward to your newest commit, and history stays one straight line. A merge commit happens when both branches have new commits. Git then creates a special commit with two parents that ties the lines together. The free Pro Git book explains both with diagrams in its chapter on basic branching and merging.

Sometimes Git stops and reports a conflict. Nothing is broken. Both branches changed the same lines, and Git asks a human to choose. Edit the marked sections into the correct result, then run git add and git commit to finish.

Branch Commands at a Glance

Command What it does
git branch Lists all local branches
git branch name Creates a branch but stays where you are
git switch -c name Creates a branch and switches to it
git switch name Switches to an existing branch
git merge name Merges that branch into your current branch
git branch -d name Deletes a branch that has been merged
git branch -D name Force deletes a branch, merged or not
git push -u origin name Publishes a branch and links it to the remote

How to Delete a Branch

Once a feature is merged, its branch has done its job. Keeping dozens of finished branches is like keeping empty pizza boxes: harmless for a while, then just clutter. Delete merged branches regularly.

# Safe delete: refuses if not merged
git branch -d feature-login

# Force delete: even if not merged
git branch -D feature-login

The small -d is the safe option. If the branch holds unmerged commits, Git stops and warns you, which has saved many developers. The capital -D deletes without asking, and commits that exist only there can be hard to recover. Use it only for a failed experiment you truly want gone. You cannot delete the branch you are standing on, so switch to main first.

Remote Branches and Push -u

So far everything happened on your own computer. A remote branch also lives on a hosting service like GitHub, so teammates can see it and you have a backup. If you mix up the tool and the website, our explainer on Git vs GitHub and what the difference really is clears that up in minutes.

# First push: publish and set upstream
git push -u origin feature-login

# After that, plain commands work
git push
git pull

# Delete the remote branch too
git push origin --delete feature-login

The -u flag is short for upstream. It links your local branch to its remote partner, so plain git push and git pull then know where to go. You need it once per branch, on the first push. For remote branches, run git branch -r.

Common Mistakes Beginners Make

Working directly on main. It feels quicker today and painful tomorrow. Even for a tiny fix, a branch keeps main safe and releasable.

Forgetting which branch you are on. Run git status before you commit. Many "lost" commits are simply sitting on the wrong branch, feeling lonely.

Letting branches live forever. A branch that drifts for weeks falls behind main, and the final merge turns into conflict city. Merge little and often.

Using -D as the default. Force delete is for experiments you meant to throw away. If you reach for it daily, something needs attention.

Vague branch names. Names like test or branch2 tell you nothing a week later. Write the purpose in the name, for example fix-payment-rounding.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between git branch and git switch -c?

git branch name only creates the branch and leaves you where you are. git switch -c name creates it and moves you onto it in one step, so your next commits land in the right place.

Can I recover a deleted Git branch?

Often, yes, for a while. If it was merged, its commits are safe inside main. If you force deleted an unmerged branch, git reflog can sometimes find the last commit so you can recreate it, but there is no guarantee, so treat -D with respect.

How many branches can a Git project have?

There is no practical limit. Branches are tiny pointers, not folder copies, so hundreds cost almost nothing. The real limit is human: delete finished branches so the list stays easy to scan.

Should every task get its own branch?

Yes, that is the normal professional habit. One branch per feature, fix or experiment keeps changes separate, makes reviews cleaner, and lets a failed idea be deleted without touching stable code.

Conclusion

Branches are the feature that makes Git feel safe. Create one with git switch -c, work and commit without fear, merge it into main when ready, and delete it with the safe -d. Publish with git push -u origin the first time, and keep names clear and branches short lived. Practise the full cycle twice on a test project today, and branching will soon feel as natural as saving a file.

event_model_payload.headline: GitLab's Unauthenticated RCE: Check, Patch and Verify in 10 Minutes
event_model_payload.summary:
If you run GitLab yourself, this is a drop-everything patch, and the trap is thinking you already did it. GitLab shipped a CVSS 10 unauthenticated RCE fix on October 21, 2026, and the patch many teams applied nine days earlier does not cover it. This post gives you the version table, the exact upgrade sequence, and the verification step most teams skip.

What actually happened

On October 21, 2026, GitLab shipped a critical patch release fixing CVE-2026-110264, an integer overflow in its regular expression compiler that GitLab rates CVSS 10.0. GitLab says that under certain conditions, a specially crafted regular expression could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on a self-managed GitLab server.

The flaw sits in Onigmo, the regular expression engine Ruby ships, which GitLab bundles inside its own packages.

The scope is what makes this one unusual. The affected range starts at GitLab 7.0, from 2014, and covers every self-managed CE and EE release below the fixed version for its branch. GitLab.com is already patched and needs no action. The researcher behind the report used the handle joaxcar and reported through GitLab's HackerOne program. GitLab keeps full technical details private for 90 days after a fix, so the public record right now is the advisory, the version table, and GitLab's two detection rules, not a full exploit write-up.

Am I affected? The version table

If you run a self-managed GitLab CE or EE install below the fixed version for your branch, you are affected, whatever your deployment type. GitLab's advisory covers Linux packages, Helm charts, Docker images and source installs alike. GitLab.com and qualifying GitLab Dedicated tenants are the only installs that need no action, and I list their exact position below the table.

Your branch Fixed release What to do
19.5 19.5.1 Upgrade to 19.5.1
19.4 19.4.3 Upgrade to 19.4.3
19.3 19.3.6 Upgrade to 19.3.6
19.2 19.2.9 Upgrade to 19.2.9
19.1 19.1.9 Upgrade to 19.1.9
19.0 19.0.10 Upgrade to 19.0.10
18.11 18.11.13 Upgrade to 18.11.13
Older than 18.11 No backport in this release Upgrade to a supported line at or above 18.11.13

One caveat on the older backports, and it matters if you are on 18.11 through 19.2. Those backports cover this critical flaw, but they do not necessarily fix every other issue in the October 21 advisory. The other fixes in that advisory are listed for 19.3.6, 19.4.3 and 19.5.1. So a backport gets you out of the CVSS 10 hole, and a move to a current branch gets you the rest of the advisory too. Plan the second step even if the first step is what you ship today.

GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include the fixes. If you are unsure which side of that line you sit on, your GitLab contact or your Dedicated version page answers it faster than guessing from a blog post, including this one.

The October 12 trap: why your last patch does not cover this

The October 12 patch fixed a different flaw, so an install patched that day is still exposed to the October 21 flaw. CVE-2026-97229, fixed October 12 in 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8, is an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular expression path. CVE-2026-110264 is separate.

Same engine family, different flaw, different fix. GitLab's detection notes place the October 21 flaw in Org-mode file rendering, a different path from the CI/CD path.

CVE-2026-97229 CVE-2026-110264
Fixed October 12, 2026 October 21, 2026
Fixed versions 19.4.2, 19.3.5, 19.2.8 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, 18.11.13
CVSS 10.0 10.0
CISA KEV status at October 30 Added October 29, 2026, federal due date November 1 Not listed
If you hold this version 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 You are patched for the first flaw only

That last row is the whole point of this section. I have seen teams close a ticket on October 12 and move on, and that ticket is not this ticket. Check your version against the October 21 table, not against your memory of patching recently. The exploitation picture also splits the same way: the sibling flaw reached CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 29, with Alpine Linux reporting probing attempts against its instance on October 20 and 21, while CVE-2026-110264 itself had no reported exploitation and no KEV listing at the October 30 checks. A quiet status for one flaw is not cover for the other, and it is not a reason to wait on either.

Check your version in 30 seconds

You need one number before you touch anything: the exact version your server is actually running, not the version you think you installed. The admin view and the command line agree with each other, so use whichever you can reach, and write the number down before you start the upgrade.



Sign in as an admin and open Help, then the version page. The version string there, such as 19.4.2, is your branch and patch level in one read. If you cannot sign in, the command line step below gives you the same number.


With shell access, run sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:env:info and read the GitLab version line. On a Linux package install, apt-cache policy gitlab-ee (or gitlab-ce for Community Edition) shows the installed version alongside the versions your package source offers.


Match the first two numbers of your version to the table above. If your version is at or above the fixed release for that branch, you are patched for CVE-2026-110264. If it is below, you are affected, even if you patched on October 12.

Patch it: the 10-minute sequence

Patching GitLab is an ordinary package upgrade on your own branch, not a major version jump, and that is good news for a same-day fix. The sequence below is the one I would run on a single-node Omnibus install, and the order matters: backup first, upgrade path second, install third, verify fourth.



Run sudo gitlab-backup create and confirm the backup file exists before you upgrade. A patch release can carry database migrations, and a backup is the only clean way back if the upgrade goes wrong. Do not skip this because the jump is small.


If you are moving within your branch to the fixed release, the jump is direct. If you are coming from an older line, check GitLab's upgrade paths documentation first, because GitLab defines required upgrade stops that must not be skipped. A skipped stop is how a routine patch turns into a broken install.


On Ubuntu or Debian with the Omnibus package, update your package lists and install the exact fixed version for your branch. For Enterprise Edition on 19.5, that looks like this:

sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install gitlab-ee=19.5.1-ee.0

Swap the package name to gitlab-ce for Community Edition and the version to your branch's fixed release, keeping the same -ee.0 or -ce.0 package suffix pattern for your edition. The package install runs gitlab-ctl reconfigure at the end, which applies migrations and restarts services. Docker and Helm installs follow the same version target through their own image tag or chart upgrade, so the table above still decides the version even when the command differs.


Run sudo gitlab-ctl status and confirm the services show as running. Read the reconfigure output for migration errors instead of assuming a clean exit code means a clean database. If a service fails to start, stop and read the error before retrying; a second install over a half-migrated database makes diagnosis harder, not faster.

Source and custom-image installs carry one extra step that Omnibus installs do not. The flaw lives in Ruby's Onigmo engine, so a GitLab you built yourself needs a Ruby that carries the underlying fix: Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 or 3.3.13, per Ruby's October 23 notice, which maps four GitLab CVEs including this one to the engine fixes. Omnibus users get their Ruby through the GitLab package itself, so the package upgrade is the Ruby fix for them. If you run your own Ruby, patching GitLab without patching Ruby leaves the engine flaw in place.

Verify the patch actually took

An upgrade that nobody verifies is a ticket closed on hope, and I have watched that exact mistake ship more than once. Verification takes under a minute, and it catches the two most common failures: the package installed but the old services never restarted, and the install landed on the wrong branch version.



Repeat the version check from the earlier section after the upgrade, in the web interface or with sudo gitlab-rake gitlab:env:info. The number must now read your branch's fixed release or higher. If it still reads the old version, the upgrade did not take, whatever the package manager said.


Run sudo gitlab-ctl status and confirm the services are running, then sign in and open a real project page. A login page that renders is not proof; a project page that loads after sign-in shows the application stack is actually up.


Write the new version, the branch target, and today's date into your change log or ticket. The next time a GitLab advisory lands, that one line is what stops the October 12 trap from happening again, because you will compare against a written version instead of a memory.

Were you already probed? What to check in logs

GitLab published two threat detections for self-managed customers looking for exploitation attempts against this flaw: "Onigmo native worker crash" and "Org mode render error burst". Those names are your search terms in your logs and monitoring, and they are worth checking even though no exploitation of this flaw had been reported at the October 30 checks.

A crash or an error burst on its own does not prove a successful attack, and GitLab's own guidance is explicit on that point. A worker can crash for ordinary reasons, and a render error burst can come from a malformed file with no attacker behind it. What you are looking for is a pattern: repeated worker crashes or render error bursts clustered in time, especially against public projects, followed by anything unusual in the same window, such as unexpected processes, changed files, or odd outbound connections.

If that pattern shows up, preserve the logs before you restart anything, finish the patch, and then treat secrets as exposed until you have reason not to. Rotate the credentials your GitLab server can read: deploy tokens, runner tokens, integration secrets, and any credentials stored in CI variables that a compromised server could reach. That rotation is the expensive part of the response, which is why the cheap part, patching before an incident, is worth doing today. If you maintain client GitLab installs, this whole check is billable, legitimate security work, and it is the same kind of emergency audit I take on through my contact section.

If you cannot patch today

GitLab published no workaround for CVE-2026-110264, so I am not going to invent one for you. Because the exact preconditions are undisclosed, no configuration change rules an instance out, and a web filter or a private-projects-only policy is not a substitute for the patch.

That honesty is the value of this section: a stopgap that sounds reassuring but is not verified would leave you exposed while feeling safe, which is worse than knowing you are exposed.

What you can do is shrink the window honestly. Put the patch in the first maintenance slot you can take, internet-facing instances first, and keep the detection names from the previous section in your monitoring until it lands. If the instance cannot go down at all, say so in your incident log, name the exposure, and do not let the ticket sit without a date. A patch with a date is a plan. A patch with no date is a hope, and hope is not a control.

The same discipline applies to the sibling flaw. If you are still on a version that predates the October 12 fix, you are carrying a flaw that is already in CISA's exploited catalog, and that one jumps ahead of everything else in this post. Patch to the October 21 version for your branch and you cover both flaws in one upgrade, which is one more reason to use the October 21 table as your target instead of patching to October 12 and stopping.

My verdict: what I would do, in order

If you run one self-managed GitLab instance, check the version now and patch it today, internet-facing instances first. Do not wait for a KEV listing, a public exploit, or a news cycle to tell you this one matters. A CVSS 10 rating from the vendor is already the full case for patching.

The October 12 confusion is the only reason this post needed to exist, so check against the October 21 table, verify the running version after the upgrade, and write the new version down.

If you run GitLab for clients, this week is a real engagement: a version audit across every install, the October 21 upgrade on each one, and a log check against GitLab's two detection names. It is the same emergency-response shape as my php2shell fix, where the same October 21 disclosure day produced a second critical patch, and the same rule applied: check, patch, verify, in that order, with no step skipped because the last patch felt recent.

FAQ

What is CVE-2026-110264?

CVE-2026-110264 is an integer overflow in GitLab's regular expression compiler, rated CVSS 10.0 by GitLab. Under certain conditions, GitLab says it could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on a self-managed GitLab server. It affects GitLab CE and EE from version 7.0 up to the fixed releases.

Which GitLab versions fix CVE-2026-110264?

The fixed releases from October 21, 2026 are 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10 and 18.11.13. Your branch decides your target: a 19.4 install goes to 19.4.3, a 19.5 install goes to 19.5.1, and so on. Anything below your branch's fixed version is still affected.

I patched GitLab on October 12. Am I covered?

No. The October 12 release fixed a different flaw, CVE-2026-97229, in the CI/CD regular expression path. The October 21 flaw, CVE-2026-110264, is separate. An install on 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 from October 12 sits below the October 21 fixed version for its branch and needs one more upgrade.

Is GitLab.com affected by CVE-2026-110264?

No action is needed on GitLab.com. GitLab says it already runs the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants on 19.3.5-internal0, 19.4.2-internal0 or later also include the fixes. This post is for self-managed CE and EE installs only.

Is there a workaround if I cannot patch today?

GitLab published no workaround for CVE-2026-110264. Because the exact preconditions are undisclosed, no configuration change rules an instance out. Patching to your branch's fixed release is the only certain protection, so treat any delay as time spent exposed and patch at the first window you can take.

Is CVE-2026-110264 being exploited in the wild?

As of the October 30 checks I cite below, GitLab had not reported exploitation of CVE-2026-110264 and it was not in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Its sibling flaw CVE-2026-97229 is a different story: CISA added it to the catalog on October 29, 2026. Do not read the quiet status of one flaw as safety for the other.

  • GitLab, Upgrade paths documentation: https://docs.gitlab.com/update/upgrade_paths/
  • Ostorlab, "GitLab Unauthenticated RCE Across 12 Years (CVE-2026-110264)": https://blog.ostorlab.co/gitlab-unauthenticated-rce-cve-2026-110264.html
  • Rescana, "GitLab CVE-2026-110264: Critical Unauthenticated RCE in Self-Managed GitLab CE/EE": https://www.rescana.com/post/gitlab-cve-2026-110264-unauthenticated-rce-october-2026
  • ZeroHunt, "GitLab CVE-2026-110264: CVSS 10 unauthenticated RCE through a rendered .org file": https://zerohunt.ai/blog/gitlab-cve-2026-110264-org-mode-regex-unauth-rce/

event_model_payload.headline: FE News 26년 11월 소식을 전해드립니다.
event_model_payload.summary:
주요소식

26년 11월 소식에서는 다음과 같은 유용한 정보들을 만나보실 수 있습니다.

​

Tailwind Labs is joining Shopify

Tailwind CSS를 만든 Adam Wathan이 Tailwind Labs의 Shopify 합류를 발표했다. Tailwind CSS를 비롯한 오픈소스 프로젝트는 계속 MIT 라이선스로 남고 Tailwind 팀이 Shopify의 지원을 받아 유지보수를 이어 가므로, 이미 쓰고 있는 팀이 당장 바꿀 것은 없다. 대신 유료 컴포넌트·템플릿 모음 Tailwind Plus와 에이전트 스킬 모음 ui.sh는 신규 가입을 받지 않으며, Wathan은 사용자와 같은 문제를 겪는 실제 커머스 제품 안에서 프레임워크를 개발하고 싶었다고 배경을 설명한다.

​

​

​

Introducing tsrs: a Port of TypeScript to Rust

Cloudflare와 VoidZero가 TypeScript 컴파일러를 Rust로 옮기는 tsrs를 Oxc 툴체인 안에서 개발한다고 발표했다. Go로 다시 작성한 TypeScript 7보다 WebAssembly 환경에 잘 맞고 메모리를 적게 쓰는 것이 목표로, 팀의 초기 벤치마크에서는 TypeScript 7.0보다 최대 8배 빠르고 메모리를 약 70% 덜 썼다. 비슷한 시기에 나온 ts-rust, Bun의 bun check, Vercel Labs의 tsc-ts도 함께 소개하며, 모두 실험 단계이므로 CI 타입 검사가 병목인 팀이라면 기존 tsc와 진단 결과를 비교하며 시험해 볼 만하다.

​

​

​

Making React Context Cheap with React Compiler

Context 값이 바뀌면 그 Context를 읽는 모든 컴포넌트가 다시 렌더링되는 비용을 React Compiler로 줄이는 방법을 다룬 글이다. 라디오 버튼 5,000개 예제에서 컴포넌트를 나누지 않고 Context를 그대로 읽게 둔 채 메모이제이션을 React Compiler에 맡기면, 클릭 처리 시간이 useSyncExternalStore 스토어나 React.memo로 나눈 방식과 비슷한 수준이 된다. 저자는 렌더링 횟수보다 렌더링 한 번의 작업량이 사용자 체감을 좌우한다며, 렌더링을 없애기보다 싸게 만드는 데 집중하라고 권한다.

​

​

​

React 19.3

실험 단계였던 과 Fragment Refs가 안정화되었다. 은 Transition으로 표시된 업데이트에서 요소의 등장, 퇴장, 갱신에 View Transition API 애니메이션을 적용하고, Fragment Refs로는 래퍼 요소 없이 형제 DOM 노드 묶음에 이벤트 리스너나 Observer를 연결할 수 있다. 컴포넌트를 서버 렌더링에서 제외하는 browser() API와 Trusted Types 지원도 추가되었으며, Strict Mode가 하이드레이션 중에도 Effect를 두 번 실행하므로 업그레이드 후에는 정리 함수가 없는 Effect부터 점검해 둬야 한다.

​

​

​

Remix 3

Remix 3이 Remix Jam 2026에 맞춰 첫 안정 버전으로 출시되었다. remix 패키지 하나에 라우터, 데이터베이스 관리, 스키마 검증, 에셋 서버, React가 아닌 자체 UI 런타임을 담은 풀스택 프레임워크이며, 기존 Remix 2 앱은 Remix 3이 아니라 React Router로 옮기게 된다. 10월 23일 나온 3.1은 코드 변경 없이 서버 렌더링을 약 두 배 빠르게 했고, 팀은 정식 출시 이후 SemVer를 지키겠다고 밝혔다.

​

​

​

>> FE News 26년 11월 소식 보러가기

◎ FE News란?

네이버 FE 엔지니어들이 엄선한 양질의 FE 및 주요한 기술 소식들을 큐레이션해 공유하는 것을 목표로 하며, 이를 통해 국내 개발자들에게 지식 공유에 대한 가치 인식과 성장에 도움을 주고자 하는 기술소식 공유 프로젝트 입니다.

매월 첫째 주 수요일, 월 1회 발행 되고 있으니 많은 관심 부탁드립니다.

event_model_payload.headline: Bridging Alloy and OpenTelemetry: the OTel engine is now in Public Preview
event_model_payload.summary:
Many Grafana Cloud customers love what Alloy offers them, but we're also seeing a growing base of users who feel the same way about the OpenTelemetry Collector. We want to make it easy for customers to make the decision that makes the most sense, regardless of their preference.

When we introduced the OpenTelemetry engine for Grafana Alloy, we set out to give teams a way to run native OTLP pipelines without giving up the power and flexibility Alloy is known for. Since then we've kept building: ironing out service installation support, enabling Fleet Management, and folding in feedback from early users. Today, as of Alloy v1.21.0, we're happy to share that the OTel engine has moved into Public Preview, running right alongside the default engine you already know. 

In this post, we'll dig into when you'd reach for each engine, walk through some of the most interesting use cases we've seen so far, and give a preview of where both engines are headed next.

The motivation behind each engine

Before diving into specific new features, let’s recap why we have two engines in Alloy.

Default engine

The default engine is a cross-ecosystem engine at its core; it's not tied to any single wire format or vendor. It can just as easily run a Prometheus pipeline, an OTLP pipeline, or a Loki pipeline, all defined using Alloy's own configuration syntax. That flexibility is what makes it a Swiss army knife: the same engine that scrapes Prometheus metrics can pull in logs over syslog for logs, ingest OTLP, scrape Prometheus metrics from embedded exporters, and route all of it to wherever it needs to go.

OpenTelemetry engine 

There's a lot to like about being able to speak every ecosystem's language. But the telemetry landscape itself is moving in the opposite direction. Rather than translating between formats, the industry is increasingly converging on a single, shared model defined by the OpenTelemetry specification. That's what an OpenTelemetry Collector actually is: a pipeline that treats OTLP as the native format end-to-end, prioritizing portability and open standards over ecosystem-bridging translation. At its core, Alloy's OTel engine is Grafana Labs' own distribution of the OpenTelemetry Collector.

Running the OTel engine

It's just a collector

The OTel engine is an OpenTelemetry Collector distribution that ships inside Alloy. It runs standard collector YAML with no translation and no Alloy syntax. If you already have a collector config, you already have an OTel engine config.

- otelcol --config=config.yaml
+ alloy otel --config=config.yaml

The rest of the CLI matches, too. validate, components, print-config, and --set all work the way they do upstream, so scripts and CI that call otelcol validate keep working.

The same goes for the tools you deploy collectors with. On the upstream Helm chart, it's two values:

image:
  repository: grafana/alloy
command:
  name: "bin/otelcol"

The OpenTelemetry Operator used to fail on the Alloy image because it had no way to set the container command. We added spec.command upstream (Operator v0.153.0 and later), so now it's one line:

spec:
  image: grafana/alloy:
  command: ["/bin/alloy", "otel"]

For a non-containerized installation, the Alloy packages can run either engine as a service. Set ALLOY_OTEL_MODE=1 and the service runs the OTel engine against config.yaml. Read our docs for more information on how to set it up by platform.

Fleet management

Managing collector configuration by hand doesn't scale past a handful of hosts, so remote configuration was one of the first gaps we closed after the initial release. As of Alloy v1.19.0, you can manage OTel engine configuration centrally with Fleet Management. The OpAMP supervisor is embedded in the Alloy binary and runs through the new experimental otel-supervisor subcommand: point it at your Fleet Management endpoint and credentials with a supervisor configuration file, and Alloy handles the connection, pulls down your pipeline configuration, and applies changes as you publish them. See the Alloy otel-supervisor reference to get started.

An escape hatch: the alloyengine extension

Sometimes the component you need only exists in the default engine today. The alloyengine extension runs Alloy configuration inside the same collector process, so you can pick up that one piece without running a second agent.

It's Experimental, and we expect it to stay that way. The two engines run side by side but can't pass data to each other directly, so anything that crosses over goes out over the network, usually OTLP.

If you reach for it, tell us why. Open an issue on the Alloy repo with the component you needed. That list is how we decide which default engine pieces become native OpenTelemetry collector components next.

Experiments with Grafana Cloud products

Heads up first: nothing in this section is supported, and you shouldn't run it in production. Part of what we're working out with the OTel engine is how Grafana Cloud's products behave when the pipeline is OTel end to end. Here's where two of them stand.

Database Observability. Today the path that works is adding your existing Alloy config to the collector you already run. Your OTLP pipelines keep doing their thing, and the extension runs database observability next to them. The Database Observability app can't tell the difference:

extensions:
  alloyengine:
    config:
      inline:
        content: |
          database_observability.postgres "default" {
            data_source_name = env("POSTGRES_DSN")
            forward_to       = [loki.write.grafana_cloud.receiver]
          }
          // ...the rest of your existing Alloy config

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc: {}
      http: {}

service:
  extensions: [alloyengine]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      exporters: [otlp_http/grafana_cloud]

A native collector path is in the works but still further off as we decide how to break the Alloy components out into OpenTelemetry native ones.

Cloud Provider Observability. Alloy's cloud provider exporters, like prometheus.exporter.gcp, work through the extension the same way. The data will be identical when run in the alloyengine extension as when run in Alloy’s default engine. The more interesting result is what happens without Alloy’s native Prometheus exporters at all. 

We've been working with the Prometheus community to make exporters embeddable as libraries, so they run as real collector receivers instead of something a collector scrapes. With a collector built to include it, the GCP exporter is just another receiver:

receivers:
  stackdriver_exporter:
    exporter_config:
      project_ids: [""]
      metrics_prefixes: [compute.googleapis.com/instance]
      aggregate_deltas: true  # off by default; Alloy turns it on

Looking beyond Cloud Provider Observability, the OpenTelemetry Collector Prometheus Distro is an official, experimental collector distribution that ships embeddable Prometheus exporters as OpenTelemetry receivers including blackbox, Postgres, Google Cloud Monitoring with stackdriver exporter and CloudWatch through yet-another-cloudwatch exporter. The receivers live in prometheus-opentelemetry-collector if you'd rather build your own with Open Telemetry Collector Builder (OCB). As they progress through the OpenTelemetry stability model we will look to add them to the OTel engine.

Looking ahead

OTel engine

So what comes next for the OTel engine now that it's in Public Preview? Making sure you can properly debug your collector is high on the list. Support bundles are a key feature for this in the default engine —a single request to /-/support packages your configuration, logs, internal metrics, runtime flags, and pprof profiles into one file you can inspect before sharing. The OTel engine has no equivalent today, so we're building an OTel-native extension to match it. Stay tuned for more updates on that front!

We also want to hear what's pulling you back to the default engine via the Alloy engine extension. The extension is there as an escape hatch, but we plan to break those pieces out into native collector components, the way we've started with Prometheus exporters. If you've reached for the extension, or held off on the OTel engine because something was missing, tell us what it was.

Default engine

The default engine isn't standing still. Most of the work ahead is about one thing: making sure your data always arrives, even when something downstream is having a bad day.

Prometheus: a better Remote Write 

Today  prometheus.remote_write is what keeps your metrics from disappearing when your backend goes down, and there’s a lot going on to improve it:

  • Smaller footprint. Keeping what’s in memory and what’s on disk as small as possible to help in high scale environments and keep restart delays minimal.

  • Pickup where you left off. Data that was in flight when Alloy restarted should still get sent.

  • Remote Write 2.0. When we moved our own internal Prometheus workloads to it, egress costs for that telemetry dropped by more than half. You can try it in prometheus.remote_write today as an experimental feature, and we're helping push it toward stable upstream.

Because prometheus.remote_write builds on upstream Prometheus, much of this work happens upstream, so it helps the whole Prometheus ecosystem, not just Alloy.

Loki: pipelines that know when something failed

Alloy's log pipelines still use a design inherited from Promtail, where components pass logs with no way to report back whether delivery worked. That's behind most of the rough edges you might have experienced: logs lost when Alloy shuts down, a slow stage holding up everything behind it, and file positions that advance before a line is actually sent. We're rebuilding the pipeline so success and failure flow back to the source:

  • No silent gaps. A file's position only moves once its lines are delivered, and Alloy drains in-flight logs on shutdown instead of dropping them.

  • Throughput that scales. A slow stage stops blocking the whole pipeline, so giving Alloy more CPU actually buys you more throughput.

  • A WAL you can rely on. We're working through the known issues to take the loki.write WAL to general availability, so logs survive an outage or a restart on disk.

Both engines are shaped by what we hear from the people running them, so tell us what you want us to focus on next. Open an issue on the Alloy repo or come find us in #alloy on the Grafana Community Slack.

event_model_payload.headline: Quick Start: C# and MongoDB - Starting and Setup
event_model_payload.summary:
In the first of the C# Quick Start series, I'll show how to set up connections between C# and MongoDB.

In future parts we'll move on and work through:

  • Database Create, Read, Update, and Delete (CRUD) operations
  • Map MongoDB to C# objects
  • Look at MongoDB aggregation
  • How to use LINQ with MongoDB

As you already know, C# is a general-purpose language and MongoDB is a general-purpose data platform. Together, C# and MongoDB are a powerful combination.

To follow along, I'll be using Visual Studio 2019 on Windows 10 and we will be connecting to a MongoDB Atlas cluster.

If you're using a different OS, IDE, or text editor, the walkthrough might be slightly different, but the code itself should be fairly similar. Let's jump in and take a look at how nicely C# and MongoDB work together.

Getting Setup
