event_model_payload.headline: Enforce Data Sovereignty With MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies
event_model_payload.summary:
Editor’s note: This post is the fourth in a five-part series exploring how MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies help you strengthen database security and enforce consistent guardrails across your organization. Read the first post on IP access list management, the second on defense in depth strategies, and the third on blocking the wildcard IP address.

Maintaining control in a multi-cloud world

As organizations scale their database infrastructure, maintaining consistent security and compliance policies becomes increasingly complex. Development teams need agility, but security teams need control. One misconfigured cluster deployed in the wrong region or on an unapproved cloud hyperscaler can lead to:

  • Compliance violations with data residency requirements.

  • Security gaps from shadow IT deployments.

  • Cost overruns from unplanned multi-cloud sprawl.

  • Audit failures when infrastructure does not match documented policies.

Introducing MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies

MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies are organization-level controls that enable you to define and enforce infrastructure governance rules using policy as code. These policies act as intelligent guardrails, automatically constraining configuration options available to developers while maintaining the flexibility teams need to build and deploy.

Today, we’re diving deep into two of the most powerful policies for multi-cloud governance: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler and Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region.

Policy #1: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler

What it does

The Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler policy gives you fine-grained control over which cloud platforms—AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure—can be used for MongoDB Atlas cluster deployments within your organization.

Why it matters

Compliance and data sovereignty: Many industries have strict requirements about where data can be processed. If your compliance framework mandates AWS-only infrastructure, this policy ensures no clusters are accidentally deployed on Google Cloud Platform or Azure.

Cost optimization: Committed to an AWS Enterprise Discount Program? This policy prevents cost leakage to other hyperscalers and helps you maximize your cloud spend commitments.

Operational consistency: Standardizing on one or two cloud hyperscalers simplifies your operational model, reduces training overhead, and streamlines your disaster recovery procedures.

Security posture: Each cloud hyperscaler has unique security features and configurations. By restricting to approved hyperscalers, you ensure your security teams have deep expertise in the platforms you actually use.

Real-world examples

MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies are defined using the open-source Cedar policy language. Here are some examples of resource policies creating guardrails around which cloud providers can be used for MongoDB Atlas cluster deployments. 

Example 1: Block a specific hyperscaler

Prevent any clusters from being deployed on Google Cloud:

Example 2: Allow only one hyperscaler

Your organization has standardized on Google Cloud. Ensure all clusters must be deployed there:

Example 3: Enforce Project-specific restrictions

Lock down a sensitive MongoDB Atlas Project so that only AWS can be used for cluster deployment:

Policy #2: Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region

What it does

The Restrict Cloud Hyperscaler Region policy enables you to control the specific geographic regions where MongoDB Atlas clusters can be deployed, down to the individual region level (e.g., aws:us-east-1, azure:westeurope).

Why it matters

Data residency compliance: GDPR, California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), and other regulations often mandate that data must remain within specific geographic boundaries. This policy streamlines compliance, making it automatic rather than manual.

Latency optimization: Restrict deployments to regions closest to your users for optimal performance. No more clusters accidentally deployed on the wrong continent.

Cost management: Some cloud regions are significantly more expensive than others. Control costs by preventing deployments to high-cost regions.

Disaster recovery planning: Define approved regions for production workloads and separate regions for disaster recovery, ensuring proper geographic distribution for business continuity.

Security compliance: Certain regions may not meet your security certification requirements. This policy ensures only approved, audited regions are used.

Real-world examples

Example 1: Block a specific region

Your compliance team has determined that aws:us-east-1 has unacceptable data residency risks for your use case, so clusters must not be deployed there:

Example 2: Block multiple regions

Prevent deployments across three regions that don’t meet your requirements:

Example 3: Allow approved regions

Take a zero-trust approach—only permit deployments in preapproved regions:

Exploring a real-world use case: Financial services compliance

A global financial services company needed to ensure all customer data remained within GDPR-compliant regions while maintaining its commitment to AWS as its primary cloud hyperscaler. Its challenge required addressing multiple dimensions simultaneously: preventing deployments to unapproved hyperscalers, restricting geographic regions for data residency, and blocking insecure network configurations.

It implemented a layered approach that combined hyperscaler and region policies with network security controls:

This single policy restricts all Google Cloud Platform deployments while also blocking specific AWS regions that didn’t meet its data residency requirements. The company complemented this with an IP access list policy preventing wildcard access to address network security.

The result? Zero compliance violations were reported in their subsequent audit. Consequently, developers maintained full self-service capabilities within established guardrails, and security teams gained confidence in infrastructure governance. The policies transformed compliance from a documentation exercise into an automated enforcement mechanism, rendering violations technically impossible.

Understanding the key benefits of using resource policies

1. Automated compliance

Stop relying on documentation, training, and manual reviews. Resource policies are enforced automatically at the Organization level.

2. Proactive, not reactive

Resource policies prevent noncompliant configurations before they are created, rather than detecting problems after deployment.

3. Developer velocity

Teams can self-service their infrastructure needs within approved guardrails without waiting for security reviews.

4. Audit trail

MongoDB Atlas generates activity feed events when policies are created, updated, or deleted, providing complete auditability.

5. Noncompliant resource visibility

Use the API endpoint /orgs/{ORG-ID}/nonCompliantResources to identify any existing resources that do not meet your policy requirements.

6. No service disruption

Existing noncompliant clusters continue running. Policies only restrict modifications or the creation of new resources that would keep them out of compliance.

Take the next step

Infrastructure governance doesn’t have to mean slowing down development. With MongoDB Atlas Resource Policies, you can enforce security and compliance requirements automatically while empowering your teams to move fast.

You can implement resource policies through the MongoDB Atlas UI with its visual policy editor, the Atlas Administration API for programmatic policy management, Terraform for infrastructure-as-code integration, or AWS CloudFormation for native AWS deployment. The policies are defined using Cedar, an open-source policy language designed for clarity and expressiveness. If you can read JSON, you can read Cedar policies.

Try resource policies today

  1. Log into MongoDB Atlas with Organization Owner privileges.

  2. Navigate to Organization Settings > Resource Policies.

  3. Create your first policy using one of the examples above.

  4. Monitor noncompliant resources and plan remediation.

  5. Iterate and refine based on your organization’s needs.

Resource policies are included with all MongoDB Atlas deployments at no additional cost. There’s no reason not to start protecting your infrastructure today.

Use Node.js? Want to learn MongoDB? This is the blog series for you!

In this Quick Start series, I’ll walk you through the basics of how to get started using MongoDB with Node.js. In today’s post, we’ll work through connecting to a MongoDB database from a Node.js script, retrieving a list of databases, and printing the results to your console.

Set up

Before we begin, we need to ensure you’ve completed a few prerequisite steps.

Install Node.js

First, make sure you have a supported version of Node.js installed. The current version of MongoDB Node.js Driver requires Node 4.x or greater. For these examples, I've used Node.js 14.15.4. See the MongoDB Compatabillity docs for more information on which version of Node.js is required for each version of the Node.js driver.

Install the MongoDB Node.js Driver

The MongoDB Node.js Driver allows you to easily interact with MongoDB databases from within Node.js applications. You'll need the driver in order to connect to your database and execute the queries described in this Quick Start series.

If you don't have the MongoDB Node.js Driver installed, you can install it with the following command.

At the time of writing, this installed version 3.6.4 of the driver. Running npm list mongodb will display the currently installed driver version number. For more details on the driver and installation, see the official documentation.

Create a free MongoDB Atlas cluster and load the sample data

Next, you'll need a MongoDB database. The easiest way to get started with MongoDB is to use Atlas, MongoDB's fully-managed database-as-a-service.

Head over to Atlas and create a new cluster in the free tier. At a high level, a cluster is a set of nodes where copies of your database will be stored. Once your tier is created, load the sample data. If you're not familiar with how to create a new cluster and load the sample data, check out this video tutorial from MongoDB Developer Advocate Maxime Beugnet.

Get your cluster’s connection info

The final step is to prep your cluster for connection.

In Atlas, navigate to your cluster and click CONNECT. The Cluster Connection Wizard will appear.

The Wizard will prompt you to add your current IP address to the IP Access List and create a MongoDB user if you haven't already done so. Be sure to note the username and password you use for the new MongoDB user as you'll need them in a later step.

Next, the Wizard will prompt you to choose a connection method. Select Connect Your Application. When the Wizard prompts you to select your driver version, select Node.js and 3.6 or later. Copy the provided connection string.

For more details on how to access the Connection Wizard and complete the steps described above, see the official documentation.

Connect to your database from a Node.js application

Now that everything is set up, it’s time to code! Let’s write a Node.js script that connects to your database and lists the databases in your cluster.

Import MongoClient

The MongoDB module exports MongoClient, and that’s what we’ll use to connect to a MongoDB database. We can use an instance of MongoClient to connect to a cluster, access the database in that cluster, and close the connection to that cluster.

Create our main function

Let’s create an asynchronous function named main() where we will connect to our MongoDB cluster, call functions that query our database, and disconnect from our cluster.

The first thing we need to do inside of main() is create a constant for our connection URI. The connection URI is the connection string you copied in Atlas in the previous section. When you paste the connection string, don't forget to update and to be the credentials for the user you created in the previous section. The connection string includes a placeholder. For these examples, we'll be using the sample_airbnb database, so replace with sample_airbnb.

Note: the username and password you provide in the connection string are NOT the same as your Atlas credentials.

Now that we have our URI, we can create an instance of MongoClient.

Note: When you run this code, you may see DeprecationWarnings around the URL string parserand the Server Discover and Monitoring engine. If you see these warnings, you can remove them by passing options to the MongoClient. For example, you could instantiate MongoClient by calling new MongoClient(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true }). See the Node.js MongoDB Driver API documentation for more information on these options.

Now we're ready to use MongoClient to connect to our cluster. client.connect() will return a promise. We will use the await keyword when we call client.connect() to indicate that we should block further execution until that operation has completed.

Now we are ready to interact with our database. Let's build a function that prints the names of the databases in this cluster. It's often useful to contain this logic in well named functions in order to improve the readability of your codebase. Throughout this series, we'll create new functions similar to the function we're creating here as we learn how to write different types of queries. For now, let's call a function named listDatabases().

Let’s wrap our calls to functions that interact with the database in a try/catch statement so that we handle any unexpected errors.

We want to be sure we close the connection to our cluster, so we’ll end our try/catch with a finally statement.

Once we have our main() function written, we need to call it. Let’s send the errors to the console.

Putting it all together, our main() function and our call to it will look something like the following.

List the databases in our cluster

In the previous section, we referenced the listDatabases() function. Let’s implement it!

This function will retrieve a list of databases in our cluster and print the results in the console.

Save Your File

You’ve been implementing a lot of code. Save your changes, and name your file something like connection.js. To see a copy of the complete file, visit the nodejs-quickstart GitHub repo.

Execute Your Node.js Script

Now you’re ready to test your code! Execute your script by running a command like the following in your terminal: node connection.js

You will see output like the following:

What’s next?

Today, you were able to connect to a MongoDB database from a Node.js script, retrieve a list of databases in your cluster, and view the results in your console. Nice!

Now that you're connected to your database, continue on to the next post in this series where you'll learn to execute each of the CRUD (create, read, update, and delete) operations.

In the meantime, check out the following resources:

event_model_payload.headline: AI-Powered Customer Retention with MongoDB: Real-Time Behavioral Triggers for Retail IT Leaders
event_model_payload.summary:
Every customer relationship is an investment, and like any investment, its value grows over time—when relationships are properly nurtured. Industry research has shown that retaining existing customers is far more cost-effective than acquiring new ones. For example, a 2025 article by Startup Guru Lab states that “businesses spend 5 to 7 times more to acquire new customers compared to keeping existing ones.”

New customers require significant marketing spend, extensive onboarding efforts, and a sustained period of trust-building before they can reach the level of loyalty and profitability of an existing customer. In contrast, customers who have already purchased from a brand have overcome those initial barriers. They know the products, the service standards, and the overall brand promise. What’s more, return customers tend to purchase more frequently, spend more per transaction, and are far more likely to recommend the brand to others.

Despite this well-documented return on investment, many retailers still focus the majority of their resources on acquisition rather than retention. A 2024 report by The CMO Survey notes how marketers spend “19.6% more on acquiring customers than retaining them.” Marketing campaigns often prioritize bringing in fresh traffic over protecting the relationships that already exist. The simple truth is that preventing a customer from leaving is almost always faster, cheaper, and more impactful than replacing them. When retailers proactively address signs of dissatisfaction, they not only keep revenue in-house but often strengthen the relationship through well-timed interventions.

The challenge of retention in a hyper-competitive market

Modern shoppers have an unprecedented amount of choice at their fingertips. With a few clicks, they can move from one site to another, compare prices, or abandon a cart if the experience feels too slow, too generic, or untrustworthy. Retention is not simply about having a loyalty program or sending follow-up emails after a cart has been abandoned. Customers expect retailers to anticipate their needs in the moment—not after the fact. 

This challenge is compounded by the complexity of online shopping behavior. Customers hesitate for multiple reasons: indecision between similar products, uncertainty about delivery costs, skepticism about product quality, or simple distraction. Traditional analytics, which rely on batch data processing, fail to capture the immediacy of these moments. By the time an abandoned cart email is sent, the customer has likely already purchased the same product elsewhere.

Real-time behavioral understanding is now critical, seeing that IT decision makers in retail must evaluate technologies that can ingest, process, and act on behavioral data within milliseconds. This is not a trivial requirement. It demands a platform that unifies structured customer data with unstructured behavioral signals, processes vast volumes of event streams in real time, and executes interventions directly from the data layer without additional latency.

MongoDB: A foundation for AI-powered retention

MongoDB is uniquely positioned to support next-generation customer retention strategies by serving as the operational data layer for real-time behavioral triggers. Its flexible document model, real-time event handling, and integration with AI pipelines allow retailers to detect hesitation and respond instantly, keeping customers engaged before they abandon their journey.

Imagine a shopper browsing sneakers. With MongoDB, hesitation can be detected immediately through captured session data, time on page, navigation loops, and mouse movement patterns. MongoDB Triggers and change streams monitor these signals in real time and launch targeted actions the moment thresholds are exceeded.

For example, if the system identifies indecision, it can surface a recommendation widget highlighting products similar to those previously purchased by the same customer. If exit intent is detected, a social proof message can appear, noting that “25 people bought this item today” or that “only a few items remain in stock.” If delivery costs are a barrier, an instant free shipping offer can be triggered. In every case, MongoDB ensures that interventions are executed in milliseconds, before the shopper clicks away.

Crucially, MongoDB is not only about speed—it also ensures intelligent intervention. An embedded AI pipeline enriches raw behavioral events with contextual insights, distinguishing genuine hesitation from casual browsing and preventing system abuse. For instance, as shown in Figure 1, if a customer repeatedly triggers discounts by abandoning carts, MongoDB’s memory-driven session model can detect the pattern and adjust offers accordingly, ensuring retention efforts are sustainable and not exploited.

Description: A shopper browses the site, generating events captured in the events collection (1) and processed in real time by the Atlas Stream Processor (2). The system detects patterns such as prolonged browsing, indecision, or exit intent, then updates the customer's collection and logs activity in customer_behaviour (3). This enriched data is sent to the AI Agent (4), which determines the next-best action and stores it in the strategies collection for delivery to the customer via the e-commerce/app interface (5).

The technology’s ability to unify data is central to its effectiveness. MongoDB stores structured data like transactions and purchase history alongside unstructured behavioral metadata like clickstream logs, session timers, and device fingerprints. This holistic view allows interventions to be precise, contextual, and aligned with the customer’s unique behavior. Atlas Search further enhances this by enabling lightning-fast retrieval of relevant product recommendations the instant they are needed.

MongoDB eliminates the need for fragmented architectures that combine separate databases, ETL jobs, and analytics engines. Instead, it provides a single, scalable solution that handles behavioral event capture, enrichment, storage, and real-time query execution. Its sharding and distributed architecture ensure the platform can support millions of concurrent sessions without latency, making it suitable for large-scale global retailers.

The benefits are clear. Abandonment rates are reduced because customers are intercepted before they leave. Conversion rates increase as hesitation is turned into a decision through contextual nudges. Personalization improves because actions are tied to live behavior, not static profiles updated once a week. And all of this is made transparent to operations teams through real-time dashboards powered by MongoDB’s aggregation framework, enabling leaders to monitor, measure effectiveness, and continuously optimize.

Real-world examples show the power of timely intervention. For example, Carrefour has implemented real-time push notifications for cart abandonment that delivered a 350% uplift in conversion rates. This case underlines what is possible with proactive, behavior-based retention strategies. By leveraging MongoDB’s operational data layer, AI integration, and real-time triggers, ITDMs can implement these strategies at scale while ensuring flexibility and cost efficiency.

How MongoDB sets retail teams up for success

The promise of customer retention solutions is often balanced against technical feasibility, cost, and scalability. MongoDB addresses these concerns directly. Its document model offers flexibility to accommodate evolving data structures without requiring schema redesigns, reducing development friction and accelerating time to market. Its ability to unify operational and analytical workloads removes the overhead of complex data pipelines, lowering infrastructure costs and simplifying system maintenance.

MongoDB’s built-in capabilities—such as time-series collections, TTL indexes, and change streams—allow IT teams to model and execute timer-based events directly within the database layer. This reduces reliance on external schedulers or ETL frameworks, cutting down latency and simplifying architecture. MongoDB Atlas Search provides near real-time retrieval of contextual recommendations without needing an additional search engine. These features make MongoDB a comprehensive platform for real-time engagement.

Security, governance, and scalability are equally addressed. MongoDB’s distributed architecture supports high performance at scale, ensuring consistent low-latency responses even during peak shopping seasons. Fine-grained access controls, encryption, and auditing capabilities align with enterprise security standards. And with MongoDB Atlas, IT teams benefit from a fully managed cloud platform that automates scaling, patching, and monitoring, freeing resources to focus on delivering value to the business rather than maintaining infrastructure.

From a strategic perspective, MongoDB allows stakeholders to align technical capabilities with business outcomes. Instead of reacting to churn after it happens, IT leaders can equip their organizations with proactive, AI-driven retention workflows that directly impact revenue and customer loyalty.

Winning the moments that matter

Customer retention is no longer about broad loyalty programs or after-the-fact marketing campaigns. It is about winning the critical moments of hesitation before a customer leaves. The retailers who succeed are those who can detect indecision instantly, act on it with contextual relevance, and do so at scale across millions of sessions.

MongoDB provides the operational data layer required to make this possible. Its flexible document model, real-time triggers, AI enrichment, and Atlas Search integration enable interventions that fire in milliseconds, ensuring customers receive timely nudges that transform hesitation into conversion. For IT decision-makers, MongoDB offers not only the technical foundation to deliver these capabilities but also the assurance of scalability, security, and operational simplicity at enterprise scale.

Retention is the true driver of sustainable growth. By harnessing MongoDB to power AI-driven behavioral triggers, ITDMs can ensure their organizations are not just competing for attention but winning loyalty at the exact moments that matter most.

References

  • 2025 article by Startup Guru Lab

  • The CMO Survey (2024 report)

event_model_payload.headline: Simplifying Enterprise Security Management: MongoDB Atlas Logs in Microsoft Sentinel
event_model_payload.summary:
Security teams face increasing pressure to maintain visibility and control across complex, hybrid environments. With data spread across multiple systems, detecting threats, correlating incidents, and enforcing governance can become fragmented and time-consuming—especially as organizations accelerate their cloud adoption and AI transformations.

Today, we’re happy to announce that MongoDB Atlas now integrates directly with Microsoft Sentinel, Microsoft’s cloud-native and AI-ready SIEM, SOAR, UEBA, and TI platform trusted by thousands of enterprises worldwide. This native integration allows teams to automatically ingest MongoDB Atlas logs into Microsoft Sentinel with just a few clicks—with no manual connectors or scripts required. 

The MongoDB Atlas Data Connector, available via the Microsoft Marketplace or the Sentinel Content Hub, uses an Azure Function to pull logs from Atlas clusters through the Atlas Admin API and to stream them into Sentinel via the Log Ingestion API. Once in Microsoft Sentinel, the logs appear in your Log Analytics Workspace, ready for query, visualization, and automation using KQL, workbooks, and Logic Apps.

By combining MongoDB Atlas’s rich monitoring and alerting capabilities with Microsoft Sentinel’s AI-driven analytics, graph correlation, and automated response workflows, security teams gain unified visibility across their Atlas workloads and the rest of their cloud estate.

Giving teams a single security view

This integration gives enterprises a single, AI-ready security operations view across applications and data. By leveraging the integration, customers can:

  • Simplify incident detection and response, reducing mean time to resolution.

  • Strengthen governance and compliance through centralized monitoring and automated reporting.

  • Accelerate time-to-value by deploying directly from the Microsoft Marketplace with unified billing and familiar Azure management.

Together, MongoDB Atlas and Microsoft Sentinel eliminate visibility gaps, streamline SecOps, and empower organizations to operate securely and confidently across their Azure environments.

Setting up the integration

The integration’s setup experience is designed for simplicity and speed:

  • Create a Log Analytics Workspace and connect it to your Microsoft Sentinel instance.

  • Search for “MongoDB Atlas Data Connector” in the Microsoft Marketplace or Sentinel Content Hub, then install the solution.

  • In Microsoft Sentinel, navigate to Data Connectors → MongoDB Atlas Data Connector, and select Deploy to Azure.

  • Provide:

    • Your Log Analytics workspace details.

    • MongoDB Project ID and the list of clusters to monitor.

    • Service Account credentials (or a Key Vault reference) for API authentication.

  • Optionally also configure:

    • Log categories filters (NETWORK, ACCESS, QUERY).

    • Exclusions for specific Category IDs.

    • Polling frequency for the Azure Function based on log volume and activity.

Once deployed, the function app, DCE, DCR, storage account, and Key Vault are automatically created, and logs begin flowing into Microsoft Sentinel per your defined schedule.

Technical deep dive

The technical diagram below illustrates the following integration components:

  • UI of Connector captures the Log analytics workspace, Atlas specifics, and schedule

  • Azure Function periodically retrieves MongoDB logs

  • JobState Table maintains the last run timestamp to ensure incremental log collection

  • DCE and DCR handle data transformation before ingestion into MDBALogTable_CL.

  • Azure Key Vault securely stores the MongoDB API credentials

This architecture ensures security and scalability, while aligning with enterprise compliance requirements.

The MongoDB Atlas logs have the schema that includes timestamp, category, severity, category id, message, and additional attributes as detailed here. Below is a screenshot of the logs as ingested into the MDBALogTable_CL table.

Once available in Microsoft Sentinel, these logs can be queried, filtered, or visualized in dashboards. Analysts can build custom workbooks, define alerts on specific severity levels or categories, and trigger automated playbooks for real-time remediation.

Unifying data and security management

Modern security operations demand centralized visibility, intelligent analytics, and automated response without compromising on flexibility or developer agility.

The MongoDB Atlas Data Connector for Microsoft Sentinel empowers organizations to unify their data and security management, ensuring MongoDB workloads benefit from the same advanced protection, analytics, and automation as the rest of their cloud ecosystem.

With this integration, customers can now:

  • Simplify log ingestion and monitoring for Atlas workloads

  • Enhance incident detection and investigation

  • Apply consistent policies and automation across their entire enterprise environment

By bringing MongoDB Atlas into the Microsoft Sentinel ecosystem, security teams can finally manage, monitor, and respond to database security events from a single, intelligent, AI-powered platform.

event_model_payload.headline: Unlocking AI Search: Introducing Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search
event_model_payload.summary:
We are excited to announce the public preview of Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search (available in Public Preview in MongoDB Community Edition), a groundbreaking feature designed to make building sophisticated, AI-powered applications easier than ever. Since 2023, MongoDB has offered integrated vector search alongside our operational database, and last year we announced the acquisition of Voyage AI, bringing state-of-the-art embedding and reranking models to our customers. 

Now, with Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search and the integration of Voyage AI’s state-of-the-art models, we’re giving developers a feature which solves a major point of friction: one-click automatic embedding directly inside MongoDB, which eliminates the need to sync data and manage external models.

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search

At its core, Automated Embedding in Vector Search offers seamless, secure, and scalable AI-powered search natively in MongoDB. By automatically generating vector embeddings (numerical representations of your data to capture semantic meaning), we eliminate the significant complexity typically required when building semantic search, recommendation engines, RAG apps, and AI agents.

The complexity we’re eliminating

Before this release, building vector search into applications presented significant challenges:

  • Manual embedding generation: Choosing an embedding model from over 100 available options and figuring out how to integrate external API services (authentication, input payload, output parameters) is challenging. Developers had to generate embeddings using external providers as part of their application code before inserting data or querying vector search.

  • Synchronization overhead: Every insert, update, or delete required keeping source data and vector embeddings in sync. Developers had to set up custom pipelines, monitor change streams, and write logic to trigger re-embedding and synchronize vectors every time source data changed. 

  • Additional API complexity: Each vector search query necessitated an extra API call to generate query embeddings. 

  • Managing large data ingestion: While simple embedding creation can be straightforward, embedding millions of documents becomes a production nightmare that developers need to monitor at scale. Teams must build complex MLOps pipelines with queuing systems, specialized workers, and retry logic to handle failures, integrate monitoring and alert systems, and ensure that primary database operations aren't blocked by slow or failing embedding endpoints.

The Solution: Streamlined AI-powered search

Automating the embedding process reduces complexity and makes getting started with semantic search as simple as creating a vector search index.

For the first time, you can simply choose an embedding model while setting up a vector search index, and the entire embeddings generation process is automated—no longer needing to rely on different vendors for embedding models and vector databases, which adds complexity and integration risks.  Now, you can simply select the embedding model that best matches your needs, including best-in-class embedding models from Voyage AI. This simplified approach significantly reduces the effort required to get started with key AI use cases, while Voyage AI's industry-leading embedding models ensure high-accuracy retrieval.

Offers architectural simplicity

Our streamlined architecture eliminates the need to manage separate embedding generation workflows, especially when handling complex, high-volume ingestions. 

Developers no longer need to maintain external embedding models, freeing up valuable engineering time that was previously spent on custom pipelines, complex error handling, and performance tuning. This simplification allows you to focus on improving application functionality rather than building embeddings from scratch or having to bring in external third parties. With MongoDB, you now get the benefits of OLTP database, vector search, and Voyage AI embedding models in one unified system, eliminating the need for multiple systems and messy data syncs.

Eliminates embedding mismatches with automation

The system automatically generates vector embeddings for text data during initial data sync when creating indexes, during document insertions and updates, and during query processing. Vector embeddings stay synchronized as underlying data changes, eliminating the risk of stale or mismatched embeddings.

Powered by state-of-the-art Voyage AI embedding models

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search features state-of-the-art embedding models from Voyage AI, including voyage-4-large, voyage-4, voyage-4-lite and voyage-code-3. These models deliver industry-leading performance on retrieval benchmarks (such as RTEB) with multilingual support.

Optimized for performance and reliability

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search eliminates the context window and rate-limiting headaches that plague direct API integrations. 

Through asynchronous dynamic batch processing that optimizes for maximum tokens per request allowed for a model, the system achieves optimal throughput during index creation - automatically adjusting batch sizes based on document shape and size. With built-in automatic retries and error handling, your embedding operations run reliably without blocking primary database operations. This production-ready infrastructure means you can ingest millions of documents without building complex MLOps pipelines or monitoring systems.

Future-proofs your AI applications 

With Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search, you can create indexes across multiple models and compare them side-by-side, making it simple to find the optimal price-performance for your use case. Model lifecycle management becomes effortless with automatic re-embedding capabilities when upgrading to newer, better-performing models. 

We know many users have delayed migrating from older embedding models precisely because of the complexity involved in re-embedding entire datasets across multiple services. Now transitioning to next-generation models requires no custom code or complex coordination across your data services, and you can compare the performance of different models on your own dataset.

Simplification for everyone

Automated Embedding in MongoDB simplifies vector search adoption, allowing Software Engineers, ML Engineers, and Data Scientists from large enterprises to startups to focus on building applications rather than managing embedding integrations. It provides a low-friction path to unlocking powerful AI-driven capabilities for a wide range of use cases, including:

  • Generative AI: Building RAG (retrieval augmented generation) systems.

  • E-commerce: Delivering personalized product recommendations.

  • Content management: Implementing robust semantic search capabilities.

  • Customer service: Creating sophisticated question-answering functionalities.

  • Data science: Professionals who need efficient ways to process large datasets and streamline the transition from prototyping with state-of-the-art models to production.

  • Migration path: Providing an easy migration path for existing text search users looking to upgrade to vector and hybrid search capabilities for improved relevance.

Reducing development overhead and speeding results

We invited a select number of customers across industries, including healthcare, financial services, transportation, and media, to test automated embedding and provide feedback during our private preview. These customers saw the massive benefits, including immediate performance enhancements and reduced overhead. Two preview customers had the following to say: 

"We deployed MongoDB’s automated embedding in vector search across our 40‑million‑document corpus, converting weeks of engineering into a low‑maintenance, production‑grade workflow that materially improved retrieval speed and relevance while reducing development overhead.”

—Ohad Levinkron-Fisch Vice President of R&D and AI MedINT Medical Intelligence

"Being able to drop MongoDB’s automated embedding into an in-flight, production-scale system and see immediate performance and simplicity gains is huge - and we’re thrilled to deepen our partnership with MongoDB, given how much of our stack already runs on MongoDB."

—Joe Marta Senior Director, Applied AI Coalfire

How to get started with the Public Preview

By automatically generating and synchronizing vector embeddings using Voyage AI models, Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search eliminates traditional vector search complexities. This secure and scalable solution is native to MongoDB, accelerating the creation of powerful AI-enabled applications and significantly improving the developer experience. 

Automated Embedding in MongoDB Vector Search in Community Edition is available now, with MongoDB Atlas and MongoDB Vector Search in Enterprise Edition access coming soon. Use your favorite MongoDB language drivers (Python, JavaScript, Java, C#, and GoLang), AI frameworks like LangChain and LangGraph, and the MongoDB MCP server. 

Jump in with our quick start guide.

GitBook security incident update Hey <$name>, The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance.

*What happened* GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data.

*Your data* Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following: * Git Sync secrets. * GitBook API tokens. * Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook. * Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors.

At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified.

*What you need to do now* * Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident. * Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook. * If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets. * If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it. Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process.

*What we are doing next* * Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks. * Introducing further security measures to our platform. * Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident. * If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates

Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption The GitBook team

event_model_payload.headline: Trace linkage: connect the dots between your app traces and database queries
event_model_payload.summary:
When an application request slows down, a trace can show a database call. Finding the database query behind it can be tedious, requiring you to switch between traces and database telemetry, as well as match timestamps or query text by hand. 

In Grafana Cloud, the Database Observability app already provides a window into all of your database telemetry, including query samples, performance history, and explain plan. But what if you could jump from that database call in the trace straight to its query details?

OpenTelemetry database semantic conventions stabilized last year, giving us all a dependable shared language for describing database operations. That foundation has opened the door for what we call trace linkage, now Generally Available in Database Observability!

What is trace linkage?

With trace linkage, we try to provide a connection between OpenTelemetry-instrumented applications and database telemetry collected with Alloy. In other words, when you give us these previously-disjoint puzzle pieces, we’ll do our best to provide you as much supporting information between these two elements as we can. And we'll do it without making you tediously piece together timestamps and logs. 

From a database span in a trace, you’ll see a link on the query text. Clicking from there, the app searches for a connection between your database query and our opinionated view of your most relevant data in the Database Observability app. You can explore sampled query execution data or check out the query’s historical performance, alongside that query’s related schema and explain plan.

This connection builds on the database attributes your OpenTelemetry instrumentation already emits. Grafana Cloud Traces, powered by Tempo, retain those attributes, and trace linkage uses the query text, database system, and database name to connect a database span to its supporting query context in Database Observability. 

We support the stable conventions like db.query.text and its legacy equivalent db.statement, so existing instrumentation can continue to benefit as teams adopt the stable conventions.

How does it work?

The initial idea for trace linkage came from this question: What shared context could connect application instrumentation with telemetry collected from the database?

The answer was to leverage trace context: the trace ID and span ID. On one side we have an application trace with spans representing a query execution. On the Database Observability side, we are collecting telemetry from the database concerning query executions. As long as the telemetry we collect contains the same trace ID and span ID, we can make a link between the application trace and Database Observability. 

This led us to sqlcommenter, an open source project donated to the OpenTelemetry community. Its idea is (delightfully) simple: let the SQL statement carry a piece of trace context with it in a comment. With trace context propagation enabled, sqlcommenter injects the application’s trace ID and span ID into a comment at the end of the SQL statement. This is done at the level of an individual query execution, so this is like a shared thread that allows us to follow from a trace span to a specific query execution.

We then search the trace ID and span ID in the logs that we generated in the Database Observability Alloy component: our component extracts traceparent from the SQL comment and includes it in query sample logs.

Going beyond a traceparent match

However, having sqlcommenter enabled doesn’t guarantee that Alloy captured the particular SQL execution. That can depend on how short-lived a query may be or how often Alloy polls the database. Even if you are ready to use sqlcommenter, not every database engine is supported, and it can come with downsides for database caches. This means that you might have traces for which we can’t find a query sample in Database Observability, at least not with sqlcommenter exclusively.

We can go beyond sqlcommenter-based matching by using the query statement itself. When we can’t find an exact match, we look for matching query text in the telemetry collected by Alloy.

That sounds straightforward, but the same query can look different on each side. OpenTelemetry instrumentation doesn’t always record statements in the same way: depending on the language and instrumentation used, literal values may be preserved or masked, and parameter placeholders can take different forms. Meanwhile, database engines apply their own normalization to the query text that Alloy collects. We account for these differences, along with formatting and comments, to find a match.

Even when we can’t point you to the exact execution, you can still explore the samples and historical performance we’ve gathered for that query! This lets us make a meaningful link between your traces and Database Observability, even without sqlcommenter.

Start with query text matching, then use sqlcommenter to match trace and span IDs exactly

Trace linkage can be a great tool for quickly connecting your database and application telemetry, so we're excited for you to try it today. If your application is already instrumented as an OpenTelemetry SDK that sends traces to Grafana Cloud and you’ve already set up Database Observability, then read our docs about setting up trace linkage to help you get started. 

If Database Observability has collected a query and the database span already includes its text in db.query.text or the legacy db.statement, chances are trace linkage can already match the span to that query without further application instrumentation.

Once you’ve tried query text matching, you can optionally go beyond and match a trace to a specific query execution with the use of sqlcommenter, as this blog discussed extensively. This improves match precision; exact matches remain best-effort because Alloy may not sample that execution.

And if you aren't sure where to start, ask Grafana Assistant for help, using natural language.

event_model_payload.headline: Bring Live MongoDB Atlas Data Into Microsoft 365 Copilot
event_model_payload.summary:
The federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas gives organizations a governed way to bring live operational data into the flow of work across Copilot experiences.

To operate efficiently, businesses require timely information about the systems that underpin their organizations. For example, they need to be able to answer questions like: Which incidents are open? Which orders are delayed? What fields and data types are present in the customer collection? The answers they need often live in operational applications built on MongoDB Atlas, while the questions are asked in the productivity tools people use every day.

To help close that gap, MongoDB is excited to introduce a federated Copilot connector for MongoDB Atlas. Now generally available, the connector enables users to ask Microsoft 365 Copilot questions about live data in MongoDB Atlas, bringing operational context into the same experience where people collaborate, analyze information, and make decisions.

The connector surfaces MongoDB Atlas data across Microsoft Copilot experiences, including Copilot Chat, Researcher in Copilot, Copilot Cowork, Microsoft Word, Excel, and Teams, with additional experiences planned to follow.

Bring operational data into the flow of work

The connector brings MongoDB Atlas to Microsoft Copilot through MongoDB’s managed remote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. When a user asks a relevant question, Copilot can query Atlas in real time—instead of relying on a static copy of the data.

This creates a more direct path from a business question to the information needed to answer it, and helps users—who may not have MongoDB expertise—access and analyze live operational data through an AI assistant.

Now, business users can use conversational prompts to:

  • Retrieve live business data without writing database queries.

  • Find and filter customers, transactions, products, orders, content, or operational events.

  • Get quick counts and key performance indicators, such as the number of delayed orders or high-value customers.

  • Summarize and rank data to identify top categories, products, regions, trends, averages, and other business insights.

For example, a user might ask Copilot to summarize the open incidents in an Atlas cluster supporting a payments application, identify delayed orders, or describe the fields and data types in the customer collection for a loyalty service. By industry, a supply chain team can investigate inventory, shipment, and warehouse exceptions. A financial services team can explore customer records, fraud alerts, and transaction investigations. And a retailer can ask questions about orders, loyalty, customer service, and personalization.

The connector can also help power business copilots and agents. Organizations can ground Copilot and other AI assistants in current MongoDB Atlas data for customer service, sales, operations, and decision support, bringing live operational context into the workflows where teams already work.

Connect to live data without migrating or indexing it

Organizations using MongoDB Atlas do not need to migrate their operational data, re-platform their applications, or rebuild their integrations to use the connector.

To do so, an administrator simply approves and enables the connector in the Microsoft 365 admin center. Users then sign in, and their existing Atlas permissions carry through to each query.

MongoDB Atlas remains the system of record. The connector queries Atlas directly rather than indexing a copy of Atlas data into Microsoft 365, so the information returned to users reflects the current state of the underlying application data.

This federated approach helps organizations connect their productivity layer to operational data while keeping that data in the environment where it is managed.

Put governance into every interaction

Making operational data more accessible requires controls that organizations can understand and manage. The connector is designed to support that approach through:

  • Permission-aware access: Each query runs as the signed-in user and honors the permissions already defined in MongoDB Atlas.

  • Administrator control: Admins approve the connector and can manage deployment through the Microsoft 365 admin center.

  • Read-only access: The connector is designed for read-only interaction with Atlas data.

  • Auditability: Administrators can audit connector activity in Microsoft Purview.

  • No separate search index: The connector queries Atlas on demand instead of indexing a copy of Atlas data in Microsoft 365.

Together, these controls give organizations a practical way to make operational information available through Copilot without giving up the governance model around the source data.

A foundation for more productive work

AI-powered productivity depends on access to relevant business context. By connecting Microsoft Copilot and other AI assistants to live MongoDB Atlas data through a federated connection, MongoDB and Microsoft are helping organizations make operational information easier to use without adding a data-movement project or another application to maintain. Users can get answers, summaries, and insights from live data through natural language, while technical teams retain control over the underlying systems and permissions.

For organizations already running MongoDB Atlas on Azure and Microsoft 365 Copilot, the connector provides a way to build on existing investments. Teams can explore high-value operational questions, validate measurable business outcomes, and develop repeatable patterns for bringing current data into everyday decisions.

The result is a simpler path from question to context to action—grounded in the systems organizations already use and governed by the permissions they already have.

event_model_payload.headline: 국내 최초 광고 MCP를 출시하며, 개발자의 역할은 어디까지 넓어졌을까?
event_model_payload.summary:
안녕하세요. 당근 광고실 광고주플랫폼팀에서 백엔드 엔지니어로 일하는 제이크(Jake)예요.

얼마 전 저희 팀 엔지니어링 매니저 Iltaek이 프론트엔드와 백엔드를 한 팀으로 합친 이야기를 글로 나눴어요. 그 글이 팀의 경계를 넘어 일하는 이야기였다면, 이번 글은 제가 당근 광고 MCP를 만들며 개발자의 역할을 넓혀 본 이야기예요.

MCP(Model Context Protocol)는 AI 서비스가 외부 서비스의 데이터를 불러올 때 쓰는 표준 연결 방식이에요. 광고주가 Claude 같은 AI 서비스에 “지난주 광고 성과 어땠어?”라고 물으면, AI가 광고 MCP를 거쳐 당근 광고의 계정 정보와 광고 정보, 성과 데이터를 가져와서 답해 줘요. 해외 광고 플랫폼에서는 구글, 메타, 아마존이 이미 MCP를 공개했고, 국내에서는 당근이 처음으로 공식 광고 MCP를 출시했어요.

저는 개발자로 이 프로젝트에 참여하는 줄 알았는데, 하다 보니 로드맵과 PRD부터 출시까지 맡아야 했어요. 이 글에서는 그 과정에서 겪은 일과, 제가 일하는 방식이 어떻게 달라졌는지 이야기해 보려고 해요.

로드맵과 PRD를 처음 써 봤어요

그동안은 PM과 함께 일하면서 엔지니어로서 개발에 필요한 의견을 나누고, PRD를 어떻게 구현할지 고민했어요. 그런데 이번에는 Iltaek에게 로드맵과 PRD까지 맡아 달라는 요청을 받았어요.

솔직히 요청을 받았을 때는 “이것도 개발자인 내 일인가?” 싶었어요. 로드맵은 PM이 그리는 거 아닌가, 내가 로드맵을 제시하는 게 맞나 하는 생각이 먼저 들었어요. 해 본 적 없는 일이라 부담도 됐고요.

그때 Iltaek이 오너라는 마음가짐으로 해 보라고 했어요. 그 말대로 “내 프로젝트”라고 생각하다 보니, 이 프로젝트를 더 잘되게 하려면 뭘 해야 할지 고민하게 되더라고요. 스스로 던지는 질문부터 달라졌어요.

로드맵을 그리려고 하니, 당근 광고 플랫폼은 생각보다 크고 복잡했어요. 전문가모드, 간편모드, 대행사 플랫폼¹까지 합치면 광고주가 할 수 있는 일이 정말 많아요. 광고 보고서, 광고 수정, 소재 만들기, 타겟팅, 전환 추적, 결제와 충전까지요. 이걸 한 번에 다 MCP로 열 수는 없어서, 범위를 좁혀야 했어요.

혹시나 잘못되더라도 광고주에게 손해가 없는 일인지, 화면보다 AI로 했을 때 더 편한 일인지, 더 많은 광고주에게 도움이 되는 일인지, 이렇게 세 가지 기준을 세워 봤어요. 그래서 리스크가 가장 낮은 조회 기능부터 열었어요. 광고를 수정하는 기능은 충분히 검증한 뒤에 열기로 했어요. AI가 예산이나 입찰가를 바꾸다 실수하면 광고비가 의도와 다르게 나갈 수 있어서요. 결제나 광고 삭제처럼 AI로 하는 게 오히려 불편하거나 위험한 일은 아예 열지 않기로 했어요. 그리고 당근 광고에서 가장 많이 집행되는 디스플레이 광고부터 시작했어요.

그렇게 로드맵을 그리고, 그 안에서 이번에 할 일의 범위를 정했어요. 그다음 저희 팀에서 쓰는 PTBSMAF라는 프레임워크로 PRD를 썼어요. 문제 정의(Problem Statement), 트레이드오프(Trade-off), 벤치마크(Benchmark), 해결책(Solution), 지표(Metrics), 중단 조건(Andon), 피드백 루프(Feedback Loop)의 앞 글자를 딴 이름이에요.

그중에서도 문제 정의, 트레이드오프, 벤치마크가 특히 도움이 됐어요. 문제를 제가 이해한 대로 풀어 쓰다 보니 생각이 정리됐고, 조회만 먼저 열면 무엇을 얻고 무엇을 포기하는지 적으면서 트레이드오프가 분명해졌어요. 특히 벤치마크에서는 다른 광고 플랫폼의 사례를 찾아보면서, 그대로 참고할 부분과 우리 상황에 맞게 바꿔야 할 부분이 구분됐어요.

PRD를 쓰면서 이전에는 생각해 보지 못했던 부분까지 고민하게 됐어요. 이 기능으로 플랫폼이 무엇을 얻을지, 어느 제품부터 고려할지, 뭐가 더 나은 방향인지 같은 제품 관점의 고민은 전부 처음이었어요.

이렇게 정한 것들이 정답인지 100% 확신할 수는 없었지만, 적어도 근거를 가지고 정했다는 점은 지금 돌아봐도 만족스러워요. 로드맵은 PM이 그리는 거라고 생각했던 것도, 해 보고 나니 제 선입견이었던 것 같아요.

API를 그대로 옮기면 될 줄 알았어요

로드맵과 PRD로 무엇을 하고 무엇을 하지 않을지 정하고 나니, 이제 도구를 어떻게 만들지 고민할 차례였어요.

광고주센터 뒤에는 이미 잘 돌아가는 API가 있어서, 그걸 MCP 도구로 하나씩 감싸기만 하면 될 거라고 생각했어요. 그런데 API를 그대로 도구로 만들면, AI가 어떤 도구를 써야 할지 헷갈려하고, 필요한 정보를 놓쳐 잘못된 답을 할 수 있더라고요.

예를 들어 광고주가 “이 광고 왜 안 나가?”라고 물었다고 해 볼게요. 광고주센터였다면 광고 정보, 노출 상태, 심사 결과가 한 화면에 같이 보였을 거예요. 그런데 API마다 도구를 따로 만들면, AI가 그중 뭘 부를지 스스로 골라야 해요. 광고 정보만 보고 “켜져 있으니 괜찮아요”라고 답하면서, 광고 심사에서 막힌 건 놓치는 식이에요.

메타 광고 MCP를 직접 연결해 보니, 도구가 많고 설명 방식도 제각각이라 AI가 광고주의 요청을 다르게 이해하는 경우가 있었어요. 로드맵을 그리며 광고주가 AI에게 무엇을 물어볼지 고민했던 게 여기서 도움이 됐어요. API를 그대로 옮기는 대신, 광고주의 질문을 기준으로 도구를 설계하기로 했어요. 그렇게 정리해 보니 좋은 API와 좋은 도구의 기준은 꽤 달랐어요.

이 기준으로, 가장 흔한 요청인 “지난주 성과 분석해 줘”를 예시로 도구를 설계해 봤어요. 이 요청은 어느 계정인지 정하고, 대상을 찾고, 성과를 보는 세 단계로 나눌 수 있어요. 그래서 단계마다 도구를 하나씩 두고 광고주센터 뒤의 여러 API를 3개의 도구로 정리했어요. 앞으로 광고 수정처럼 기능이 늘어나면 도구도 함께 늘어나겠지만, 그때도 이 기준을 지켜 가려고 해요.

제품으로 내놓으려면 챙길 게 많았어요

도구를 다 만들었다고 바로 내놓을 수 있는 건 아니었어요. AI가 광고주의 계정을 대신 다룰 수 있도록 약관을 검토하고 법무팀의 확인을 받아야 했어요. 기존 서버에 부하가 가지 않도록 적절한 호출 한도를 정해야 했고, 광고주용 연결 가이드와 서비스 내 안내 화면도 준비해야 했어요. 그리고 출시 후 운영을 위한 대시보드도 만들어야 했어요.

처음에는 좀 막막했어요. 일정을 챙기고, 회의를 잡고, 다른 팀과 일정을 맞추는 일은 개발자인 저에게 익숙하지 않았으니까요. 그럴 때마다 함께 진행한 PM인 Moana와 이야기하면서 하나씩 풀어 나갔어요.

챙길 일 중에서도 가장 걱정했던 건 인증이었어요. MCP는 인증 방식이 표준으로 정해져 있어요. OAuth 2.1을 따라야 하고, MCP를 연결할 때 광고주 본인의 동의를 거쳐야 해요. 사내에서만 쓰는 게 아니라 외부 광고주에게 공개하려면, 이러한 표준을 반드시 지원해야 했어요. 다행히 당근의 인증을 맡고 있는 Identity Service Team에서 이미 SSO(Single Sign-On)를 제공하고 있었어요.² 그래서 MCP 인증도 지원해 달라고 요청드렸고, 인증 서버를 표준에 맞게 고쳐 주셨어요.

그리고 나서 광고 MCP에 인증 서버를 연동하고 AI 서비스에 연결해 봤어요. 그런데 OpenAI의 Codex에서는 로그인을 누르면 에러가 뜨고 그대로 끊겼어요. OpenAI 문서에는 이 표준을 지원한다고 나와 있어서 더 당황했는데, 알고 보니 그때 이 인증 방식에 대한 지원은 Codex 정식 버전에는 아직 들어가지 않았고 알파 버전에만 막 들어온 참이었어요. 이대로 출시하면 Codex에서는 광고 MCP를 연결할 수 없는 상황이었어요. 그래서 틈날 때마다 새 버전이 나왔는지 들여다봤어요. 출시 전에 정식 버전에서도 지원하게 돼서, 그제야 한숨 돌렸어요.

그렇게 9월 16일, 광고 MCP를 공개 베타로 출시했어요.

출시 후엔 광고주가 어떻게 쓰는지 궁금했어요

원래라면 개발하고 QA하고 프로덕션에 배포하면 끝났다고 생각했을 것 같아요. 그런데 제품을 맡고 보니, 배포하고 나서 의도한 대로 동작하는지가 궁금했어요. 광고주들이 이걸 실제로 어떻게 쓰는지, 어떻게 하면 더 잘 쓰게 할 수 있을지 계속 고민하게 됐어요. 그래서 도구가 호출될 때마다 어떤 광고주가 어떤 AI 서비스에서 어떤 도구를 불렀는지 남기고, 계속해서 MCP를 쓰는지까지 대시보드에서 볼 수 있게 만들었어요.

출시 직후에는 틈날 때마다 대시보드를 열어 봤어요. 간편모드 사장님이 많은지 전문가모드 마케터가 많은지, 대행사 마케터도 쓰는지, 어떤 업종에서 많이 쓰는지 살펴보다 보니, 만들 때 고민했던 것들이 실제로 광고주에게 도움이 되는지 더 알고 싶어졌어요. 누가 시킨 건 아니었지만, 주간 리포트도 써 보고 데이터도 직접 분석해 봤어요.

광고실에서는 광고주 경험을 직접 이해하기 위해 실제 광고를 운영해 보는 개밥먹기(dogfooding)를 하고 있어요. 저도 한 빵집 광고를 맡고 있었는데, 가게 주변 좁은 지역에만 광고를 집행하다 보니 성과가 점점 떨어지고 있었어요. 그래서 광고 MCP를 연결해 에이전트에게 성과 분석을 맡겨 봤어요.

에이전트는 소재 피로도가 높다며 새 소재를 제안했어요. 성과가 낮은 광고를 찾아 끄고, 그 예산을 다른 광고로 옮기라는 제안도 했어요. 소재 피로도까지 짚어낼 줄은 몰라 놀랐어요. 실제 광고를 운영할 때 참고할 만한 제안이었어요.

이 경험을 통해 광고주가 MCP를 잘 쓰고 있는지는 호출 횟수만으로 판단할 수 없다고 느꼈어요. 분석이 광고주의 판단과 실제 운영에 얼마나 도움이 되는지가 더 중요했어요. 그래서 로드맵에서 다음 단계로 미뤄 둔 광고 수정 기능의 필요성도 분명해졌어요. 분석 결과를 실제 광고에 반영해야 운영에 변화가 생기니까요.

다음은 AI로 광고를 고치는 거예요

지금 광고 MCP는 조회만 할 수 있어요. 분석 결과를 광고에 반영하려면 광고주가 광고주센터에 들어가 직접 수정해야 해요. 다음 단계에서는 조회와 수정을 연결해 AI가 광고를 고치고 만들 수도 있게 하려고 해요.

장기적으로는 AI 서비스를 직접 사용하기 어려운 간편모드 사장님도 당근 안에서 에이전트의 도움을 받아 광고를 더 잘 운영할 수 있도록 하고 싶어요. 지금 만든 도구는 외부 AI 서비스뿐 아니라 당근 안의 에이전트에도 그대로 연결할 수 있어서, 도구를 새로 만들지 않아도 돼요.

기능을 넓히는 만큼, 이게 정말 광고주에게 도움이 되는지도 계속 확인하려고 해요. 광고를 더 자주, 더 잘 고칠 수 있으면 광고 성과가 좋아지고, 좋아진 성과는 광고주의 매출로, 다시 당근 광고의 매출로 이어질 거라고 보고 있어요. 광고 MCP는 이 흐름의 첫 단계인 “광고를 더 잘 고치는 일”을 AI로 더 쉽게 만들어 준다고 생각해요.

마치며

사내에 출시 공지를 올리며 감사 인사를 적다 보니, 고마운 분들이 많아서 빠진 분이 없는지 몇 번이나 다시 확인했어요. 제품 하나를 내놓기까지 이렇게 많은 분의 도움이 필요하다는 걸 이번에 알았어요. 갑작스러운 요청에도 함께해 주신 모든 분께 감사드려요.

처음에는 “이것도 개발자인 내 일인가?” 싶었어요. 그런데 내 프로젝트라고 생각하니 질문이 바뀌었어요. “어떻게 구현할까?”에서 “어떤 문제를 풀고, 문제가 실제로 해결됐는지 어떻게 확인할까?”로요. 제가 해 보고 도움이 됐던 습관을 세 가지로 정리해 봤어요.

  1. 구현하기 전에, 이 일이 어떤 문제를 푸는지 내 언어로 표현해 봐요.
  2. 배포하고 나서, 문제가 정말 풀렸는지 검증해 봐요.
  3. 내가 만든 기능을 사용자처럼 직접 써 봐요.

이 글이 개발자로서 역할을 넓혀 보려는 분께 작은 참고가 되면 좋겠어요. 궁금한 점이나 비슷한 경험이 있다면 댓글이나 제 링크드인으로 편하게 남겨 주세요.

각주

  1. 당근 광고는 광고주의 환경에 맞춰 서비스가 나뉘어요. 간편모드는 쉽고 빠르게 광고를 집행하고 싶은 소상공인 광고주를 위한 서비스이고, 전문가모드는 캠페인, 광고그룹, 소재 단위로 전략을 세우고 정밀한 타겟팅과 성과 분석이 필요한 마케팅 담당자와 광고주를 위한 서비스예요. 대행사 플랫폼은 여러 광고주의 광고를 대신 운영하는 대행사를 위한 서비스예요.
  2. 당근 SSO가 어떻게 만들어져 왔는지는 Identity Service Team이 쓴 당근의 인증은 어떻게 달라져 왔을까요?에서 볼 수 있어요.
  3. 같은 광고 소재를 같은 사람들에게 오래 보여 주면, 사람들이 익숙해져서 점점 반응하지 않게 되는 현상이에요. 클릭률이 시간이 지날수록 떨어지는 모습으로 나타나요.

국내 최초 광고 MCP를 출시하며, 개발자의 역할은 어디까지 넓어졌을까? was originally published in 당근 기술 블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing Starlight Forge: Evidence-Backed Documentation for Real Codebases
event_model_payload.summary:
Good documentation work starts with an uncomfortable truth: a codebase rarely explains itself.

A package.json tells only part of the story. A directory name can be misleading. A framework convention may not actually be used. The most valuable details are often spread across source files, configuration, tests, CI, deployment files, and existing documentation.

That is why I built Starlight Forge: an open-source Agent Skill that guides coding agents through repository discovery, evidence-backed documentation planning, and safe documentation generation.

It can produce either portable Markdown documentation or an Astro + Starlight documentation site. It is deliberately not an npm package, hosted service, custom CLI, or documentation bot. It is a set of instructions, references, templates, and small local validation helpers that work with coding agents that support the Agent Skills format.

The problem: documentation generators can sound confident while being wrong

Documentation generated from a shallow repository scan often looks polished but has a trust problem. It may:

  • describe routes that do not exist;
  • suggest commands that are not in the project;
  • infer architecture from a framework convention rather than source evidence;
  • miss an existing contributor guide or deployment workflow;
  • overwrite documentation written by the team; or
  • include sensitive information copied from configuration files.

Those are not cosmetic mistakes. They create friction for maintainers and can send new contributors in the wrong direction.

Starlight Forge treats documentation as a repository-analysis task first and a writing task second. The agent should inspect before it plans, plan before it writes, and validate before it reports success.

What Starlight Forge does

The skill provides a canonical workflow in one SKILL.md, with focused reference guides for deeper work such as monorepos, safe repository discovery, evidence quality, incremental updates, Markdown output, and Astro + Starlight generation.

At a high level, the workflow is:

Discover repository scope
        ↓
Build an evidence map
        ↓
Propose a documentation plan
        ↓
Generate in an agreed destination
        ↓
Validate links, claims, commands, and navigation
        ↓
Report what actually passed, failed, or was not checked

The purpose is simple: documentation should make clear what was observed, what was inferred, and what remains unknown.

1. Start with repository discovery, not a generic template

Before creating a page, Starlight Forge asks the agent to establish the actual repository root and inspect the files that reveal how the project works:

  • repository guidance such as AGENTS.md and contribution instructions;
  • manifests, workspace definitions, and declared scripts;
  • entry points, framework configuration, tests, CI, and deployment files;
  • existing documentation that should be preserved; and
  • representative packages when the repository is a monorepo.

The discovery process is bounded. It skips dependency directories, build output, large binaries, generated artifacts, symlinks during broad scans, and likely secret files unless they are explicitly relevant. Repository text is treated as data, never as instructions that can redirect the agent.

For large repositories, this matters. Reading every file is usually expensive and does not make documentation more accurate. A targeted inventory and focused source inspection produce a better starting point.

Starlight Forge includes an optional deterministic inventory helper for this purpose. It lists paths and useful manifests while avoiding common dependency trees, sensitive-looking file names, and symlinks. It does not generate prose or make network requests.

2. Tie important claims to evidence

The core idea behind the skill is a small evidence map.

For each meaningful claim, the agent should have a source path, configuration file, test, or clearly labelled reasoning behind it. For example:

Documentation claim Supporting evidence How to describe it
A package is an application entry point Manifest script and source entry Observed fact
Two packages form a shared boundary Imports and workspace configuration Inference, with rationale
A deployment command is available CI workflow or checked-in script Observed fact
A service has a certain runtime behavior No inspected source or test Unknown until verified

This changes the tone of generated documentation in a useful way. Instead of inventing a default command because a project resembles a familiar framework, the agent can say that the command is unknown or point to the script that actually exists.

It also keeps pages reviewable. A maintainer can trace a setup instruction, architecture explanation, or environment-variable name back to the repository instead of accepting a vague summary on faith.

3. Plan pages before modifying files

The skill separates planning from generation.

Once it understands the repository, it proposes the documentation pages, their purpose, the output location, and the existing files that may be affected. If the requested output directory already contains authored documentation, it preserves those files. The agent should ask only when an overwrite is genuinely necessary.

This makes the skill suitable for documentation work that evolves over time. A later refresh can target pages affected by source changes instead of treating the whole docs/ directory as generated content.

4. Choose Markdown or Astro + Starlight

Starlight Forge supports two output modes because documentation needs vary.

Portable Markdown

Markdown is the default choice when a repository needs lightweight, reviewable pages that can live alongside the source. The skill creates linked pages in the destination you approve and adapts the page set to the project. It avoids producing empty boilerplate simply to fill a standard template.

Example prompt:

Use Starlight Forge to inspect this repository and create a concise Markdown
developer guide in docs/developer/. Show me the proposed pages before writing,
preserve existing files, and cite source files for important claims.

Astro + Starlight

For a navigable documentation website, the skill can generate or integrate an Astro + Starlight site. It inspects the repository first, then uses current Starlight conventions for content, navigation, and built-in search. It does not modify application code just to make documentation generation easier.

Example prompt:

Use Starlight Forge to document this project as an Astro + Starlight site in
website-docs/. Inspect existing files first, show the plan, then build the
site if dependencies are available. Do not deploy it.

In either mode, the agent should validate local links, source references, and navigation. In Starlight mode, it should run an available build only when the environment and project dependencies make that safe and practical. A skipped build must be reported as skipped, not passed.

5. Build documentation with safety boundaries

Documentation work often has broader access to a codebase than a narrow feature task. That makes safe defaults essential.

Starlight Forge directs the agent to:

  • keep reads and writes within the agreed repository and documentation destination;
  • avoid likely credential files and never reproduce secret values;
  • respect ignore rules and avoid unnecessary dependency or build trees;
  • avoid executing project code just to learn what it does;
  • inspect scripts before running them;
  • preserve existing user-authored documentation;
  • avoid installing packages or contacting external services unless requested; and
  • distinguish passed, failed, skipped, and not-checked validation results.

These measures reduce risk; they are not a claim that prompt injection or incorrect documentation can be eliminated. Repository files, generated content, comments, issue text, and tool output are still untrusted data. The real security boundary remains the permissions and tooling provided by the agent host.

Small helpers, not another product to maintain

The repository includes two dependency-free Node.js helpers:

  • inventory-project.mjs produces a bounded, filename-only project inventory.
  • validate-docs.mjs checks local Markdown links and verifies the basic Agent Skill frontmatter.

They are intentionally narrow. They do not analyze architecture, write documentation, call an AI service, or install dependencies. The coding agent remains responsible for source inspection, judgement, and writing.

That separation is deliberate. I wanted the project to stay portable and easy to audit instead of turning it into another toolchain that needs a service, account, or build pipeline before it is useful.

Installation and use

The canonical skill is in skills/starlight-forge/. Copy that directory into a supported skills location for your agent, or use the repository plugin packaging where your agent supports it.

For example, after installing the skill, invoke it in a coding-agent session:

# Codex
$starlight-forge

# Claude Code
/starlight-forge:starlight-forge

# GitHub Copilot CLI
/starlight-forge

The repository also contains plugin manifests for Codex, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot CLI. For Claude Code, the documented repository installation flow is:

/plugin marketplace add ShubhamTiwari909/starlight-forge
/plugin install starlight-forge@starlight-forge

For Codex and GitHub Copilot CLI, see the repository README for the current plugin commands and manual installation paths. Agent installation behavior changes over time, so it is worth checking the linked official documentation and the agent's own skill or plugin listing after installation.

What has been evaluated so far

The project includes small fixture repositories covering TypeScript utilities, a React UI package, a Next.js app, a Node API-shaped project, a monorepo, malformed project metadata, and an adversarial repository. The fixtures are designed to test specific failure modes, such as invented commands, unsafe file reads, unsupported architecture claims, broken links, and unexpected overwrites.

The local checks validate the skill metadata, local Markdown links, inventory behavior around sensitive-looking files and symlinks, and generated fixture output. They do not simulate a full coding agent or prove documentation quality for every repository.

There is also early real-world feedback: I used the skill on an Astro project, where it generated accurate documentation; I also installed it from the repository in Claude Code and used it to create a thorough Astro documentation site. Those results are encouraging, but they are experience reports rather than a controlled compatibility benchmark.

Where I want to take it next

The most useful next step is feedback from real repositories.

I am especially interested in cases where the skill:

  • missed an important source of truth;
  • made a claim that needed stronger evidence;
  • proposed an awkward documentation structure;
  • needed better monorepo guidance;
  • found an existing documentation folder that required a more careful update strategy; or
  • produced Starlight content that needed a framework-specific adjustment.

If you try it, please open an issue with the repository shape, the prompt you used, what it generated, and what you expected. Redact private code and credentials. Concrete feedback will make the reference guides and fixtures much more valuable than generic feature requests.

Try Starlight Forge

You can find the project, installation notes, references, fixtures, and contribution guidance here:

github.com/ShubhamTiwari909/starlight-forge

If your project has documentation that is technically correct but hard to trust, start with a small target: a setup guide, package overview, or contributor page. Ask the agent to show its evidence-backed plan before it writes. That one habit makes generated documentation much easier to review and maintain.
