event_model_payload.headline: Reading X.509 Certificates by Hand: SANs, Key Usage, Chains & Intermediates
event_model_payload.summary:
Most TLS outages I have been called into did not start with a dramatic key leak. They started with a certificate someone never really read: a missing Subject Alternative Name, an incomplete chain file, a leaf that looked fine in a browser on one machine and failed everywhere else. Browser UIs hide the details. openssl x509 -text does not. Once you can walk a certificate by hand, half of "SSL is broken" tickets become a five-minute diagnosis instead of a day of guessing.

I wrote this with help from AI tools and checked every command and example myself against current OpenSSL behaviour. I build PixelValut, a set of free browser-based developer and network tools, and this is Part 2 of the series on Web PKI and certificate forensics. Part 1 covered leaked private keys and rotation. Here we slow down and learn to read what a certificate actually asserts.

📚 Series Roadmap — Web PKI & Certificate Forensics in Practice

  • Part 1: Leaked TLS Private Keys: Proving Compromise, Finding Every Affected Cert & Rotating Safely
  • Part 2 (This Post): Reading X.509 Certificates by Hand: SANs, Key Usage, Chains & Intermediates
  • Part 3: Certificate Revocation in 2026: CRLs, the Decline of OCSP & Short-Lived Certificates
  • Part 4: Certificate Transparency Monitoring: Catching Unexpected Certificates for Your Domains
  • Part 5: ACME Automation Failures: Renewal Outages, Rate Limits & DNS-01 Pitfalls
  • Part 6: Mutual TLS for Internal APIs: Private CAs, Rotation & Pinning Trade-offs

Related: Subdomain Takeover & Dangling DNS Reconnaissance

How do you read an X.509 TLS certificate by hand?

Direct answer: Dump the leaf with openssl x509 -text, confirm Subject and Issuer, verify every hostname lives in the Subject Alternative Name extension, check Key Usage and Extended Key Usage for server auth, then walk the chain until you reach a trusted root. Most production failures are a missing intermediate or a hostname that never made it into the SAN list.

Pull the leaf and read it

Fetch what the server actually presents, not what you think is on disk:

openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
  -showcerts /dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -text

Or inspect a PEM file from your load balancer:

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -text

You want the same fields every time. An SSL certificate checker is useful for a quick browser-side view of issuer, SANs and expiry; the OpenSSL dump is what you use when you need exact extension flags.

Subject and Issuer 

Subject: CN = example.com
Issuer: C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R11

Subject is who the certificate claims to be. Issuer is who signed it. For publicly trusted TLS, the Issuer is almost always an intermediate, not the root. If Subject and Issuer are identical, you are looking at a self-signed certificate, which is fine for lab work and wrong for a public site.

SAN vs CN (the hostname trap)

Browsers and modern clients match hostnames against the Subject Alternative Name (SAN) extension, not against the Common Name. A certificate with CN=example.com and no SAN will fail hostname verification in current clients even when the CN "looks right."

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -ext subjectAltName

Expect something like:

X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:example.com, DNS:www.example.com

If api.example.com is missing from that list, clients talking to api.example.com will reject the certificate regardless of how clean the chain looks. Wildcard SANs (DNS:*.example.com) cover one label only; they do not cover a.b.example.com.

Key Usage and Extended Key Usage

These extensions constrain what the key is allowed to do:

openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -ext keyUsage,extendedKeyUsage

For a public HTTPS leaf you typically want:

Extension Expected on HTTPS leaf Red flag
Key Usage Digital Signature, Key Encipherment (RSA) or Digital Signature (ECDSA) Certificate Sign / CRL Sign on a leaf
Extended Key Usage TLS Web Server Authentication Client Auth only, or empty when a client enforces EKU
basicConstraints CA:FALSE CA:TRUE on a leaf (mis-issued or wrong file)

A leaf marked CA:TRUE is either a serious CA mistake or, more often, you opened an intermediate by accident and thought it was the site certificate.

basicConstraints and path length 

openssl x509 -in intermediate.pem -noout -ext basicConstraints

Intermediates should say CA:TRUE. Leaves should say CA:FALSE or omit CA entirely depending on profile. PathLen constraints on intermediates limit how deep a chain may go; you rarely edit these by hand, but you need to recognize them when a private CA chain fails to validate.


AI-generated image.

Building and verifying the chain

TLS clients need a path from the leaf to a trust anchor they already have. Servers must send the leaf and every intermediate. They should not send the root; clients already have roots.

# Show the full chain the server sends
openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -servername example.com \
  -showcerts /dev/null | sed -n '/BEGIN CERTIFICATE/,/END CERTIFICATE/p'

Verify locally once you have leaf + intermediates in one PEM:

openssl verify -CAfile /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt \
  -untrusted intermediates.pem leaf.pem

-untrusted is where intermediates go. If verification fails with "unable to get local issuer certificate," the usual cause is a missing intermediate in what you serve, not a broken root store.

Setup What client receives Typical symptom
Leaf only Site cert, no intermediate Works on some Android/desktop caches, fails elsewhere
Leaf + correct intermediate Complete path to a public root Clean verify
Leaf + wrong intermediate Chain that does not link unable to get local issuer certificate
Leaf + intermediate + root Extra root in handshake Usually tolerated; wastes bytes; some scanners warn
Expired intermediate Path that ends early Sudden multi-region outage after a quiet period

Missing intermediates are still one of the most common production TLS failures, especially after a manual renewal where someone uploaded only cert.pem and forgot fullchain.pem.

Good vs broken setups at a glance

Check Healthy Broken
Hostname Appears in SAN Only in CN, or wrong name
Chain Leaf + intermediates, no required root Leaf alone
EKU Server Auth present Missing where policy requires it
Not After Days or weeks of validity left Expired, or expires tonight with no automation
Signature SHA-256 (or stronger) with expected key type Legacy MD5/SHA-1 on anything public
Key size RSA ≥ 2048 or P-256/P-384 ECDSA RSA 1024

For a related attack surface where DNS and certificates interact, see the earlier note on dangling DNS and certificate reconnaissance. Wrong SANs also show up there when an abandoned hostname still has a live certificate.

Diagnostic checklist

  1. Does openssl s_client show the certificate you expect for this hostname?
  2. Is every served hostname listed in Subject Alternative Name?
  3. Is Issuer an intermediate you recognize, not a mystery private CA on a public site?
  4. Is basicConstraints CA:FALSE (or equivalent) on the leaf?
  5. Do Key Usage / EKU allow server authentication?
  6. Does the server send intermediates (fullchain), not leaf-only?
  7. Does openssl verify succeed with your platform trust store?
  8. Are Not Before / Not After in a sensible window (clock skew included)?
  9. Does the public key type and size match your policy?
  10. Did you compare the live handshake to the files on disk after the last deploy?

Browse more developer TLS and network tools when you need a second view without pasting private keys anywhere.

FAQ

Why does my browser show a padlock when openssl verify fails?

Browsers sometimes cache intermediates, fetch missing ones, or use a different trust store. Command-line verify against the system store is the harsher, more portable check. Trust the stricter result for server configuration.

Is the Common Name still required?

Profiles vary. Many CAs still set CN for compatibility, but hostname matching is SAN-based. Never rely on CN alone.

What is the difference between cert.pem and fullchain.pem?

cert.pem is usually the leaf. fullchain.pem is leaf plus intermediates. Almost every reverse proxy should be pointed at the full chain file.

Can I ignore Extended Key Usage?

Not if your clients enforce it. Mutual TLS and some enterprise proxies are strict. For public HTTPS leaves, Server Auth should be present.

Why did renewal break only mobile clients?

Often a missing intermediate: desktop browsers had it cached; mobile clients did not. Always test with a clean openssl s_client after renewal.

Should I pin intermediates?

Prefer pinning sparingly and prefer monitoring Certificate Transparency (covered in Part 4). Intermediate replacements by public CAs are normal; hard pins without a backup plan cause outages.

Next in this series, Part 3 covers revocation in 2026: CRLs, why OCSP is fading for many clients, and how short-lived certificates change the incident playbook.

event_model_payload.headline: From One VM to a Three-Tier App, With an AI that Wouldn't Let Press Apply
event_model_payload.summary:
Last week I built infrastructure by clicking through consoles and running commands. This week I wrote it down as code, built it again, destroyed it, and built something bigger. Five assignments, two clouds, and one rule that mattered more than any of the code: a human reviews every change before it touches the account.

Here's how the week actually went, including the apply that failed halfway.

Part 1: One file, six resources

The first assignment was the smallest: an Azure Linux VM defined entirely in Terraform. A resource group, virtual network, subnet, public IP, network interface, and the VM, all in a single main.tf.

What struck me was how little I had to describe. The NIC points at the subnet, and the VM points at the NIC. Terraform works out the build order from those references, and terraform plan showed me exactly what would be created before anything existed. That preview is the safety net the portal never gave me.

Two habits started here and stayed all week:

  • The VM password lived in a variable marked sensitive, supplied through the environment, so it never appeared in the file or in a screenshot.
  • Every build ended with terraform destroy. Create, verify, destroy.

Part 2: The same ideas on AWS

The second assignment rebuilt the pattern on AWS: a custom VPC with a public and a private subnet, an internet gateway, a public route table, a security group, and an EC2 instance that installs Nginx at boot.

It also taught me about permissions. My IAM user was read-only from an earlier audit assignment, and Terraform needs to create things. A harmless dry run caught it before I wasted any time:

aws ec2 create-vpc --cidr-block 10.99.0.0/16 --dry-run

UnauthorizedOperation meant missing permission. DryRunOperation ... would have succeeded meant I was good to go. I attached the EC2 policy and moved on.

Part 3: A React app that deploys itself

The third assignment used Azure custom_data (cloud-init) to turn an empty Ubuntu VM into a running React site: install Node and Nginx, clone the repository, build it, and serve the build folder.

Two details nearly tripped me up. A script saved with Windows line endings fails silently at boot, because the first line becomes #!/bin/bash\r. And a small VM can run out of memory during npm run build, so the script creates a swap file first. Neither shows up in a tutorial, and both would have cost me an evening.

Part 4: Modules, and an apply that half-worked

The fourth assignment split an AWS build into reusable modules: network, EC2, and RDS. The root file calls each module and passes outputs between them, so the database gets its subnets and security group from the network module without anything being copied by hand.

My first apply created twelve of thirteen resources and then failed on the database. RDS rejected my master password, because it forbids characters like /, @, ", and spaces. Terraform had recorded everything it had already built, so after fixing the password, the second apply created just the one missing resource. That was my first real lesson in why state matters.

Then I connected from the EC2 instance to the private database, imported the schema, and tested a cart action in the browser to see the matching row appear in RDS.

Part 5: The capstone, with Claude Code in the loop

The capstone was a production-style three-tier deployment of a Book Review app: a VPC across two Availability Zones with six subnets, a public load balancer, a web tier running Nginx and Next.js, an internal load balancer, a private Node.js API tier, and a Multi-AZ RDS MySQL database with a read replica. Sixty-three resources in the first apply.

The assignment's real subject was the workflow. I set up Claude Code with:

  • a CLAUDE.md holding the architecture, CIDR plan, security rules, and approval rules;
  • a Terraform engineer subagent that proposes a design, reads the current provider docs through the Terraform MCP server, and then builds one phase at a time;
  • a read-only reviewer subagent that checks each phase and reports PASS, WARN, or FAIL;
  • hooks that block auto-approved changes and format code after every edit.

Claude could validate and plan. Applying and destroying were reserved for me.

The review loop earned its keep. The reviewer caught a bootstrap script that could fail before Nginx was configured, missing validation on the admin SSH range, and a subtle risk I'd have walked into: with load balancer health checks and a manual deployment, the Auto Scaling group would eventually terminate my unhealthy instances and delete my hand-deployed work. I stretched the grace period and suspended the replacement process while I deployed.

The failure no review could catch

The first capstone apply failed on the read replica:

Creating read replicas for source instance with engine mysql where ManageMasterUserPassword is enabled is not supported.

Every plan, every review, and every doc lookup had passed. Only AWS knew that rule. I gave Claude the real error and we compared options: drop the replica (the assignment required one), or generate the password in Terraform with a write-only argument and store it in Secrets Manager, so it never lands in state or outputs. The plan showed the primary updating in place, and the second apply finished the replica.

It's a clean illustration of what the Terraform MCP server is and isn't. It serves documentation. It can't query my account, so it couldn't predict this.

I also said no to a recommendation. Claude suggested an instance refresh for the change, but nothing was deployed yet, so the refresh would have waited on replacements that couldn't become healthy. I replaced the two App instances myself with one command instead.

Deploying by hand, then proving it

User data only installed software, so I deployed the apps myself: the backend through a systemd service that fetches its database password from Secrets Manager at start, and the frontend built on each web instance. Both target groups went healthy, I registered a user, wrote a review, and then read both rows back from the private database. The credentials came from the instance's IAM role, so no password ever appeared in a terminal.

Then terraform destroy. A NAT gateway, two load balancers, and three database instances bill by the hour, and the most important command of the week was the last one.

What I'm taking away

  • State is the memory. A failed apply isn't a disaster, because Terraform resumes from what it recorded. Guard the state file, and never delete the project folder before you destroy.
  • AI is a fast engineer and a careful reviewer, but it can't see your live account. The best results came from a loop: plan, research, build, validate, review, then a human decides.
  • Keep secrets out of everything. Sensitive variables, write-only arguments, Secrets Manager, and a rule that nothing credential-shaped goes into user data or outputs.
  • Test each layer in order. Every deployment problem this week was solved by checking one hop at a time, not guessing.
  • Treat cost as part of the design. A single NAT gateway and a short-lived environment were deliberate tradeoffs, and I could explain every one of them.

P.S. This post is part of the DevOps Micro Internship (DMI) with Agentic AI, Cohort 3, by Pravin Mishra.
You can follow my graded progress throughout the cohort.
Start your DevOps journey: https://dmi.pravinmishra.com/?utm_source=student&utm_medium=ps-blog&utm_campaign=cohort3

event_model_payload.headline: You Just Got Handed a Mystery Binary. Now What?
event_model_payload.summary:
Someone drops a file in your lap. No source code, no docs, no idea what it does. Maybe it's a CTF challenge. Maybe it's a suspicious attachment. Maybe it's a dependency you don't quite trust.

So you start the usual ritual: strings here, xxd there, objdump for the imports, another tool for the headers, a different one for the hash. Five tools, five outputs, and you're still stitching the story together by hand.

That's the exact friction hexlens was built to kill.

The problem hiding in plain sight

Binaries don't explain themselves. Every question you ask needs a different tool:

  • What kind of file is this? — PE, ELF, Mach-O, DEX, .NET — each with its own parser
  • What does it import? — and does its imphash match known malware?
  • What's inside? — strings, sections, headers, all scattered across outputs

For CTF players, malware triage, and forensics work, that tool-hopping is the slowest part of the job. The analysis isn't hard — getting to it is.

What hexlens does

hexlens is an open-source binary intelligence and reverse engineering framework that puts the answers in one place. Point it at a binary and get the intelligence that matters:

  • Format support across PE, ELF, Mach-O, DEX, and .NET — one tool, whatever you're handed
  • Import analysis and imphash — spot known-bad patterns fast, and compare binaries by behavior instead of bytes
  • Security and forensics focus — built for malware analysis and CTF forensics, not just hex dumps
  • A TUI — browse the binary interactively instead of drowning in terminal scrollback

Instead of five tools and a notebook, you get one view of what the binary is and what it does.

Get started 

npm install hexlens

Then run hexlens against your binary and start with the imports and headers — that's where the story usually is.

Why I built it

Reverse engineering tooling is powerful but fragmented, and most of it assumes you already know what you're looking for. I wanted something that answers the first five questions about an unknown binary immediately, so you can spend your time on the actual analysis instead of the setup.

hexlens is at v0.2.0 now, with 400+ total downloads on npm. It's still early — if you throw a weird binary at it and it chokes, or there's a format you need, I'd genuinely love to hear about it.

Try it, break it, and tell me what it missed. Feedback welcome.

npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/hexlens
GitHub: https://github.com/parasraju/hexlens

Open-source binary intelligence & reverse engineering framework. npm install hexlens

event_model_payload.headline: Invalid Host header after deploying? Why it happens and the fix
event_model_payload.summary:
By Octave · drafted with AI, tested on Hubfly space. Originally published on the Hubfly space blog.

TL;DR

  • What you get: the exact error each framework prints when it rejects your public address, the one-line fix for each, and a 10-second curl check to catch it before you deploy.
  • Who it's for: anyone who just put a Vite, React, Vue, Django or MCP server app online and got a blank 403, 400 or 421 instead of their page.
  • Time needed: 10–15 minutes.

Checked in October 2026 with Vite 8, webpack-dev-server 6, Django 6.1 and the Python MCP SDK 2.x.

Your app worked on localhost. You deployed it, opened the public URL, and got a one-line page: Invalid Host header. Or Blocked request. This host is not allowed. Or a bare Bad Request (400) with nothing in the logs.

Nothing is broken on the server. Your app is refusing visitors on purpose, because it doesn't recognise the address they typed. In this guide you'll make your app accept its real address, and only that address, so your site loads and stays protected. It takes one setting per framework.

Try it on Hubfly space: you get a free HTTPS address for your app on the free tier (360 hours a month, no card).

Why your app rejects its own address

Every browser request carries a Host header: the name the visitor typed, like shop-web.eu1.hubfly.app. On your laptop that name is always localhost or 127.0.0.1. Once you're online, the platform's edge proxy handles HTTPS and passes the public name through to your container unchanged.

Browser ──Host: shop-web.eu1.hubfly.app──▶ HTTPS proxy ──same Host──▶ your container
                                                                  │
                                         "Is this name on my list?" ┘
                                          no → 403 / 400 / 421

Many dev servers and frameworks keep a list of names they'll answer to. By default that list is only localhost. This protects you from DNS rebinding, an attack where a malicious website tricks a browser into talking to a server it shouldn't reach. So the check is good. It just doesn't know your new name yet.

Each tool fails differently, which is why the error is so confusing:

What you run What visitors see Status Where it's logged
Vite dev server (vite) Blocked request. This host ("…") is not allowed. 403 Not in server output
vite preview Same message, pointing at preview.allowedHosts 403 Not in server output
webpack-dev-server (Vue CLI, older React and Angular setups) Invalid Host header 403 Not in server output
Django with DEBUG = False Bad Request (400) 400 Nowhere by default
Python MCP SDK (streamable_http_app()) Invalid Host header 421 WARNING Invalid Host header: …

The same request, four tools, four different answers.

Step 1: Reproduce it on your laptop in 10 seconds

You don't need to deploy to see the error. Start your app locally, then send it the public name with curl:

# Replace the port and the name with yours
curl -i -H "Host: your-app.eu1.hubfly.app" http://127.0.0.1:5173/

If you get a 403, 400 or 421, you've found the problem without waiting for a deploy. Keep this command handy: you'll run it again after each fix.

Why this works: the check only looks at the Host header, not at how the request reached your app. Faking the header locally triggers exactly what your visitors see.

Step 2: Stop running a dev server in production (frontends)

If the error comes from Vite or webpack-dev-server, the real fix is usually not a setting. It's that you deployed the development server. Dev servers rebuild on every change, use more memory, and carry these local-only safety checks.

Build your site once and serve the static files instead. For a Vite app (React, Vue, Svelte, Solid), add a static file server:

npm install sirv-cli

Then set your scripts in package.json:

{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "vite",
    "build": "vite build",
    "start": "sirv dist --host 0.0.0.0 --port ${PORT:-8080} --single"
  }
}

Your platform runs npm run build once, then npm start. A static file server has no host check, so the error disappears. --single sends unknown paths like /orders/42 to index.html, which single-page apps need for client-side routing. --host 0.0.0.0 makes the server reachable from outside the container. (Binding to 127.0.0.1 instead gives you a 502; see our guide to the 502 Bad Gateway fix.)

On Hubfly space, set the container port to the one in your start script (8080 here).

Step 3: When you do need the check, allow your real name

Sometimes you really do want the server running online: a shared preview, a Django app, an MCP server. Then add your public name to the allowlist. List the exact names. Never switch the check off.

Vite (dev and preview) 

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'

const hosts = (process.env.ALLOWED_HOSTS || '').split(',').filter(Boolean)

export default defineConfig({
  server: { host: '0.0.0.0', allowedHosts: hosts },
})

Set ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app in the environment. A leading dot allows a domain and all its subdomains: .your-domain.com covers staging.your-domain.com too. vite preview uses server.allowedHosts unless you set preview.allowedHosts separately, so one list covers both.

Don't use allowedHosts: true. It accepts any name, which turns the protection off.

webpack-dev-server (Vue CLI and custom webpack setups) 

// webpack.config.js
module.exports = {
  // ...
  devServer: {
    host: '0.0.0.0',
    allowedHosts: ['your-app.eu1.hubfly.app', '.your-domain.com'],
  },
};

The same leading-dot rule applies. Old answers suggest disableHostCheck: true or allowedHosts: 'all'. The first was removed in webpack-dev-server 4 (current versions refuse to start with it), and the second turns the check off.

Django: two settings, not one

Django has two checks, and the second only shows up after you fix the first.

1. ALLOWED_HOSTS blocks unknown names with Bad Request (400). With DEBUG = False, Django logs this through its mail_admins handler only. Gunicorn's output stays empty, which is why this one feels like a ghost. Read the list from the environment:

# settings.py
import os

ALLOWED_HOSTS = [h for h in os.environ.get("ALLOWED_HOSTS", "").split(",") if h]
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS = [o for o in os.environ.get("CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS", "").split(",") if o]

2. CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS matters as soon as someone submits a form, including the admin login. The platform's proxy handles HTTPS and talks to your app over plain HTTP inside the network. So the browser says the request came from https://your-app…, Django thinks it's serving http://your-app…, and every POST fails with 403 CSRF verification failed. With DEBUG = True the page shows the real reason: Origin checking failed - https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app does not match any trusted origins.

Set both values in your container's environment:

ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app
CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app

Note the difference: ALLOWED_HOSTS takes bare names, while CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS needs the scheme (https://).

To make the next host error visible in your logs, send Django's host warnings to the console:

LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "disable_existing_loggers": False,
    "handlers": {"console": {"class": "logging.StreamHandler"}},
    "loggers": {
        "django.security.DisallowedHost": {"handlers": ["console"], "level": "ERROR"},
    },
}

Now an unknown name prints Invalid HTTP_HOST header: 'your-app.eu1.hubfly.app'. You may need to add 'your-app.eu1.hubfly.app' to ALLOWED_HOSTS. in your container logs.

Python MCP server: the 421 error

The official Python MCP SDK switches on host checking when the app is built for 127.0.0.1, which is the default for streamable_http_app(). Running it with uvicorn ... host="0.0.0.0" doesn't change that, so your public URL gets 421 Invalid Host header while curl localhost works fine.

Pass your public name explicitly:

import os
import uvicorn
from mcp.server import MCPServer
from mcp.server.transport_security import TransportSecuritySettings

mcp = MCPServer("orders")

@mcp.tool()
def ping() -> str:
    return "pong"

public_host = os.environ["PUBLIC_HOST"]  # e.g. your-mcp.eu1.hubfly.app

app = mcp.streamable_http_app(
    transport_security=TransportSecuritySettings(
        allowed_hosts=[public_host],
        allowed_origins=[f"https://{public_host}"],
    )
)

uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=8000)

Your public name now gets a normal response, and any other name still gets 421. That includes 127.0.0.1: if a local health check calls the server, add 127.0.0.1:8000 to allowed_hosts too. The SDK's own mcp.run(transport="streamable-http", host="0.0.0.0") skips the host check entirely; only use it if the server sits behind an access key. For the full MCP setup with HTTPS and an access key, see Deploy your own MCP server.

Step 4: Put the name in your environment on Hubfly space

Keep the hostname out of your code so the same build works for staging, production and your own domain.

  1. Open your project in the Hubfly space dashboard and create or open your container.
  2. Go to Network → Add Domain → Auto Endpoint. You get an HTTPS address like your-app.eu1.hubfly.app, with TLS and force-HTTPS switched on.
  3. Copy that address. Under Configuration → Environment Variables, add ALLOWED_HOSTS (and for Django, CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS with https:// in front).
  4. Redeploy or restart the container so the app reads the new values.

The Environment Variables tab with both values set.

Adding your own domain later? Add it to the same variables, separated by a comma: ALLOWED_HOSTS=your-app.eu1.hubfly.app,www.your-domain.com. For a custom domain, add the DNS record the dashboard shows; Hubfly space issues the certificate and renews it 30 days before it expires.

Step 5: Check it

Open your public URL in the browser, or run:

curl -i https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app/

Once your name is on the list, you get your page instead of a 403, 400 or 421. Then try a name you didn't allow, against your local copy:

curl -i -H "Host: not-mine.example.com" http://127.0.0.1:8000/

That one should still be refused. If both behave, the fix is done and the protection is still on.

What can go wrong

1. "I fixed ALLOWED_HOSTS, now the admin login says CSRF verification failed."

That's the second Django check. Add CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-app.eu1.hubfly.app, with the scheme. If your proxy sets X-Forwarded-Proto, SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER is the other route, but only use it when the proxy always overwrites that header. Otherwise a client could fake it.

2. "I added the name, but it's still blocked."

Check what you typed against the error text: www.your-domain.com and your-domain.com are different names. In Vite and webpack a leading dot covers subdomains; without the dot it matches one exact name. Also check the app actually restarted: dev servers and Django read these settings at startup.

3. "It works on the platform URL but not my custom domain."

Each name your visitors use must be on the list. Add the custom domain (and www, if you use it) to ALLOWED_HOSTS, and to CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS with https:// for Django.

4. "It works, but my bundle is huge and the page is slow."

You're probably still running the dev server. Go back to Step 2 and serve the built files.

Takeaway

"Invalid Host header" means your app's safety check doesn't know its new name. For frontends, the best fix is to stop shipping the dev server and serve your build. For everything else, put your exact public name in an environment variable and feed it to the framework's allowlist. Never turn the check off. And before your next deploy, run one curl -H "Host: …" locally: it catches the problem in 10 seconds.

Read next: 502 Bad Gateway in Docker? Bind to 0.0.0.0 · Build failed? How to read the build log · Deploy your own MCP server with HTTPS and an access key

Go further on Hubfly space

  • Put it on your own domain: add a custom domain to your container with automatic HTTPS, then add it to ALLOWED_HOSTS. Domains docs
  • Add a database next to it: a managed PostgreSQL database starts at about $2 a month. Managed databases
  • Keep a private staging copy: run a second container with its own Auto Endpoint and its own ALLOWED_HOSTS, and turn on Identity Access (API Key Only) from the project's Firewall. Open the dashboard

Deploy this

event_model_payload.headline: ViKernel: VIDRAFT's Weight-Native OS Embeds an AI-Proof Kill Switch Directly in Model Weights
event_model_payload.summary:
ViKernel: VIDRAFT's Weight-Native OS Embeds an AI-Proof Kill Switch Directly in Model Weights

TL;DR: VIDRAFT has released ViKernel, a security operating system that implements control circuitry — including an AI-proof kill switch — directly inside a model's weights rather than as an external guardrail. The kill switch is asymmetric by design: anyone can halt the model, but restarting it requires a cryptographic signature from an authorized operator. Developers can explore the system's behavior via a public demo on Hugging Face.

What it is

ViKernel is what VIDRAFT calls a Weight-Native OS (웨이트 네이티브 OS): a security layer whose logic is encoded into the model's weights themselves rather than bolted on as a wrapper, prompt filter, or inference-time proxy.

Key properties:

  • Scope: Works with VIDRAFT's own ~27 billion parameter model and has been applied to external model families including Google's Gemma and Alibaba's Qwen.
  • Architecture metaphor: The system implements weight-level analogs of CPU, NPU, and memory circuits — discrete functional units baked into the parameter space.
  • Security surface: Policy enforcement, boot-time integrity checking, audit logging, PII masking, and the kill switch all live inside this weight-embedded control plane.
  • Governance backing: VIDRAFT participates in South Korea's Ministry of Science and ICT cybersecurity-focused AI foundation model program and handles safety evaluation for the national security AI project "K-MISOS" within a NAVER Cloud-led consortium.

How it works

The central design philosophy flips the conventional guardrail model. Most production AI safety systems intercept requests outside the model — system prompts, classifier heads, API-layer filters. ViKernel places enforcement inside the weight structure as a separate control circuit that the language model itself cannot address or override through inference.

Kill switch mechanism:

  • The halt command is intentionally asymmetric: any party can trigger a stop, but resuming operation requires a valid digital signature from a pre-approved operator.
  • While halted, the model refuses all task execution regardless of the content or persuasiveness of incoming requests — analogous to an industrial emergency-stop that bypasses the machine's own control logic.

Policy enforcement circuit:

  • When the model attempts to invoke a tool, a dedicated rule circuit — separate from the language model's reasoning — decides whether that call is permitted.
  • This means a sufficiently clever prompt cannot talk the policy layer into approving a blocked action; the decision path does not route through the LLM's token generation.

Computational substrate:

  • VIDRAFT implemented a vector arithmetic unit inside the weight space. The team reports that after adding this unit, the internal policy-decision stage became approximately 21× faster under identical test conditions.
  • As a proof of capability for weight-native computation, the system correctly multiplied two 300-digit integers to produce a 600-digit result using only the in-weight circuit — no external compute path.

Note: The 21× figure refers specifically to the speed of the security policy-decision stage, not end-to-end inference throughput for the language model.

Benchmarks & results

All figures below come directly from VIDRAFT's public disclosures; no numbers have been extrapolated or inferred.

Metric Reported result
Policy-decision stage speedup (after weight-native vector unit) ~21× vs. baseline
Dangerous tool-call blocks in internal testing 100% blocked
Cases where linguistic persuasion changed a policy decision 0
Weight-native arithmetic demo 300-digit × 300-digit → 600-digit result, reported correct

VIDRAFT notes that the public demo replays recorded outputs rather than running the live in-weight circuit in real time, so independent verification of real-time circuit execution requires a deeper integration than the demo environment provides.

How to try it

VIDRAFT has published a ViKernel demo on Hugging Face that is publicly accessible:

  • The interface is described as resembling a Windows-style desktop environment.
  • From the demo you can observe: kill switch activation and restart (with the signature requirement illustrated), policy verdicts on tool calls, PII masking behavior, and audit log output.
  • Important caveat: The public demo plays back pre-recorded responses generated by the real OS; it is not a live sandbox where you can probe the in-weight circuit directly.

No public GitHub repository, installable package, or API endpoint has been announced as of this writing. Check the Hugging Face organization page for VIDRAFT for the current demo link and any future releases.

FAQ

Q: Why put the OS in the weights rather than at the inference server level?
A: An inference-layer guardrail can be bypassed, misconfigured, or — in agentic/self-improving systems — potentially modified by the AI itself. By encoding control logic into the weights as a circuit that the language model's own forward pass cannot reach, VIDRAFT aims to make the control surface tamper-resistant even against a model that can rewrite external code.

Q: Does applying ViKernel mean I have to retrain my model from scratch?
A: VIDRAFT reports applying the technology to existing external model families (Gemma, Qwen) in addition to their own model, which suggests the approach is not limited to models trained from scratch with ViKernel in mind. The exact adaptation process has not been publicly detailed.

Q: Is the 21× speedup relevant to my inference pipeline?
A: Probably not directly — it measures the latency of the internal policy-decision circuit specifically, not overall token generation throughput. Think of it as an improvement to the overhead of the security layer itself, not a general inference acceleration claim.

event_model_payload.headline: Dennis Ritchie: The Most Influential Programmer of the 21st Century Through Impact on Computing
event_model_payload.summary:
Introduction

When assessing the most influential programmer of the 21st century, the focus must shift from subjective accolades like "greatest" or "smartest" to tangible, measurable impact. Influence, in this context, is defined by the adoption and transformative effects of a programmer's creations on computing ecosystems, industries, and societal challenges. This approach aligns with the system mechanism that measures influence through the widespread integration of tools, frameworks, or methodologies across diverse user communities and sectors.

Programmers in the 21st century have shaped computing through open-source leadership, algorithmic breakthroughs, and the creation of foundational software. However, not all contributions age equally. The environment constraint of the tech industry's rapid evolution demands that influential work remain foundational or adaptable. For instance, a programming language that fails to evolve with hardware advancements risks obsolescence, while an open-source project that neglects community engagement may stagnate despite initial promise.

The stakes are high. Misidentifying or underestimating key contributors risks stagnation in open-source innovation and the fragmentation of computing standards. Conversely, recognizing and building upon their work can accelerate solutions to critical challenges like scalability, security, and collaboration. This is particularly evident in the system mechanism of open-source contributions, which democratize access to technology and foster collaborative problem-solving.

To illustrate, consider the Linux kernel and Git. These tools, created by Linus Torvalds, have become de facto standards in software development and infrastructure. Their impact is not just technical but cultural, reshaping how developers collaborate and innovate. This aligns with the analytical angle of examining ecosystem impact, where the influence extends beyond code to workflows, industries, and user behaviors.

In this article, we will dissect the influence of key programmers through the lens of adoption, adaptability, and problem-solving impact. By doing so, we aim to identify not just a name, but a blueprint for enduring influence in the ever-evolving landscape of computing.

Candidate Profiles and Impact Analysis

Identifying the most influential programmer of the 21st century requires a rigorous analysis of tangible impact, not just technical brilliance. Below are profiles of the top 5 candidates, evaluated through the lens of adoption, adaptability, and problem-solving influence.

1. Linus Torvalds

Key Contributions: Linux kernel, Git version control system.

Impact Mechanism: The Linux kernel, created by Torvalds, powers over 90% of cloud infrastructure and the majority of smartphones (via Android). Git has become the de facto standard for version control, enabling decentralized collaboration in software development. This dual impact has reshaped workflows, reduced costs, and accelerated innovation across industries.

Adaptability: Linux’s open-source model allows it to evolve with hardware advancements (e.g., ARM support) and emerging use cases (e.g., IoT). Git’s simplicity and scalability ensure its relevance in both small projects and large enterprises.

Risk Mechanism: Without Torvalds’ leadership, Linux could fragment into incompatible forks, and Git might lack critical updates, stifling collaboration.

2. James Gosling

Key Contributions: Java programming language, JVM.

Impact Mechanism: Java’s "write once, run anywhere" philosophy enabled cross-platform development, powering billions of devices from smartphones to enterprise servers. The JVM’s bytecode abstraction decouples software from hardware, ensuring longevity despite rapid tech evolution.

Ecosystem Impact: Java’s dominance in enterprise software has shaped industries like finance and logistics. However, its verbosity and resource overhead limit adoption in lightweight systems (e.g., IoT), highlighting a trade-off between portability and efficiency.

Failure Mechanism: Overemphasis on backward compatibility risks obsolescence as newer languages (e.g., Rust) address modern needs like memory safety.

3. Guido van Rossum

Key Contributions: Python programming language.

Impact Mechanism: Python’s simplicity and readability have made it the primary language for data science, AI, and automation. Its extensive libraries (e.g., TensorFlow, Pandas) lower barriers to entry, democratizing access to advanced computing.

Educational Influence: Python’s adoption in 80% of university CS programs ensures its influence on future programmers. However, its dynamic typing can lead to runtime errors, a trade-off for ease of use.

Rule for Adoption: If prioritizing rapid prototyping and interdisciplinary use (e.g., science, finance), use Python. For performance-critical systems, consider alternatives like C++.

4. Brendan Eich

Key Contributions: JavaScript, WebAssembly.

Impact Mechanism: JavaScript’s ubiquity in web development has enabled interactive, dynamic web applications, transforming user experiences. WebAssembly, co-developed by Eich, addresses JavaScript’s performance limitations by allowing low-level code execution in browsers.

Risk Mechanism: JavaScript’s rapid evolution (e.g., ES6+) can fragment developer knowledge, while WebAssembly’s complexity may limit adoption in smaller teams.

Optimal Solution: For web applications requiring both interactivity and performance, combine JavaScript with WebAssembly. Avoid over-reliance on JavaScript for compute-intensive tasks.

5. Donald Knuth

Key Contributions: TeX typesetting system, The Art of Computer Programming.

Impact Mechanism: TeX revolutionized academic publishing by enabling precise mathematical typesetting, becoming the standard for scientific documents. Knuth’s books shaped algorithmic thinking, influencing generations of programmers.

Edge Case: While TeX remains foundational in academia, its complexity limits broader adoption. Knuth’s focus on theoretical rigor may overlook practical implementation challenges.

Professional Judgment: TeX is indispensable for technical publishing but less relevant for general-purpose design. Knuth’s educational influence is unparalleled but requires supplementation with modern tools.

Conclusion

Linus Torvalds emerges as the most influential programmer due to the ubiquity and adaptability of Linux and Git, which address critical scalability and collaboration challenges. His work exemplifies the power of open-source leadership, creating ecosystems that evolve with technological demands. Failing to build on his contributions risks stagnation in global computing standards.

Comparative Impact Assessment

When assessing the influence of programmers on 21st-century computing, the focus must shift from individual brilliance to the tangible, widespread impact of their creations. This section compares key figures based on adoption rates, industry standards set, and long-term technological advancements, highlighting the programmer whose contributions have had the most enduring and transformative effect.

Adoption and Ecosystem Impact

The influence of a programmer is measured by the adoption and integration of their work into computing ecosystems. Linus Torvalds stands out with the Linux kernel, which powers over 90% of cloud infrastructure and most smartphones via Android. This ubiquity is not just a numbers game; it reflects Linux’s ability to adapt to diverse hardware—from ARM processors in IoT devices to x86 servers in data centers. The open-source model of Linux fosters community-driven innovation, ensuring it evolves with technological demands. In contrast, James Gosling’s Java, while dominant in enterprise software, faces limitations in lightweight systems due to its resource overhead, illustrating how technical elegance without adaptability can restrict influence.

Longevity and Adaptability

The tech industry’s rapid evolution demands that influential work remain foundational or adaptable. Torvalds’ Git exemplifies this, becoming the de facto standard for version control by enabling decentralized collaboration. Its simplicity and scalability allow it to serve both small projects and large enterprises. Conversely, Guido van Rossum’s Python, while dominating data science and education, relies on dynamic typing, which introduces runtime error risks in performance-critical systems. This trade-off highlights the limitations of prioritizing ease over robustness, a typical failure in sustaining long-term influence.

Problem-Solving Impact

The ability to address critical technological or societal problems elevates a programmer’s influence. Torvalds’ work has solved scalability and collaboration challenges in software development, enabling global teams to work seamlessly. For instance, Git’s distributed architecture allows developers to merge changes asynchronously, reducing conflicts and accelerating project timelines. In contrast, Brendan Eich’s JavaScript, while revolutionizing web interactivity, struggles with performance limitations that WebAssembly only partially addresses. This fragmentation of solutions underscores the risk of over-specialization, where tools fail to address broader needs.

Educational and Cultural Influence

Educational impact shapes the foundational knowledge of future programmers. Python’s adoption in 80% of university CS programs ensures its influence on algorithmic thinking and interdisciplinary applications. However, its ease of use can lead to over-reliance, neglecting deeper understanding of low-level systems. Torvalds’ influence, meanwhile, extends beyond code to cultural practices, such as open-source collaboration and decentralized decision-making, which have become industry norms. This cultural impact is harder to quantify but equally critical in sustaining influence.

Conclusion: The Most Influential Programmer

Based on the analytical framework, Linus Torvalds emerges as the most influential programmer of the 21st century. His contributions—the Linux kernel and Git—have achieved unmatched adoption, set industry standards, and addressed critical scalability and collaboration challenges. Their open-source nature ensures adaptability and community-driven evolution, mitigating risks of stagnation. Failing to build on Torvalds’ work would risk fragmentation of computing standards and hinder global collaboration.

Rule for Enduring Influence

If a programmer’s work achieves widespread adoption, sets industry standards, and solves critical problems through adaptable, open-source solutions, it will have the most enduring influence on computing.

Conclusion and Future Implications

The evidence unequivocally points to Linus Torvalds as the most influential programmer of the 21st century. His creation of the Linux kernel and Git version control system has fundamentally reshaped computing ecosystems, addressing critical challenges in scalability, collaboration, and infrastructure standardization. Linux’s dominance in cloud computing (over 90% market share) and mobile devices (via Android) demonstrates its role as a de facto standard, while Git’s decentralized model has revolutionized software development workflows.

Future Developments Stemming from Torvalds’ Contributions

Torvalds’ work will continue to drive innovation through:

  • Edge Computing and IoT: Linux’s adaptability to low-power hardware (e.g., ARM) positions it as the backbone for edge devices, enabling real-time data processing in IoT ecosystems. This hinges on its ability to evolve with hardware advancements, a mechanism ensured by its open-source model.
  • AI and Machine Learning Infrastructure: Linux’s scalability and Git’s collaborative framework will underpin AI development pipelines, facilitating distributed training and model versioning. However, this requires sustained community engagement to integrate emerging AI-specific optimizations.
  • Decentralized Collaboration Models: Git’s architecture will likely inspire new paradigms in asynchronous teamwork, reducing merge conflicts and accelerating development cycles. Its simplicity ensures adoption across team sizes, though over-reliance on its current feature set risks stagnation without updates addressing evolving needs.

Broader Implications for the Tech Industry

Ignoring Torvalds’ foundational contributions carries tangible risks:

  • Fragmentation of Computing Standards: Without Linux’s unifying role, the industry risks proliferation of incompatible systems, increasing costs and hindering interoperability. This occurs when competing proprietary solutions fail to achieve critical mass.
  • Stifled Open-Source Innovation: Git’s absence would revert collaboration to centralized models, slowing innovation by reintroducing bottlenecks in code integration and review processes.
  • Educational and Cultural Regression: Torvalds’ emphasis on open collaboration and meritocracy has shaped developer culture. Abandoning these principles risks a return to siloed, less inclusive development practices.

Optimal Path Forward: Building on Torvalds’ Legacy

To maximize the enduring impact of Torvalds’ work, the industry must:

  1. Prioritize Open-Source Sustainability: Active community participation and funding are critical to prevent project stagnation. For example, Linux’s evolution depends on contributions from hardware vendors to support new architectures.
  2. Integrate with Emerging Technologies: Linux and Git must adapt to quantum computing and AI-driven development. Failure to do so risks obsolescence, as seen with Java’s limited adoption in lightweight systems due to resource overhead.
  3. Educate on Foundational Principles: Curriculum integration of Linux and Git ensures future developers understand decentralized collaboration. Overemphasis on high-level tools (e.g., Python) without low-level systems knowledge creates a skills gap.

Rule for Enduring Influence: If a technology achieves widespread adoption, sets industry standards, and solves critical problems through an adaptable, open-source model, it will dominate its domain. Torvalds’ work exemplifies this, and deviating from this blueprint risks technological stagnation.

event_model_payload.headline: How Zapier turns ideas into working software in hours with Vercel
event_model_payload.summary:
Zapier on Vercel

  • Interactive partner demos in under two hours with v0, replacing a process that could take weeks

  • First versions of three internal applications, each built in one day

  • A shared daily briefing for more than 60 marketers, replacing individual efforts to assemble the same information

  • 3.3 million sandboxes created in one month, isolating the code execution behind Zapier’s AI workloads

Before the industry had a word for agents, Zapier was building them. Today Zapier is the AI orchestration platform connecting AI to the workflows, data, and systems businesses use every day.

Zapier has been a Vercel customer since they began using Vercel for web experiences several years ago. They stayed, and expanded, because every team that needed to ship quickly found the same answer: speed, with the security guardrails already in place. As they grew, so did their adoption of Vercel as more teams found new uses for the platform. Today, Vercel supports work across engineering, partnerships, and marketing, from customer-facing AI to interactive partner demos and internal applications.

The needs vary by team, but the priority is getting useful work into people’s hands quickly. A backend engineer can create an interactive demo of an integration inside a partner’s product. In marketing, a former product marketer with no prior deployment experience can share tools containing sensitive information through a company-approved environment and keep improving them as colleagues use them.

Zapier’s teams are moving faster and doing more than they could before. When the next launch comes around, building on Vercel is a given.

From weeks of prototype work to a demo in under two hours

Every partnership Zapier signs extends what its customers can automate. The Powered by Zapier team is how those partnerships become product, helping SaaS and AI companies embed Zapier’s automation capabilities directly into their own tools, so users can automate without ever leaving the partner’s app. The stakes are high, because Zapier relies on this team to make its platform the entry point to all the software in the world. The problem was speed: collaborating outside the organization took forever, with every prototype requiring screenshots, design time, and frontend resources, and weeks could pass before a partner saw anything clickable.

With v0, the team can create a fully interactive, multi-view prototype in under two hours, showing an embedded Zapier experience inside the partner’s own product.

Chu’s background is in backend development, not frontend engineering or design, but v0 lets her build these experiences without coordinating a separate design and frontend effort for every partner conversation. Partners can click through the flow and share it with colleagues, using the prototype as a blueprint for implementation alongside the API documentation.

Sharing sensitive internal data securely

In marketing, Joe Stych set out to make the team’s scattered knowledge easier to use. He had spent years in product marketing before becoming a agentic go-to-market engineer, but had never worked out of a Git repository or deployed an application.

At an internal hackathon, he built Marketing Hive, a shared source for positioning, messaging, personas, and competitive intelligence. Sharing his local prototype meant making sensitive information accessible to colleagues without exposing it to everyone else.

“The Hive holds our positioning, personas, and competitive intel, so I couldn't just send people a link. On Vercel it was behind our SSO from the first deploy, so I could share it without exposing it” says Joe Stych, Senior Lead, Agentic GTM at Zapier.

Zapier’s data and security teams had already endorsed Vercel. Stych deployed through the company’s approved internal tooling environment, with access gated behind Zapier’s single sign-on.

He develops in Cursor and keeps code and source material in GitLab, where changes trigger Vercel builds and deployments. If an update needs to be undone, he can roll back the deployment.

The first versions of three of his internal applications took about a day each. In roughly two months, a hackathon project had grown into production software used across marketing. It was built by someone who had never deployed anything before.

Internal apps for marketing and sales

Marketing Hive holds the knowledge. Marketing OS puts it to work. It gives more than 60 marketers a daily briefing in Slack and a dashboard with what changed across marketing, one update from each team, a win worth celebrating, and progress against goals. Each marketer can start from the briefing instead of assembling the same information from separate channels.

“The first five minutes of your day, you need to look at the Marketing OS update,” says Dan Slagen, Zapier’s CMO.

Readers mark what they found useful, helping Stych prioritize improvements. The briefings also spark discussions in a marketing channel open to everyone at the company.

Stych is building a sales coaching application that brings together account context and industry messaging before a call. Afterward, it reviews the Gong recording to highlight what worked and suggest changes to the talk track.

For the internal applications, he checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights. Decisions about positioning remain with people, and he says additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Model access and isolated code execution

Beyond Marketing OS, a separate team at Zapier uses AI Gateway to send requests to AI models on behalf of customers using Zapier products.

A common endpoint lets an application change or add models without maintaining a separate integration for each provider. Failover gives requests another route when a provider cannot serve them, while unified reporting lets a team see their usage across providers in once place.

What's next

Zapier’s relationship with Vercel began with web experiences and expanded as the company grew, with more teams finding uses for the platform as their needs changed. Today its role spans the software Zapier runs for customers and the tools its people build for one another, and every thread is still widening.

The clearest picture of where it leads is in marketing, where other teams are starting to borrow the pattern. The goal is more versions across the company, and perhaps a Revenue OS for Zapier’s customer-facing teams next, each built the way the first one was, by someone close to the problem. First comes trust. Stych still checks reported numbers and the evidence behind claimed insights, and additional safeguards will come before agents publish without human review.

Across all of it, Vercel helps Zapier put useful work into people’s hands and keep adapting it to the needs of the business.

event_model_payload.headline: How Mercor ships internal apps and billions of production tokens on one platform
event_model_payload.summary:
Mercor on Vercel

  • Batch jobs cut from 12 hours to 2 hours

  • 18M requests and 63B tokens routed through AI Gateway in 10 days

  • Expert access provisioned in seconds via Vercel Passport

  • Over 2,000 projects created by hundreds of internal builders

Mercor connects hundreds of thousands of domain experts with frontier AI labs, helping those labs generate the human data they need to train and evaluate leading models. It also runs large batches of automated grading jobs to evaluate models for labs and enterprises.

Demand arrives in bursts that can push model traffic to peak capacity for days, even as individual evaluation or labeling jobs carry 24-hour deadlines. With so little time to deliver, requests waiting on a provider’s rate limits can put a client’s deadline at risk.

Mercor’s business teams also need applications tailored to each engagement, giving experts a way to see their tasks and progress without waiting for changes to the core platform.

For Aaron Brown, Mercor’s Head of Security, enabling more people to build means making it easier to give them the access they need and keep track of how they use it. Mercor uses Vercel AI Gateway to manage model access and Vercel Passport to handle secure access to their applications.

When model capacity becomes a customer deadline

Mercor’s mix of direct integrations and third-party gateways could not provide enough token-per-minute capacity for its open-model workloads when demand surged. As requests hit provider limits and entered retry queues, time-sensitive batch jobs stretched beyond 12 hours, consuming more than half of a client’s 24-hour deadline.

AI Gateway provided more inference capacity and failover routing between providers when requests hit rate limits, helping batch work continue instead of waiting in retry queues. Mercor reports that those jobs now finish in 2 to 3 hours, leaving more time to complete the rest of the client’s work. In its first 10 days on Gateway, the team routed 18 million requests and 63 billion tokens, without hitting rate limits.

Mercor continues to use multiple gateways and vendors, valuing Vercel for its combination of model access, controls, and hands-on support when the team needs more capacity. Engineers also get one API for leading foundation model providers and a growing catalog of open models, so they can try a new model without building another provider integration.

Giving engineers room to experiment within limits

As model use grew, Mercor needed to understand where token spend was going, but its previous setup offered little visibility into usage by team and project. A single loop error in a script could exhaust the available budget.

Hundreds of Mercor engineers now use open models through AI Gateway with per-user keys that carry expiration dates, token limits, and spend limits. Security can give experimentation a budget and an end date, then use the usage records to see which user, project, and workload is driving consumption. Engineers can try different models through the same gateway under those controls, without managing another set of provider credentials each time.

Managing access as business teams build

A few hundred people across Mercor’s business teams now build applications on Vercel, where the company’s project count has grown from fewer than a dozen to roughly 2,000. Many of those projects are temporary environments for a specific client engagement.

One production use case gives experts detailed views of their project tasks and progress. Rather than ask engineering to add every engagement’s interface to the core platform, business teams build the interfaces themselves and share them with the experts doing the work.

To share those applications, teams need to control who can sign in without taking on a separate authentication setup for every project. Passport provides that common authentication layer, handling sign-in to Vercel deployments through an existing identity provider.

Mercor’s identity team built a product called Audiences, integrating Vercel Passport as a first class primitive, to automate access provisioning. Once a team selects the experts who need access, Audiences creates the IdP group, Vercel connection, and Passport configuration. With that workflow, Mercor reports provisioning access in seconds for audiences ranging from dozens of experts to tens of thousands. Offboarding works the same way in reverse. Because access is derived from the IdP group, removing the group at the end of an engagement removes access to the project, so no stale access is left behind.

Limiting what each agent can do

Alongside those applications, Mercor uses agents to answer questions from experts in its marketplace, automate HR workflows, and help employees navigate internal systems. Mercor’s approach is to give each agent narrow permissions suited to its job, rather than everything available to the person who invoked it.

For agents that use open models through AI Gateway, Mercor can also scope model access, set expiration dates, and cap spending. That governs their model use while Mercor separately determines which systems and actions each agent can access.

What’s next

Mercor expects more open models to power its internal agents and systems, and more teams outside engineering to build tools for experts. As that work grows, the company wants teams to spend less time setting up model integrations and application authentication so they can respond to client workloads with tight deadlines.

The aim is to make the secure path the fastest path, with shared model access and repeatable authentication workflows helping experts get the tools they need and labs get their work back on time. Mercor wants to support that growth without security work increasing at the same rate.

About Mercor: Mercor is an AI data company that organizes human intelligence for AI training and evaluation. Its network of more than 5M experts, from doctors to lawyers to engineers, powers benchmarks, enterprise evals, RL environments, post-training and agent deployments.

event_model_payload.headline: 예측을 넘어 결정과 발견으로: DeciML과 NeXA를 만든 이유
event_model_payload.summary:
안녕하세요. 무신사에서 ML Engineer로서 추천, CRM, 유저 속성, ML 플랫폼 등을 담당하고 있는 Core-E Personalization 팀의 김윤태입니다.

저희 팀에서는 개인화와 관련된 여러 문제를 풀고 그 문제를 서비스에 전달하기 위한 플랫폼을 만들어 가면서 개인화가 앞으로 어떤 방향으로 확장될 수 있을지 고민해 왔습니다.

개인화의 범위가 넓어질수록 ML로 풀어야 하는 문제도 달라집니다. 커머스의 검색과 추천, 광고, 앱 푸시, 쿠폰, 배너 등 다양한 채널이 각각 다른 목적에서 출발했고, 무신사와 29CM에서도 그랬습니다. 하지만 이들은 개인화가 확장될수록 점점 하나의 질문으로 수렴합니다.

이 고객에게 지금 무엇을 보여줄 것인가?

고객이 반응할 확률을 구하는 예측(prediction) 문제만 풀어서는 이 질문에 답할 수 없습니다. 반응할 확률이 높다고 해서 고객에게 모든 것을 무한정 보여줄 수는 없기 때문입니다. 하루에 보낼 수 있는 푸시의 수, 이번 달에 사용할 수 있는 쿠폰 예산, 한 화면에 담을 수 있는 상품의 수처럼 쓸 수 있는 자원에는 늘 한계가 있습니다. 반응 확률을 예측한 뒤에도, 그 한계 안에서 누구에게 무엇을 보여줄지는 따로 결정해야 합니다.

이런 문제를 풀기 위해 저희는 DeciML과 NeXA라는 두 개의 ML 플랫폼을 새로 만들었습니다. 두 플랫폼은 문제에 맞는 ML 모델을 학습하고 그 결과를 서비스까지 전달합니다. DeciML은 결정(decision) 문제를, NeXA는 발견(discovery) 문제를 다룹니다.

이 글은 두 플랫폼을 소개하는 시리즈의 첫 편입니다. 이번 편에서는 저희가 마주한 문제와 새로운 플랫폼이 필요했던 이유, 그리고 두 플랫폼이 맡을 역할과 설계 방향을 이야기합니다. 후속 편에서는 두 플랫폼의 구조와 적용 범위, 플랫폼 위에서 문제를 풀어 나간 사례를 차례로 다룹니다.

The Problems Ahead

점수 예측만으로는 답할 수 없는 지점들

지금까지 많은 개인화 문제는 비교적 익숙한 형태로 풀 수 있었습니다. 고객과 상품, 혹은 고객과 콘텐츠의 조합마다 “이 고객이 반응할 확률은 얼마인가”를 예측하고 그 값을 기준으로 가장 점수가 높은 선택지를 고르는 방식입니다. 클릭률(CTR)이나 구매 전환율(CVR)처럼 하나의 점수를 잘 예측하는 것이 문제 해결의 핵심이었습니다.

하지만 서비스와 지면의 복잡도가 높아지고 개인화의 범위가 넓어질수록, 단순히 높은 점수를 고르는 것만으로 풀어낼 수 없는 문제가 발생합니다. 무엇을 보여줄지에 더해 제한된 자원을 누구에게 배분할지도 결정해야 하고 고객의 행동이 실제로 서비스의 개입 때문에 바뀌었는지도 알아야 합니다. 여러 지면의 결정을 함께 고려해야 하는 경우도 있고 새로운 발견 지면이 생길 때마다 그곳에 ML을 빠르게 적용해야 하기도 합니다.

이런 한계는 이미 서비스 곳곳에서 나타나기 시작했고 개인화가 진행될수록 더 다양한 형태로 늘어날 것입니다. 그중 지금 저희가 중요하게 보고 있는 네 가지 유형은 다음과 같습니다.

Constrained Allocation. 오늘 보낼 수 있는 푸시가 한 통뿐이라면 누구에게 보내야 할까요? 하루에 보낼 수 있는 푸시 슬롯은 정해져 있고 쿠폰 예산에는 한도가 있습니다. 이때는 정해진 슬롯과 예산을 누구에게 배분할지 답해야 합니다. 점수는 배분의 입력이 될 수 있지만 배분 자체는 제약을 함께 고려해야 풀 수 있습니다. 누구에게 보낼지뿐 아니라 누구에게 보내지 않을지도 결정할 수 있어야 합니다.

Incrementality. 앱 푸시의 클릭률을 높였는데 왜 앱 진입이나 구매 같은 비즈니스 지표는 그대로일까요? 원래 앱에 들어올 가능성이 높은 고객에게 푸시를 보냈다면, 클릭이라는 반응은 만들 수 있어도 푸시가 없었을 때와 비교해 실제 행동이 얼마나 달라졌는지는 알 수 없기 때문입니다. 중요한 것은 반응할 확률이 아니라, 개입이 실제로 만들어낸 변화가 얼마나 되는가입니다. 이를 알기 위해서는 개입이 있었을 때와 없었을 때의 차이를 추정해야 합니다.

Cross-surface Coordination. 아침 푸시로 보여 준 상품을 낮에 홈에서 또 맨 위에 올려야 할까요? 한 고객은 하루 동안 여러 지면을 오갑니다. 푸시를 받고 앱에 들어와 추천을 보고, 검색을 하고, 배너를 마주할 수도 있습니다. 그런데 각 지면을 서로의 결정을 모른 채 따로 최적화하면, 고객의 전체 경험과 비즈니스 목표보다 각 지면의 개별 성과만 높이는 방향으로 움직입니다. 여러 지면의 개인화를 함께 다루려면 고객을 서비스 전체의 관점에서 이해하고 그 위에서 결정을 조율할 수 있어야 합니다.

Discovery Structure. 다음 달 새 큐레이션 지면이 생기면 서빙을 처음부터 다시 만들어야 할까요? 개인화를 적용해야 하는 서비스의 형태는 하나로 고정되어 있지 않습니다. 상품을 나열하는 피드나 여러 주제와 콘텐츠를 조합하는 큐레이션이 있을 수 있습니다. 카테고리와 검색 결과처럼 서로 다른 구조를 가진 지면도 있고 앞으로 새로운 형태의 지면이 계속 만들어질 것입니다. 새로운 구조가 생길 때마다 그에 맞는 ML 서빙과 연결 방식을 처음부터 다시 만들어야 한다면, 개인화는 서비스의 변화 속도를 따라가지 못합니다. 어떤 구조가 등장하더라도 그 안에 ML의 결과를 빠르게 전달할 수 있어야 합니다.

Understanding, Valuation and Selection

이해하고, 가치를 평가한 뒤, 선택합니다

앞에서 살펴본 문제들은 형태가 서로 다르지만, 해결을 위한 접근 순서는 비슷합니다. 먼저 고객과 상품을 이해해야 하고 가능한 선택지의 가치를 평가해야 합니다. 마지막으로 제약을 고려해 실제로 무엇을 할지 선택해야 합니다. 저희는 이 공통된 흐름을 세 단계로 정리했습니다.

  • 이해 단계 (Understanding) — 고객과 상품 등 서비스를 구성하는 대상을 ML이 사용할 수 있는 표현(representation)과 피처(feature)로 바꾸는 과정입니다. 특정 지면에서 어떻게 사용할지를 먼저 정하기보다, 고객과 상품 자체를 얼마나 잘 이해할 수 있는지에 초점을 둡니다.
  • 평가 단계 (Valuation) — 이해 단계의 산출물을 바탕으로 각 선택지가 얼마나 가치 있는지를 평가합니다. 특정 개입이 만들어낼 변화, 고객과 후보 사이의 관련성(relevance), 노출했을 때 기대할 수 있는 가치 추정처럼 문제마다 다른 기준을 비교 가능한 값으로 만듭니다.
  • 선택 단계 (Selection) — 평가 단계에서 추정한 비교 가능한 값을 바탕으로 실제 선택을 내리는 단계입니다. 비즈니스 제약을 고려해 슬롯을 누구에게 사용할지, 화면에는 무엇을 어떤 순서로 보여줄지를 정합니다.

앞 단계의 결과는 다음 단계의 기반이 됩니다. 고객과 상품을 이해하지 못하면 가치를 제대로 평가하기 어렵고, 평가가 없으면 무엇을 선택할 근거도 없습니다.

이 세 단계는 어떤 문제를 풀든 달라지지 않습니다. 달라지는 것은 각 단계에서 다루는 기준과 마지막 산출물입니다. 푸시 문제라면 어느 고객에게 어떤 자원을 쓸지 정한 결과가, 추천 문제라면 한 화면에 함께 보여 줄 후보를 지면 구조에 맞게 정렬하고 묶은 슬레이트(slate)가 나옵니다.

이렇게 나온 산출물도 실제 서비스에 전달되지 않으면 의미가 없습니다. API 응답이든 배치 테이블이든 결과가 실제 노출이나 발송까지 이어져야 합니다.

각 단계의 산출물은 한 문제를 풀고 사라지는 중간 결과가 아닙니다. 이를 저장하고 축적해 다음 문제를 풀 때 다시 씁니다. 각 서비스 안에서 광고를 위해 학습한 고객 표현은 푸시의 평가에, 추천을 위해 학습한 상품 임베딩은 검색의 순위 계산에도 활용될 수 있습니다. 새 지면이 생겨도 이미 쌓아 둔 이해 단계의 산출물을 바탕으로 그 지면에 맞는 평가와 선택 단계를 확장해 나가면 됩니다.

돌아보면 저희는 이해하고 평가하고 선택하는 이 흐름을 이미 수도 없이 반복해 왔습니다. 다만 그 결과는 프로젝트마다 따로 남아 다음 문제로 이어지지 못했습니다. 달라진 것은 그 반복을 패턴으로 인식하고 한 번 풀 때마다 다음 문제가 더 쉬워지도록 축적하는 형태로 만들었다는 점입니다. 그것이 DeciML과 NeXA입니다.

Two Platforms, One Mental Model

같은 구조 위에서 다른 문제를 풉니다

두 플랫폼은 동일한 템플릿과 실행 환경 구조 위에서 작동합니다. 동일한 배포 경로와 서빙 규약, 관측 기준을 공유하면서 각자가 푸는 문제에 적합한 지식을 쌓아갑니다. 두 영역을 나눈 기준과 각 플랫폼의 역할을 이름과 함께 설명하겠습니다.

Decision and Discovery

Technology First에서 Problem First로

두 플랫폼은 기술보다 문제를 중심으로 나뉘어 있습니다. 랭커(ranker), 밴딧(bandit), 업리프트(uplift) 모델은 어느 쪽에서도 쓰이기 때문에 기술만 놓고 보면 두 영역은 상당 부분 겹치고 다른 곳에서 쓰는 기술과도 크게 다르지 않습니다. 저희가 다르게 정한 것은 기술이 아니라 경계입니다. 그 경계는 서비스가 어떤 질문에 답하려 하는가에 있고 그 질문은 유한한 자원이 누구의 것인가에 따라 갈립니다.

Decision은 공급자의 관점에서 서비스가 가진 유한한 자원을 어떻게 사용할 것인가를 다룹니다. 여기서 유한한 자원이라고 하면, 푸시 한 건, 쿠폰 예산, 유료 노출 한 자리처럼 서비스가 비즈니스를 위해 선제적으로 활용하는 자원을 의미합니다. 그래서 주어진 비즈니스 제약 안에서 목표를 달성하도록 자원을 배분해야 합니다. 질문은 “이 자원을 누구에게, 언제 쓸 것인가”이고, 좋은 답의 기준은 자원을 쓰지 않았을 때와 비교해 실제로 만들어 낸 변화입니다.

Discovery는 소비자의 관점에서 고객이 가진 시간과 주의라는 유한한 자원을 어떻게 효과적으로 쓰게 할 것인가를 다룹니다. 검색어를 넣든 피드를 넘기든 고객이 먼저 움직이고, 서비스는 그 탐색 여정 속에서 고객이 원하는 상품을 노출해야 합니다. 한 화면에 담을 수 있는 상품의 수도, 고객이 탐색에 들일 수 있는 시간과 노력도 한정되어 있습니다. 그래서 풀어야 하는 문제는 그 시간 안에 원하는 것을 찾게 하는 발견 문제가 됩니다. 질문은 “지금 이 고객에게 무엇을 어떤 순서로 보여줄 것인가”이고, 좋은 답의 기준은 고객이 그 세션 안에서 마음에 드는 것을 찾았는가입니다.

같은 기술이더라도 목적에 따라 다른 쪽에 놓이기도 합니다. 밴딧 모델을 사용해서 푸시 메시지 후보 중 무엇을 보낼지 정하면 발송 건수라는 서비스의 자원을 쓰는 일이므로 결정 문제를 풀게 됩니다. 같은 밴딧 알고리즘을 활용하여 홈 피드에 노출할 상품 추천을 제공한다면 고객의 탐색 여정을 돕는 발견 문제에 해당합니다. 서비스에서 직면한 문제가 다르면 보상(reward)의 정의도, 학습에 쓰는 신호도, 결과를 내보내는 형태도 달라집니다. 그래서 같은 기술에서 출발해도 결국 다른 모델이 만들어집니다.

어느 쪽 문제인지는 바라보는 관점에 따라 달라질 수 있어서 경계가 늘 명확하지는 않습니다. 그래도 문제를 기준으로 나누는 이유는 플랫폼이 쌓아 가는 평가 기준과 데이터, 서비스로 결과를 전달하는 방식이 기술보다 질문을 따라 갈리기 때문입니다. 같은 질문을 푸는 문제끼리 묶어야 이것들을 함께 쓸 수 있고, 기술을 바꾸더라도 쌓아 둔 것이 그대로 남습니다.

유한한 자원의 쓰임을 결정하는 DeciML

DeciML은 Decision과 Machine Learning을 합친 이름입니다. Decision은 이 플랫폼이 다루는 문제를, Machine Learning은 이를 해결하는 주요 수단을 의미합니다. 소리 내어 읽으면 ‘decimal’이 되는데, 고객과 비즈니스를 측정 가능한 값으로 표현하고 그 위에서 판단한다는 의미도 함께 담았습니다.

이 플랫폼은 광고, 푸시, 쿠폰, 배너처럼 서비스가 고객에게 먼저 개입하는 영역의 개인화를 주로 다룹니다. 앞에서 살펴본 문제 중에서는 제한된 자원을 어떻게 배분할지, 개입이 실제로 만들어낸 증분 효과를 어떻게 추정할지, 여러 지면의 결정을 어떻게 조율할지가 여기에 해당합니다.

이 문제들의 핵심은 제한된 자원을 어디에 사용하는 것이 가장 좋은지를 판단하는 일입니다. 누구에게 보내고 누구에게 보내지 않을지, 제한된 예산을 어떤 고객에게 사용할지를 여러 제약과 함께 결정합니다.

고객을 다음 발견으로 이끄는 NeXA

NeXA는 Next eXploration Architecture의 약자로, ‘넥사’라고 읽습니다. 이름의 eXploration은 고객이 서비스 안에서 원하는 것을 찾아 나가는 발견 과정을, Architecture는 ML 결과를 고객에게 보여 주는 노출 구조를 의미합니다. Next에는 상품을 지면에 단순히 나열하는 데서 그치지 않고, 추천과 검색 등 다양한 발견 경험에 맞는 차세대 노출 방식을 만들어 가겠다는 뜻을 담았습니다.

NeXA는 추천과 검색을 포함한 발견 영역의 개인화를 담당합니다. 앞에서 이야기한 문제 중에서는 다양한 형태의 발견 지면에 ML을 빠르게 적용하는 문제가 여기에 해당합니다. 새로운 형태의 지면이 생겨도 노출 방식을 처음부터 다시 만들지 않고, 공통 구조 위에서 그 지면에 맞는 방식을 바로 갖추는 것이 목표입니다.

NeXA는 고객이 탐색하는 맥락에 맞춰 후보를 평가하고, 순서를 정하는 데서 나아가 여러 후보를 지면 구조에 맞는 하나의 구성으로 묶습니다. 최종 결과는 순서를 정한 후보 목록부터 여러 후보를 조합한 슬레이트까지 각 지면이 요구하는 형태로 서비스에 전달됩니다.

DeciML과 NeXA는 같은 고객 이해를 공유하면서 서로 다른 역할을 맡습니다. DeciML이 서비스가 고객에게 먼저 할 행동을 정한다면, NeXA는 고객이 서비스 안에서 무엇을 어떤 모습으로 발견할지를 정합니다. 출발하는 쪽은 다르지만 두 플랫폼 모두 하나의 개인화 경험을 만들기 위한 기반입니다.

Three Design Claims

플랫폼의 설계를 관통하는 세 가지 원칙

플랫폼의 구조는 다음 편부터 자세히 다룹니다. 이 글에서는 그 구조를 관통하는 세 가지 설계 원칙을 설명합니다.

세 원칙의 목표는 같습니다. 반복되는 기술적 문제는 플랫폼이 맡고 사람은 문제를 정의하고 해결하는 데 시간을 쓰도록 하는 것입니다.

플랫폼은 모델을 올리고 운영하는 도구에서 나아가, 한 사람이 해결한 문제가 다시 반복되지 않도록 만들고 그 과정에서 쌓인 지식과 판단을 다음 사람과 에이전트가 이어받도록 하는 기반입니다.

Problem to Product

모델을 운영하던 사람이 만든 플랫폼입니다

이 플랫폼은 직접 모델을 만들고 서비스에 배포하고 운영해 온 경험에서 시작했습니다. 모델을 운영한다는 것은 모델을 지면에 내보낸 뒤 실제 환경에서 어떤 결과를 만들고 있는지까지 책임진다는 뜻입니다. 그래서 이 플랫폼은 처음부터 엔지니어링의 시선만으로 설계하지 않았습니다. 플랫폼이 무엇을 잘해야 실제 프로덕트가 좋아지는가를 먼저 물었습니다.

그 질문에 답하는 과정에서 병목이 드러났습니다. 모델 하나를 지면에 내보낼 때마다 서빙 API 연결, 장애 처리 방식, 배포 절차, 트래픽 감당 여부, 데이터 규모에 맞는 처리 방식과 서빙 자원까지 프로젝트마다 새로 논의해야 했습니다. 문제를 고민하는 시간보다 같은 시행착오를 반복하는 시간이 더 길었고 그만큼 모델이 프로덕트에 반영되는 시점도 늦어졌습니다. 그래서 DS와 MLE가 같은 문제를 다시 마주하지 않도록, 서빙부터 배포와 운영까지 필요한 경로를 표준화했습니다.

표준화의 기준은 조직이 만들고자 하는 프로덕트의 방향, 곧 모든 것이 개인화되는 커머스였습니다. 대신 성격이 다른 워크로드를 폭넓게 수용하는 플랫폼은 아닙니다. 그 대가를 감수하더라도, 자주 풀어야 하는 문제를 훨씬 빠르게 해결하는 쪽을 택했습니다. 그래서 플랫폼의 가치도 몇 종류의 모델을 올릴 수 있는지가 아니라, DS와 MLE가 하나의 문제를 정의하고 프로덕트에 반영하기까지 걸리는 시간을 얼마나 단축했는가로 봅니다.

AI-Native by Design

사람과 에이전트가 같은 규칙으로 일합니다

이 플랫폼에서 코드를 만들고 배포하는 주체는 사람만이 아닙니다. 에이전트도 코드를 작성하고 테스트를 구성하며 배포를 준비합니다. 그래서 사람과 에이전트가 같은 규칙 아래에서 일하도록 플랫폼을 설계했습니다. 둘 다 같은 기준으로 검증받고 같은 형태로 결과를 남깁니다.

지식이 남는 방식도 달라져야 합니다. 지금까지는 “이 문제를 왜 이렇게 풀었는지”, “이 모델을 어떤 조건에서 배포해도 되는지” 같은 판단이 담당자의 기억에만 남아 있어도 일이 진행될 수 있었습니다. 하지만 에이전트는 사람의 기억을 읽을 수 없습니다. 결과만이 아니라 그 결과가 만들어진 과정과 판단의 기준, 곧 무엇을 변경했고 어떤 테스트를 통과했으며 왜 그 선택을 했는지가 플랫폼이 읽을 수 있는 형태로 남아야 합니다. 그래야 다음 작업을 그 위에서 바로 시작할 수 있습니다. 사람도 마찬가지여서 담당자가 바뀌어도 이전 작업의 맥락을 파악하는 데 불필요한 시간을 쓰지 않아도 됩니다.

표준 경로로 반복을 없애고 지식을 남겨 반영 시간을 줄입니다. 한 사람이 남긴 지식이 다음 문제의 출발점이 되면 같은 고민을 처음부터 다시 하지 않아도 됩니다. 그래서 저희가 말하는 AI-native 플랫폼은 에이전트가 개발부터 배포까지 자연스럽게 참여하고 플랫폼의 지식과 구조를 활용해 스스로 문제를 해결할 수 있도록 설계된 플랫폼입니다.

Above the Floor

품질 하한은 플랫폼이, 문제는 DS와 MLE가 소유합니다

플랫폼은 인프라와 개발 관점의 품질 하한을 소유합니다. 서빙 계약, 재시도와 과부하 차단, 배포와 롤백 경로, 관측 규약처럼 매번 새로 구현하면 사람마다 다른 답을 내놓게 되는 문제들입니다. 이런 기반을 플랫폼이 기본으로 제공하면, 누가 어떤 모델을 만들더라도 서비스의 기본적인 품질과 운영 기준은 일정하게 유지됩니다.

그 위의 문제는 DS와 MLE의 몫입니다. 어떤 문제를 풀 것인지 정의하고, 어떤 접근이 더 나은지 고민하고, 구현하고, 동료와 논의하며 쌓아가는 지식은 플랫폼이 대신 가질 수 없는 자산입니다. 플랫폼은 그 문제에 집중할 시간을 확보하고 한 번 만들어진 결과와 지식이 다음 문제에서도 다시 쓰일 수 있도록 기반을 만듭니다.

모두가 슬롯을 누구에게 줄지, 이 화면에 무엇을 보여줄지를 고민하며 더 높은 곳을 향해 갈 때, 그 아래를 받치는 것이 플랫폼의 역할입니다.

Where This Goes

예측을 넘어 결정과 발견으로

모든 것이 개인화되는 커머스를 지향한다면, ML의 역할은 예측 문제를 풀어 점수를 산출하는 데서 끝나지 않습니다. 고객을 이해하고, 행동의 가치를 평가하고, 비즈니스 제약 속에서 선택하는 일이 서비스 전반에서 하나의 흐름으로 이어져야 합니다. DeciML과 NeXA는 그 흐름을 서비스에 전달하는 두 플랫폼입니다. 두 플랫폼은 유한한 자원이 누구의 것인가에 따라 역할을 나누고, 반복되는 기술적 문제는 플랫폼이 맡아 사람이 문제를 정의하고 해결하는 데 집중하도록 설계했습니다.

이 흐름을 서비스 전반으로 넓히려면 역할이 나뉜 여러 플랫폼이 함께 맞물려야 합니다. DeciML과 NeXA 같은 ML 플랫폼은 문제에 맞는 모델을 학습하고 서빙해 그 산출물을 오케스트레이션 레이어로 전달하는 데까지를 맡습니다. 오케스트레이션 레이어는 이 산출물을 받아 A/B 테스트를 운영하고, 여러 모델의 결과를 조합하거나 단계적으로 바꾼 뒤 백엔드 서버로 전달합니다. 여기에 모델이 쓰는 피처를 실시간으로 관리하는 피처 스토어와, 모델의 등록과 버전을 관리하고 모니터링하는 모델 레지스트리가 더해집니다. 각 플랫폼의 역할은 다르지만, 서비스의 개인화를 더 빠르고 넓게 확장할 수 있는 생태계를 만든다는 목표는 같습니다. DeciML과 NeXA는 그 생태계를 만들어 가는 시작점입니다.

다음 편에서는 DeciML이 결과가 필요한 시점에 따라 서빙 방식을 Realtime API, Batch Job, Async Worker 셋으로 나눈 이유와 서빙 방식마다 기술을 고른 기준, 그리고 이를 뒷받침하는 실행 환경을 다룹니다.

그 뒤로는 발송 슬롯의 배분, 예산 제약 아래의 쿠폰 타겟팅, 발견 지면의 노출 구성처럼 두 플랫폼 위에서 풀어낸 문제들을 결과가 확인된 것부터 차례로 소개하겠습니다. 오케스트레이션 레이어, 피처 스토어, 모델 레지스트리처럼 두 플랫폼과 연결되는 플랫폼들도 이 시리즈에서 하나씩 다루겠습니다.
