event_model_payload.headline: A ghost moved into my terminal. It runs on Gemma, and it never leaves my laptop
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

The first time I ran it for real, Gemma said nothing at all. Eight commands, eight empty lines. The ghost was there, it just wouldn't speak. That turned out to be the most honest bug I've ever hit in a Halloween project, and I'll get to it.

What I Built

haunted-terminal is a ghost that moves into your zsh, and it doesn't just leave comments. It haunts the place.

When you open a terminal:

  1. The ghost rises. A full-screen ASCII ghost fades in out of the dark, bobs, blinks, and fades away.
  2. The music starts. A horror soundtrack loops for as long as any haunted tab is open, and stops when you close the last one.
  3. The welcome card appears. The same ghost floats beside your status (is Gemma awake, is the music on, where you are) until you press a key.
  4. Then it stays. About one command in three, it whispers a line about what you just did. Every few commands, something in the room makes a sound: a whispered boo right behind your ear, a wolf, a witch cackling, chains on stone.

The ghost is a programmer who died in 1987 at a VT100 terminal, halfway through a COBOL migration. He is cold, a little jealous of the living, and he never gives advice.

He also has one job that is not a joke. Before you press Enter on rm -rf, git push --force, git reset --hard, DROP TABLE or curl ... | sh, he stops you and asks if you're sure.

And on November 1 and 2, for Día de los Muertos, the welcome card turns marigold, and the ghost builds a small ofrenda for everything you deleted that day.

The ghost is Gemma 4 E2B, running on my laptop through llama.cpp. Nothing I type goes to a server.

Demo

A two-minute tour: the ghost rising, the welcome card, real Gemma whispers on git status, npm test and a typo, a wolf howl from the ElevenLabs sounds, the rm -rf guard, the Día de los Muertos card, and how to install it. Turn the sound on.

Every ghost line in that picture is real Gemma output. A few more from the test runs:

$ git log --oneline -5
  👻 Five commits remain, the ghosts of my forgotten logic.
$ git checkout feature/login        (exit 128)
  👻 The branch is gone, just like my last memory of warmth.
$ git status
  👻 The changes remain, just like the dust on this old screen.
$ npm test                           (exit 1)
  👻 That error is familiar; the same ghost in the machine.

Website: haunted-terminal-lovat.vercel.app, with the same ghost animated in your browser and a button to play the soundtrack.

Code

ankitjha1405 / haunted-terminal

A local Gemma ghost that haunts zsh

👻 haunted-terminal

A ghost moves into your terminal. Open a tab and it rises out of the dark while a horror soundtrack starts. Then it stays. It whispers about the commands you run, and stops you before you rm -rf.

The ghost is Gemma 4, running on your own machine through llama.cpp. Your shell history never leaves your laptop.

 Website · Built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

Every ghost line above is real Gemma output from a laptop, about half a second each.

Hacktoberfest 2026 · Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

This is my entry for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4: Ghost in the Machine. The week asks for a spooky build with open-source AI at its core. Here the ghost is the open model: Gemma 4, running on your own laptop, gives the…

View on GitHub

Two files do the work, with no dependencies beyond Python's standard library: ghost.zsh (the hooks) and ghost (everything else).

How I Built It

The architecture is small. ghost.zsh hooks into zsh in two places. After every command, precmd hands the command and its exit code to the ghost. Before Enter, a wrapped accept-line widget runs the safety check. When a terminal opens, it starts the music and plays the intro. The ghost script talks to llama-server's OpenAI-compatible endpoint, draws the animations, and manages the sound.

Most of what I learned came from things going wrong.

1. The ghost that wouldn't speak

That first live run: eight commands, eight empty replies. The raw response showed why. Gemma 4 starts thinking as soon as it gets a system prompt, and it spent all 60 of its tokens reasoning about how to be a ghost:

"content": "",
"reasoning_content": "Thinking Process:\n\n1. **Analyze the Request & Persona:**..."

One flag fixed it: "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false}. A ghost should blurt, not deliberate. There's now a test so this can't quietly come back.

2. "Another…"

Once it spoke, it started a lot of lines the same way: Another triumph. Another failure. Another branch lost. So I measured it. I wrote eval_ghost.py, which runs 40 everyday commands (git, npm, docker, typos, failed builds) through the ghost three times and checks every reply.

Then I added four example replies to the prompt, told it to notice one concrete detail of the command, and skipped commands like ls and cd that aren't worth a ghost's breath. Here's the before and after, 120 replies each:

Check Before After
Replied at all 100% 100%
Under 20 words 100% 100%
Gave no advice 100% 100%
No emoji, quotes or hashtags 100% 100%
Didn't open with "Another" 82% 97%
One sentence 82% 88%
Median reply time 0.7 s 0.7 s

Most of the remaining "two sentence" replies are fragments like "Five commits. Such a brief, pathetic life for code.", which honestly suit him. The examples cost no speed: llama-server caches the shared prompt, so old and new run at the same median.

3. The safety check is not the model

A warning before rm -rf has to be instant and right every time, so it's plain pattern matching. Gemma only does the part where being creative is the point. The same script tests it:

Safety check Result
Dangerous commands caught 19/19
Harmless look-alikes left alone 19/19 (was 17/19)

The two false alarms were grep -r 'DROP TABLE' migrations and echo 'drop table' > notes.txt. Now DROP only counts inside a database client like psql or mysql.

4. Secrets never reach the model

Even a local model shouldn't see your keys, and the ghost could repeat one on screen. Before a command reaches Gemma, anything that looks like a secret is blanked: export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-..., --password=..., Bearer tokens, https://user:token@..., and GitHub, Slack and AWS key formats. npm test stays npm test. echo $GITHUB_TOKEN stays too, because a variable name isn't a secret.

5. A voice that talked too much

My first version had ElevenLabs read every ghost line aloud. It was too much within a minute. A ghost that talks constantly isn't scary. A sound you didn't expect is.

So now the shell keeps a counter. After every one to three commands (two on average, which I checked over 30 commands), it plays one of seven horror sounds made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API: a breathy boo, a wolf howl, a witch's cackle, a creaking door, a moan, dragging chains, overlapping whispers. Each is generated once and cached. After that they cost no credits, work offline, and ElevenLabs never sees a single command.

6. Colours that didn't exist

The welcome card's title came out garbled on my Mac, with some letters invisible. macOS Terminal.app can't display 24-bit colour, and I had used it for a gradient. The card now uses only the 256-colour palette, with a solid white title and a violet base.

The rest

  • The ghost is a signed distance field: a circle for the head and a box with a wavy hem for the body, drawn in @$% and lit by a violet and green halo. The website draws its hero with the same math in JavaScript.
  • The welcome card redraws in place 20 times a second until you press a key, and that key isn't typed into your prompt.
  • One music player serves every tab. An atomic lock file stops two tabs from starting two players. (They did, the first time. Testing caught it.) Each shell registers itself, and the music stops when none are left.
  • No server, no ghost. If llama-server is down, the ghost stays silent in milliseconds. It never blocks the shell.
  • Tests: 15 unit tests, plus an interactive zsh test that drives a real shell through a pseudo-terminal. It types rm -rf, presses n, and checks the folder survived. GitHub Actions runs them on every push.

I built this with Claude Code as my pair programmer.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A terminal sees everything: file paths, hostnames, branch names, half-typed secrets, the command you ran at 2 a.m. I would never pipe that into a hosted API to get a joke back.

With an open-weight model I don't have to. Gemma runs on my machine, so:

  • It works offline. On a plane, in a basement, with Wi-Fi off.
  • My shell history stays mine. No account, no logs on someone else's server.
  • It costs nothing to run. A ghost that comments hundreds of times a day would be a real bill on a paid API. Here it's zero.
  • No lock-in. GHOST_URL points at any OpenAI-compatible server. Swapping Gemma for another open model is one flag to llama-server.

This only works because open models are now small and good enough to sit next to your shell and answer in under a second. A year ago this would have been a cloud API with a privacy policy. Now it's a file on my disk.

Prize Categories

  • Best Use of Gemma: Gemma 4 E2B is the ghost, running locally through llama.cpp, with thinking turned off, example-driven prompting, and a measured before and after.
  • Best Use of ElevenLabs: seven horror sound effects made with the ElevenLabs sound effects API, played at random every one to three commands and cached so they work offline.
  • Best Use of GitHub Copilot: GitHub Actions runs the unit tests and a zsh syntax check on every push.

Music: "Horror Music" by kiravale, via Pixabay. Code: MIT. Demo video: built with the onetake motion skill (PolyForm Noncommercial), narrated with the open Kokoro TTS model. The terminal in it is redrawn from the ghost's own code, and every ghost line in it is real Gemma output.

event_model_payload.headline: It's Halloween, So Here's My Field Guide to the Monsters Already Living in Your Stack
event_model_payload.summary:
Seven creatures, one per audit: the Zombie process, the Ghost cron, the Trojan paste, the Spider at the door, the Gremlin in CI, the Kraken in the schema, and the Daemon you should adopt. Each with its habitat, its detection one-liner, and its banishment.

Every infrastructure has a bestiary. Nobody writes it down, which is why the monsters keep winning. Mine got catalogued one audit at a time over a year of confessions on this blog — seven distinct creatures, every one still living in somebody's production right now. It's Halloween, so: name them, detect them, banish them. Or adopt them, in one case. Field guides are honest about which animals are pets.

The Zombie 🧟
Died once, kept walking. Deprecated services still serving, restart loops older than the intern who "fixed" them.

# dead-but-walking in the process table
ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,comm | awk '$3 ~ /^Z/'
# and the container flavor: restart loops
docker ps -a --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Status}}' | grep -iE 'restart|back-off'

Banish: graveyard rules — kill it fully (process, DNS, keys, CI variables) or adopt it with an owner. Half-killed zombies are how sequels happen.

The Ghost 👻
The spirit of a departed colleague, still doing their job. Ours ran at 3:07 AM and reconciled invoices.

for u in $(cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd); do
  crontab -l -u "$u" 2>/dev/null | grep -vE '^\s*#|^\s*$' | sed "s/^/$u: /"
done   # every line that can't name an owner, on purpose, is a ghost

Banish: the séance — owner, purpose, loud failure, or a funeral. Plus staleness alerts: a ghost that stops working is an incident nobody feels for three weeks.

The Trojan 🐴
Arrives as a gift, opens the door from inside. Pasted snippets, dependency diffs, October PRs titled fix typo.

git diff main...HEAD | grep -nE 'process\.env|os\.environ|getenv'      # env going somewhere
git diff main...HEAD | grep -nE 'base64|eval\(|atob'                   # obfuscation
git diff main...HEAD | grep -nE 'curl .*(-d|--data)|wget |fetch\('     # new outbound call

Banish: review before merge even at twenty lines; provenance comments; pin what you can pin. Most Trojans aren't malicious — just someone else's bug, fossilized with full rights.

The Spider 🕷️
The internet's automated fauna, patiently trying every handle. Lives on your public address and every port you forgot

# before: the porch the spiders sit on
ss -tlnp | grep -E '0\.0\.0\.0|::'          # listeners facing everyone
journalctl -u ssh --since yesterday | grep -c 'Failed password'

# after (no public IP, default-deny, managed ingress): both commands return silence
krova tcp list web-1                        # empty. no porch, no spiders.

Banish: don't fight it at the door; remove the door. My spider population went extinct in a weekend and I did nothing heroic — just changed the default. (The one entry where my hosting is the whole spell: Krova Cubes ship with no public address.)

The Gremlin 👺
Feeds on observation. The CI-only failure, the bug that vanishes under the debugger, timestamps disagreeing by exactly one hour in exactly one region.

# evict its conditions: unseeded randomness and un-pinned clocks in tests
grep -rnE 'Math\.random|random\.random|Date\.now|time\.now' tests/ src/ \
  | grep -viE 'seed|fake|clock'             # every hit is a gremlin bed

Banish: you don't kill gremlins, you bore them out: fixed clocks, seeded randomness, reproducible builds. Boredom is the only exorcism that holds.

The Kraken 🐙
Too big to fight, too central to flee. Tentacles in every schema; migrations scheduled in quarters; a cloud labeled LEGACY.

# count the tentacles before you wake it
grep -rc 'legacy_orders' --include='*.sql' --include='*.py' --include='*.ts' . \
  | sort -t: -k2 -rn | head

Banish: nobody slays the Kraken. Build seams, route one tentacle at a time around it, let it sleep. Anyone selling you a slaying is selling you an outage.

The Daemon 😇
The only monster that works for you. Night-shift process keeping caches warm, certs renewed, queues drained. A daemon is not a demon — it's a guardian spirit we forgot to thank.

systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running --no-pager \
  | awk '{print $1}' | grep -vE '^\.|systemd|ssh|cron'   # your daemons
# adoption papers per daemon: owner, runbook path, silence alert

Banish: absolutely not. Adopt: name it, log it, alert on its silence. A daemon with an owner is infrastructure; a daemon without one is next year's Ghost.

The honest part
None of these are moral failures. Every stack I've audited hosted at least four of the seven simultaneously. The monsters aren't the shame; the unnamed monsters are. An inventory turns fear into a checklist, and a checklist turns 3 AM into Tuesday.

And the seventh entry is the lesson: the difference between a guardian and a ghost is rarely the creature. It's whether somebody wrote its name down.

Name your monsters
Tonight of all nights: run the seven detections. Seven chairs at the table; see who sits down. Then write the field guide — one page per monster: habitat, tells, banishment, or adoption papers if it earns them.

event_model_payload.headline: I Built a Sector Rotation Map in Python. A Shuffle Test Humbled It.
event_model_payload.summary:
This week I shipped a sector rotation map for Indian stocks. It plots NSE sector and thematic indices against the Nifty 500 and sorts them into four corners: Leading, Weakening, Lagging and Improving.

Then the obvious question hit me: does it actually tell you anything? If you buy whatever is Leading, do you beat the market? And do sectors really travel clockwise around the map, the way every explainer says?

So I rebuilt the whole thing in Python, ran it over ten years of weekly data, and checked. This post is the build: the maths, the code, two bugs, and a shuffle test that took my favourite finding away. The story version, with more charts, is on Medium (linked at the end).

Not investment advice. I built the data platform and the map used here. Data runs from July 2016 to 23 October 2026.

The maths

Every week, for every sector:

rs    = 100 * sector / nifty_500                  # relative strength
ratio = 100 * wma(rs, 5) / wma(rs, 15)             # has it been gaining ground lately?
mom   = 100 * ratio / ratio.shift(5)               # is that speeding up or fading?

wma is a weighted moving average, where the newest week counts most. Dividing the 5-week average by the 15-week one gives a number around 100. Above 100 means relative strength has been rising recently, so the sector has been outperforming the Nifty 500 over the last few weeks. The momentum line compares today's ratio with five weeks ago. Above 100, that outperformance is accelerating.

Two numbers, two thresholds at 100, four corners:

q = np.where(ratio >= 100, np.where(mom >= 100, "Leading", "Weakening"),
             np.where(mom >= 100, "Improving", "Lagging"))

The formula was the easy part. Every mistake I made was in the data handling.

Getting the data

I pulled daily levels for 21 indices and the Nifty 500 from the data API I built. Responses are paginated, so a small helper follows meta.next_cursor until has_more is false. The from date is 2015, so the 15-week averages have time to warm up before the test starts in July 2016.

Weekly bars, finished weeks only 

iso = daily.index.isocalendar()
weekly = daily.groupby([iso.year, iso.week]).last()
weekly.index = [pd.Timestamp.fromisocalendar(y, w, 5) for y, w in weekly.index]
if weekly.index[-1] >= pd.Timestamp.today().normalize():
    weekly = weekly.iloc[:-1]  # this week hasn't finished yet

Grouping by ISO week and taking the last close gives one bar per week, holiday weeks included. Each week is labelled with its Friday, and if that Friday hasn't passed, the week is dropped. Run it on a Wednesday without that check and you're treating three days as a full week. My first version dropped the last week unconditionally, which quietly threw away a finished week whenever I ran it on a weekend.

The live map had a cousin of this bug. In weekly mode, a freshness check that looked at the wrong date decided, in the middle of the week, that every sector was stale, and the map came up empty. The fix was to compare each sector's last session with the map's as-of date.

The bug that almost fooled me

My first version built the daily table like this:

daily = pd.concat(series, axis=1).sort_index().ffill()

Forward-filling looks harmless. Holidays differ a little between indices, so why not carry the last price forward?

Because three of the indices (Healthcare, Consumer Durables, Oil & Gas) have a stray data point in mid-2016 and no continuous data until 2020. ffill() took that one price and copied it forward for years. Healthcare got about four years of invented, perfectly flat history.

Nothing errored, but the answer flipped. With the fill, Improving sectors beat the Nifty 500 over the next quarter by 0.30% on average. Without it, they lagged by 0.36%.

I caught it only because an earlier prototype built the weeks differently and the two disagreed. The fix was to delete .ffill():

daily = pd.concat(series, axis=1).sort_index()

GroupBy.last() already skips missing values inside a week, so holidays are fine, and a week with no data at all stays empty. The rolling averages see the gap, return NaN, and drop out instead of inventing a trend.

A second, smaller one, which a reviewer caught: I first computed the 13-week forward return after dropping the empty rows. Across a gap, shift(-13) then jumps 13 rows, not 13 weeks. The forward return is now computed on the full weekly series, before anything is dropped.

Checking it against the live map

Before trusting the backtest, I printed the latest week and compared it with the live page. All 21 indices matched the live page to two decimals on both ratio and momentum. IT: ratio 104.76, momentum 104.49. Pharma: 101.35 and 99.30. MNC: 97.33 and 98.19.

Result one: Leading doesn't predict much

For every weekly reading from July 2016, I recorded the corner and whether the sector beat the Nifty 500 over the next 13 weeks:

           weeks     avg beat_benchmark
quadrant
Improving   1707  -0.36%          47.9%
Lagging     3620  -0.28%          47.0%
Leading     3443  +0.47%          50.1%
Weakening   1616  +0.21%          47.8%

Any sector-week beat the benchmark 48.3% of the time, so Leading is about two points better. But the 13-week windows overlap, which makes 10,386 readings worth far fewer independent ones. When I kept only non-overlapping quarters, Weakening (+1.14%, 132 readings) came out ahead of Leading (+0.26%, 253). That flip looks like noise, so I wouldn't treat either number as an edge. These are also price indices, so dividends are left out. That slightly understates sectors that yield more than the Nifty 500.

Result two: the shuffle test

The clockwise rotation looked like the real finding. 67.0% of the 2,233 corner changes went clockwise.

Then I asked what random data would do. For each sector, I took the longest unbroken stretch of its real weekly moves, shuffled their order, rebuilt a relative-strength path, and ran the exact same map on it, 30 times:

s = rs.dropna()
run = (s.index.to_series().diff() > pd.Timedelta(weeks=2)).cumsum()
s = s[run == run.value_counts().idxmax()]  # longest unbroken stretch only
moves = np.log(s).diff().dropna().to_numpy()
path = np.exp(np.log(s.iloc[0]) + np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rng.permutation(moves))]))
fake.append(readings(pd.Series(path, index=s.index))[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"])

real sectors: 2233 quadrant changes, 67.0% clockwise
shuffled data: 66.2% clockwise (range 63.6% to 68.0%)

The shuffled data rotates clockwise just as reliably: real sectors, at 67.0%, sit inside the shuffled range. Even the median time in Leading is the same: six weeks for real sectors, five to six for shuffled ones.

The reason is in the maths. The momentum axis is roughly the rate of change of the ratio axis. When momentum is above 100, the ratio is rising, so the dot moves right; below 100 it moves left. Right along the top and left along the bottom is clockwise, for any wiggly series, like a pendulum's position against its speed. And because the ratio compares a short and a long average of the same series, it swings around 100 for any input, so those loops circle the centre of the map. The rotation comes from the indicator itself. It's still a nice way to see a sector's recent path. It just isn't evidence of a cycle you can trade.

The full script

Set TAPETIDE_API_TOKEN and run it. It prints the latest map, the results table, the clockwise count and the shuffle test.

import os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import requests

API = "https://api.tapetide.com/v1"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['TAPETIDE_API_TOKEN']}"}
SECTORS = ["nifty-it", "nifty-bank", "nifty-private-bank", "nifty-psu-bank", "nifty-fmcg",
           "nifty-pharma", "nifty-auto", "nifty-metal", "nifty-realty", "nifty-energy",
           "nifty-financial-services", "nifty-infrastructure", "nifty-media", "nifty-mnc",
           "nifty-pse", "nifty-cpse", "nifty-commodities", "nifty-india-consumption",
           "nifty-consumer-durables", "nifty-healthcare-index", "nifty-oil-and-gas"]
ORDER = ["Leading", "Weakening", "Lagging", "Improving"]


def closes(slug, start="2015-01-01"):
    rows, params = [], {"from": start, "limit": 1000}
    while True:
        body = requests.get(f"{API}/indices/{slug}/levels", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60).json()
        rows += body["data"]
        if not body["meta"]["has_more"]:
            break
        params["cursor"] = body["meta"]["next_cursor"]
    s = pd.DataFrame(rows)
    return pd.Series(s["close"].values, index=pd.to_datetime(s["date"]), name=slug)


daily = pd.concat([closes(s) for s in SECTORS + ["nifty-500"]], axis=1).sort_index()
iso = daily.index.isocalendar()
weekly = daily.groupby([iso.year, iso.week]).last()  # last real close per week; empty weeks stay NaN
weekly.index = [pd.Timestamp.fromisocalendar(y, w, 5) for y, w in weekly.index]
if weekly.index[-1] >= pd.Timestamp.today().normalize():
    weekly = weekly.iloc[:-1]  # this week hasn't finished yet


def wma(x, n):
    weights = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    return x.rolling(n).apply(lambda v: v @ weights / weights.sum(), raw=True)


def readings(rs):
    ratio = 100 * wma(rs, 5) / wma(rs, 15)               # is relative strength rising lately?
    mom = 100 * ratio / ratio.shift(5)                   # is that speeding up or fading?
    q = np.where(ratio >= 100, np.where(mom >= 100, "Leading", "Weakening"),
                 np.where(mom >= 100, "Improving", "Lagging"))
    next_13w = rs.shift(-13) / rs - 1                    # beat the benchmark next quarter?
    d = pd.DataFrame({"rs": rs, "ratio": ratio, "mom": mom, "quadrant": q, "next_13w": next_13w})
    return d[d["ratio"].notna() & d["mom"].notna()]


def clockwise_share(frames):
    moves = [(a, b) for d in frames for a, b in zip(d["quadrant"], d["quadrant"].iloc[1:]) if a != b]
    return np.mean([ORDER[(ORDER.index(a) + 1) % 4] == b for a, b in moves]), len(moves)


rs_all = {s: 100 * weekly[s] / weekly["nifty-500"] for s in SECTORS}
frames = [readings(rs)[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"] for rs in rs_all.values()]
panel = pd.concat(frames, keys=SECTORS, names=["sector", "week"])
print(panel.xs(panel.index.get_level_values("week").max(), level="week").round(2)
      .sort_values("ratio", ascending=False).drop(columns="next_13w").to_string())

test = panel.dropna(subset=["next_13w"])
print(test.groupby("quadrant")["next_13w"].agg(
    weeks="size", avg=lambda v: f"{v.mean():+.2%}", beat_benchmark=lambda v: f"{(v > 0).mean():.1%}"))
share, n = clockwise_share(frames)
print(f"real sectors: {n} quadrant changes, {share:.1%} clockwise")

# The same map built from shuffled weekly moves: same sizes, no real pattern.
rng = np.random.default_rng(11)
shuffled = []
for _ in range(30):
    fake = []
    for rs in rs_all.values():
        s = rs.dropna()
        run = (s.index.to_series().diff() > pd.Timedelta(weeks=2)).cumsum()
        s = s[run == run.value_counts().idxmax()]  # longest unbroken stretch only
        moves = np.log(s).diff().dropna().to_numpy()
        path = np.exp(np.log(s.iloc[0]) + np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rng.permutation(moves))]))
        fake.append(readings(pd.Series(path, index=s.index))[lambda d: d.index >= "2016-07-01"])
    shuffled.append(clockwise_share(fake)[0])
print(f"shuffled data: {np.mean(shuffled):.1%} clockwise (range {min(shuffled):.1%} to {max(shuffled):.1%})")

What I'd try next

  • A better null model. Shuffling weekly moves breaks every streak. A block shuffle that keeps short runs intact would be a tougher test.
  • The daily map. The live page also has a daily version with 14/36/8 settings.
  • Run every new pattern past random data first. That one is less an idea than a rule now.

The live map is at tapetide.com/insight/sector-rotation, on Tapetide, the data platform I built. The findings and charts are in the companion piece on Medium. Not investment advice.

event_model_payload.headline: I Built RepoGeist: An Open-Source AI That Uncovers the Ghosts in Your Git History
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine.

There is code in your repository that nobody can see anymore.

It had a filename. Someone spent an afternoon writing it. Another developer changed it three weeks later. Then one commit removed it, the branch moved on, and the reason slowly disappeared from the team's memory.

Git remembers the code. It does not explain the story.

What I Built

RepoGeist is a privacy-first Git archaeology application that reconstructs a repository's past and lets you investigate it with a local open-weight AI model.

The deterministic half reads real Git objects. It counts commits and contributors, traces file activity, identifies quiet branches, finds files deleted from the analyzed HEAD, and retrieves their last historical versions without modifying the working tree.

The generative half turns selected evidence into explanations. Ghost Chat answers questions about the repository. Commit Autopsy interprets a bounded diff. The Repository Speaks transforms factual milestones into a haunted chronicle, technical documentary, or developer retrospective. Answers include references to the commits and files supplied as evidence.

My interpretation of “Ghost in the Machine” is both literal and practical: the ghosts are deleted modules, abandoned experiments, and decisions whose authors are no longer in the room.

Demo

Demo video: Watch on YouTube

The most revealing route through RepoGeist's synthetic demo repository is:

  1. RepoGeist analyzes ten deterministic commits and a stale experiment branch.
  2. The Graveyard reveals auth/legacy.py, which no longer exists at HEAD.
  3. Code Resurrection displays its final historical version directly from Git.
  4. Ghost Chat receives the deletion commit, related authentication changes, and bounded metadata.
  5. The answer explains what the evidence proves. If Git never documents why it happened, RepoGeist says the motivation is unknown.

That last constraint matters. A confident ghost that invents history is just a hallucination wearing a costume.

Code

AryanSharma9917 / repogeist

👻 RepoGeist

Every repository has a past. Some commits still haunt it.

RepoGeist is a privacy-first Git archaeology platform. It reconstructs real repository history, finds code absent from HEAD, surfaces quiet branches, retrieves historical source, and lets a local open-weight model explain the evidence without sending source code to a third party.

Built for the Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge — Week 4, Ghost in the Machine.

What works

  • Secure import beneath one configured repository root
  • Deterministic commit, contributor, file, language, activity, and branch analysis
  • Deleted-file detection and read-only historical content retrieval
  • Searchable timeline, repository graveyard, and responsive Spectral Terminal UI
  • Evidence retrieval and locally hosted Ollama chat with commit/file citations
  • Bounded-diff commit autopsies and three evidence-grounded story styles
  • Markdown and JSON investigation reports
  • Analysis jobs with real stage-based progress
  • Reproducible ten-commit synthetic demo plus stale experiment branch
  • Docker Compose, API tests, typechecking, production build, and CI

The…

View on GitHub

Repository: github.com/AryanSharma9917/repogeist

The repository includes Docker Compose, a reproducible demo-repository generator, FastAPI OpenAPI documentation, architecture and security guides, automated tests, and CI that does not require downloading model weights.

How I Built It

The frontend is built with Next.js and TypeScript. The backend uses FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, and SQLite. RepoGeist invokes native Git using argument arrays with hooks disabled; it never executes code from an analyzed repository. A configured repository-root boundary prevents the API from browsing arbitrary paths on the host.

The core architectural decision was to keep Git facts separate from AI prose:

Git repository
  -> deterministic extraction
  -> SQLite evidence records
  -> bounded keyword/entity retrieval
  -> local Ollama prompt
  -> evidence-linked response

RepoGeist uses the open-weight Qwen2.5 3B model through Ollama by default. Both the runtime URL and model name are configurable. The model never receives the entire repository; it sees a bounded evidence packet containing relevant commit metadata, changed paths, deletion records, and, for a commit autopsy, a limited diff.

Repository content is treated as untrusted data. A commit message could contain prompt-injection text, so the system prompt explicitly says that repository-derived text is evidence, not instructions. The model receives no tools for shell execution, arbitrary file access, secret access, repository mutation, or outbound requests.

The application remains useful without Ollama. If local AI is unavailable, only the AI endpoints return setup guidance. The factual dashboard, timeline, Graveyard, Code Resurrection, and deterministic reports still work.

What I verified

  • Six backend tests pass against real temporary Git repositories.
  • Ruff linting and TypeScript checking pass.
  • The Next.js production build succeeds and generates eleven application routes.
  • Docker Compose configuration and the frontend/backend Docker builds succeed.
  • The backend container completed a real demo import, ten-commit analysis, Graveyard lookup, and historical-source retrieval.
  • The installed frontend dependency tree reports zero known vulnerabilities.
  • A real Ollama run with qwen2.5:3b produced a Ghost Chat answer citing the authentication deletion commit and auth/legacy.py while correctly acknowledging that the exact motivation was undocumented.
  • A real Haunted Chronicle returned chronological inline citations and a complete evidence panel.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Repository history can contain unreleased features, internal names, security fixes, and architectural clues. Sending all of it to a closed hosted API by default would be the wrong privacy model.

Local inference changes the product, not just its cost. Source code, Git history, prompts, and model responses can remain on the developer's machine. RepoGeist works without an AI subscription, and a team can swap models, inspect the grounding prompt, adjust retrieval, or work completely offline. The deterministic analyzer is open to inspection, so users can distinguish facts extracted from Git from interpretations generated by the model.

Open-weight is not automatically the same as unrestricted open source, and every model's license still deserves review. However, the ability to possess and run the weights locally is what makes RepoGeist's privacy promise technically credible.

The Spirit of It

The moment I want the demo to land is not the animated title. It is a small sentence beneath a polished AI answer:

The file was removed in this commit, but the repository does not document the developer's exact motivation.

That admission is the heart of RepoGeist. Git archaeology is not necromancy. We can recover evidence, preserve context, and tell a compelling story, but we should not put words in the mouths of developers who are not there to correct us.

Sometimes respecting the dead means letting the record end where it ends.

event_model_payload.headline: SaaS Backup & Disaster Recovery: RPO, RTO and PITR
event_model_payload.summary:
A nightly pg_dump to the same VPS is not a backup strategy. It is a file that disappears with the disk, the compromised root account or the provider incident that took the server down in the first place, and even when it survives it can only take you back to 2 AM. For a SaaS product, the real questions are how much data you can afford to lose (RPO), how long you can afford to be down (RTO), and whether anyone has actually restored from your backups recently.

At Loop Origin we run Laravel and Node SaaS platforms on VPS infrastructure for clients, and backup design is part of every server setup and maintenance engagement. This is the setup I deploy by default, with the configuration, restore commands and drill schedule.

What is a good backup and disaster recovery setup for a SaaS on a VPS?

Direct answer: Combine continuous database archiving for point-in-time recovery (PostgreSQL WAL with pgBackRest or WAL-G, MySQL binary logs) with periodic full backups pushed to versioned, write-protected object storage in a separate account and region. Define RPO and RTO per tier, encrypt everything, and run a timed restore drill every month.

RPO and RTO tiers: pick one per system, not per company

RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. They drive cost, so set them per system rather than declaring "zero data loss" for everything.

Tier Typical RPO Typical RTO Mechanism Fits
Tier 0 Seconds Minutes Streaming replica plus WAL/binlog archiving, scripted failover Payments, orders, core tenant data
Tier 1 Minutes 1-4 hours Continuous WAL/binlog archive plus daily full backup, restore to new VPS Most B2B SaaS primary databases
Tier 2 24 hours 1 day Nightly full backup to object storage Analytics copies, internal tools
Tier 3 Rebuildable Days Infrastructure as code, no data backup Caches, queues, search indexes rebuilt from source

Most clients I work with land on Tier 1 for the primary database and Tier 2 or 3 for everything else. Redis queues and Elasticsearch-style indexes are usually Tier 3: rebuild them from the database instead of backing them up. My guide on running Laravel queues in production covers why failed jobs should live in the database rather than only in Redis.

Why dumps alone are not enough

A logical dump (pg_dump, mysqldump) is a consistent snapshot at one moment. If a bad migration or an accidental DELETE without a WHERE runs at 4:40 PM, a nightly dump takes you back to the previous night and you lose the day. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) closes that gap: restore the last full physical backup, then replay the database's change log up to the second before the mistake.

Dumps are still useful for moving individual tenants, seeding staging and long-term archives. They are just not the recovery mechanism for the primary.

PostgreSQL PITR with pgBackRest

postgresql.conf changes (restart required for archive_mode and wal_level):

wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'
archive_timeout = 60          # force a WAL segment switch at least every 60s

/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf:

[global]
repo1-type=s3
repo1-s3-bucket=acme-db-backups
repo1-s3-endpoint=s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
repo1-s3-region=eu-central-1
repo1-path=/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=4
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-cipher-pass=
compress-type=zst
start-fast=y

[main]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main

Initialize, verify and schedule:

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main stanza-create
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main check          # confirms WAL archiving works
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=full backup   # weekly via cron/systemd timer
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=diff backup   # daily
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main info

archive_timeout = 60 is what makes the RPO roughly one minute on a quiet database: without it, a low-traffic system may not fill and ship a 16 MB WAL segment for a long time.

The restore you will run when someone drops a table at 16:40:

sudo systemctl stop postgresql
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --delta \
  --type=time --target="2026-10-31 16:39:00+05" --target-action=promote restore
sudo systemctl start postgresql

In practice I restore to a new server first, verify the data, then cut over or copy the missing rows back. Restoring over the only production copy removes your ability to try again.

WAL-G is the main alternative: archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p', wal-g backup-push $PGDATA for base backups, and wal-g backup-fetch $PGDATA LATEST plus restore_command = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p' and recovery_target_time for PITR. I prefer pgBackRest for its built-in check, retention and parallel restore, and WAL-G where a team already uses it.

MySQL and MariaDB PITR with binary logs 

# my.cnf
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = /var/lib/mysql/binlog
binlog_format = ROW
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 1209600   # 14 days, longer than your full-backup interval
sync_binlog = 1

Take a consistent full backup with Percona XtraBackup for large databases, or mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 for smaller ones (--source-data replaced --master-data in MySQL 8.0.26). Ship binlogs off the server continuously, for example with mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never running on a backup host.

Recovery: restore the full backup, read the binlog file and position recorded in it, then replay up to just before the incident:

mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2026-10-31 16:39:00" \
  binlog.000412 binlog.000413 | mysql -u root -p

--stop-datetime is interpreted in the local time zone of the machine running mysqlbinlog, a detail that has caught more than one team restoring on a UTC server.

Object storage: where backups survive the incident

The repository must survive the loss of the server and of the credentials on it:

  • Separate account or project for the backup bucket, with a write-only key on the server. A stolen server key should not be able to delete backups.
  • Versioning plus object lock (S3 Object Lock, or the equivalent on S3-compatible providers that support it) with a retention period longer than your detection window.
  • A different region or provider from the primary VPS.
  • Client-side encryption (pgBackRest's repo1-cipher-type, or restic for file backups) with the passphrase stored outside the server.
  • File uploads (storage/app, user uploads) backed up with restic or rclone, or written directly to object storage in the first place.

Cost drivers, compared

Component What drives cost How to control it
Object storage Total stored size × retention Compression (zstd), differential backups, retention limits
Request and egress fees Restore downloads, frequent small uploads Choose providers with low egress; restore drills to the same region
Standby replica (Tier 0) A second always-on server Use only for systems that truly need minute-level RTO
Restore drill servers Hours of a temporary VPS per month Script the drill, destroy the server afterwards
Engineer time Setup, monitoring, drills Automate checks and alerts; document the runbook

For most Tier 1 SaaS databases the storage bill is small next to the replica and engineering time. My VPS vs managed PaaS cost comparison shows where managed databases with built-in PITR change the calculation.

Failure modes I have seen

  • Archiving silently broken. archive_command fails, WAL piles up in pg_wal and the disk fills. Monitor pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and the age of last_archived_time.
  • Backups nobody restored. Encryption passphrase lost, wrong PostgreSQL major version, missing extensions. Only a drill finds these.
  • Same blast radius. Backups in a bucket the compromised server can delete.
  • Binlog retention shorter than the backup interval. A gap makes PITR impossible past the last full backup.
  • Forgotten tenants' files. The database restores, but uploaded documents do not.
  • Shared-database multi-tenancy surprises. Restoring one tenant from a shared physical backup needs a side restore and a selective copy; plan it. My multi-tenant SaaS database architecture guide covers the trade-offs.

Monthly restore drill runbook

  1. Provision a clean VPS from infrastructure code.
  2. Restore the latest full backup plus WAL or binlogs to a target time from yesterday.
  3. Time it end to end; compare against your RTO.
  4. Run integrity checks: row counts on key tables, latest order or invoice timestamp, application smoke test.
  5. Restore a sample of uploaded files and open them.
  6. Record duration, issues and the backup set used in the runbook.
  7. Destroy the drill server and rotate any credentials it used.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time between the last recoverable point and the incident. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. A system can have a one-minute RPO and a four-hour RTO, and the two are engineered with different tools.

Is pg_dump enough for a production SaaS database?

Not as the only mechanism. It restores to the moment the dump ran, so anything after that is lost. Use physical backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, and keep logical dumps for tenant exports, staging data and long-term archives.

pgBackRest or WAL-G?

Both provide base backups, WAL archiving to object storage, compression, encryption and PITR. pgBackRest has a built-in configuration check, retention management and parallel restore. WAL-G is lighter and common in container setups. Choose the one your team will monitor and drill.

How often should I test restoring backups?

At least monthly for production databases, and after any major version upgrade, storage change or backup configuration change. A drill should restore to a fresh server, be timed against your RTO and include an application-level check, not just a successful exit code.

Should backups be stored in the same cloud provider?

A different region at minimum, and ideally a separate account with write-only credentials from the server and object lock enabled. A different provider adds protection against account-level incidents at the cost of egress fees during restores.

Do I need to back up Redis?

Usually not, if Redis holds caches, sessions and queues that can be rebuilt or retried. Keep durable state such as failed jobs and anything business-critical in the main database. Back up Redis only if it is your primary store for data you cannot regenerate.

Follow & Connect

event_model_payload.headline: Python Error Handling: try, except and finally Explained with Examples
event_model_payload.summary:
Originally published on CodingCush.

Python error handling uses a try block to run risky code, an except block to catch and handle any error that happens, and a finally block for code that must run no matter what, such as closing a file. Instead of letting your whole programme crash with a red error message, you catch the problem, show a friendly message, and keep the rest of your code running safely.

What Is Error Handling in Python?

Every programme meets problems sooner or later. A user types letters where a number should go. A file you expected is missing. A network connection drops halfway through a download. In Python, these problems are called exceptions, and when one happens Python normally stops the programme and prints a long traceback — helpful for you as the developer, terrifying for your user.

Error handling is simply your plan for those moments. You tell Python: "Try this code, and if something goes wrong, do this instead of crashing." It is a bit like wearing a seatbelt. You do not plan to crash, but you are very glad it is there on the one day you need it.

Python gives you four keywords for this job: try, except, else and finally. The official tutorial walks through the same ideas in the Python documentation on errors and exceptions, and it is worth keeping that page open while you learn.

The Basic try and except Block

The simplest form needs only two parts. Put the risky code inside try, and put your rescue plan inside except:

try:
    number = int(input("Enter a number: "))
    print("You entered:", number)
except ValueError:
    print("That was not a valid number. Please try again.")

If the user types 42, everything works and the except block is skipped completely. If the user types hello, int() raises a ValueError, Python jumps straight into the except block, and the friendly message appears instead of a crash. The programme keeps running afterwards, which is the whole point.

Notice that we named the exact error, ValueError. Python has many built-in exception types, and the full list of built-in exceptions in the documentation shows what each one means. Catching a specific error is almost always better than catching everything, because it stops you from hiding real bugs by accident.

Catching Different Errors in Different Ways

Real code can fail in more than one way, and each failure may need a different response. You can stack several except blocks under one try, and Python uses the first one that matches:

try:
    numerator = int(input("Enter the top number: "))
    denominator = int(input("Enter the bottom number: "))
    result = numerator / denominator
    print("Result:", result)
except ValueError:
    print("Please enter whole numbers only.")
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("You cannot divide by zero. Even Python has limits.")

Here, typing letters triggers the first block, while typing 0 as the denominator triggers the second. Each problem gets a message that actually describes it, which makes your programme far easier to use — and far easier to debug later.

You can also catch several errors with one block by grouping them in brackets, and you can read the error message itself with as:

try:
    age = int(input("Enter your age: "))
    print("Next year you will be", age + 1)
except (ValueError, TypeError) as error:
    print("Something went wrong:", error)

The variable error holds Python's own description of the problem. Printing it during development is a great habit, because it tells you exactly which line complained and why.

The official Python tutorial — reading and writing files is where most beginners meet their first exceptions.

The else Block: Code That Runs Only on Success

The optional else block runs only when the try block finishes with no error at all. Beginners often ask why it exists, when they could simply put the code at the end of try. The answer is clarity and safety: code inside try is protected by your except blocks, so an error there could be caught and hidden by mistake. Code in else is not protected, so any error it raises will still surface properly.

try:
    file = open("scores.txt", "r")
    content = file.read()
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("The scores file could not be found.")
else:
    print("File loaded successfully.")
    print(content)
    file.close()

If the file opens and reads cleanly, the else block runs. If the file is missing, only the except message runs. This pattern pairs naturally with our guide on how to read and write files in Python, where the same open, read and close steps are explained in full.

The finally Block: Code That Always Runs

The finally block is the tidy-up crew. Its code runs whether the try block succeeded, failed, or even returned early. That makes it perfect for releasing resources: closing files, closing network connections, or unlocking something you locked.

try:
    file = open("notes.txt", "r")
    print(file.read())
except FileNotFoundError:
    print("notes.txt does not exist yet.")
finally:
    print("Finished — cleaning up now.")

Whatever happens above, that final message prints. In real projects the finally block usually closes the file instead of printing, so the file is never left open by accident. An open file that never closes can lock the file for other programmes and quietly waste memory, which is nobody's idea of fun.

try, except, else and finally Compared

Here is the whole flow in one table:

Block When it runs Typical job
try Always, first Holds the risky code you want to protect
except Only when a matching error happens Handles the problem with a message or a fallback
else Only when no error happens Runs follow-up code that depends on success
finally Always, last Cleans up: closes files and connections

A useful way to remember it: try is the attempt, except is the rescue, else is the celebration, and finally is switching the lights off when you leave — it happens every single time.

Raising Your Own Exceptions

Sometimes your own code needs to report a problem. Use the raise keyword to trigger an exception on purpose, usually when input breaks a rule your programme depends on:

def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative.")
    print("Age set to", age)

try:
    set_age(-5)
except ValueError as error:
    print("Error:", error)

Writing small helper functions like this is much easier once functions feel natural, so if they still feel new, work through our beginner-friendly guide to Python functions explained with examples first. Raising clear errors early stops bad data from travelling deep into your programme, where it becomes much harder to trace.

Common Mistakes Beginners Make

Catching everything with a bare except. Writing except: with no error type catches every possible problem, including typos and real bugs, and then hides them. Your programme looks calm while quietly doing the wrong thing. Name the error you expect instead.

Leaving the except block empty. An except block that does nothing is like a smoke alarm with the batteries removed. At minimum, print or log what went wrong.

Putting too much code in try. Keep the try block small, covering only the lines that can actually fail. A huge try block makes it hard to know which line caused the error.

Forgetting finally for cleanup. If you open something inside try, close it in finally (or use a with statement for files), so it closes even when an error interrupts you.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the difference between try and finally in Python?

The try block holds code that might raise an error. The finally block holds cleanup code that runs after everything else, whether an error happened or not.

Can I use try without except in Python?

Yes, if you pair it with finally. A try and finally combination is valid and is used purely for guaranteed cleanup. A try block must have at least one except or a finally after it.

What happens if an error is not caught?

Python stops the programme and prints a traceback showing where the error happened. Nothing after that line runs, which is why catching expected errors makes your programme feel much more polished.

Should I catch all exceptions with except Exception?

Only as a last-resort safety net, for example at the very top of a programme, and always log the error when you do. For normal code, catch the specific exception you expect, such as ValueError or FileNotFoundError.

Conclusion

Error handling is what separates a script that works on a good day from a programme you can trust every day. Use try for risky code, except to handle specific problems with clear messages, else for code that should only run on success, and finally for cleanup that must always happen. Start small — wrap your user input and file reading first — and your Python programmes will instantly feel calmer, kinder and far more professional.

event_model_payload.headline: Your agent's log has 1,509 rows and zero denials. That is the problem.
event_model_payload.summary:
An agent that never refuses anything is not a working agent. It is a script with a credit card.

I keep seeing the same artefact offered as proof of control: a log where every row says allowed. Fifteen hundred rows, zero denials, exported to CSV for the auditor. It proves traffic. It does not prove that anything was ever stopped.

What a refusal actually looks like

A deny record is small and boring on purpose:

{
  "v": 1,
  "prev": "",
  "ts": "2026-10-31T09:14:02+00:00",
  "decision": "deny",
  "policy": "spend_limit_per_call",
  "requested": {"amount_usdc": 40},
  "limit": {"amount_usdc": 5},
  "subject": "agent:invoice-runner",
  "signature": "ed25519:..."
}

Four properties make it evidence rather than a note:

  1. It exists only when something was refused. If the file is empty, either nothing was stopped or nothing was checked. Both are answers.
  2. It chains. prev binds each record to the one before it; deleting a row breaks every row after it.
  3. It is signed offline. A verifier checks the chain and the signature without trusting the service that produced it.
  4. It names the policy and the numbers. "Denied" is an opinion; "asked 40, limit 5, policy spend_limit_per_call" is a fact.

The question that breaks most demos

Show me one refusal from last week, with the policy that fired.

Most systems cannot answer it, because denials are logged at the same level as successes and thrown away first.

What this is not

It is not a compliance certificate, and it does not make an agent safe. It makes one narrow claim verifiable: this action was stopped, at this time, under this policy, and the record has not been edited since. Everything else still needs a human.

If you already keep such a log, the only thing I would ask: can someone verify it without your dashboard? If yes, you are ahead of most teams shipping agents today.

I build attest, a deterministic verifier for agent artefacts — schema, emptiness, provenance, and mandate authority, one Ed25519-signed verdict. The deny log is public: https://attest.rta.lat/deny-evidence

event_model_payload.headline: Cuéntame: a local Gemma interviewer that preserves the words you actually said
event_model_payload.summary:
What I Built

In Panama, the Day of the Dead on November 2 can mean visiting a grave, cleaning it, and remembering someone through ordinary details: a Sunday meal, a phrase they repeated, the sound of a familiar place. I wanted a tool for collecting those details while the people who know them can still tell the story.

Cuéntame is a small command-line interview. Gemma runs locally through Ollama and asks one question at a time about a person you want to remember. The program saves the answers as a Markdown page. The model is allowed to ask; it is not allowed to write the person's life story. The saved page is assembled by Python from the exact answers entered by the storyteller.

My interpretation of Ghost in the Machine is a question that helps a living person remember, without pretending to be the person who is gone.

Demo

The repository has a clearly fictional formatting example:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

That command does not call a model. For the actual interview, run Ollama with gemma4:e2b, then:

python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Gemma proposes each next question using the earlier questions and answers. A fictional answer such as “Hacía arroz con coco los domingos” goes into the file verbatim. If you never answer who taught Elena to cook, the file does not claim to know.

I ran this short end-to-end check with the locally installed gemma4:e2b model and a fictional answer:

$ python3 cuentame.py --nombre 'Elena (ficticia)' --preguntas 1
¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?
> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.
Guardado en recuerdos/recuerdo-elena-ficticia.md

The resulting page contains the prompt and the original answer:

## 1. ¿Cuál es un recuerdo de comida que te gustaría compartir sobre Elena?

> Hacía arroz con coco los domingos.

The output lives under recuerdos/, which is excluded from Git. The CLI refuses to overwrite an existing memory. The public examples contain fictional answers only.

Code

yosef7 / cuentame

Local family-memory interview with Gemma and Ollama

Cuéntame

Una pequeña entrevistadora local para conservar recuerdos familiares sin pedirle a la IA que invente una biografía. Gemma, mediante Ollama en 127.0.0.1, propone una pregunta a la vez. El archivo final copia literalmente las respuestas de la persona entrevistada. Los vacíos quedan abiertos.

Proyecto creado para Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge: Week 4, tema Ghost in the Machine. La demo ficticia y las pruebas de código no equivalen a una ejecución real del modelo.

Uso

Requiere Python 3.10+ y Ollama. Descarga un modelo Gemma compatible con tu equipo y usa su nombre exacto con --modelo. El valor predeterminado es gemma4:e2b.

ollama pull gemma4:e2b
python3 cuentame.py --nombre "Elena" --modelo gemma4:e2b

Para ver solo el formato de salida, sin modelo:

python3 cuentame.py --ejemplo

Los resultados van a recuerdos/, excluido de Git. El programa no sobrescribe archivos existentes. El ejemplo usa una persona y…

View on GitHub

The project uses Python's standard library, the local Ollama /api/generate endpoint, and an open-weight Gemma model. It is MIT licensed. The README explains installation and testing; no cloud account or API key is needed.

How I Built It

The boundary is intentionally narrow:

Storyteller's answers
       |              previous Q&A
       |                  |
       |                  v
       |           local Gemma -> next question
       v
Python copies exact answers -> private Markdown file

ask_question() sends the interview history only to 127.0.0.1:11434. The prompt asks for one short, open question and forbids fabricated facts or impersonation. The program rejects empty, multiline, overlong, or non-question replies. The model response is displayed as a question; it is never used as a memory answer.

render_memory() writes the storyteller's responses as block quotes. It does not ask Gemma for a summary. That is a deliberate technical choice: a fluent summary can introduce a detail nobody said. A source-grounded keepsake is more useful than a beautiful invented biography.

The first live run revealed a practical Gemma 4 issue: with a short output limit, the model spent its tokens in its internal thinking field and returned no visible question. Setting think: false in the Ollama request produced a short question. There are three focused tests for the local request, history passed to the model, invalid model output, and literal preservation of an answer. I also completed the one-question live check above. A full family interview remains untested and should be reviewed by the storyteller.

Why Open Innovation Matters

Family recollections are private. An open-weight model running on the same laptop lets the interview continue without sending those answers to a hosted model. Markdown is a portable output: a family can read it years later without the original app or a subscription. Python and Ollama are replaceable pieces rather than a service that must remain online.

This does not prove a memory is historically accurate. The storyteller may misremember, and Gemma may ask a poor or leading question. The person using the tool should skip a question that feels wrong and review the file before sharing it. What the program can guarantee is narrower and testable: it does not turn generated prose into an attributed family fact.

Prize Category

I used Gemma as the local question generator, so this project also fits Best Use of Gemma. The same core is needed for the general Week 4 theme; no other partner service is claimed.

Prepared with AI assistance. The author approved publication.

event_model_payload.headline: Giving an AI assistant a memory of your Google search traffic that does not go stale
event_model_payload.summary:
Picture this.

You ask your AI assistant which pages bring in the most search traffic. It answers with confidence. The numbers are from three months ago, for a site you stopped managing in August.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just kept a memory of data that is no longer true.

I wanted a memory of Google search traffic that stays current, and that forgets what it should. So for Mergetober I built a Google Search Console connector for Cognee. The code lives in PR #584 for issue #4793.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph that an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Search Console. You sign in with Google, pick your properties, and it syncs how they perform in search.

Search Console gives you numbers, not prose. One row per date, query and page would be millions of documents, and an LLM would read every one. So the connector groups the data by calendar month. Each month of a property becomes:

  • an overview: totals, devices, top countries, top queries and top pages;
  • one document per top page, with the queries that led to it.

All of a property's documents share one node set. The same query in two months becomes one entity in the graph, so you can ask how it changed.

source = google_search_console_source(
    sites=["sc-domain:example.com"],  # leave it out for every verified property
    months=3,
)
await cognee.remember(source, dataset_name="search_console",
                      primary_key="id", write_disposition="merge")

Sign-in is OAuth 2.0 with the read-only scope. Run login.py once, in the browser, and the token is cached in a private file.

Data that is late and sampled

Two things make Search Console different from a normal source.

First, the newest data is late and preliminary. Google publishes final numbers about two days behind, and it can still revise the last days. So the connector reads final data only. A month stays open until it is a few days older than that lag. An open month is read again on every run. Then it is read one last time and closed, and a closed month is never read again. Only documents whose text changed are sent on, so an unchanged run makes no LLM call.

Second, the data is sampled. Google returns the top rows by clicks and leaves out rare queries for privacy. That means a query that disappears from a response is not a deleted query, and the rows never add up to the totals. Every document says so.

What gets forgotten

A property you remove, deselect, or lose verification on is forgotten whole, with its documents. I added a few safety rules, because a wrong delete is worse than a missed one:

  • A failed request never deletes anything. The run stops and the next one starts from the same spot.
  • A month that suddenly comes back empty keeps its documents. Google having a bad moment is more likely than every click vanishing.
  • If Google throttles the sync, it stops cleanly and keeps the months it already read. It waits a minute at most at a time, because a sync holds Cognee's lock. The next run picks up where it stopped.
  • If the account suddenly sees no verified property, the run stops instead of forgetting everything.

The real test

First I tested against a fake: an in-memory copy of the Search Console API. It aggregates real fact rows, sorts by clicks, hides the newest days, and withholds rare queries. 110 tests pass on Python 3.10 and 3.12, and on Cognee 1.6.4 and 1.6.6. They include a run of the whole Cognee pipeline with a mocked LLM. The 106 that skip that pipeline run also pass on Python 3.14. But a fake only proves what you thought to fake.

So I signed in with a real Google account. I created an OAuth client, went through the browser consent, and listed my properties. Google returned my one property, with siteOwner permission. I then ran the connector against it twice.

Here is the honest part. My only property is a personal portfolio, and it had no search traffic in the last 80 days. So the real sync found no data. It created no documents and raised no errors. The second run skipped the two closed months:

run 1  {'sites': 1, 'periods': 3, 'closed': 0, 'documents': 0, ...}
run 2  {'sites': 1, 'periods': 1, 'closed': 2, 'documents': 0, ...}

The bug only a real Google could find

That empty property showed me something my fake got wrong.

When there is no data, I expected Google to answer with an empty response. It does not. For a query with no dimensions, it returns one row of zeros: {'clicks': 0, 'impressions': 0, ...}.

My code read "one row" as "there is data". It would have written an overview that says "0 clicks" for every empty month. Worse, it would have walked straight past my own safety rule. A month that had real documents and then got a zero row back would have been overwritten with zeros, instead of being kept.

Now a row with zero impressions counts as no data. I changed the fake to behave the way Google does, so a test fails if this comes back.

The same run settled a smaller question. Google accepts the lowercase type and dataState values that I send.

What I did not test

I did not test any of this against real traffic: documents built from real queries and pages, a recall on real data, a changed month, or forgetting a real property. Those paths are covered by the fake-API tests and the mocked-LLM pipeline test, not by a live account. I also never saw a real 429 from Google.

Rare queries are left out of the lists by design. A long tail of low-click pages shows up in the totals only. Sitemaps and URL inspection are not ingested. The README lists these.

Try it

The example is in packages/connector/google-search-console/examples/. You need a Google Cloud project with the Search Console API enabled, an OAuth client of type Desktop app, and a verified property. The README walks through it.

If you point it at a property with real traffic, I would love to hear what breaks.

event_model_payload.headline: Run your own model endpoint on a rented GPU with vLLM: your own API key, an SSH tunnel, and an optional LoRA adapter
event_model_payload.summary:
Short answer: rent a GPU with SSH access, install vLLM in a fresh Python environment, start it so it listens only on the instance's own localhost, require an API key of your own, and reach it from your machine through an SSH tunnel. If you have a LoRA adapter for the same base model, vLLM can serve it next to the base model under its own name. When you are done, copy out what you need and destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU, and the GPU rental in this guide is ours. Each step ends with a "What to check" line, because versions, flags and defaults change.

Which kind of endpoint is this?

CloudGPU's terms (section 6) say that each running instance with a service URL gets a public HTTPS address; these URLs are "hard to guess but they are not authenticated by default", and if you need authentication you configure it inside your instance, for example an API key on your Ollama deployment. The docs say that templates that serve an API, such as Ollama and ComfyUI, get such a URL.

This guide takes a different route on purpose. You rent a raw GPU, run vLLM on it, and do not publish any URL: the server listens only on the instance's own localhost, requires your own API key, and you reach it through an SSH tunnel from your machine. That gives you an endpoint only you can use, as long as you keep the SSH access and the key to yourself.

vLLM's own security guide is clear about the limits of the key: --api-key protects only the endpoints under the /v1, /v2, /inference and /cohere prefixes, other endpoints on the same server are not covered, and it says not to rely on --api-key alone. It also notes that some underlying components may listen on all network interfaces. So treat the key as one layer, keep the tunnel as the way in, and do not send anything to the instance that you would not put on a rented machine.

Read these things first

  1. The license of your base model. An adapter sits on top of a base model, so the base model's license applies to what you serve. The walkthrough uses Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, whose model card lists the Apache-2.0 license (read 2026-10-27). If you use a small Llama or Gemma model instead, read the Llama 3.2 Community License or the Gemma Terms of Use first, including what they say about derivative models. This guide gives no legal conclusions.
  2. What your adapter was trained on. Use only data you have the right to use; CloudGPU's acceptable use policy (section 1.8) prohibits training on datasets you do not have rights to use. If your adapter was trained on text generated through DeepSeek's API and you publish its outputs, DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) require you to label published outputs as AI-generated (section 3.1).
  3. CloudGPU's terms. Read the terms before you rent. Section 1 says compute comes from third-party data centres and supplier networks, which can change, so this guide does not claim your data stays on any particular machine.

What you need

  • A CloudGPU account with balance. GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page. Payment is by card or USDT (payments).
  • A terminal with ssh, scp and Python 3 on your own machine.
  • Optional: a LoRA adapter trained on Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, stored in the usual Hugging Face PEFT layout (a folder with adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors), for example the one from the self-critique guide in this series. Without an adapter, do everything below and skip the adapter parts; you will serve the base model only.

What to check: ssh -V prints a version, and python3 --version prints a version. If you have an adapter, its folder contains the two files above.

Step 1: make your endpoint key and look at your adapter (on your own machine)

The key is a long random string that only you and the server know. Generate one:

python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"

Keep it in a password manager. Make a new one for every instance; never reuse a key from another service.

If you have an adapter, open adapter_config.json in its folder and note two fields: base_model_name_or_path and r (the LoRA rank).

What to check: the command printed a long random string that you have stored somewhere other than a shell history you share. For an adapter, base_model_name_or_path is mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (if not, the adapter belongs to another base model and this guide's command will not match it), and r is a number you can compare with the rank limit in Step 4.

Step 2: rent a raw GPU

On Deploy, choose Raw GPU and a card. The CloudGPU docs say that every template is a ready-made image with root SSH and that for anything a template does not cover you rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. The docs' GPU table lists 16 GB as the minimum VRAM for models from 0.5B to 8B parameters; vLLM also needs Linux and an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher, according to its installation page. A 7B model in 16-bit needs memory for the weights plus a cache for requests, so a card with more than the minimum is the easy fix if the server reports it cannot fit.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. If you have an adapter, upload its folder from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -r -P  ./adapter-selfloop @:/workspace/

What to check: ssh -p @ connects, nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and (with an adapter) ls /workspace/adapter-selfloop shows adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors.

Step 3: install vLLM in a fresh environment

The vLLM installation page recommends uv for the Python environment. uv can be installed from PyPI (see the uv installation page). On the instance:

pip install uv
cd /workspace
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto

These lines follow the vLLM page as read on 2026-10-27; if the page now shows different commands, use its commands.

What to check: with the environment active, vllm --version prints a version, and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" prints True. If the install stops with an error, read the error text and the troubleshooting parts of the vLLM page.

Step 4: start the server on localhost, with your key

Use your own key in place of . With an adapter:

cd /workspace && source .venv/bin/activate
nohup vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key  \
  --tokenizer-mode hf \
  --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 16 \
  --lora-modules selfloop=/workspace/adapter-selfloop \
  > /workspace/vllm.log 2>&1 &

Without an adapter, remove the --enable-lora, --max-lora-rank and --lora-modules lines.

What the flags do, from the vLLM serve reference and LoRA page: --host 127.0.0.1 keeps the HTTP server on the instance's localhost; --api-key makes requests under /v1 carry that key; --tokenizer-mode hf uses the Hugging Face tokenizer instead of letting auto pick the mistral_common tokenizer for Mistral models; pinning it is meant to match how an adapter was trained with the Hugging Face tokenizer, so drop the flag if your adapter was trained another way; --lora-modules name=path registers the adapter under the name selfloop; --max-lora-rank must be at least the adapter's r and the docs list the allowed values (the default is 16), so if your r from Step 1 is larger than 16, use the next allowed value. The key is visible in the instance's process list while the server runs, which is one more reason to use a fresh key per instance.

Wait until the log says the server is ready before you send a request. If the process exits, read the end of the log with tail -n 50 /workspace/vllm.log. A message about memory for the cache is fixed by adding --max-model-len 8192 or by choosing a card with more memory.

What to check: on the instance, curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models | head -n 1 prints an HTTP status line that is not a success (an authentication error is expected, because you sent no key), and curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer " http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models prints JSON that lists the base model and, with an adapter, selfloop.

Step 5: open the tunnel and call your endpoint (on your own machine)

In one terminal, open the tunnel. Nothing is printed while it runs; leave it open:

ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -p  @

If local port 8000 is already used, pick another local port (for example -L 8001:127.0.0.1:8000) and use it in the URLs below. In a second terminal:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer "

Now the same request through the OpenAI SDK (pip install openai on your own machine). Put this in a file named ask.py:

import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key=os.environ["ENDPOINT_KEY"])

BASE = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
ADAPTER = "selfloop"  # delete this name from the loop below if you started without an adapter

question = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

for name in (BASE, ADAPTER):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=name,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    print("==", name)
    print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
    print()

Run it with the key in an environment variable, not in the file:

export ENDPOINT_KEY=""
python3 ask.py "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

Any tool that lets you set an OpenAI-compatible base URL and a key can use the same two values (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and your key) while the tunnel is open.

What to check: the curl call lists the model names you expect; ask.py prints one answer per model name; and a call with a wrong or missing key is refused rather than answered. If the tunnel command prints "address already in use", use another local port. Reading two answers is not a test of your adapter; for that, use questions the adapter never saw and compare them yourself, as in the self-critique guide.

Step 6: stop, copy out what you need, destroy

Close the tunnel with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Before you destroy anything, copy what you want to keep. The docs have a section called "What to save before you destroy an instance"; read it in the CloudGPU docs. For example, copy the server log from your own machine:

scp -P  @:/workspace/vllm.log ./

Then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). Minutes spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed. The endpoint key was meant for this instance only; do not reuse it.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your Dashboard, and the curl call from Step 5 now fails to connect.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • This is your own endpoint, with your own API key, reached through your own SSH tunnel. It is not a public URL.
