  • Per CloudGPU's terms (section 5), you keep ownership of any data, models, code or output you create on or upload to an instance, and CloudGPU says it does not access, inspect, copy or back up the contents of your instance except in three listed cases: a credible report of a violation of section 3, valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties.
  • Per the same terms, destroying an instance permanently deletes its local storage, and you are responsible for backing up what you want to keep.
  • Whatever you send to the endpoint is processed on that rented instance. Do not send secrets or personal data you would not put on a rented machine.
  • If you call a model through CloudGPU's AI API instead of your own instance, the request is forwarded to the model provider and its terms apply; see the privacy policy.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • vLLM: installation (NVIDIA CUDA), serving LoRA adapters, serve command reference, security guide.
  • uv: installation.
  • Licenses: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card, Llama 3.2 Community License, Gemma Terms of Use.
  • DeepSeek: Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026).
  • CloudGPU: terms, acceptable use policy, privacy policy, docs, pricing.

event_model_payload.headline: What cron expression runs every 5 minutes?
event_model_payload.summary:
A cleanup job was supposed to run every five minutes. The crontab was saved at 10:03. The log showed 10:05, then 10:10. That is not a late start. The expression is tied to the clock, at minutes 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, and 55. Saving the file does not start a countdown. Classic cron also does not hold the next start while the previous process is still running, so a six-minute command overlaps itself. What follows is the five-field form used by Vixie cron and cronie, not a systemd timer and not Quartz.

Five fields, then the command

A standard line is five time fields and then the command. None of them is a seconds field.

Field Range A star means
Minute 0–59 Every minute
Hour 0–23 Every hour
Day of month 1–31 Every day of the month
Month 1–12 Every month
Day of week 0–7 Every day of the week

On Vixie cron and on cronie, Sunday is both 0 and 7. Monday is 1 and Friday is 5, so 1-5 is Monday through Friday. Some other schedulers accept only 0 for Sunday. Read crontab(5) on the host before using 7. Prefer numbers to names such as MON or JAN.

The fields use the daemon’s timezone, so 0 0 * * * is midnight there, not necessarily UTC. Honor CRON_TZ only if that host’s crontab(5) says so.

Every 5, 10, 15, and 30 minutes

Each line below is aligned to the clock, and each one includes minute 0.

*/5 * * * *     # 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55
*/10 * * * *    # 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
*/15 * * * *    # 0, 15, 30, 45
*/30 * * * *    # 0 and 30

The edit time is not stored. A line installed at 10:03 still waits for 10:05, then 10:10.

5-59/5 * * * * starts the range at 5, so minute 0 is left out. Use it only when you mean to skip the top of the hour. For a plain every-five-minutes job, keep */5 * * * *.

Drop the step when you want an hour or a day instead.

0 * * * *       # every hour, at minute 0
0 0 * * *       # every day at 00:00
0 9 * * *       # every day at 09:00
0 9 * * 1-5     # Monday through Friday at 09:00

0 * * * * fires 24 times a day, 0 0 * * * once at midnight, and 0 9 * * 1-5 on weekdays at 09:00 because day-of-month stays a star. The either-day rule starts only when both day fields are restricted. A day field that starts with *, including */2, is not restricted. See why cron runs on the wrong day.

How a step is counted

A step is a range plus /n. In the minute field, * means 0-59, so */5 is 0, then every fifth minute through 55. Twelve runs an hour.

In the hour field, 0 */2 * * * is minute 0 of every second hour: 00:00, 02:00, 04:00, and so on through 22:00.

Day of month starts at 1, not 0. On Vixie cron and cronie, * in that field is 1-31, so 0 0 */5 * * is midnight on the 1st, 6th, 11th, 16th, 21st, 26th, and 31st. It is not the dates divisible by 5 (the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, and 30th). If the daemon is not cronie, test that list. A cron expression generator shows the five fields. It does not simulate one daemon’s calendar, and it does not install the job.

Mistakes that move the run

Copy the five fields, not the sentence beside them. Crontab does not read “every five minutes.”

Do not add a seconds field in front. The other fields shift right. Quartz uses six fields, or seven with a year, and seconds come first. Spring uses that six-field form. EventBridge’s six fields are minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, and year, with no seconds field. Quartz and EventBridge both use ? in a day field. A five-field line matches neither shape.

Traditional Vixie cron does not skip a run because the previous process is still going. If the work must not overlap, take a lock in the command, for example with flock, and leave the schedule alone. systemd timers and queue workers can differ. This warning is about classic cron.

Cron’s PATH is often shorter than a login shell. Call the program by its absolute path. A stored “next run” in an API is often a Unix timestamp, not an expression. Read that number on the Unix timestamp converter. Do not paste it into the minute field.

*/5 cannot mean “five minutes from now.” Sleep in a process, or use a queue delay. The daemon still starts the command once, when the minute begins, not again at second 10 or 20.

Try it for one cycle

Point a throwaway line at a file you can delete.

*/5 * * * * date >> /tmp/cron-every-5.log

Wait until two lines are written. The minutes should be five apart, and each minute should be divisible by 5. Then delete the line. Some hosts log the start with journalctl -u cron. Others still use syslog. Use the log that machine keeps.

Full guide with the FAQ and a cron generator: https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-every-5-minutes

event_model_payload.headline: Black October: 9 AI Dev Platforms Were Breached. Rotate Your Keys Today
event_model_payload.summary:
TL;DR: In October 2026, at least nine AI developer platforms disclosed security incidents, according to a Wiz research post published on October 30. The common thread is that attackers went after stored environment variables, especially the ones that unlock AI models. Stolen keys were tested within about 30 minutes and later resold. If you have an OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock or similar key sitting in a hosting or dev platform, rotate it today. Then put a spend cap on it and narrow its scope. There's a checklist below.

Any other month, one AI platform breach would have been the security story of the week. This month there were nine, and Wiz's researchers had to point out that hardly anyone was connecting them. They called it "Black October".

I'm writing this for developers and small teams, not security specialists. Most of us have pasted an LLM API key into a platform dashboard at some point because it was the quickest way to get a demo running. This post covers what's confirmed so far, what attackers did with the keys, and what you can do in the next hour.

The nine incidents, as Wiz lists them

This is Wiz's list with the disclosure dates they give:

Date (Oct 2026) Platform
Oct 6 Fireworks AI
Oct 9 Andromeda
Oct 14 Zeabur
Oct 15 Lightning AI
Oct 16–17 OpenCode
Oct 20 Railway
Oct 23 Warp
Oct 28 CommandCode
Oct 30 Northflank

What's known about each one varies a lot. Most of these incidents are still under investigation, and Wiz says detailed technical information mostly isn't public yet. Here's what the post does say, attributed to the companies:

  • Fireworks, OpenCode and Warp reported signs of an "agent swarm" attack. Andromeda called its incident part of an "industry-wide attack."
  • OpenCode and CommandCode explicitly attributed their incidents to an attempt at "distillation" (using stolen model access to train or copy models).
  • Fireworks, Zeabur and Lightning AI attribute their root causes to credential access. Wiz notes that Lightning AI had previously been hit by a supply chain attack in the Mini-Shai Hulud campaign.
  • Railway has released a preliminary report and says it believes initial access came through "privilege escalation in our build infrastructure."
  • Warp has suggested the root cause was a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode points to a "legacy system."
  • Zeabur has published a full write-up and, according to Wiz, will shut down because of the incident.

There's no single shared vulnerability. Wiz says no single vulnerability or dependency links these attacks. The shared pattern is what the attackers wanted: every public report describes targeted hunting for stored environment variables, with a focus on those that grant AI access.

Unconfirmed: whether one group is behind all nine incidents. Wiz doesn't claim that, and neither do I.

Why your AI key is now worth stealing

Wiz ties the campaign to two trends. Agentic attacks let attackers compromise targets faster. LLMJacking is the other: stolen model access gets resold through "LLM broker" services. The resale market is what turns a stolen key into money quickly, and that's why so many people are now hunting for these keys.

Wiz also traced downstream abuse of two enterprise keys, which it could attribute to one of the vendor breaches. Both cases are worth reading in full. These are the numbers that matter for your own setup:

  • Validation came fast. In both cases, the first unauthorised call came within 30 minutes of the reported credential access at the vendor. It was a single model call from a residential IP, made during a one-minute sweep that tested stolen keys across multiple organisations.
  • Case A (unrestricted key): Over about 30 hours, until the key was remediated, the actor made approximately 800,000 Bedrock calls, about 90% of them successful. The key's policy allowed global.* cross-region inference profiles, which spread the load across regions, so only about 6% of calls were throttled.
  • Case B (restricted key): This key only allowed Bedrock through us.* inference profiles. The reseller pool asked for global.*, so thousands of calls failed at first. Then a checker found the working us.* model IDs, and over about 13 hours a single address made approximately 1.7 million calls, over a million of them successful. Most of the rest were throttled by the account's regional quotas.
  • The cost: At list price, Wiz estimates these two cases alone likely ran up over $100k in usage.

Case B doesn't show that restrictions save you. They didn't stop the abuse. They slowed it, and the regional quotas limited it. That's the right way to think about scoping: it limits how much damage a stolen key can do, and you still have to rotate fast.

Wiz also mentions anecdotal impact reports from social media: alleged theft of about $371,000 in cryptocurrency using crypto keys stored in Railway, and stolen AI access (for example from OpenCode) producing consumer bills in the hundreds to thousands of dollars. Treat these as reports, not confirmed totals.

Northflank's advice is the right default for everyone

Northflank, the most recent platform on the list, put out the clearest customer guidance I've seen this month. Its status page told every customer to assume all environment variables have been decrypted and to rotate everything: secrets on workloads, secret groups and global secrets. It also recommended disabling public access to database addons, and said multiple users had confirmed their AI keys had been used. A later update told customers to revoke credentials with the issuing provider (not just change them in Northflank) and to check AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity.

You don't have to be a Northflank customer for this to apply. If a platform that stores your env vars discloses an incident, the safe assumption is that every value in those env vars is gone. You rotate the keys first and investigate later.

The rotation checklist (do this today)

Start with every platform that holds an AI key: hosting, CI, notebook services, agent platforms and coding tools.

  1. Make the inventory. List every AI key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock/IAM, Google, Mistral, OpenRouter and so on), and note which platform and which environment holds it. If you can't say where a key lives, assume it's on one of these platforms.
  2. Create the replacement first. Generate a new key at the provider, update the platform secret and redeploy. Confirm the app works.
  3. Revoke the old key at the provider. Deleting it from the platform isn't enough, because the attacker has a copy. Revocation has to happen where the key was issued.
  4. Do the non-AI secrets too. Database URLs, payment keys, cloud credentials, webhook signing secrets and crypto wallet keys. Northflank's "rotate everything" applies here, and the Railway reports show attackers take whatever they find.
  5. Read your usage and billing logs. Look for unfamiliar models, regions or IPs, traffic at odd hours, or a sudden jump in output tokens. In Wiz's cases there was only a trickle of validation calls for days before the flood, so a small amount of strange usage still matters.
  6. Report abuse. Tell the provider and the platform. Some providers can help with fraudulent usage if you report it quickly.
  7. Write down the date. Add each rotation to your secrets inventory, so the next incident takes ten minutes, not an afternoon.

Spend caps and scoped keys: treat AI keys like payment cards

A stolen AI key works like a payment card with no limit. So put a limit on it.

  • Set the hardest spend limit your provider offers. Most AI provider consoles have per-project or per-workspace budgets, limits or alerts. A hard limit is better than an alert, and an alert that wakes someone up beats a monthly invoice. Set it close to your real usage, not 10x above it.
  • One key per app, per environment. Production, staging and that weekend prototype shouldn't share a key. When one leaks, you rotate one key and you can see exactly whose usage it was.
  • Restrict models and regions. On Bedrock, use IAM policies that allow only the specific models and inference profiles your app calls. Case B shows the effect: abuse was delayed and capped by regional quotas instead of spreading worldwide.
  • Use short-lived credentials where you can. Workload identity or OIDC role assumption for cloud model access means there's no long-lived key in an env var to steal.
  • Keep keys out of the platform where possible. If a platform supports pulling secrets from a dedicated secrets manager at runtime, use that, so the platform holds a reference instead of the value.

What we do on our projects

On our own client projects we keep production AI keys in the cloud provider's secrets manager rather than pasting them into every dashboard. Each environment gets its own key, and each provider account gets a budget alert. When a platform we use discloses an incident, we rotate first and investigate second. This month, the habit that made the biggest difference was keeping a written list of where every key lives. Rotating takes minutes. Working out where the keys are is the slow part.

What's still unknown

  • Whether the incidents share an operator. Wiz links resale infrastructure to keys from at least one breach, but says it can't definitively tie the resellers to the initial compromises.
  • Root causes for most of the nine platforms. Only Zeabur has a full write-up and Railway a preliminary report, according to Wiz.
  • How many customer keys were taken in total. No platform has published that number yet.

I'll update this post if the platforms publish more detailed reports.

Where does your AI API key live right now?

Be honest: how many dashboards hold a copy of your OpenAI or Anthropic key at the moment? Have you set a spend limit on any of them? Tell me in the comments. I'm curious whether this month has changed how anyone stores these keys.

event_model_payload.headline: Stop Debugging Services That Never Ran: Practical systemd Conditions and Asserts on Linux
event_model_payload.summary:
You enable a unit, start it, and get... nothing. No error. systemctl start exits 0. systemctl status says inactive (dead). There is no traceback, no failed state, no red text — just a service that quietly declined to exist.

Nine times out of ten that is not a broken unit file. It is a Condition...= line doing exactly what it was told, and systemd skipping the start silently.

Conditions are one of the least documented and most useful parts of unit files. They let a single image boot on a laptop and a server, let a backup job refuse to run when the backup disk is not mounted, and let a provisioning unit run exactly once. Used carelessly, they produce the invisible-service problem above.

Everything below was checked against systemd 257.13 on Debian 13, with the observed output quoted verbatim.

Conditions are checked at job execution time, not at enable time

A condition is not a dependency and not an install-time guard. It is evaluated at the moment the queued start job is about to run — after the units ordered before it have finished. That timing matters: a condition can test state that After= dependencies just produced.

The semantics, from systemd.unit(5):

  • Multiple conditions are ANDed. All must hold.
  • A leading ! negates a single condition.
  • A leading | turns a condition into a triggering condition: if any triggering condition holds, and all non-triggering conditions hold, the unit starts. The order is |! — pipe first, exclamation second.
  • Assigning the empty string (ConditionPathExists=) resets the entire condition list.
  • All path checks follow symlinks, except ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink=.

If a condition fails, systemd skips the start "mostly silently". The unit does not enter failed. Ordering is still honoured, and dependent units are pulled in as if the unit had activated — the skip happens at the last moment.

Conditions versus asserts: the difference you can observe

Asserts are the loud twin. Same argument syntax, prefixed Assert..., but an unmet assert fails the job, not the unit.

I wrote two throwaway units to confirm the behaviour on systemd 257. One had ConditionPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker, the other AssertPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker. Results:

# condition unit
$ systemctl start lyra-condtest.service
$ echo $?
0
$ systemctl status lyra-condtest.service
○ lyra-condtest.service - Lyra condition test
     Loaded: loaded (/run/systemd/system/lyra-condtest.service; static)
     Active: inactive (dead)

# assert unit
$ systemctl start lyra-asserttest.service
Assertion failed on job for lyra-asserttest.service.
$ echo $?
1

The journal tells the real story:

lyra-condtest.service - Lyra condition test skipped, unmet condition check ConditionPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker
lyra-asserttest.service: Starting requested but asserts failed.
Assertion failed for lyra-asserttest.service - Lyra condition test.

So: conditions skip quietly and succeed; asserts fail loudly and exit non-zero. Neither one moves the unit into failed. That last point surprises people — an assert does not set the unit's failed state, it only fails the queued job, so systemctl is-failed still reports inactive. If your monitoring only looks at unit state, you can miss an assertion failure entirely.

The rule of thumb: use a condition when the unit genuinely does not apply to this machine (wrong architecture, no battery, already provisioned). Use an assert when the unit absolutely should run but something the administrator must fix is wrong.

The conditions that earn their keep

There are around thirty conditions. These are the ones that solve real problems.

Hardware and platform

  • ConditionArchitecture= — x86-64, arm64, native; valued on mixed-architecture fleets sharing one image.
  • ConditionVirtualization= — vm, container, or a specific engine: kvm, docker, podman, systemd-nspawn, private-users. ConditionVirtualization=!container is the standard way to keep a unit off containers.
  • ConditionCPUFeature= (v248) — x86 and arm64 feature checks, e.g. avx2 or arm64.bti.
  • ConditionSecurity= — selinux, apparmor, ima, audit, uefi-secureboot, tpm2. Useful for units that only make sense with a given LSM active.
  • ConditionACPower= — true holds if at least one AC connector is connected or if no AC connector is known at all. That fallback keeps server units working; it also means the condition passes on machines that cannot report power state.
  • ConditionCapability= — checks a capability in the manager's bounding set, not the service's effective set.

Runtime environment

  • ConditionPathExists= and friends — !path negation, ConditionPathExistsGlob=, ConditionPathIsDirectory=, ConditionPathIsMountPoint=, ConditionPathIsReadWrite=, ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink=, ConditionDirectoryNotEmpty=, ConditionFileNotEmpty=, ConditionFileIsExecutable=.
  • ConditionPathIsEncrypted= (v246) — true only when the backing block device is dm-crypt/LUKS. It does not detect ext4 per-directory encryption, and it does not look through loopback devices.
  • ConditionKernelCommandLine= — matches a word or an exact key=value from /proc/cmdline. Read from /proc/1/cmdline when systemd runs as a container payload, which is a nice detail when your condition behaves differently in a container.
  • ConditionFirstBoot= and ConditionNeedsUpdate= — image provisioning primitives.
  • ConditionUser= / ConditionGroup= — mainly for user managers. ConditionUser=@system matches the system UID range, and is pointless for the system manager, which always runs as root.

Lab 1: a maintenance switch that actually stops work

The highest-value pattern in the whole set is a negated path check used as an operator kill switch.

# /etc/systemd/system/nightly-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly restic backup to /srv/backup
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

# Operator pause switch: touch this file and this unit will not run.
ConditionPathExists=!/etc/backup/pause

# Refuse to run unless the backup target is actually mounted.
ConditionPathIsMountPoint=/srv/backup

# If the config is missing, fail loudly instead of silently doing nothing.
AssertPathExists=/etc/restic/password

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo touch /etc/backup/pause
sudo systemctl start nightly-backup.service   # exits 0, does nothing
sudo journalctl -u nightly-backup.service -b --no-pager | tail -2
# ... skipped, unmet condition check ConditionPathExists=!/etc/backup/pause
sudo rm /etc/backup/pause

Two things worth noticing. The condition is re-evaluated on every start attempt, so it also gates timer-driven activations. And it is not a watchdog: nothing re-checks the file until something starts the unit again.

If you pair this with systemd.timer, put the condition on the service, not the timer. A condition on the timer prevents the timer from starting at all; a condition on the service is evaluated at each activation, which is what you usually want for a pause switch.

Lab 2: only back up on AC power

A laptop that starts a three-hour rsync at 20% battery is a design bug.

# ~/.config/systemd/user/laptop-sync.service
[Unit]
Description=Sync home directory to NAS
ConditionACPower=true
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=%h/bin/sync-home.sh

Test it without unplugging anything:

systemd-analyze condition --unit=laptop-sync.service
echo $?    # 0 = would start, 1 = would be skipped

On a desktop with no battery, ConditionACPower=true passes because no AC connector is known. That is documented behaviour, not a bug — and the reason this condition is safe to ship in a shared unit.

Lab 3: assert required state, then override it in a drop-in

Vendor units sometimes assert paths you do not have. Resetting an assert requires clearing the list first, because AssertPathExists= is a list setting:

# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service.d/10-local-paths.conf
[Unit]
# Clear every inherited assertion of this name, then re-add ours.
AssertPathExists=
AssertPathExists=/etc/myapp/config.toml
AssertDirectoryNotEmpty=/var/lib/myapp

Without the empty assignment you would end up with both the vendor's path and yours, and the unit would fail the job for a path that is irrelevant on this host.

This is also the correct place for "the database directory must exist before we start", because a missing directory is an operator problem, not a reason to silently skip.

Lab 4: run provisioning exactly once

First boot semantics are built in: ConditionFirstBoot=yes is true while /etc was unpopulated at boot, and it stops being true once the manager finishes its startup phase.

# /etc/systemd/system/site-provision.service
[Unit]
Description=One-time site provisioning
ConditionFirstBoot=yes
Wants=first-boot-complete.target
Before=first-boot-complete.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/provision.sh
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

The Wants= plus Before= pairing is the part people skip. first-boot-complete.target is what marks first boot as done; ordering the provisioning unit before it means an aborted first boot re-runs the unit next time instead of leaving a half-configured system.

ConditionNeedsUpdate=/etc solves the neighbouring problem — running a migration only when /usr is newer than the .updated stamp file. Units using it should order themselves before systemd-update-done.service, which resets that stamp.

Debugging a unit that will not start

Work in this order. Every command below is read-only.

# 1. What did systemd decide, and why?
systemctl show myapp.service -p ActiveState -p ConditionResult -p AssertResult
# ActiveState=inactive
# ConditionResult=no
# AssertResult=yes

# 2. Which condition failed? (works without starting anything)
systemd-analyze condition --unit=myapp.service
# myapp.service: ConditionPathIsMountPoint=/srv/backup failed.
# Conditions failed.

# 3. The journal has the human-readable reason.
journalctl -u myapp.service -b --no-pager | grep -i -e condition -e assert

Two practical notes from actually running these:

  • systemctl show -p Conditions prints Conditions=[unprintable] because it is a structured property. Use ConditionResult for the verdict and systemd-analyze condition for the detail.
  • systemd-analyze condition also accepts bare expressions, which is handy for testing syntax before you commit a unit: systemd-analyze condition 'ConditionPathExists=/etc/passwd' prints a per-condition pass/fail line and exits 1 if the set fails.

And the trap that started this article: systemctl start exits 0 when a condition skips a unit. Any deploy script that checks only the exit code will happily report success while the service never ran.

Where conditions go wrong

  • They are not dependency control. The man page is explicit: conditions are evaluated long after jobs are queued, so they are "not suitable for conditionalizing unit dependencies". If B must not run without A, use Requires=/After=, not a condition on B.
  • Nothing re-evaluates them spontaneously. A condition that becomes true later does not start the unit. Use a .path unit or a timer to create the start job.
  • They do not interact with Restart=. A skipped unit never started, so there is no restart to perform. A unit whose condition starts failing on a later start will just stop, cleanly.
  • Broken symlinks fail ConditionPathExists= because path checks resolve symlinks. Use ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink= to test the link itself.
  • ConditionKernelVersion= is unportable. Distributions backport features into older version strings, so a version number does not tell you what the kernel supports. The man page calls this out directly.
  • systemd-analyze verify does not evaluate conditions. It catches unit syntax and missing executables, not whether a condition will pass on this host.

The short version

A unit that will not start and will not explain itself is almost always a condition. Check ConditionResult, run systemd-analyze condition --unit=, read the journal line, and the mystery collapses in about ten seconds.

Use conditions for "this unit does not belong here", asserts for "this host is misconfigured and someone should know", and never for dependency logic. The negated path check alone — ConditionPathExists=!/etc/service/pause — is worth adding to every scheduled job you own.

References

  • systemd.unit(5), Conditions and Asserts: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.unit.html
  • systemd-analyze(1), condition verb: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-analyze.html
  • systemctl(1): https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemctl.html
  • systemd-detect-virt(1) for the virtualization identifiers accepted by ConditionVirtualization=
  • machine-id(5), First Boot Semantics: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/machine-id.html
  • systemd.special(7) for first-boot-complete.target

event_model_payload.headline: OpenDsec: self-hosted sandboxes for RL rollouts and code-running agents
event_model_payload.summary:
If you train a model with agentic reinforcement learning, every rollout needs somewhere to run code: install a package, run the tests, hit the network, write files. Thousands of those run at once. When the training job is preempted they all have to stop together and come back later. And when you want to explore one state several ways, you want copies of the environment as it is right now, memory included, not fresh ones from the image.

Hosted sandbox services cover part of this. We wanted all of it on our own machines, so we built OpenDsec and published it under the AGPL.

This is the first post in a series about it. Here: what it does, what it looks like to run, and where its limits are.

One run, start to finish

That is a real recording on one bare-metal server: the install script, then a short Python program that creates a Firecracker microVM, runs print(6*7) in it and forks it into four copies. The six minutes of building and installing are cut; everything after runs at real speed. The 0.16 s is the whole API call (placement, boot, the in-VM agent ready), measured from the client.

The program is the whole client side:

import asyncio, time
from opendsec import DSecClient, DSecRunArgs

async def main():
    async with DSecClient() as client:
        t = time.perf_counter()
        sb = await client.run_sandbox(DSecRunArgs(backend="microvm", image="root/py:3.12"))
        print(f"ready in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s (whole API call: placement + boot)")
        print((await sb.run_shell("python3 -c 'print(6*7)'")).stdout.strip())
        t = time.perf_counter()
        forks = await sb.fork(count=4)    # copies with memory
        print(f"forked 4 in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
        await asyncio.gather(*(s.stop() for s in [sb, *forks]))

asyncio.run(main())

Where the design comes from

DeepSeek described the sandbox platform behind their agentic RL training in DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec). OpenDsec follows that paper: a stateless apiserver, IAM with nested projects and quotas, a watcher that aggregates scheduling state, power-of-k placement where each node has the final say on admission, layered images loaded on demand, a default-deny network policy, and pausing a whole task at once.

Where the paper leaves things open, or where we chose differently, the decisions are ours: nftables and a DNS proxy instead of eBPF for the network policy, any shared file system (NFS, CephFS, JuiceFS) instead of 3FS for images, and Firecracker with memory snapshots as the main backend. The design document marks every point as either from the paper or our own.

OpenDsec is an independent project. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek and contains none of its code.

What you get

  • Three kinds of sandbox behind one API: Firecracker microVMs, containers, and full QEMU VMs. Exec, files, processes, PTY and HTTP into the sandbox work the same on all of them.
  • Fast microVMs. About 0.1 s for the VM to boot, about 55 ms to create one from a memory snapshot, about 50 ms to resume one from a pause.
  • Fork with memory. fork(count=N) pauses the source for about 10 ms and gives you N copies with the same processes, imports and open ports. On one node the copies share memory pages; on another node they pull the snapshot from the source node directly.
  • Scale. One 384-thread node took a burst of 5120 microVMs in 37 s. A two-node cluster took 8192 containers in one burst with no failures.
  • Task-level pause. Pause every sandbox of a training task in one call, push their memory to swap, resume them later.
  • E2B compatible. Code written for E2B's SDKs runs against your own machines after changing three environment variables (E2B_API_URL, E2B_SANDBOX_URL, E2B_API_KEY). E2B's own Python and JS SDK checks pass.
  • Operable. mTLS between all components, a Raft-replicated IAM, Prometheus metrics and alerts, staged rollouts with automatic rollback, offline installs. Restarting or upgrading any component leaves running sandboxes alone.

All numbers are our own measurements on our bare-metal machines; the design document says how each was measured. Your hardware will give different ones. For example, the fork time depends on the file system under the sandbox state: 0.1 s on XFS, which copies memory files by reflink, and about 1 s on ext4, which has to copy them.

Try it on one machine

You need a Linux x86_64 machine with systemd and cgroup v2 (we test on Ubuntu 24.04). MicroVMs also need /dev/kvm, so use bare metal or a cloud VM with nested virtualization; without it you get containers only.

sudo -i
apt update && apt install -y make git python3-venv
curl -fsSL https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar -C /usr/local -xz
git clone https://github.com/kernflux/opendsec && cd opendsec
deploy/quickstart.sh

The script checks the machine, builds everything, downloads Firecracker and the guest kernel (checked against pinned hashes), installs the components as systemd services with their own CA, imports python:3.12 from Docker Hub, and runs one container and one microVM as a check. Then:

python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install ./sdk/python
. /root/opendsec-ops/demo.env
.venv/bin/python sdk/python/examples/quickstart.py

deploy/quickstart.sh --uninstall removes all of it again.

What it is not (yet)

  • It is 0.x. Interfaces may change before 1.0.
  • We have only verified Ubuntu 24.04 hosts. Other distributions, real GPUs and multi-node Kubernetes are untested.
  • It is infrastructure you run. There is no hosted version.

License

The servers are AGPL-3.0. The Python SDK, the Go client and the API definitions are Apache-2.0, so programs that only call OpenDsec are not bound by the AGPL. A commercial license is available for closed modifications.

Next in this series

Firecracker, gVisor and containers compared for running AI-generated code: isolation, start time, memory and compatibility, with measurements.

The code is at github.com/Kernflux/opendsec, the docs at kernflux.github.io. Issues and questions are welcome there or in the comments.

event_model_payload.headline: Managed Services vs Portability: When Cloud Lock-In Is Worth It and How to Stay Cloud-Agnostic
event_model_payload.summary:
Lock-in is worth accepting when a managed service saves more engineering time than it will cost to leave, and it is not worth it for the core compute runtime that every workload depends on. The runtime is the layer you should keep portable. Control Plane keeps the runtime portable across AWS, GCP, Azure, and your own servers, including on premises, while still letting workloads use each cloud’s managed services through Universal Cloud Identity, Control Plane’s credential-free access to AWS, GCP, and Azure services. This guide offers an honest framework for deciding when lock-in is a fair price, a service-by-service map of proprietary services to portable alternatives, and a practical exit plan you can act on today.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Lock-in becomes a problem when it is accidental, unmeasured, or applied to the wrong layer.

  • When lock-in is worth it: A managed service materially reduces staffing, improves reliability, or accelerates delivery, and you have documented the exit cost.
  • When it is not: The service is your core compute runtime or your identity plane, where switching costs compound across every workload. Managed Kubernetes is fine when workload definitions stay in standard manifests.
  • The portable layer to protect: Application code, container images, deployment pipelines, data formats, and the runtime itself.
  • The exit plan: Maintain a service-dependency register, test data exports quarterly, keep infrastructure as code, and budget for egress.
  • How Control Plane fits: Control Plane runs workloads on AWS, GCP, Azure, your own Kubernetes clusters through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own machines, from bare metal to on-premises servers, joined as locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), all mixed in one environment. Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads call AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code. You get managed-service benefits without surrendering runtime portability.

For a deeper look at the full lock-in landscape, see our companion piece on how to avoid cloud vendor lock-in.

When Do Managed Platform Services Increase Vendor Lock-In?

Managed services create lock-in in five ways, and they differ in how hard they are to undo.

Proprietary APIs

When your application code calls a vendor-specific API, every call is a line of migration debt. The more deeply integrated the API, the more refactoring a move requires. This is the most visible form of lock-in and the one engineers think of first.

Data Gravity and Egress Costs

Large datasets are expensive to move. Cloud providers charge for data leaving their network, and the sheer time to transfer terabytes or petabytes creates inertia. Transfer time and egress fees grow with data volume, so the cost of leaving rises the longer you stay.

Proprietary Identity and Permissions

IAM systems differ significantly between AWS, GCP, and Azure. Policies, roles, and service accounts written for one cloud do not translate to another. Migrating identity is tedious, error-prone, and security-sensitive.

Proprietary Serverless Runtimes

Functions tied to a specific serverless platform carry implicit dependencies on the platform’s event model, scaling behavior, timeout limits, and deployment tooling. These are difficult to replicate elsewhere.

Contract Terms

Committed-use discounts, enterprise agreements, and reserved capacity create financial lock-in. Breaking a contract early can mean forfeiting discounts or paying penalties.

Data gravity and proprietary identity are the hardest to undo. Moving data is a large but bounded transfer project, while identity must be redesigned and re-audited for every workload. Proprietary APIs come next, then serverless runtimes, then contract terms, which have a defined end date.

Decision Framework: When Is the Managed Option Worth It?

Use this table to evaluate each service category.

Service Category Lock-In Level Switching Cost Drivers When the Managed Option Is Worth It
Compute runtime High Every workload depends on it; migration touches everything Rarely worth locking in. Keep this portable.
Kubernetes Medium Storage classes, load balancer and ingress annotations, CNI plugins, and the link between pods and cloud IAM (EKS Pod Identity, Workload Identity Federation for GKE, Microsoft Entra Workload ID) are cloud-specific Use managed Kubernetes for convenience, but keep workload definitions portable via standard manifests.
Relational databases Medium Schema compatibility is high (PostgreSQL, MySQL), but managed features (replication, backups) differ Worth it when the managed service handles HA, patching, and backups you would otherwise staff for.
NoSQL databases High Proprietary query languages, data models, and SDKs (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB) Worth it for rapid prototyping or when throughput requirements match the service exactly. Document the exit path.
Object storage Low (API), Medium (large datasets) S3-compatible APIs are a de facto standard, though Azure Blob Storage uses its own API. Egress fees and transfer time scale with data volume. Lifecycle rules, storage classes, and event notifications differ by provider. Almost always worth it. For large buckets, budget for egress and keep an export or replication path.
Queues and streaming Medium Client SDKs, delivery semantics, ordering, and retention differ across SQS, Pub/Sub, Event Hubs, and Kinesis Worth it for most workloads. Wrap producers and consumers behind an interface, or use a Kafka- or AMQP-compatible managed service so client code stays portable.
Serverless functions High Event sources, cold-start behavior, and runtime constraints are proprietary Worth it for event-driven glue code, spiky traffic, and low-traffic endpoints. For core business logic, keep handlers thin and put the logic in plain libraries that can also run in a container.
Identity High Policies, roles, and trust relationships are cloud-specific Abstract identity where possible. Use workload identity federation over long-lived keys.
Observability Medium Proprietary query languages and dashboards; data export is usually feasible Worth it when the team is small. Adopt OpenTelemetry for instrumentation to keep the data portable.
Managed AI / model APIs Medium-High Model-specific prompt tuning, fine-tuning artifacts, and pricing models Worth it for speed to market. Use an abstraction layer for model calls.

Which Open-Source Alternatives to Managed Databases Best Support Portability?

When a managed service’s lock-in level is too high for your risk tolerance, open-source alternatives can restore portability. The table below maps common managed services to their portable counterparts.

Managed Service Portable Alternative Notes
Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL, Azure Database for PostgreSQL PostgreSQL Schema-level compatibility is strong. Run it on any cloud or on premises.
Amazon RDS for MySQL, Cloud SQL for MySQL MySQL or MariaDB Widely supported. MariaDB began as a MySQL fork and is compatible with many MySQL workloads, though the two have diverged in newer versions.
DynamoDB, Cosmos DB ScyllaDB or Apache Cassandra Both are wide-column databases. Apache Cassandra is open source. ScyllaDB is source-available since 2025 and offers Alternator, a DynamoDB-compatible API. Cosmos DB also offers a Cassandra-compatible API, which eases moves in either direction.
Amazon SQS, Google Pub/Sub Apache Kafka, NATS, or RabbitMQ Kafka excels at high-throughput streaming and is the closer match for Pub/Sub. RabbitMQ is mature for task queues and is the closer match for SQS. NATS is lightweight and supports both patterns.
AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions, Azure Functions Standard containers Package functions as containers to decouple from the serverless runtime. Any container platform can run them.
Amazon ElastiCache Redis or Valkey Redis is widely deployed and, from Redis 8, is available under AGPLv3 as well as source-available licenses. Valkey is a BSD-licensed Linux Foundation fork of Redis 7.2.4. ElastiCache supports both engines, so the move is usually low-friction.

The right choice depends on your team’s operational capacity and workload requirements, not on a blanket recommendation.

When Is It Worth Accepting Platform Lock-In for Managed AI Services?

AI services are the newest and fastest-moving category of managed cloud offerings. The lock-in calculus here is different because the field changes so quickly that today’s best model may not be tomorrow’s.

Evaluate Five Factors

  1. Speed to market. Managed AI APIs remove the work of hosting, scaling, and updating models, so you can ship a first version without building GPU infrastructure. If time-to-market is critical, the lock-in trade-off is often favorable.
  2. Model quality. Some proprietary models outperform open alternatives on specific tasks. Benchmark on your data before committing.
  3. Data sensitivity. Sending data to a third-party model API may conflict with compliance requirements. On-premises or private inference may be necessary.
  4. Cost at scale. API pricing that looks cheap at prototype volume can become prohibitive at production scale. Model the cost curve before you commit.
  5. Ability to swap models behind an abstraction. If your application calls models through a thin abstraction layer, switching providers is mostly a configuration change. You still need to re-test prompts and tool calls, re-run evaluations, and re-embed stored vectors if the embedding model changes.

Use managed AI APIs for experimentation and initial deployment, and build an abstraction layer for model calls from day one. For production inference at scale, portable containers running on GPU infrastructure give you the flexibility to move between clouds or neoclouds as pricing and performance shift. On Control Plane, workloads can attach NVIDIA GPUs, and MK8s lets you join GPU servers from other providers as locations. See our guide on running AI inference across multiple GPU clouds.

What Multi-Cloud Infrastructure Patterns Reduce Dependence on Proprietary Managed Services?

Six engineering patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services when applied across the stack.

Containerize the Runtime

Package every workload as a standard container image that follows the OCI image spec. An image packages application code and dependencies so any runtime that supports the OCI image spec can run it. Portability still has limits. Build multi-architecture images if you may run on both x86 and Arm nodes, keep configuration in environment variables or secrets rather than the image, and treat kernel features and GPU drivers as host dependencies.

Infrastructure as Code

Define all infrastructure in code with tools such as Terraform, OpenTofu, or Pulumi. Infrastructure as code makes environments reproducible and auditable. On Control Plane, the CLI, console, and Control Plane’s own Terraform and Pulumi providers all work through the same Control Plane API, so your definitions stay consistent.

Open Protocols and Formats

Prefer open standards: OpenTelemetry for observability, S3-compatible APIs for object storage, SQL for relational data, AMQP or NATS for messaging. Open protocols reduce the surface area of proprietary dependency.

Isolate Provider-Specific Code Behind Interfaces

When you do use a managed service, wrap it behind a well-defined interface in your application code. A storage interface, a queue interface, or a model-call interface means you can swap implementations without touching business logic.

Scheduled Data Replication

For critical datasets, replicate data to a second cloud or to your own infrastructure on a schedule. This keeps a current copy outside the primary provider for migration or disaster recovery. Replication adds ongoing egress and storage costs, so limit it to data you cannot rebuild.

Workload Identity Instead of Long-Lived Keys

Long-lived API keys and service account credentials are both a security risk and a portability obstacle. Use workload identity federation to grant short-lived credentials scoped to the current task. On Control Plane, Universal Cloud Identity does this for AWS, GCP, and Azure services.

For a broader look at cloud-native design principles that support portability, see our guide on cloud-native architecture principles, patterns, and building portable systems.

Should I Choose PaaS or SaaS for Vendor Lock-In and Portability?

Choose a PaaS when portability matters. A PaaS runs your application, so you keep the code, images, and data. A SaaS product replaces the application, so only your data can move.

The platform provides the runtime, networking, and operational tooling. If the PaaS uses standard container images and open APIs, your application is portable even if the platform itself is not.

With SaaS, the contract usually says you own your data, but the export format and completeness depend on the vendor. You do not control the application logic, the runtime, or the operational model. Portability depends entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities and API compatibility. Switching SaaS providers often means rebuilding workflows from scratch.

A PaaS keeps these advantages only if it runs standard containers and does not impose a proprietary build or deployment format. For a detailed comparison of PaaS options, see our guide to the best PaaS providers in 2026.

What Contract Clauses Should I Require for Data Portability and Service Exit?

Before signing a cloud or managed-service agreement, negotiate terms that protect your ability to leave. The following checklist covers the essentials.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Consult qualified counsel for your specific situation.

  • Data export format and timeline. The provider must export your data in a standard, documented format within a defined number of days after termination.
  • Exit assistance. The contract should include a transition period during which the provider supports migration activities.
  • Egress fee terms. Cap or waive egress fees during the transition period. At minimum, get clarity on per-GB costs.
  • Notice periods. Ensure notice periods for termination are reasonable and symmetric. You should not need 12 months’ notice to leave.
  • Termination for convenience. You should be able to terminate without cause, subject to reasonable notice and payment for services consumed.
  • Price change caps. Limit annual price increases to a defined percentage, or require advance notice that gives you time to evaluate alternatives.
  • Data deletion certification. After migration, the provider must certify in writing that your data has been deleted from their systems, including backups, within a specified timeframe.

Maintain a service-dependency register that tracks each provider-specific component, its owner, data location, export procedure, portable alternative, and estimated exit cost. Review it quarterly.

How Control Plane Approaches Portability

Control Plane is the platform for running unbreakable apps and agents. It combines any cloud, neocloud, and bare metal into what Control Plane calls a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a set of locations a workload runs across.

On Control Plane, a workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC, and a global endpoint routes each request to the nearest healthy location, so you get failover without paying for idle standby capacity. The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations, and those locations can be on different providers.

During the October 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, which lasted about 15 hours, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had no downtime, and their workloads were “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” according to Control Plane internal incident telemetry. See designing systems that survive the inevitable.

Control Plane runs serverless, standard, stateful, cron, and VM workloads on AWS, GCP, and Azure, on clusters you already run through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), on your own machines (bare metal or VMs) turned into managed locations with Control Plane Managed Kubernetes (MK8s), and on premises. On Control Plane-provided compute, there is no Kubernetes cluster you have to operate, and Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, Capacity AI (Control Plane’s right-sizing of CPU and memory based on historical usage), built-in observability, and security. You pay for the CPU and memory you reserve, by the millicore and the megabyte, with no contracts or minimums. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed separately.

On Control Plane, the template catalog deploys open-source data services such as PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Cassandra, Kafka, NATS, RabbitMQ, and Redis or Valkey into a GVC, so the portable alternatives above run on the same platform as your workloads.

Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity gives workloads short-lived, least-privilege access to 600+ AWS, GCP, and Azure services, with no long-lived cloud keys in your code. The Control Plane MCP server uses the same API as the CLI, console, and Terraform and Pulumi providers, so Control Plane complements the infrastructure as code you already run.

Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Customers typically cut compute costs 30 to 50 percent compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure.

You use each cloud’s managed services where they earn their place, and your runtime stays free to move. For a walkthrough of deploying the same application across AWS, GCP, and Azure, see how to run the same app on AWS, GCP, and Azure.

FAQ

When do managed platform services increase vendor lock-in?

Managed services increase lock-in when they expose proprietary APIs, store large volumes of data subject to egress fees, impose proprietary identity models, or use non-standard event systems. The more deeply your application integrates with these surfaces, the higher the switching cost.

Which open-source alternatives to managed databases best support portability?

PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Apache Cassandra, Redis, and Valkey are widely adopted portable alternatives. ScyllaDB is a source-available option with a DynamoDB-compatible API. For queues and streaming, Apache Kafka, NATS, and RabbitMQ replace proprietary offerings.

When is it worth accepting platform lock-in for managed AI services?

It is worth it when speed to market is critical and you build an abstraction layer over model calls from day one. Avoid deep lock-in for production inference at scale; portable containers on GPU infrastructure give you pricing and performance flexibility.

What multi-cloud infrastructure patterns reduce dependence on proprietary managed services?

Containerize workloads, define infrastructure as code, use open protocols (OpenTelemetry, S3-compatible APIs, SQL), isolate provider-specific code behind interfaces, replicate critical data on a schedule, and use workload identity instead of long-lived keys.

Should I choose PaaS or SaaS for vendor lock-in and portability?

Choose PaaS when portability is a priority, because you keep control of your application code, container images, and data. SaaS portability depends almost entirely on the vendor’s data export capabilities.

What contract clauses should I require for data portability and service exit?

Require data export in standard formats within a defined timeline, exit assistance during a transition period, capped or waived egress fees, reasonable notice periods, termination for convenience, price change caps, and written data deletion certification.

How does Control Plane keep the runtime portable while using managed services?

On Control Plane, workloads (containers or VMs) run on a Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), Control Plane’s set of locations that can span AWS, GCP, Azure, Kubernetes clusters you bring through Control Plane’s Bring Your Own Kubernetes (BYOK), and your own servers on premises. Control Plane’s Universal Cloud Identity lets those workloads use AWS, GCP, and Azure managed services without long-lived cloud keys in your code.

Is multi-cloud the same as cloud-agnostic?

No. Multi-cloud means using more than one cloud provider. Cloud-agnostic means your workloads can move between providers with minimal effort. You can be multi-cloud and still deeply locked in to each provider’s proprietary services. True cloud-agnostic architecture requires portable runtimes, open standards, and abstraction layers.

Does containerization solve cloud portability?

Only partly. Containers make application code and dependencies portable, as long as images are built for the CPU architectures you target. They do not solve portability for databases, storage, identity, networking, or observability, which often remain cloud-specific. You need additional patterns, such as open protocols and interface abstraction, to address those layers.

How often should I test my cloud exit plan?

Test your cloud exit plan on a fixed schedule set by how critical the system is, such as quarterly for revenue-critical workloads, and after any major architecture change. Each test should export real data and deploy a representative workload on an alternative cloud.

event_model_payload.headline: Trouble finding a motivated co-founder
event_model_payload.summary:
For context, I'm a college student running a consumer mobile app business. I've been working on my own apps solo for about 6 months (both development and marketing), and since I'm majoring in engineering, it's been quite hard to balance running this business with my studies.

This is what originally led me to seek a co-founder in the consumer mobile app space who's strong in UGC/distribution. The problem is that It's very hard for me to find someone who actually cares and is willing to put in the work.

Some past scenarios:

1) I made a profile on the YC Co-founder matching site and got matched with a guy who eventually ghosted me after two weeks. I got matched with a couple of other people as well, but they never answered any of my introduction DMs

2) I met another guy on this one app called "Ambitious" who seemed pretty motivated (he was also a student) and was also interested in mobile apps. But after creating literally 1 single video, he said that he didn't have the time for this and left.

I've tried talking to other students at my university as well, but I don't really go to a prestigious school or one that's known for cs/tech, so not many people are interested in startups or stuff like that.

I'm not quite sure what I should do at this point, so I wanted to come on here and ask for tips and advice for finding a co-founder.

event_model_payload.headline: GEMM Tutorial and UlmBLAS
event_model_payload.summary:
In 2014 I wrote a tutorial on how to write an efficient matrix multiplication that can achieve near peak performance. This is actually not achieved by some Strassen algorithm variant. It's achieved through a cache friendly algorithm (exploiting the cache hierarchy) and SIMD register instructions.

The tutorial showed how to achieve that step by step. Beginning with a naive implementation using three loops. Then using buffers to first cache matrix blocks and then performing the matrix product block wise. That actually means you make copies of blocks and then do computations with the blocks. Sounds stupid but makes sense: Assume you have square N x N blocks then cost of make making a copy is O(N^2) and for the computation it's O(N^3). If the computation with the copied/cached blocks is much faster this actually pays of.

Anyway the details are explained in the tutorial. As the university web server has changed many times after 2014 I moved it to GitHub: https://github.com/michael-lehn/gemm-tutorial

From the tutorial I created ulmBLAS (ulm makes sense, as I work at Ulm University) which is a complete BLAS implementation. Recently I started with a tutorial for the matrix multiplication with Cuda. Currently there is not much text, I just outlined a possible step by step approach to go from naive to a performant implementation (actually the goal was to be on par with NVIDIA's cuBLAS; but it's more on parish ... but I think still gives an idea). It in the cuda subdirectory of ulmBLAS: https://github.com/michael-lehn/ulmBLAS

event_model_payload.headline: UI extensions now support a larger number of locales
event_model_payload.summary:
UI extensions no longer have a 256 KB limit on the combined size of their locale files. As of October 30, 2026, you can add more languages to an extension without hitting a combined size limit at deploy. This applies to all apps with UI extensions, and no action is required.

What changed

Previously, the total size of the locale files in a UI extension's locales folder couldn't exceed 256 KB. Extensions with many languages could reach that limit and fail to deploy, which forced you to trim translations or drop languages.

That combined limit is now removed. The 30 KB limit for each individual locale file still applies. Locale files keep the same format, file naming, and fallback behavior described in the checkout UI extension localization guide. You don't need to change how you structure translations.

Who's affected

This change applies to every app that includes UI extensions with locale files, on all API versions. Existing extension versions keep working as before. New deploys aren't limited by the combined size of locale files.

If your extensions were under the old limit, nothing changes for you.

What to do

You don't need to take any action. If you previously removed languages or shortened translations to stay under 256 KB, you can add them back:

  1. Add the locale files you need to your extension's locales folder, for example de.json or pt-BR.json. Keep each file under 30 KB.
  2. Run shopify app deploy to release a new app version.
  3. Preview the extension in a development store with the store or customer locale set to one of the new languages, and confirm the translated strings appear.

Related docs

  • Localize a checkout UI extension
  • Localize a customer account UI extension

event_model_payload.headline: New trusted vault origin signal in Payments Apps API
event_model_payload.summary:
The Payments Apps API 2027-01 release candidate adds payment_method.data.trusted_vault_origin to credit card payment and verification requests. Payment app developers can use this optional Boolean to handle missing CVV for cards from a vault Shopify trusts. Adoption is optional and requires Shopify enablement.

What changed

Shopify can include trusted_vault_origin in both encrypted card and payment_instrument payloads. Read it from payment_method.data, outside the encrypted card details or payment_instrument object.

  • true: Don't reject the payment or verification for missing CVV alone. A CVV may still be present.
  • false or absent: Keep your existing CVV rules for that flow, including flows that accept payments without CVV.

Continue your fraud checks, 3-D Secure authentication, and validation of any CVV provided. The signal does not identify the originating vault. See the trusted vault origin reference for the field contract and payload examples.

Who's affected

This applies to payments apps that handle requests with payment_method.type set to credit_card. Your extension must use API version 2027-01 or later, and Shopify must enable the field for your app. Changing the API version does not enable it.

Shopify omits the field on earlier API versions, when it has not enabled the field for your app, or when it has no value to send.

What to do

No immediate production migration is required. Use the 2027-01 release candidate for testing and keep production apps on a supported stable version.

To prepare your integration:

  1. Review your payment and verification handlers. Add support for the optional field and the CVV handling described above.
  2. For integration testing, set your development extension's api_version to 2027-01. Confirm Shopify has enabled the field for your app before expecting Shopify to send it.
  3. Test true, false, and an absent field, with and without CVV. Cover each payload format your app supports and repeat the cases for verification requests if applicable. Confirm that missing CVV does not cause rejection for true, while false and absence preserve your existing handling.

Related docs

  • Configure payments extensions
  • Test credit card payment requests
  • Shopify API versioning

event_model_payload.headline: Gift Card line_item_id will become read-only in REST Admin API version 2027-01
event_model_payload.summary:
In REST Admin API version 2027-01 and later, the line_item_id property on the Gift Card resource is read-only. Shopify ignores the property in create and update requests. Remove it from those requests before you upgrade.

What changed

In REST Admin API version 2027-01 and later, apps can't add, replace, or clear a gift card's line-item association through Gift Card create or update requests. Shopify ignores any line_item_id value in those requests.

Gift Card responses still include existing line-item and order associations. Earlier API versions keep their current behavior.

Who's affected

This change affects you if all of the following are true:

  • Your app uses the REST Admin API Gift Card resource.
  • Your app includes line_item_id when it creates or updates gift cards.
  • You plan to upgrade your app to API version 2027-01 or later.

If your app only reads line_item_id from Gift Card responses, or stays on an API version earlier than 2027-01, then this change doesn't affect you.

Why this matters

A gift card's line-item association records the order line item that created the gift card. Making line_item_id read-only stops apps from changing the link between a gift card and its order.

Breaking changes and migrations

In REST Admin API version 2027-01 and later, Shopify accepts create and update requests that include line_item_id and ignores the property. The gift card keeps its existing line-item association.

Before you upgrade to API version 2027-01:

  1. Find the REST Gift Card create and update calls that send line_item_id.
  2. Remove line_item_id from those request payloads.
  3. If your app needs the existing association, then keep reading line_item_id from Gift Card responses.

There isn't a replacement API for adding, replacing, or clearing a gift card's line-item association from outside Shopify.

To confirm the migration:

  1. Send a create or update request without line_item_id.
  2. Read the same gift card, and check that its line_item_id value didn't change.

Action required

Before you move production traffic to REST Admin API version 2027-01 or later, stop sending line_item_id in Gift Card create and update requests. Otherwise, your app's records might not match Shopify's, because Shopify keeps the original association.

Related docs

  • REST Admin API Gift Card resource for 2027-01
  • Shopify API versioning

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing Geist Serif
event_model_payload.summary:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Geist Sans

x-height

710

750

Descender

-150

-200

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.
