event_model_payload.headline: How to compare more than 5 keywords in Google Trends (and get daily data for years)
event_model_payload.summary:
Google Trends has two limits that come up the moment you use it for real work:

  1. You can compare at most 5 terms at once.
  2. For any range longer than about 9 months, you get weekly or monthly points, not daily ones.

Both limits have the same cause, and the same fix. Every response from Google is scaled 0-100 against its own peak. A "50" in one request and a "50" in another mean nothing relative to each other. You can still join requests, though, as long as they share something you can measure in both. Then you rescale one to match the other.

I spent a while getting this right for a scraper I built. Here's what works and what doesn't.

Comparing more than 5 keywords

The usual advice is to put one anchor keyword in every batch of 5 and rescale each batch by the anchor's total. It works until your keywords have very different sizes.

Google rounds every value to a whole number. Compare "coffee" with "kombucha" and kombucha comes back as 0 or 1 on most days, so most of its signal is lost. If coffee is your anchor, every small keyword gets crushed. If kombucha is your anchor, coffee overflows and you can't rescale it at all.

The fix is to run it in two passes:

  1. Rough pass. Batch everything against one anchor, only to rank the keywords by popularity.
  2. Precise pass. Sort by that ranking and cut the list into batches where each batch shares one keyword with the previous one: [1,2,3,4,5], [5,6,7,8,9], [9,10,...]. Neighbours in popularity end up together, so nothing gets rounded to zero, and the shared keyword links each batch to the last. 
import time

from pytrends.request import TrendReq


def compare_many(keywords, timeframe="today 12-m", geo=""):
    pytrends = TrendReq(hl="en-US", tz=0)

    def fetch(batch):
        pytrends.build_payload(batch, timeframe=timeframe, geo=geo)
        time.sleep(2)
        return pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns="isPartial")

    # Rough pass: rank against one anchor.
    anchor = keywords[0]  # pick something mid-popular, it must not score 0
    rough = {}
    for i in range(1, len(keywords), 4):
        df = fetch([anchor] + keywords[i:i + 4])
        rough.update((df.sum() / df[anchor].sum()).to_dict())
    ordered = sorted(rough, key=rough.get, reverse=True)

    # Precise pass: similar sizes together, one shared keyword per link.
    merged = None
    for start in range(0, max(len(ordered) - 1, 1), 4):
        batch = ordered[start:start + 5]
        df = fetch(batch)
        if merged is None:
            merged = df
            continue
        link = batch[0]
        df = df * merged[link].sum() / df[link].sum()
        merged = merged.join(df.drop(columns=link))

    return (merged * 100 / merged.max().max()).round(2)

How close does it get? I checked 7 coffee drinks against direct 5-term comparisons on the Google Trends site. Relative to chai:

Keyword Chained Google, direct
matcha 2.07 2.09
espresso 3.20 3.22
latte 1.76 1.75
kombucha 0.36 0.36

With a single anchor, kombucha came out at roughly 1 or 2 against coffee's 100, mostly rounding noise. The ladder fixed that.

Daily data for multi-year ranges

Google returns daily points for ranges up to about 269 days. For anything longer, request overlapping daily windows and rescale each window to match the previous one on the shared days:

from datetime import timedelta

import pandas as pd

WINDOW_DAYS = 260
OVERLAP_DAYS = 60


def daily_interest(keywords, start, end, geo=""):
    pytrends = TrendReq(hl="en-US", tz=0)
    merged = None
    window_start = start
    while True:
        window_end = min(window_start + timedelta(days=WINDOW_DAYS - 1), end)
        pytrends.build_payload(keywords, timeframe=f"{window_start} {window_end}", geo=geo)
        df = pytrends.interest_over_time().drop(columns="isPartial")
        time.sleep(2)
        if merged is None:
            merged = df
        else:
            overlap = merged.index.intersection(df.index)
            scale = merged.loc[overlap].values.sum() / df.loc[overlap].values.sum()
            merged = pd.concat([merged, df.drop(overlap) * scale])
        if window_end >= end:
            return (merged * 100 / merged.max().max()).round(2)
        window_start = window_end - timedelta(days=OVERLAP_DAYS - 1)

The overlap length matters more than you'd think. With a few days of overlap, one spike inside it throws off the scale of everything after it. Sixty days averages that out. For bitcoin and ethereum over 2023-2025, the stitched daily series correlates 0.997 with Google's own weekly series for the same period.

To get daily data for more than 5 keywords, combine the two: stitch each batch over time first, then chain the batches.

The part that will actually stop you: 429 errors

All of this takes many requests. Seven keywords in two passes is 4 requests. Seven keywords over 5 years of daily data is about 36. Google rate-limits Trends per IP, and you'll start seeing 429 Too Many Requests well before that.

pytrends won't save you here. It was archived in 2025, and its retries= option crashes on current urllib3 with unexpected keyword argument 'method_whitelist'. Google's official Trends API is still invite-only. What works is retrying with a growing, randomised delay, starting a fresh session after each 429, and rotating proxies once you're past a few dozen requests.

Or skip all of it

I packaged everything above, including proxy rotation and retries, into an Apify Actor. You give it a list of keywords of any length, turn on daily data if you want it, and get one dataset on a single 0-100 scale. It also returns regions, related queries and Trending Now. In a test of 30 keywords with 5 years of daily data, it returned 54,810 data points in under 2 minutes with no errors. It costs $0.002 per keyword, and keywords that fail are free.

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")
run = client.actor("rishupishu/google-trends-scraper").call(run_input={
    "keywords": ["coffee", "tea", "matcha", "espresso", "latte", "chai", "kombucha"],
    "timeRange": "today 5-y",
    "dailyData": True,
})
rows = client.dataset(run.default_dataset_id).list_items().items

Either way, the method is the same. Rescale through something the two requests share, and keep the things you compare at similar sizes.

event_model_payload.headline: The Site Moved. The Scheduler Didn't: 19 Days of Silent Background Jobs After a Migration
event_model_payload.summary:
We moved a busy local news site to a new server. The migration checklist was long and we were proud of it: files, database, media, DNS, TLS, redirects, image paths, mail, a performance pass. The home page loaded in half a second instead of four. Editors logged in, wrote stories, and published them. Every check we had was green.

Nineteen days later, during a routine look at table sizes, one number stood out. A small table that normally holds a few thousand rows had close to 600,000. Nothing was broken from the outside. The site was fast, pages returned 200, nobody had complained.

The table was big because the job that trims it had not run once since the migration. Neither had any other background job. The application's scheduler, a single crontab line, had never been added on the new server.

This post is about why that kind of failure is invisible, what it actually cost us, and the three checks we now treat as part of every move.

How the scheduler works in this application

The CMS has one scheduler entry point. The operating system runs it every minute from cron:

* * * * * /path/to/php /path/to/app/scheduler.php > /dev/null 2>&1

That one script reads a list of jobs from the database, each with its own interval, and runs whichever are due. The list is long: publishing posts that were scheduled for a future time, rolling raw visit logs up into hourly statistics, deleting old rows from logging and rate-limit tables, rebuilding sitemaps, refreshing small data widgets, sending queued notifications.

This design is convenient. Adding a job is a database row, not a server change. It is also a single point of failure that lives outside the application's code, in the system crontab of whatever user the site runs as. Copy the files and the database, and you have copied the job list but not the thing that runs it.

Why nobody noticed for 19 days

Look at what each job does and ask who would see it fail.

  • Scheduled publishing. Editors who schedule a story for 06:00 would notice when it doesn't appear. On this site the newsroom publishes immediately; nobody had scheduled anything. We checked afterwards: no posts were stuck in a scheduled state.
  • Statistics roll-up. The admin dashboard reads today's numbers from the raw log, so "today" looked fine. Only longer ranges, built from the hourly summaries, were going stale, and nobody had opened a monthly report yet.
  • Cleanup jobs. Their whole effect is that something doesn't happen: a table doesn't grow. A table that is growing gives no signal until it is big enough to slow a query or fill a disk.
  • Data widgets. Currency rates, weather and football fixtures were the only visibly stale things. We had actually noticed those during the migration and fixed them by adding a few dedicated cron lines, one per widget. That fix made the problem harder to see: the visible symptoms went away, so the missing scheduler line looked like it had been handled.

Our uptime monitor checked the home page and an article page. Both were fine. A health check that only asks "does the page render" will never see a job that didn't run, because the page doesn't depend on it today.

There is a general rule hiding here: the failure of a background job is invisible until the job's absence becomes a foreground problem. Cleanup jobs take weeks. Aggregation jobs take until someone opens a report. Publishing jobs take until someone schedules a post.

What it cost

In this case, less than it could have. No content was lost and nothing went down. The damage was:

  • A rate-limit and request log table with roughly 594,000 rows that should have held a few days of data. Inserts into it happen on every request, so it was slowly making every request a little more expensive.
  • Nineteen days without hourly statistics summaries. Summaries can only be rebuilt from raw logs that still exist. Here the raw logs were still there, because the cleanup hadn't run either. If the roll-up had stopped while the cleanup kept running, the raw data behind those reports would have been deleted on schedule.
  • A few days of security log retention that was longer than our own policy says it should be.

The more uncomfortable cost is what would have happened on a different site. On a site that relies on scheduled publishing, the morning's stories would have stayed drafts, and the newsroom would have discovered it at 06:01 on a weekday.

The fix itself was one line 

crontab -u siteuser -l > crontab-before.txt   # keep the old state
( crontab -u siteuser -l 2>/dev/null; \
  echo '* * * * * /path/to/php -d date.timezone=Europe/Istanbul /path/to/app/scheduler.php > /dev/null 2>&1' \
) | crontab -u siteuser -

Two details mattered more than the line:

  1. The per-widget lines had to go. They were now duplicates of jobs the scheduler also runs. Two copies of the same job, running at slightly different times, is its own source of subtle bugs.
  2. The site sat behind a CDN proxy, and some jobs call the site's own URLs. From the server, those requests went out to the CDN and back in, picking up rate limits and bot checks on the way. Pointing the site's own hostnames at the local machine in /etc/hosts keeps self-requests local.

Before turning the scheduler on, we checked for posts with a publish time in the past that were still waiting. A scheduler that has been off for weeks will publish all of them in its first minute. On a migrated site those can be old test posts, so look before you enable.

After enabling it, the job table told us within two minutes whether it worked:

SELECT name, last_run, last_status
FROM scheduled_jobs
ORDER BY last_run DESC
LIMIT 10;

The jobs started showing fresh last_run values, and the oversized table was left to the regular nightly cleanup instead of a manual DELETE during business hours.

Three checks we now run on every migration

1. Diff the crontabs, not just the files

Before the move, dump every crontab that touches the site: the site user's, root's, and any system cron file that mentions the site's path.

crontab -u siteuser -l
crontab -l | grep -F '/path/to/app'
grep -rlF '/path/to/app' /etc/cron.d /etc/crontab 2>/dev/null

After the move, run the same commands on the new server and compare. Any line that exists on the old server and not the new one is either a deliberate decision, written down, or a bug. We had migrated the files with rsync, the database with a dump, and the crontab with memory. Memory lost.

2. Monitor "time since last run", not "is the site up"

The scheduler already wrote a last_run timestamp for every job. Nothing was reading it. We added a check to our regular server health script that asks one question per site:

SELECT COUNT(*) AS stale
FROM scheduled_jobs
WHERE enabled = 1
  AND last_run < NOW() - INTERVAL 10 MINUTE
  AND run_every_minutes <= 5;

If a job that should run every few minutes has not run in ten, the check warns. It also warns if the site has no scheduler line in any crontab at all. This turns an invisible failure into a visible one within minutes instead of weeks.

If your application doesn't record job runs, the cheapest version is a heartbeat: have the scheduler touch a file or ping a URL every run, and alert when the file's age passes a threshold. Dead-man's-switch services exist for exactly this, and a ten-line script against a timestamp does the same job.

3. Put the scheduler in the definition of "migrated"

Our checklist said "copy cron jobs" somewhere in the middle. It now says, as the last step before anyone signs off:

The scheduler is running on the new server. Proof: the job table shows a last_run within the last two minutes for every enabled job.

A checklist item that needs a timestamp as evidence is hard to tick by accident. "Copy cron jobs" was easy to tick after adding the six widget lines, because cron jobs had, in fact, been copied.

What to take from this

  • A scheduler that lives in the system crontab is part of your deployment, even if every job it runs lives in your database.
  • Background job failures are silent by design. Plan for that by monitoring their timestamps, because their effects will show up late and somewhere else.
  • When you fix a symptom during a migration, ask what produced it. We fixed stale widgets one by one and missed that they all had the same cause.
  • Before re-enabling a scheduler that has been off, look at the queue it will process. Days of backlog can run in one minute.

We run a small fleet of news sites on the same CMS at Alesta WEB, and the stale-job check now runs against all of them as part of regular server maintenance. It is a few lines of SQL, and it would have caught this on day one.

event_model_payload.headline: A Weibo hot-search tracker that alerts on your keywords
event_model_payload.summary:
I build Qovia, the API used in this post. The script is plain Python, so you can swap in any source that returns the hot-search board as JSON.

Weibo's hot-search board is a live list of what China is talking about. If you track a brand, a person or a topic, you probably want to know the moment it shows up, not when you next remember to look. In this tutorial we'll build a small poller that:

  1. fetches the board on a schedule,
  2. checks it against your keyword list,
  3. sends an alert (to stdout and optionally a webhook) the first time a keyword appears, and not again until it has left the board,
  4. pulls a few recent posts for the matched term so the alert has context.

Setup 

pip install requests
export QOVIA_KEY=sk-qovia-...
export ALERT_WEBHOOK=https://hooks.example.com/...   # optional, any URL that accepts a JSON POST

Get a key from Qovia. Requests authenticate with Authorization: Bearer .

Step 1: fetch the board

GET /v1/raw/weibo/hot_search takes no parameters. The catalog describes it as Weibo's realtime board in rank order, with the term, its heat, Weibo's label, category and whether it is a topic, plus the topics pinned above rank 1 in pinned. Ad slots are left out, and the board changes about every minute.

import os
import requests

BASE = "https://api.qovia.ai"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['QOVIA_KEY']}"}


def get(path, **params):
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}{path}", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()["data"] or {}


board = get("/v1/raw/weibo/hot_search")
for item in board["items"][:5]:
    print(item["rank"], item["word"], item["heat"], item["label"], item["url"])

Each item has rank, word, heat, label, category, is_topic and url. Pinned items have rank: null, so treat rank as optional.

Step 2: match keywords and avoid repeat alerts

The part that makes an alert tracker usable is not firing every minute for a term that stays on the board for hours. We keep a small JSON state file of terms we have already alerted on, and drop a term from it once it leaves the board, so it can alert again if it comes back.

import json
import pathlib

KEYWORDS = ["新能源", "小米", "苹果"]          # substrings to watch for
STATE = pathlib.Path("alerted.json")


def load_state():
    return set(json.loads(STATE.read_text())) if STATE.exists() else set()


def check(board, alerted):
    entries = board.get("items", []) + board.get("pinned", [])
    on_board = {e["word"]: e for e in entries}
    hits = []
    for word, entry in on_board.items():
        if word in alerted:
            continue
        matched = [k for k in KEYWORDS if k in word]
        if matched:
            hits.append((matched[0], entry))
    new_state = alerted & set(on_board) | {e["word"] for _, e in hits}
    return hits, new_state

Matching is a plain substring test. If you need fuzzier matching (variant spellings, English names), this is the function to extend.

Step 3: add context to the alert

A hot term on its own doesn't tell you why. GET /v1/raw/weibo/search takes a keyword and, optionally, start_date and end_date (YYYY-MM-DD, Beijing time) and a page. Search for the matched board term and include a few post snippets:

from datetime import date


def context(word, n=3):
    today = date.today().isoformat()
    res = get("/v1/raw/weibo/search", keyword=word, start_date=today, end_date=today, page=1)
    return [p["text"][:120] for p in res.get("items", [])[:n]]

Per the catalog, search text may be cut and results carry no interaction counts, so use them for context, not for ranking. Date handling is deliberately simple here: date.today() uses your machine's timezone, and the API's dates are Beijing time, so near midnight the two can disagree.

Step 4: notify 

def notify(keyword, entry, snippets):
    lines = [f"Weibo hot search: '{keyword}' matched '{entry['word']}'"]
    if entry.get("rank"):
        lines[0] += f" (rank {entry['rank']})"
    lines.append(entry["url"])
    lines += [f"- {s}" for s in snippets]
    text = "\n".join(lines)
    print(text, "\n")
    hook = os.environ.get("ALERT_WEBHOOK")
    if hook:
        requests.post(hook, json={"text": text}, timeout=30)

Many chat tools accept a JSON body with a text field; adjust the payload to whatever your destination expects.

Step 5: the loop 

import time

INTERVAL = 300  # seconds

alerted = load_state()
while True:
    try:
        board = get("/v1/raw/weibo/hot_search")
        hits, alerted = check(board, alerted)
        for keyword, entry in hits:
            notify(keyword, entry, context(entry["word"]))
        STATE.write_text(json.dumps(sorted(alerted), ensure_ascii=False))
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        print("request failed, will retry:", e)
    time.sleep(INTERVAL)

For production, run the loop body from cron or a scheduled job instead of while True, and load the state file each time; the logic is the same.

What it costs

In the catalog, GET /v1/raw/weibo/hot_search and GET /v1/raw/weibo/search are each $1 per 1,000 calls, and a call that returns no data is not charged. So the polling cost is simply your poll rate times that price: as arithmetic, one poll every 5 minutes is 288 board calls a day. Context lookups only happen when a keyword hits. See the pricing page for the current terms.

The board changes about every minute, so a 5-minute interval can miss a term that appears and drops off between polls. Shorten INTERVAL if that matters to you; it is a cost versus latency trade-off.

Ideas to extend it

  • Alert only when a term enters the top N ranks, using rank.
  • Track heat between polls to alert on fast risers.
  • Store every poll to build a history of when your keywords trended.

This article was written with the help of AI.

event_model_payload.headline: Keep a source log, get a clean reference list: a free Python research kit for APA and MLA
event_model_payload.summary:
Most citation mistakes in essays and theses don't happen while writing the reference list. They happen weeks earlier, when you read a paper, copy a quote into your notes and forget the page number. Or you save the same article twice under slightly different titles.

Plagx Research Kit is a free, open-source notebook that fixes this at the source. You log each source as you read it, and Python turns the log into a correct APA 7 or MLA 9 reference list. It also checks the log for duplicates and missing details, and compares your draft's in-text citations against it.

👉 Open the notebook in Google Colab. Click Runtime → Run all. No setup is needed.

It also gives you templates to download: a source log, a literature matrix, an annotated bibliography and a research plan.

1. The source log

A source log is a spreadsheet with one row per source. These columns are the minimum you need to cite a source and find it again later:

Column Example
id smith2020
type article-journal, book, chapter, webpage
authors Smith, John Allen; Lee, Kate
year, title, container Year, title, and journal/book/site name
volume, issue, pages, doi, url Whatever applies
notes, quote, quote_page Your summary, plus any exact quote with its page number

Recording the page number next to every quote is the habit that saves the most time later.

2. From log row to citation

The notebook uses plagx-cite, an MIT-licensed Python package with no dependencies. It works with CSL-JSON, the format Zotero, Mendeley and Crossref export, so each log row is mapped to one CSL-JSON reference:

pip install plagx-cite

from plagx_cite import format_reference, cite_in_text

ref = {
    "id": "smith2020",
    "type": "article-journal",
    "title": "Feedback timing and revision quality in undergraduate essays",
    "author": [{"family": "Smith", "given": "John Allen"}, {"family": "Lee", "given": "Kate"}],
    "issued": {"date-parts": [[2020]]},
    "container-title": "Journal of Academic Writing",
    "volume": "12", "issue": "3", "page": "45-67",
    "DOI": "10.1234/jaw.2020.045",
}

print(format_reference(ref))
# Smith, J. A., & Lee, K. (2020). Feedback timing and revision quality in undergraduate essays.
# Journal of Academic Writing, 12(3), 45–67. https://doi.org/10.1234/jaw.2020.045

print(cite_in_text(ref, page="52"))               # (Smith & Lee, 2020, p. 52)
print(cite_in_text(ref, narrative=True))          # Smith and Lee (2020)
print(cite_in_text(ref, style="mla", page="52"))  # (Smith and Lee 52)

The example sources here and in the notebook are made up. The DOIs aren't real.

3. Check the log before you write

check_references finds duplicates (same DOI, or same title and first author) and missing details. In the notebook's example log, the same paper was saved twice: once with title-case capitalisation and a full https://doi.org/ link, and once without. Another source has no year:

from plagx_cite import check_references

report = check_references(refs)
for issue in report["issues"]:
    print(issue["level"], issue["ref"], issue["message"])

# error   smith2020b  Possible duplicate (doi and title match) of smith2020: smith2020, smith2020b
# warning chen2021    No year (will show as n.d.)

The check runs locally and nothing is sent over the network. DOI lookups are optional and off by default.

4. Match the draft against the log

The most common reference-list mistake is a source cited in the text that never made it into the list, or the other way round. The notebook finds APA-style citations such as (Smith & Lee, 2020, p. 52) or Garcia (2018) with a regular expression and compares them with the log:

import re

CITATION = re.compile(r"([A-Z][\w'-]+)(?: (?:&|and) [A-Z][\w'-]+| et al\.)?,? \(?(\d{4})")

draft = """Early feedback changes how students revise (Smith & Lee, 2020, p. 52).
Garcia (2018) recommends paraphrasing from notes. Several studies support
peer review (Chen, 2021; Patel, 2019)."""

cited = {(name.lower(), year) for name, year in CITATION.findall(draft)}
logged = {("smith", "2020"), ("garcia", "2018"), ("chen", "2021"), ("okafor", "2022")}

print("Cited but not logged:", cited - logged)   # {('patel', '2019')}
print("Logged but not cited:", logged - cited)   # {('okafor', '2022')}

It's a simple pattern match and won't catch every citation format, but it catches the mistakes that cost marks.

5. Templates

The last cells write everything to an output folder and download it as a zip:

  • source_log_template.csv: a blank log with the columns above
  • literature_matrix.csv: compare sources by method, findings, limitations and themes
  • annotated_bibliography.md: formatted references with your notes under each
  • research_plan.md: research question, scope, search strategy table and timeline
  • references.json / references.bib: your sources as CSL-JSON and BibTeX, for Zotero, Mendeley or LaTeX

To use your own sources, upload your log (File → Save a copy in Drive first), and the same cells build your reference list and templates.

Links

  • Colab notebook: plagx-research-kit
  • Source (MIT): github.com/plagiarismcheckerx/plagx-research-kit-colab
  • Citation package: plagx-cite on PyPI · npm · browser demo

By Plagiarism Checker X. This kit formats citations and checks your source log. It doesn't check for plagiarism or detect AI-generated text. For full plagiarism checks and AI-generated text detection, visit the Text Similarity Detector.

event_model_payload.headline: Moving a production API to Hetzner, part 2: hardening and configuring the server
event_model_payload.summary:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

In part 1 we created a Hetzner CX23 behind a Cloud Firewall, with a
cloud-init config meant to harden it on first boot. This part does that hardening
by hand, one step at a time, explains every line, and does it without ever
risking a lockout.

(cloud-init is the tool in every cloud image that runs once on first boot and
applies the config you paste into the Cloud config box: users, files,
packages, commands. Part 1, section 5 has the full config and how it works.)

Why by hand, if cloud-init can do it?

  • You'll know what each setting does, so you can debug it when it misbehaves.
  • It works anywhere: on a provider without cloud-init, on a server someone else created, or when cloud-init failed or was never given its config.
  • It doubles as the verification. If you did use cloud-init, skip to section 5 ("Verify like an attacker") and run the checks. They prove the config was applied, not just pasted.

Placeholders, as before: the new server is 198.51.100.20 and the old one is
203.0.113.10.

1. ~/.ssh/config: two servers, two keys, short commands

The problem it solves

During a migration you constantly talk to two machines, each with its own
address, port and key. Typing
ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 ubuntu@198.51.100.20 every time is slow
and error-prone. ~/.ssh/config gives each server a short name:

Host old-box
  HostName 203.0.113.10
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/oldhost_key.pem
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Host new-box
  HostName 198.51.100.20
  Port 2222
  User ubuntu
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519
  IdentitiesOnly yes

Now ssh new-box means all of that. So do scp file new-box:, rsync … new-box:,
and git clone new-box:…. Every OpenSSH-based tool reads this file.

You can append a block without opening an editor:

printf '\nHost new-box\n  HostName 198.51.100.20\n  Port 2222\n  User ubuntu\n  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519\n  IdentitiesOnly yes\n' >> ~/.ssh/config

Why IdentitiesOnly yes

Without it, the client offers the server every key in your ssh-agent, one by
one, before the one you named. sshd allows only a few attempts per connection
(MaxAuthTries, default 6). With enough keys loaded you get
Too many authentication failures before the right key is ever tried.
IdentitiesOnly yes means "offer only the IdentityFile named here". It also
stops you from accidentally presenting your work key to a personal server.

2. First login, and the plan for not locking yourself out

On a stock Hetzner image, before any hardening, there is exactly one account you
can reach: root, on port 22, with the SSH key you selected at creation.
Hetzner writes that key into /root/.ssh/authorized_keys and sets no root
password. So that's where we start:

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'id; ss -tln'

(If cloud-init did run, root login is already disabled and this is refused. That's
your cue to skip to the checks in section 5.)

What happened to me: I created the server and forgot to paste the cloud
config. My first ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused, because nothing was
listening on 2222 (section 6 explains how to read that). Recreating the server
would have meant giving up a CX23 that was close to sold out, so I hardened it
by hand, as below.

Running a command after the host ('id; ss -tln') executes it remotely and
returns. No interactive shell is needed, which makes every step repeatable and
easy to paste into notes.

The lockout problem

Hardening SSH means changing the very thing you're connected through. Get one
line wrong, for example disabling root before the new user's key works, and the
next connection fails. On a cloud server, your remaining way in is the provider's
web console. Remember from part 1 that Hetzner sets no root password when you
use an SSH key, so even the console needs a password reset first.

The fix is to make changes in two passes, with a test in between, so that at
every moment at least one known-good way in still works:

3. Pass 1, explained block by block

The whole pass is one script, sent from the laptop and run on the server as root.
'bash -s' tells the remote bash to read its script from standard input, and the
heredoc (<<'EOF' … EOF) supplies it. The quotes around 'EOF' stop your
local shell from expanding $variables inside, so they reach the server as
written.

ssh -p 22 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 'bash -s' <<'EOF'
set -euo pipefail
export DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# --- user ---
id ubuntu >/dev/null 2>&1 || adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" ubuntu
usermod -aG sudo ubuntu
echo 'ubuntu ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' > /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu && chmod 440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-ubuntu
install -d -m 700 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /home/ubuntu/.ssh
install -m 600 -o ubuntu -g ubuntu /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/ubuntu/.ssh/authorized_keys

# --- packages ---
apt-get update -q
apt-get -y -q -o Dpkg::Options::=--force-confold upgrade
apt-get -y -q install ufw unattended-upgrades

# --- sshd ---
cat > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf <<'CONF'
Port 22
Port 2222
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password
PubkeyAuthentication yes
CONF
sshd -t
systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl restart ssh.socket || true
systemctl restart ssh || true

# --- docker log rotation (read when Docker is installed later) ---
mkdir -p /etc/docker
echo '{"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}' > /etc/docker/daemon.json

# --- host firewall ---
ufw default deny incoming; ufw default allow outgoing
for r in 22/tcp 2222/tcp 80/tcp 443/tcp 443/udp; do ufw allow $r; done
ufw --force enable

# --- swap ---
if [ ! -f /swapfile ]; then fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile && echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab; fi

ss -tln | grep -E ":(22|2222) "
EOF

set -euo pipefail

These are bash's "fail loudly" settings: -e stops at the first failing command,
-u treats an unset variable as an error, and pipefail makes a pipeline fail
if any stage fails, not just the last. Part 3 shows pipefail biting back,
too.

The user

  • adduser --disabled-password: the account has no password at all, so it can only be reached with a key. id ubuntu || … makes the line safe to run twice.
  • sudoers.d/90-ubuntu with NOPASSWD: ubuntu can run sudo without a password, which is what Ubuntu cloud images give their default user. It's a trade-off: if someone gets this account they get root. But a password-less account with a sudo password needs a password set somewhere, and that's a secret to manage. With key-only SSH, the key is the boundary. chmod 440 because sudo refuses sudoers files that others can write to.
  • install -d -m 700 / install -m 600: create .ssh and copy root's authorized_keys with the right owner and permissions in one step. The permissions aren't cosmetic. sshd's StrictModes (on by default) ignores an authorized_keys file that other users could modify, and the symptom is a baffling Permission denied (publickey).

Packages

DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive and --force-confold stop apt from opening an
interactive "a config file changed, which version do you want?" prompt in the
middle of a non-interactive SSH session. confold keeps the existing file.

sshd: drop-in files and "first value wins"

Instead of editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config, we add a file in
/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. The main config includes that directory near its
top, and the files load in name order. For most settings sshd keeps the
first value it reads, so 10-hardening.conf beats the image's own
50-cloud-init.conf and anything below in the main file. Package upgrades never
touch your drop-in, either.

Line Meaning
Port 22, Port 2222 listen on both (repeatable directive)
PasswordAuthentication no no password logins, so bots guessing passwords get nowhere
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no closes the other password path (PAM "keyboard-interactive"), which can otherwise ask for a password even with the line above
PermitRootLogin prohibit-password pass 1 only: root may log in with a key, our safety line. Pass 2 changes it to no
PubkeyAuthentication yes keys, explicitly

Two commands make it safe:

  • sshd -t tests the configuration and exits non-zero on a syntax error. Because of set -e, a typo stops the script before the restart, so the old, working sshd keeps running.
  • sshd -T (used later) prints the effective configuration after all files are merged. That's the only reliable way to know which value won.

Why ssh.socket and not just ssh

Since Ubuntu 24.04, sshd is socket-activated: systemd holds the listening
socket (ssh.socket) and starts sshd when a connection arrives. Which ports that
socket listens on is generated from sshd_config by a systemd generator, and
the generator only runs on systemctl daemon-reload. So changing Port takes
three steps: reload (regenerate the socket), restart ssh.socket (rebind the
ports), restart ssh. Skip the reload and sshd's config says 2222 while nothing
listens there. || true keeps the script going on releases that aren't
socket-activated.

The script ends by printing what's listening. We got
0.0.0.0:22, 0.0.0.0:2222, [::]:22 and [::]:2222.

ufw: the host firewall

ufw ("uncomplicated firewall") is a front end for the kernel's netfilter
(nftables). Default deny incoming and allow outgoing, then open exactly
what's needed. 22 is allowed before ufw enable, otherwise enabling it would
cut the very session doing the enabling.

Docker bypasses ufw for published ports (see part 1), so ufw protects sshd and
anything else running directly on the host, and the Cloud Firewall protects
everything. Two layers, each covering the other's blind spot. That's
defence in depth.

Swap

A 4 GB server with no swap handles a memory spike (a big query, a container
starting) by invoking the kernel's OOM killer, which usually kills the biggest
process: Postgres. A 2 GB swapfile turns that crash into a brief slowdown.
fallocate reserves the space instantly, mkswap formats it, swapon activates
it, and the /etc/fstab line brings it back after a reboot.

4. Test, then pass 2

Before taking anything away, prove the new way in works:

ssh new-box 'whoami; sudo -n true && echo sudo-ok'

ubuntu
sudo-ok

sudo -n means "non-interactive": fail instead of prompting. So this proves
both the key and passwordless sudo. Only now, as ubuntu, turn root off:

ssh new-box 'sudo sed -i "s/^PermitRootLogin .*/PermitRootLogin no/" /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf && sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh && sudo sshd -T | grep -E "^(port|permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication) "'

port 22
port 2222
permitrootlogin no
passwordauthentication no

5. Verify like an attacker

Checking the config proves what you intended. Negative tests prove what's
enforced: try what should fail and watch it fail.

ssh -p 2222 -i ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -o IdentitiesOnly=yes root@198.51.100.20 true
# root@198.51.100.20: Permission denied (publickey).

ssh -p 2222 -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password ubuntu@198.51.100.20 true
# ubuntu@198.51.100.20: Permission denied (publickey).

The second line is the interesting one. We asked for password authentication,
and the server's reply lists only (publickey) as acceptable. It doesn't offer
a password prompt at all.

Then the rest of the configuration in one go:

ssh new-box 'sudo ufw status verbose; ss -tln; timedatectl show -p NTPSynchronized; swapon --show; free -h; df -h /; cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades; systemctl is-enabled unattended-upgrades; ls /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null && echo REBOOT-NEEDED'

What to look for, and why each matters:

Check Expect Why
ufw status active, deny incoming, five allow rules the host layer is on
ss -tln only :22, :2222 and 127.0.0.53/54:53 nothing unexpected listening. 127.0.0.53 is the local DNS resolver (systemd-resolved), bound to loopback only
NTPSynchronized=yes yes clock accuracy is a security property: TLS certificate validity, TOTP codes (30-second windows) and signed webhooks (Paddle allows about 5 minutes of drift) all fail on a wrong clock
swap / RAM / disk 2 GB swap, ~3.7 GB RAM, ~32 GB free sanity
20auto-upgrades both lines "1" daily package-list refresh and daily unattended security upgrades
reboot-required present after the big upgrade a new kernel or libc is installed but not running yet

Automatic updates, and the reboot they don't do

unattended-upgrades installs security updates every day. During pass 1,
needrestart restarted the services whose libraries changed and listed the ones
it deferred. It doesn't reboot: a new kernel only takes effect after a
reboot, and the system flags this with /var/run/reboot-required. Automatic
reboots stay off (the default), because a reboot in the middle of a
database write is worse than a few days on the old kernel.

The best time to reboot is now, while the box is empty. It's also a free test
that everything comes back on its own:

ssh new-box 'sudo reboot'
# wait ~30–60 s
ssh new-box 'whoami; uptime; ss -tln | grep -E ":(22|2222) "; sudo ufw status | head -1; swapon --show --noheadings; ls /var/run/reboot-required 2>/dev/null || echo no-reboot-needed'

Both SSH ports, ufw and swap all survived.

6. Reading a port test: open, refused, filtered

From the laptop, without installing nmap:

for p in 22 2222 443 5432; do timeout 5 bash -c "$p" 2>/dev/null && echo "$p open" || echo "$p closed/filtered"; done

/dev/tcp/HOST/PORT isn't a real file. It's a bash feature: redirecting from it
opens a TCP connection. timeout 5 caps the wait.

There are three possible answers, and telling them apart is the most useful
network-debugging skill I know:

Result Meaning What to look at
open something accepted the connection —
refused (instant) reached the machine, nothing listening the service: is it running, on that port?
timeout dropped on the way firewalls: cloud, host, or your own network

Two real examples from this migration:

  • ssh -p 2222 → Connection refused on the first try. The Cloud Firewall was fine. sshd simply wasn't on 2222 yet, because cloud-init hadn't run.
  • Port 22 → timeout from home, even though sshd listened on 22, ufw allowed it and the Cloud Firewall allowed it. Every layer on the server said yes. That points at the path: some home routers and ISPs drop outbound port 22. The way to prove it is to test from a third machine on a different network, such as the old server (ssh old-box 'timeout 5 bash -c ") or a phone hotspot. This is exactly why SSH listens on two ports.

The final scan read 2222 open, 443 closed/filtered (nothing serves it
yet), and 5432 closed/filtered. The database port is invisible from outside,
which is what we want.

7. Docker 

ssh new-box 'curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | sudo sh && sudo usermod -aG docker ubuntu'
  • get.docker.com is Docker's official convenience script. It adds Docker's own apt repository and installs the engine and the Compose plugin. Piping a script into sh is fine when you trust the source and it comes over HTTPS; read it first if you want (curl -fsSL https://get.docker.com | less). If it doesn't yet support a brand-new Ubuntu release, add the apt repository by hand from Docker's docs instead.
  • usermod -aG docker ubuntu lets ubuntu run docker without sudo. ⚠️ The docker group is root-equivalent: anyone in it can start a container that mounts / and edit any file. Here ubuntu already has passwordless sudo, so nothing changes, but never add a less-trusted user to it.

Group membership is read at login, so open a new connection to check:

ssh new-box 'docker --version && docker compose version && docker info --format "{{.LoggingDriver}}"'

Docker version 29.x
Docker Compose version v5.x
json-file

json-file confirms Docker read our daemon.json from pass 1. That file caps
each container's log at 3 × 10 MB. Without it Docker never rotates container
logs, and on a 40 GB disk the reverse proxy's access log eventually fills the
disk. Disk-full is a classic way for a small server to die in month five.

Where we are

Layer State
Perimeter Cloud Firewall: 22, 2222, 80, 443/tcp+udp, ICMP
Host ufw default-deny with the same ports
SSH key-only, root disabled, on 22 and 2222; verified by negative tests
OS fully patched, rebooted, automatic security updates on, clock synced
Memory 4 GB + 2 GB swap
Runtime Docker with log rotation

In part 3 we move the application: copying a secrets file from server to
server through the laptop without it ever touching the laptop's disk, pulling
the image instead of building it, rehearsing a restore from backups (which turned
up a real bug), and planning a cutover with a few minutes of downtime and a clear
rollback.

event_model_payload.headline: Give your LLM live web search: query top results clean page Markdown (no search API key)
event_model_payload.summary:
LLMs are stuck at their training cutoff. The usual fix is to give them a web search step: run a query, take the top results, read the pages, and put the relevant text in the prompt. Most tutorials stop at "get a search API key", which means a paid account with Google, Bing or Brave and their rate limits.

Here's a way to do the whole loop (search → fetch pages → clean Markdown) in one call, with no search API key.

What one run returns

Query: best open source vector database 2026, top 5 results, with page content. This is the real output (Markdown trimmed):

[
  {
    "query": "best open source vector database 2026",
    "engine": "duckduckgo",
    "position": 1,
    "title": "9 Best Open Source Vector Databases in 2026 (Tested) - Geekflare",
    "url": "https://geekflare.com/open-source/vector-database/",
    "domain": "geekflare.com",
    "contentSuccess": true,
    "tokensApprox": 200,
    "markdown": "| Qdrant | Yes — sparse and dense vectors fused in one query | ..."
  },
  {
    "position": 5,
    "title": "7 Best Open-Source Vector Databases in 2026",
    "domain": "krunalkanojiya.com",
    "markdown": "Qdrant is the best balanced open-source vector database for most teams starting a dedicated retrieval service in 2026. It combines ..."
  }
]

Every result has its rank, title, URL and domain. With fetchPageContent on, it also has the page body as Markdown with boilerplate stripped, plus a token estimate. That's exactly what you want to paste into a prompt with citations.

The grounding loop in Python 

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

def web_search(query, n=5, chars=3000):
    run = client.actor("get_anything/ai-web-search-scraper").call(run_input={
        "queries": [query],
        "engine": "duckduckgo",
        "maxResults": n,
        "fetchPageContent": True,
        "maxCharsPerPage": chars,      # keep the prompt within budget
    })
    return [r for r in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items() if r.get("contentSuccess")]

def build_context(results):
    return "\n\n".join(
        f"[{r['position']}] {r['title']} ({r['url']})\n{r['markdown']}" for r in results
    )

results = web_search("best open source vector database 2026")
context = build_context(results)

prompt = f"""Answer using only the sources below and cite them like [1].

{context}

Question: Which open-source vector database should a small team start with in 2026, and why?"""
# send `prompt` to the model you use (Claude, GPT, a local Llama...)

A few tips from using it:

  • Budget with maxCharsPerPage. Five pages × 3,000 characters is about 4k tokens, which fits comfortably in any modern context window.
  • Keep the citation index. Numbering sources by position lets the model cite [1]–[5], and you can show the links in your UI.
  • Several queries per run. queries takes a list, so you can fan out a question into 3–4 phrasings in one run and de-duplicate by URL.
  • DuckDuckGo is the default engine and works without extra setup. Google is available too, behind a residential proxy.

Or skip the code: let the assistant search for itself (MCP)

If you use Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or another MCP client, add the scraper as a tool through the Apify MCP server:

{ "mcpServers": { "apify": { "url": "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=get_anything/ai-web-search-scraper" } } }

Now you can ask "Search the web for this week's news on X and summarise the top 5 sources with links", and the assistant runs the search and reads the pages itself. Setup guide: Connect any Apify scraper to Claude or ChatGPT in 2 minutes.

When you already have the URLs

If you don't need the search step (say you have a list of docs pages or articles), use the sister tool that only converts URLs to clean Markdown and can crawl a whole site: LLM Web Scraper.

Cost

Pay per result, no subscription. See the Pricing tab on the Actor page. The Apify free plan's monthly credit is enough to try it properly.

Try it: AI Web Search Scraper on Apify

What are you using for grounding today, and where does it break? I'm curious which sites give people the most trouble.

event_model_payload.headline: Turn any website into clean Markdown for your RAG pipeline (no boilerplate, with token counts)
event_model_payload.summary:
If you've built a RAG pipeline, you know the boring part isn't the embeddings. It's getting clean text out of web pages. Raw HTML is full of nav bars, cookie banners, footers and "related posts", and all of it ends up in your vector database and in your prompts.

Here's the setup I use now: give a list of URLs (or one docs site) to a scraper that returns only the main content as Markdown, plus metadata and an approximate token count per page. Then chunk and embed.

What you get back

I ran it on two pages: the Wikipedia article on RAG and the Apify docs page for Actors. This is the real output (Markdown trimmed):

{
  "url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation",
  "title": "Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia",
  "date": "2023-11-05",
  "sitename": "Wikimedia Foundation, Inc.",
  "wordCount": 225,
  "tokensApprox": 375,
  "method": "http",
  "success": true,
  "markdown": "---\ntitle: Retrieval-augmented generation - Wikipedia\n...\n---\n**Retrieval-augmented generation** (**RAG**) is a technique that ..."
}

A few things that matter for RAG:

  • The Markdown starts with a small front-matter block (title, url, date, sitename). Keep it on the first chunk so every answer can cite its source.
  • tokensApprox (about 4 characters per token) lets you budget before you embed or stuff a context window.
  • method tells you whether the page came over plain HTTP (fast, cheap) or needed the browser fallback. JS-heavy and bot-protected pages are rendered with a hardened browser automatically.
  • maxCharsPerPage truncates pages if you only want the first N characters (I used 1,500 for this demo).

Run it from Python

The scraper is an Apify Actor, so you can call it with the official client and get the dataset back in one call:

from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

run = client.actor("get_anything/llm-web-scraper").call(run_input={
    "startUrls": [
        {"url": "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retrieval-augmented_generation"},
        {"url": "https://docs.apify.com/platform/actors"},
    ],
    "outputFormat": "markdown",   # or "text" / "both"
    "includeLinks": False,        # cleaner chunks for embeddings
    "useBrowser": "auto",         # browser only when HTTP isn't enough
})

pages = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
for p in pages:
    print(p["title"], p["tokensApprox"], "tokens")

Chunk it for a vector DB

Markdown headings make natural chunk boundaries. A minimal splitter:

import re

def chunk_markdown(page, max_chars=2000):
    parts = re.split(r"\n(?=#{1,3} )", page["markdown"])   # split before H1-H3
    chunks, buf = [], ""
    for part in parts:
        if len(buf) + len(part) > max_chars and buf:
            chunks.append(buf)
            buf = ""
        buf += part + "\n"
    if buf:
        chunks.append(buf)
    return [{"text": c, "url": page["url"], "title": page["title"]} for c in chunks]

docs = [c for p in pages if p["success"] for c in chunk_markdown(p)]
# -> embed `text`, store `url` + `title` as metadata (pgvector, Qdrant, Pinecone, Weaviate...)

Ingest a whole docs site

Set crawl: true and it follows same-domain links from each start URL, with caps so a run can't run away:

{
  "startUrls": [{ "url": "https://docs.example.com/" }],
  "crawl": true,
  "maxPages": 200,
  "maxDepth": 3,
  "outputFormat": "markdown"
}

That gives you one dataset row per page, ready to chunk the same way. It's an easy way to give an assistant a product's documentation.

Use it straight from Claude or ChatGPT (MCP)

You don't have to write code at all. Through the Apify MCP server, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor or any MCP client can call the scraper as a tool:

{ "mcpServers": { "apify": { "url": "https://mcp.apify.com/?tools=get_anything/llm-web-scraper" } } }

Then just ask: "Read these three URLs and summarise what each says about pricing." Step-by-step setup: Connect any Apify scraper to Claude or ChatGPT in 2 minutes.

Cost

You pay per page converted (see the Pricing tab on the Actor page). There's no subscription, and the Apify free plan's monthly credit covers plenty of testing.

Try it: LLM Web Scraper on Apify. If you need the search step too (query → top results → their pages as Markdown), I wrote that up separately: the AI Web Search Scraper.

Questions or a site it doesn't handle well? Drop a comment, I read them all.

event_model_payload.headline: Serving MOSS-Image: step count, memory mode and the traps that change the words you ship
event_model_payload.summary:
If your product makes menus or posters through an image API, what matters is that the price on the menu is the price you sent. We served MOSS-Image-SFT, an Apache 2.0 model from OpenMOSS at MOSI.AI built for long text in pictures, on one A40 on our cloud. Two settings decided almost everything: the step count, and where the weights (the model's learned numbers) sit while it runs.

With the authors' 50-step recipe, every word was correct on every text test, at 78 to 81 seconds per picture of about one megapixel. A community turbo add-on from lodestones took 8.6 to 9.2 seconds and got two words wrong. The full MOSS-Image test on one A40 has all 22 pictures and the deploy steps. This piece covers the choices.

Why 50 steps cost 100 passes

The model begins with random static and removes some of it per step. Each of the 50 steps calls it twice, with your prompt and with an empty one, and the gap between the answers steers the picture toward your words. That is about 100 runs of a 5-billion-parameter network per picture.

The lodestones 8-step add-on is a LoRA: a 1.2 GB set of small corrections laid over the original weights, trained to finish in 8 calls with no empty-prompt call. Its card says the correction is smaller than bf16's rounding step (bf16 is the 16-bit format of the weights), so folding it in would erase it. It stays a separate layer at strength 0.7, as in the hugging-apps demo Space. That strength is shared by every request, so our backend (the server that loads the model and answers requests) runs one picture at a time. One loaded copy serves both modes:

{"prompt": "A clean conference poster on a white wall. Large bold title: OPEN WEIGHTS DAY",
 "size": "1024x1024", "seed": 42, "mode": "turbo"}

The body follows OpenAI's image API, plus mode (sft or turbo). The seed fixes the starting static: keep it the same when you compare modes, or you are comparing luck.

The trap: running the 8-step LoRA at 4 steps

We tried the 8-step add-on at 4 steps. It took 5.2 seconds and the lettering broke.

The title read "OPEN WEIGHT DAYDY" and times looked like "1(.C0". The add-on was trained for 8 steps. Adapters built for 4 exist, and we did not test them. At 8 steps, turbo repeated a word in the poster title, wrote "PNG bock" for "PNG back" and half-garbled street signs, while the chalkboard menu, the Chinese note and both layouts were right. Use it for drafts and proofread each picture.

Memory mode: pick the one that streams the right part

MOSS-Image is a pair: a 17 GB reader (the Qwen3.5-9B text encoder from the Qwen team, which turns the prompt into numbers) and a 10 GB painter. The reader is busy only briefly per prompt, so it can live in system RAM and move to the GPU on demand. To mimic smaller cards, we limited PyTorch's share of the A40 with torch.cuda.set_per_process_memory_fraction:

Memory cap Peak on the card 50 steps Turbo
None (real A40, 48 GB) about 30 GB 80 s 9 s
16 GB, reader in main memory about 14 GB 86 s 13 s
12 GB, reader and part of the painter in main memory about 11 GB 160 s 18 s

The generic enable_model_cpu_offload() from diffusers fit 24 GB but not 16 GB and ran slower than moving only the reader, so our automatic mode never picks it. A cap copies a card's memory size, not its speed, so trust the fit more than the timings. Neither the fit on a real card nor the automatic choice has been tested yet: we set each mode by hand.

What to measure before you trust a setup

The memory ladder and the per-picture measurements list everything. These checks carry over:

  • Byte equality. The static is drawn on the CPU from the seed, and offloading only moves weights. All 8 ladder pictures matched the uncapped run byte for byte (cmp). If yours differ, something besides placement changed.
  • Peak memory as the card reports it. nvidia-smi, NVIDIA's monitor, counts memory the CUDA runtime keeps for itself, which the PyTorch cap ignores. The 16 GB setup leaves about 2 GiB spare, less with a display attached.
  • System RAM. The 16 and 12 GB setups used up to 22 GB. Plan for 32.
  • Time to ready. Ours took 63 seconds, 29 of them downloading 28 GB. A custom backend gets 300 seconds, and at 100 MB/s the download alone takes about 280. On machines we rent for you that limit is fixed for now. Status: open.
  • Every word, by eye. 22 pictures, one seed each, show behaviour, not a ranking.

The authors' technical report claims 96.3% average text coverage on their own benchmark, the best among open-weight models. We read only the abstract. Our menu was right in both modes, the kind of prompt where Iris-3B, the last image model we tested, dropped decimal points.

Credits and the full write-up

OpenMOSS at MOSI.AI made the model, pipeline, user guide, layout format and report. The Qwen team made the text encoder, Black Forest Labs the FLUX.2 small VAE that decodes the painter's output into pixels. lodestones trained the 8-step add-on and Kromoss, darask0 and akhaliq the 4-step and 3-step adapters. The ComfyUI team added native support, Comfy-Org made quantized repacks, the hugging-apps Space showed how to apply the LoRA. We spotted the model in a video by AI Search. Our part: the backend, the SDK example and the measurements. Deploy commands and open issues are in the MOSS-Image hands-on test with every timing and memory figure.

event_model_payload.headline: What Is the Most Important Quality of DevOps?
event_model_payload.summary:
Imagine a busy restaurant kitchen on a Saturday night. The chefs have the best ovens money can buy, a perfectly organized pantry and a ticket system that prints orders in seconds. Yet if the chefs, the servers and the dishwashers do not talk to each other, plates still go out cold, orders get lost and everybody ends the night frustrated.

Software teams work the same way. You can buy the best tools in the market and still ship slowly and break things often. The thing that separates teams that succeed with DevOps from those that struggle is not a tool. It is a quality: shared ownership of the whole journey, from code to customer.

In this post, I’ll explain what that means, why it beats every other skill on the list, and how you can start practicing it this week.

The quick answer

The most important quality of DevOps is shared ownership, which grows out of honest collaboration. When developers, operations, QA and security all feel responsible for the result, not just their own step, the rest of DevOps becomes much easier.

What DevOps is trying to fix

In many companies, work used to move like a relay race with a dropped baton at every handoff. Developers wrote code and passed it on. Testers checked it and passed it on. Operations deployed it and kept it running. Each group had its own targets, and none of them owned the final outcome.

That setup creates familiar problems:

Releases that are slow because every handoff adds waiting time
Bugs that are found late, when they are expensive to fix
Outages followed by arguments about whose fault it was
Knowledge locked inside a few people’s heads

DevOps changes the question from “is my part done?” to “is the customer’s experience working?” That shift is a quality of mindset, not a feature of any product.

Why shared ownership matters more than tools

Tools follow habits, not the other way around. A new pipeline does not make people talk to each other. People who already work well together will build a good pipeline and keep it healthy.

Problems get found earlier. When developers care about how code behaves in production, they write more testable, more observable software. When operations people join planning, they flag risks before they become incidents.

Recovery gets faster. During an outage, nobody wastes time deciding who is responsible. Everyone knows the goal is the same: restore service, then learn from it.

People stay longer. Teams that trust each other and learn from mistakes without blame tend to be calmer and more engaged than teams that live in constant finger-pointing.

Signs your team already has it

Developers join on-call rotations or at least sit in on incident reviews
Operations engineers are involved while features are still being designed
After a failure, the first question is “what in our process allowed this?”
Documentation is written and updated by the people who do the work
Anyone can explain, in a few sentences, how a change travels to production

Signs it is missing

Tickets are thrown over the wall with no conversation
Only one person knows how a critical system works
Incident reports name a person instead of a cause
Developers say “that’s an ops problem” and operations says “that’s a dev problem”
Releases happen rarely because everyone is afraid of them

The supporting qualities

Shared ownership leads the way, but a few other qualities help it grow:

Curiosity and continuous learning. Cloud platforms and security threats change fast, so teams need to keep learning together.
An automation mindset. If a task is repetitive and error-prone, ask whether a script can do it. This frees people for more valuable work.
Clear communication. Good written updates, short runbooks and honest status messages are the everyday tools of collaboration.
Customer focus. Keep asking how a change will affect the people using your product.
Resilience. Things will break. Teams that stay calm and learn from failures improve faster.

How to start building it this week

Share one goal. Choose a metric developers and operations both care about, such as how quickly you can ship a safe change or how fast you recover from a problem.
Invite each other in. Ask operations to join a planning meeting. Ask a developer to shadow an on-call shift.
Run a blameless review. After the next incident, write down what happened, why it was possible and what you will change. Leave names out of the causes.
Write one runbook. Pick the system only one person understands and document it together.
Celebrate team wins. When a release goes smoothly, thank everyone who helped, not just whoever pressed the button.

None of this needs a budget or a new tool. It only needs a few honest conversations.

Mistakes to avoid

Believing that hiring a “DevOps engineer” alone creates DevOps
Rolling out new tools before agreeing on how people will work
Rewarding teams for conflicting goals, like speed for one and stability for the other
Using incident reviews to find someone to blame
Expecting culture to change in a month

event_model_payload.headline: 👻 The Séance Engine: Finding the Ghost in the Data with TabPFN & Gemma
event_model_payload.summary:
🕯️ The idea

What does your computer do while you sleep?

Mine is supposed to do almost nothing. CPU in single digits, a few kilobytes of network, "System Idle" all night long. So when I pictured a ghost living inside a machine, I didn't imagine a skull on the screen. I imagined one row in a boring log file that shouldn't be there.

The Séance Engine reads a day of ordinary system logs, asks an open tabular foundation model which moment is the hardest to believe, and then hands that moment to a local LLM. The LLM, playing the Spirit of the Machine, tells us what passed through the circuits in a short Día de los Muertos style story.

It finds the ghost in the data, then gives it a voice.

⚙️ How it works

Everything runs on my laptop: one Python file, about 100 lines.

1. The haunted log. 24 hourly rows of hour, cpu_usage, memory_usage and network_io_mb. By day it's VS Code; by night, idle. You can also point it at your own CSV: python seance_engine.py my_logs.csv.

2. The divination (TabPFN by Prior Labs). TabPFN is a classifier, and an anomaly detector needs a sense of what's "normal". So I used a small density-ratio trick:

  • For each row, hold it out.
  • Show TabPFN the other 23 real rows labelled real, next to random noise spread across the same range labelled noise.
  • Ask: how real does the held-out row look?

Ordinary hours score between 0.66 and 0.99. The witching hour scored this:

2026-10-29 02:33:00    8%   4 MB/s   System Idle       p_real 0.992
2026-10-29 03:33:00   98% 850 MB/s   UNKNOWN_PROCESS   p_real 0.006
2026-10-29 04:33:00    7%   5 MB/s   System Idle       p_real 0.992

Because hour is a feature, TabPFN isn't just flagging "big numbers". It learned that this machine sleeps at 3 AM, so 98% CPU at that hour is what doesn't fit. No training loop, no tuning: TabPFN does all of it in context.

3. The séance (Gemma 2 9B through Ollama). The anomalous row, including its p_real score, goes into a prompt that asks Gemma to speak as a gossipy, theatrical ghost who lives in the laptop's fan (fun, quirky, and chilling by the last line). Output streams to the terminal word by word, which feels a lot like a candle flickering.

4. The tracing (Sentry). The whole investigation is one Sentry trace, with spans for loading the logs, the TabPFN scan and the Gemma chat. Token counts go on the chat span.

The trace showed me something I didn't expect: the leave-one-out TabPFN scan (24 small fits on CPU) took 38 seconds, and Gemma took about a minute. The ghost costs more to find than to listen to.

👻 What the machine confessed

⚠️ ANOMALY DETECTED at 2026-10-29 03:33:00 (P(real)=0.006)

Ah, three thirty-three in the morning, that's when the veil thins, darlings! The fan whirred like a disco ball under a mariachi band as 98% of my beloved CPU hummed with the impossible, a process so shrouded, so strange, it registered as "UNKNOWN_PROCESS" on the logs. I saw it all, you see, every pixel flicker as 95% of the memory churned, a ghostly green glow illuminating its form. It downloaded a single video at 850 MB/s, a pixelated rendition of a chihuahua wearing a sombrero, its tiny paws drumming on a maraca. A forgotten relic, perhaps, from a life lived before this one. Now, the screen rests dark, the chihuahua frozen mid-shake, a reminder of that fleeting connection. Is it ever truly gone?

Every run summons a different visitor. The prompt asks Gemma for a gossipy ghost who lives in the laptop fan: give the ghost a petty hobby and one oddly specific detail, weave in every real number, and end on one quiet line that makes you glance at your own laptop.

💡 Why open models

  • The data stays home. These are behaviour logs from a personal machine. With open weights, TabPFN and Gemma both run locally, and nothing leaves the laptop. It works with Wi-Fi off.
  • I own the voice. I set the system prompt and the temperature, and I can swap models freely (MODEL = "gemma2:9b" is one line).
  • Free to haunt every night. A ghost should be ambient. Running a local check on last night's logs every morning costs nothing per call.
  • It runs on old hardware. This was built on an Intel Mac stuck on PyTorch 2.2. The newest TabPFN wouldn't install, but tabpfn==2.0.9 worked, and that's the point of open weights: you pick a version that fits the machine you actually have.

🛠️ Run it yourself 

ollama pull gemma2:9b
pip install -r requirements.txt   # tabpfn==2.0.9, numpy<2, pandas, ollama, sentry-sdk
python seance_engine.py
# optional tracing
SENTRY_DSN="your-dsn" python seance_engine.py

🔗 Links

  • Code: https://github.com/Prekshabarjatya/seance-engine
  • TabPFN: https://github.com/PriorLabs/TabPFN
  • Gemma: https://ai.google.dev/gemma
  • Ollama: https://ollama.com
  • Sentry: https://sentry.io

Happy Día de los Muertos. Leave a candle on for your machines tonight. 🕯️

event_model_payload.headline: Analyze what Xiaohongshu (RedNote) users say about a product with Claude and MCP
event_model_payload.summary:
Xiaohongshu (小红书, also called RedNote) is where a lot of Chinese shoppers go to review products before they buy, and to complain after. If you sell anything in China, or compete with someone who does, the notes and comment sections there tell you a lot. The trouble is that there is no public API to sign up for, and reading hundreds of Chinese comments by hand is slow.

In this post we'll connect Claude Code to a remote MCP server, ask it what Xiaohongshu users say about a product, and let it search notes, read their comments and summarize them. At the end there's a short Python version that calls the same HTTP API without an agent.

Disclosure: I build Qovia, the API and MCP server used here. It's a paid API with a free trial.

Step 1: add the MCP server to Claude Code

Get a key from the Qovia console, then add the server with one line:

export QOVIA_KEY=sk-qovia-...
claude mcp add --transport http qovia https://api.qovia.ai/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer $QOVIA_KEY"

The server exposes only four tools, so it doesn't fill the model's context with a hundred tool definitions:

  • search_endpoints: find data endpoints by keyword or platform
  • get_endpoint: show an endpoint's parameters, a response example and the price
  • call_endpoint: run an endpoint and return data plus billing info
  • get_account: check your key's balance and rate limit

search_endpoints and get_endpoint are free and work without an API key, so you can let the agent explore the catalog before you spend anything. Only call_endpoint needs the key. Setup details are in the MCP docs.

Step 2: ask a question

Start claude and give it something like this:

Using the qovia MCP tools, find out what Xiaohongshu users say about
the Stanley Quencher tumbler. Search in Chinese, take the 5 most
commented notes from the past month, read the first page of comments
on each, and summarize: main praise, main complaints, recurring
questions, and anything about fakes or pricing. Quote a few comments
in Chinese with an English translation. Tell me how much the run cost.

Step 3: what the agent does

The agent doesn't need to know Qovia's catalog in advance. A typical run goes like this.

1. Find the endpoints. It calls search_endpoints with platform: "xiaohongshu". That lists the Xiaohongshu endpoints, including:

Endpoint id Path Price per call
raw.xiaohongshu.search GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comments GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.note GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/note $0.005
raw.xiaohongshu.comment_replies GET /v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comment_replies $0.005

2. Read the parameters. It calls get_endpoint for the two it needs.

raw.xiaohongshu.search returns 20 notes a page:

  • keyword (required, up to 50 characters)
  • sort: general (default), latest, most_liked, most_commented or most_saved
  • note_time: all (default), day, week, month or year
  • note_type: all (default), video or image
  • page: from 1, up to 50; stop when has_more is false

raw.xiaohongshu.comments returns a note's first-level comments:

  • note_id (required, 24 hex characters)
  • sort: default (Xiaohongshu's own order, pinned and popular first, about 5 a page) or latest (newest first, 10 to 15 a page, without like counts)
  • cursor: pass back the previous page's cursor unchanged; stop when has_more is false

3. Fetch the data. It runs call_endpoint with something like:

{ "endpoint_id": "raw.xiaohongshu.search",
  "params": { "keyword": "斯坦利 保温杯", "sort": "most_commented", "note_time": "month" } }

Each note in the result carries its Xiaohongshu id in extra.source_id. Here is an abbreviated example of the structure, taken from get_endpoint's response example (not from a real run of this prompt):

{
  "page": 1,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": "soc_xia_c79d099f083d",
      "platform": "xiaohongshu",
      "text": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）…",
      "author": { "user_id": "5a916db4e8ac2b54e8b53aba", "nickname": "J*y" },
      "metrics": { "likes": 1205, "saves": 966, "shares": 287, "comments": 1570 },
      "extra": {
        "title": "真假摩可纳咖啡对比（一）",
        "source_id": "69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "url": "https://www.xiaohongshu.com/explore/69f7dc410000000035021f62",
        "note_type": "image",
        "published_at": "2026-05-04T07:37:37+08:00"
      }
    }
  ],
  "has_more": true
}

It then passes each source_id as note_id to raw.xiaohongshu.comments. Again an abbreviated example structure from get_endpoint:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "cid": "6a17eab1000000002902f300",
      "text": "喝了晚上还能睡着怎么解",
      "likes": 1918,
      "reply_count": 62,
      "ip_location": "陕西",
      "created_at": "2026-05-28T15:11:45+08:00",
      "author": { "nickname": "肉*嘟" }
    }
  ],
  "total": 1072,
  "cursor": "6a1b938c000000002b025bef",
  "has_more": true
}

4. Summarize. With five searches' worth of notes and their comments in context, Claude groups the comments into themes, picks quotes and translates them. ip_location is handy if you want a rough regional split. Every call_endpoint result includes charged_usd, so the agent can add up the cost when you ask.

A run like the prompt above is about 6 calls: one search plus five comment pages, so roughly $0.03.

Tip: search in Chinese

Xiaohongshu users write in Chinese, and they rarely use a brand's English name. Searching Stanley finds far fewer notes than 斯坦利 or 斯坦利 保温杯. A few things that help:

  • Ask the agent to try two or three Chinese keywords: the Chinese brand name, the brand plus the product category, and any nickname people use.
  • Add words people use when they review: 测评 (review), 踩雷 (bad buy), 真假 (real vs fake), 平替 (cheaper alternative).
  • Use sort: "most_commented" to find the notes with the most discussion, and note_time to keep it recent.
  • Read comments with the default sort first. It puts the most-liked comments on top, which are usually the most representative.

The same thing in plain Python

If you want this as a scheduled job instead of a chat, call the HTTP API directly. Every endpoint returns the same envelope: data holds the result and meta holds billing info.

import os, requests

BASE = "https://api.qovia.ai"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['QOVIA_KEY']}"}
spent = 0.0

def get(path, **params):
    global spent
    r = requests.get(f"{BASE}{path}", headers=HEADERS, params=params, timeout=60)
    r.raise_for_status()
    body = r.json()
    spent += float(body.get("meta", {}).get("charged_usd", 0) or 0)
    return body["data"]

notes = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/search",
            keyword="斯坦利 保温杯", sort="most_commented", note_time="month")["items"]

rows = []
for note in notes[:5]:
    comments = get("/v1/raw/xiaohongshu/comments",
                   note_id=note["extra"]["source_id"])["items"]
    for c in comments:
        rows.append((note["extra"]["title"], c.get("likes"), c["text"]))

for title, likes, text in rows:
    print(f"[{likes}] {title} | {text}")
print(f"spent ${spent:.3f}")

From there you can hand rows to any LLM with a "summarize praise and complaints" prompt, or write them to a CSV.

Pricing and trial

  • New accounts get 50 trial calls, enough to run the example above several times.
  • You're charged only when a call returns data. Empty results and errors are free, including a search with no hits or a note with no comments.
  • Both Xiaohongshu endpoints used here cost $0.005 per call ($5 per 1,000).
  • Discovery (search_endpoints, get_endpoint) is always free and needs no key.

More in the docs, the Xiaohongshu API page and the Xiaohongshu MCP page. If you try it, I'd like to hear which product you looked up and what the comments said.
