event_model_payload.headline: Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Practical Case Study of Amazon EC2
event_model_payload.summary:
Introduction

Cloud computing has changed the way individuals and organizations access and manage computing resources. Traditionally, businesses had to purchase physical servers, storage devices and networking equipment before they could deploy applications. This required significant financial investment, technical expertise and continuous maintenance.

Today, cloud computing provides an alternative through different service models, one of which is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explores the concept of IaaS, its features, benefits and challenges, using Amazon Web Services (AWS), particularly Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2), as a case study.

1. What Is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud computing model that provides virtualized computing resources such as servers, storage and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing physical servers and installing them in an office or organization, users can rent computing resources from a cloud service provider.

The cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, including the servers, networking equipment and data centres, while customers manage their operating systems, applications and data.

For example, a business that wants to host a website does not necessarily need to purchase a physical server. It can rent a virtual server from an IaaS provider and use it to host its website.

3. Case Study: Amazon Web Services (AWS) EC2

Amazon Web Services (AWS) is one of the major cloud computing platforms. One of its infrastructure services is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2).

Amazon EC2 provides virtual servers, known as instances, that allow individuals and organizations to run applications in the cloud.

Rather than purchasing physical servers, customers can launch EC2 instances, select their preferred operating systems and configure the resources required for their applications.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Consider a university that wants to develop an online course registration system.

Traditionally, the university might need to purchase physical servers, install operating systems, configure networking and provide storage facilities before deploying the application.

With Amazon EC2, the university can:

  1. Create an AWS account.
  2. Select an appropriate virtual server (EC2 instance).
  3. Choose an operating system, such as Linux or Windows Server.
  4. Configure the server's computing capacity, including memory and processing power.
  5. Configure network access and security settings.
  6. Install and deploy the university's course registration application.
  7. Increase or decrease computing resources as the number of users changes.

For instance, during course registration periods, many students may access the system simultaneously. The university can increase its computing capacity to accommodate the increased demand and reduce it when traffic decreases.

This demonstrates how IaaS provides flexibility and scalability.

Important Components of Amazon EC2

Some important components include:

  • EC2 Instances: Virtual servers used to run applications.
  • Amazon Machine Images (AMIs): Templates containing the operating system and other configurations required to launch instances.
  • Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS): Provides persistent storage for EC2 instances.
  • Security Groups: Act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic.
  • Instance Types: Determine the computing resources available, including CPU, memory and networking capacity.

4. Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

1. Reduced Hardware Costs

Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.

2. Scalability

Computing resources can be increased or decreased depending on application requirements.

3. Flexibility

Users can select different operating systems, server configurations and storage options.

4. Faster Deployment

Virtual servers can be launched without waiting for physical hardware to be purchased and installed.

5. Remote Management

Administrators can manage their cloud infrastructure through AWS management tools and interfaces.

5. Challenges and Limitations of IaaS

Despite its benefits, IaaS also has some limitations.

1. Security Responsibilities: Although the cloud provider manages the physical infrastructure, customers remain responsible for securing their operating systems, applications, access permissions and data.

2. Internet Dependency: Accessing cloud infrastructure generally requires a reliable internet connection.

3. Cost Management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when unused resources continue running.

4. Technical Knowledge: Users need some knowledge of operating systems, networking, security and server administration to manage their infrastructure effectively.

6. Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how organizations obtain and manage computing resources. It reduces the need for physical infrastructure while providing flexibility, scalability and faster deployment of applications.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how IaaS works by allowing users to rent virtual servers, configure their computing environments and deploy applications without purchasing physical servers.

For organizations such as universities, businesses and startups, IaaS provides an alternative to traditional infrastructure management.

As cloud computing continues to develop, understanding IaaS is important for students, developers and organizations interested in modern computing technologies.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

  2. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). What is Amazon EC2?

  3. Amazon Web Services. (n.d.). Amazon EC2 Documentation

event_model_payload.headline: Logging AI tool usage without logging sensitive data
event_model_payload.summary:
When a team adds an AI feature, the first debugging instinct is to log everything: the full prompt, the full response, the user's message. It works. It also means your logs now hold a copy of every customer email, contract and support ticket that went through the feature, sitting in a system with weaker access controls than your database and a much longer memory.

You need logs. You need them to debug bad answers, answer audit questions and keep costs under control. You don't need them to be a second copy of your customers' data.

Here's a practical middle path.

Decide what the logs are for

Before writing any code, list the questions your logs must answer. For most small teams it's these:

  1. Debugging: which prompt version and model produced this answer, and did the call fail?
  2. Audit: who (which user or service) used the AI feature, when, and on what record?
  3. Cost: how many tokens did we use, by feature and by customer?
  4. Safety: did a call get blocked, filtered or flagged?

Notice that none of these needs the full text of the prompt or the response. That's the key idea: log metadata by default, and content only by exception.

The default log record

This is the record to write for every call:

import hmac
import json
import logging
import os
import time
import uuid

log = logging.getLogger("ai_usage")


FP_KEY = os.environ["AI_LOG_FP_KEY"].encode()   # random secret, not in code


def fingerprint(text: str) -> str:
    """Keyed, non-reversible fingerprint so identical inputs can be grouped."""
    return hmac.new(FP_KEY, text.encode("utf-8"), "sha256").hexdigest()[:16]


def log_ai_call(*, feature, prompt_name, prompt_version, model, actor_id,
                record_id, prompt_text, response_text, usage, status, started):
    # started: value of time.monotonic() taken before the call
    usage = usage or {}                      # failed calls often have no usage data
    call_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "feature": feature,                  # e.g. "ticket_summary"
        "prompt": prompt_name,
        "prompt_version": prompt_version,
        "model": model,
        "actor_id": actor_id,                # internal user or service id, not an email
        "record_id": record_id,              # e.g. ticket id
        "input_chars": len(prompt_text),
        "input_fp": fingerprint(prompt_text),
        "output_chars": len(response_text or ""),
        "input_tokens": usage.get("input_tokens"),
        "output_tokens": usage.get("output_tokens"),
        "status": status,                    # "ok", "error", "blocked"
        "latency_ms": int((time.monotonic() - started) * 1000),
    }))
    return call_id

With this, you can trace any answer to a prompt version and a record, add up costs by feature, and see failure rates, all without storing a word of the customer's text.

A note on the fingerprint: a plain hash of short or predictable text (an email address, a yes/no answer) can be reversed by guessing, so the fingerprint is keyed with a secret (AI_LOG_FP_KEY), so it can't be checked by guessing without the key. The fingerprint is for grouping long, varied inputs ("were these two calls the same request?"), not for hiding identifiers. Identifiers like emails shouldn't go into it in the first place.

When you do need content: redact first

Sometimes you need to see what was sent, for example while fixing a specific bug. When that happens, log a redacted sample, not the raw text, and only when a flag is switched on.

A simple redaction pass catches the most common sensitive patterns:

import re

PATTERNS = [
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:sk|pk|api|key|token|ghp|xox[bp])[-_][A-Za-z0-9_-]{12,}\b", re.I), "[SECRET]"),
    (re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+"), "[EMAIL]"),
    (re.compile(r"\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b"), "[CARD]"),
    (re.compile(r"(?"), "[PHONE]"),
]


def redact(text: str, limit: int = 500) -> str:
    for pattern, label in PATTERNS:
        text = pattern.sub(label, text)
    return text[:limit]

Order matters: run the most specific patterns first. Secrets go before emails, cards and phone numbers, or a phone pattern can eat the digits in the middle of a key and leave the rest in the log.

import os

DEBUG_CONTENT = os.getenv("AI_LOG_CONTENT") == "1"

call_id = log_ai_call(...)  # same call as above

if DEBUG_CONTENT:
    log.info(json.dumps({
        "event": "ai_call_content",
        "call_id": call_id,
        "prompt_sample": redact(prompt_text),
        "response_sample": redact(response_text or ""),
    }))

Be honest about the limits. Regular expressions catch emails, phone numbers, card-like numbers and obvious keys. They won't catch names, many provider key formats (cloud access keys, bearer tokens), addresses, medical details or anything written in free text. That's why content logging stays off by default, is switched on for a short time for a specific problem, and is truncated. If your feature handles health, financial or legal information, don't log content at all; reproduce the problem with test data instead.

Keep content logs somewhere separate, for less time

Metadata and content have different risks, so treat them differently:

Metadata log Content sample log
Default Always on Off; switched on per incident
Who can read it Engineering and whoever handles costs A named few engineers
How long it's kept As long as your audit needs (agree this with whoever owns compliance) Days, not months
Where Your normal log system A separate log stream or index with its own access rule and expiry

Most log platforms let you route by a field (here, event) and set a separate retention period per stream. Use that, so content samples expire automatically and nobody has to remember to delete them.

Don't forget the other copies

Your own logs are only one place prompts end up:

  • The AI provider. Check their data retention and training settings for your account, and turn off anything you don't need. Write down what you chose and why.
  • Error trackers. Exception reports often capture local variables, including the prompt. Configure them to scrub request bodies and the variables that hold prompt text. Provider error messages sometimes echo part of the prompt too, so log the exception type (type(exc).__name__) and status code, not str(exc).
  • Analytics and tracing tools. If you trace requests end to end, make sure spans don't attach the full prompt as an attribute.
  • Chat and tickets. When someone pastes a "bad answer" into a team chat to discuss it, that's a copy too. Share the call_id instead, and look the details up where access is controlled.

What auditors usually ask

If you work with larger clients, sooner or later someone will ask how you control AI use. The metadata log answers most of it:

  • Which features use AI, and which models? (feature, model)
  • Who used them, on which records? (actor_id, record_id)
  • Can you show a change history for prompts? (prompt_version, plus your repository history)
  • How long do you keep AI-related data, and who can see it? (your retention table above)

Being able to answer those from a dashboard, rather than by searching raw text, is a good sign you've got the balance right.

A short checklist

  1. Write a metadata record for every AI call: feature, prompt version, model, actor, record, tokens, status, latency.
  2. Never put emails or other identifiers into actor_id or the fingerprint.
  3. Keep content logging off by default; when it's on, redact and truncate.
  4. Send content samples to a separate stream with short retention and narrow access.
  5. Review provider retention settings, error-tracker scrubbing and tracing attributes.
  6. Share call IDs in chat, not prompts.

Good AI logs tell you what happened without telling everyone what your customers said.

Ahmed Vaseer is Founder & CEO - Ingenious Concepts, an AI-first technology and digital growth agency. 80+ projects, ISO 27001 certified via Global CB.

event_model_payload.headline: UIDesignRequiresCompatibility ends with the iOS 27 SDK: finding the code that paints over Liquid Glass
event_model_payload.summary:
When iOS 26 introduced Liquid Glass, many teams added one key to Info.plist and moved on: UIDesignRequiresCompatibility, set to YES, keeps the earlier design. Apple's page for the key always called it temporary ("Temporarily use this key while reviewing and refining your app's UI"), and now it has an end date in practice: "The system ignores this key when you build for iOS 27 or later."

The SDK you build with is not entirely your choice. App Store submissions says that starting April 2027, iOS apps uploaded to App Store Connect "must be built with the iOS & iPadOS 27 SDK or later". Today the Upcoming Requirements page still asks for the iOS 26 SDK, so this is a planning item, not an emergency.

Deleting the key is one line. The real work is finding where your own code fights the new bars.

What actually needs review

Apple's Adopting Liquid Glass puts it this way: custom backgrounds and appearances in bars "might overlay or interfere with Liquid Glass". In a typical UIKit app that has been around since iOS 15, that code looks like this (from the test fixture I use below):

let navigation = UINavigationBarAppearance()
navigation.configureWithOpaqueBackground()
navigation.backgroundColor = .harborNavy
navigation.shadowColor = .clear
UINavigationBar.appearance().standardAppearance = navigation
UINavigationBar.appearance().scrollEdgeAppearance = navigation

let tabs = UITabBarAppearance()
tabs.configureWithOpaqueBackground()
tabs.backgroundColor = .white
UITabBar.appearance().isTranslucent = false

UIToolbar.appearance().barTintColor = .harborNavy

None of this is wrong; it is a brand decision made for an older design. With the opt-out ignored, it sits on top of a material the system wants to draw.

Listing it with glassready

I wrote an open-source CLI, glassready, that reads a native iOS, Flutter or React Native/Expo project and lists the opt-out and these places. It does not build, run or change anything. On the native-uikit-optout fixture from its repository:

npx @mcamdali/glassready

Excerpt of today's output (glassready 0.1.3, rules liquid-glass@2026.10.27, exit code 1):

Harbor · native iOS · .
target Harbor: opts out of Liquid Glass (Harbor/Info.plist)

The Liquid Glass opt-out is ignored when built with the iOS 27 SDK; 4 custom styles to review first

ERROR    GLS001 Liquid Glass opt-out that the iOS 27 SDK ignores
         Harbor/Info.plist:42
WARNING  GLS002 Bar appearance with its own background
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:28
WARNING  GLS002 Bar appearance with its own background
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:38
WARNING  GLS003 Bar colour or translucency set the old way
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:42
WARNING  GLS003 Bar colour or translucency set the old way
         Harbor/AppDelegate.swift:44
INFO     GLS006 Blur layer without a Liquid Glass counterpart
         Harbor/PortMapViewController.swift:5
INFO     GLS008 Fixed bar height or safe-area arithmetic
         Harbor/PortMapViewController.swift:26
         A number added to the safe-area insets.

1 error, 4 warnings, 2 info

The last finding is the subtle one. The fixture places a panel 49 points above the bottom safe area, the height of the classic tab bar:

summary.bottomAnchor.constraint(
    equalTo: view.bottomAnchor, constant: -(view.safeAreaInsets.bottom + 49)),

The report's fix: constrain to safeAreaLayoutGuide instead of adding a bar height, do not read the tab bar's frame for layout, and check the screen with the tab bar minimized as well.

The fixes the report gives

Each finding names a fix. For the bars, condensed from the report:

  • Opaque appearances (GLS002): remove configureWithOpaqueBackground() and the background and shadow settings, or apply them only before iOS 26 with if #available(iOS 26.0, *). Move the brand colour to tintColor and the title text attributes.
  • barTintColor, isTranslucent = false (GLS003): remove them, or keep them only for earlier versions; use tintColor for the bar's buttons.
  • Blur layers (GLS006): behind a floating panel, use UIGlassEffect on iOS 26 and later and keep the blur as the fallback; over a photo or a map, keep it.

The repository also has the same app after these fixes. The report on it:

target Harbor: no opt-out (Harbor/Info.plist)

Ready for Liquid Glass: no opt-out and no custom bar styles found
Impact: none (0 of 100)
Already uses: UIGlassEffect

0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 info

React Native, Expo and Flutter

In React Native the opt-out sits in ios//Info.plist; in Expo it can sit in ios.infoPlist in app.json. On the React Native 0.88.1 fixture (native stack around JavaScript bottom tabs), glassready reports, among others:

WARNING  GLS101 Native stack header with its own background
         App.tsx:54
         headerStyle.backgroundColor paints the header.
INFO     GLS102 Tab bar drawn in JavaScript
         App.tsx:29
         createBottomTabNavigator draws the tab bar in JavaScript.

The rule data explains the second one: a JavaScript tab bar "keeps its look" with the iOS 27 SDK while the native headers and sheets around it become Liquid Glass. For Flutter, the rules flag Cupertino bars that Flutter draws itself and UiKitView platform views next to Flutter widgets.

What the simulator showed

The repository records a simulator comparison from 27 October 2026, which I did not repeat here: the same UIKit app built with Xcode 27.1, with and without the key. On iOS 27.0 the screenshots match, so the key is ignored; on iOS 26.4 they differ. While the key stays, one build shows two designs depending on the device.

Limitations

From the README, and they matter:

  • Patterns, not a compiler. The rules are regular expressions over source text with comments and strings blanked. Generated code, macros or unusual shapes can be missed or matched by mistake.
  • Only the app's own sources. Pods, Swift packages outside the app folder, node_modules and Flutter plugins are not read.
  • .xcconfig files are not read; app.config.js/.ts are read as text, not run.
  • A warning is not a verdict. A brand colour on a bar can be a deliberate decision; the warning says where the code paints over the bar. Look at the screen on an iOS 27 simulator and decide.
  • The impact score sorts projects; in the README's words, "it does not grade the design."

Try it

In your app folder (Node.js 22.12 or later):

npx @mcamdali/glassready
npx @mcamdali/glassready --fail-on error --format markdown --output glassready.md

The second writes a Markdown report for a pull request and fails only on the ignored opt-out (exit 1 on the fixture above).

The opt-out answers how the app will look. Whether it will launch at all with the same SDK is a separate check, covered in "Built with the iOS 27 SDK, a UIKit app without a scene stops at launch".

Repository: github.com/muhittincamdali/glassready (MIT).

Muhittin Camdali is a mobile engineer (iOS, Flutter, React Native) and the author of glassready.
