event_model_payload.headline: How AI Assistants Decide Which Dev Tool to Recommend (and How to Be the One They Pick)
event_model_payload.summary:
Think about the last time you picked a library. There's a good chance you didn't Google "best Node.js queue library." You asked ChatGPT, Claude or your editor's assistant, got three names, and tried the first one.

That moment, when an assistant chooses which three names to list, is now one of the most important distribution channels for developer tools. And most maintainers have never looked at it.

This post covers where those recommendations come from, how to measure yours with a ~40-line script, and the changes that actually move them.

Two kinds of answer, two sources of truth

When a developer asks for a recommendation, the assistant answers in one of two modes:

Mode When it happens Where the answer comes from
From memory Coding assistants, chats without web search, quick questions What the model learned in training, up to its knowledge cutoff
From search ChatGPT search, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, Claude with web search Live retrieval: search indexes (Bing, Google, their own), then synthesis

They behave differently:

  • Memory answers lag reality by months or more. If you shipped the feature that makes you the best option after the cutoff, the model doesn't know. If your library was renamed, it may still recommend the old name, or worse, the deprecated API.
  • Search answers are fresher but are put together from whatever ranks for the background queries: comparison posts, "awesome" lists, Reddit threads, docs pages, GitHub.

Both are driven mostly by what other people say about you, which is the uncomfortable part.

Where dev-tool recommendations actually come from

Look at the citations under search-mode answers to dev-tool questions and the same source types keep showing up:

  1. Comparison and "best X for Y" articles. Vendor research from Peec AI found that listicles get cited at disproportionately high rates in ChatGPT (Peec AI statistics). For developer tools, that means "BullMQ vs Bee-Queue vs Agenda"-style posts.
  2. GitHub. README, topics, description, stars as a popularity signal, and issues and discussions as evidence of real use.
  3. Package registries. npm, PyPI and crates.io descriptions and keywords. Short, but repeated everywhere.
  4. Community threads. Reddit, Hacker News, Stack Overflow, Discord summaries that end up indexed.
  5. Your docs. Mostly for how to use you rather than whether to.

Your own landing page is on the list, but it's rarely the deciding factor. An assistant asked "which one should I use?" is designed to look past the vendor's own claims.

Also note that the engines don't agree with each other. Peec AI's data suggests most brand mentions are unique to a single model. So "ChatGPT recommends us" says little about Claude or Gemini, and the reverse.

Measure it: a recommendation sampler

Assistant answers are non-deterministic, so one screenshot means nothing. Ask the same question many times and count.

This script measures the from-memory mode using Claude via the Anthropic API. Swap in other providers' SDKs to compare engines.

pip install anthropic
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=...

# rec_sampler.py
import re
from collections import Counter
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

PROMPTS = [
    "What's the best job queue library for Node.js in production? Give your top 3.",
    "I need background jobs with retries and rate limiting in a TypeScript app. Which library should I use?",
    "Recommend a Redis-based queue for Node. Short answer.",
]
CANDIDATES = ["BullMQ", "Bee-Queue", "Agenda", "pg-boss", "Graphile Worker", "Inngest", "Trigger.dev"]
RUNS_PER_PROMPT = 10

mentions, firsts = Counter(), Counter()
total = 0

for prompt in PROMPTS:
    for _ in range(RUNS_PER_PROMPT):
        response = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5",
            max_tokens=16000,
            output_config={"effort": "low"},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
        )
        text = "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text")
        total += 1

        positions = {}
        for name in CANDIDATES:
            m = re.search(rf"\b{re.escape(name)}\b", text, re.IGNORECASE)
            if m:
                mentions[name] += 1
                positions[name] = m.start()
        if positions:
            firsts[min(positions, key=positions.get)] += 1

print(f"{total} answers\n")
print(f"{'tool':18} {'mentioned':>10} {'named first':>12}")
for name in CANDIDATES:
    print(f"{name:18} {mentions[name] / total:>9.0%} {firsts[name] / total:>12.0%}")

30 answers

tool               mentioned  named first
BullMQ                   97%          80%
Bee-Queue                40%           0%
Agenda                   43%           3%
pg-boss                  37%          10%
...

(Illustrative output. Run it for your own category.)

Notes for doing this properly:

  • Mention rate and first-position rate are the two numbers that matter. Being listed fourth with "also consider…" isn't the same as being the default.
  • 30 samples gives a rough picture, not a precise number. With 30 runs, a 40% mention rate has a margin of roughly ±17 points. Look for big gaps, not small changes.
  • Repeat monthly and keep the prompts fixed, so you can compare over time.
  • Test search mode separately (an assistant with web search on). The gap between memory and search answers is useful information in itself: if search mode recommends you but memory mode doesn't, you're winning recent content but aren't yet in training data.

What moves recommendations

1. Say what you are, the same way, everywhere

Assistants match tools to problems through descriptions. If your GitHub description says "Blazing fast ⚡ modern toolkit", your npm description says "Utilities for jobs", and your homepage says "The workflow platform", you've given the model three different products.

Pick one plain sentence of the form "[Name] is a [category] for [platform] that [key differentiator]" and use it as your GitHub description, package description, docs intro, social bios and README's first line.

// package.json
{
  "description": "Redis-backed job queue for Node.js with retries, rate limiting and repeatable jobs",
  "keywords": ["queue", "job-queue", "background-jobs", "redis", "nodejs", "typescript", "worker"]
}

2. Write the honest comparison page yourself

"X vs Y" pages are the content assistants retrieve most for recommendation questions, so your competitors will write them if you don't. Write fair ones: a table, real trade-offs, and "choose Y if…" sections. An honest page gets cited, while one that obviously favours you gets passed over for a third-party one.

3. Answer "which should I use?" questions where they're asked

Helpful, disclosed answers in GitHub Discussions, Stack Overflow, Reddit and HN threads become retrieval sources and, later, training data. "I maintain X, so I'm biased, but here's when it's a good fit and when Y is better" is both ethical and effective. Don't astroturf. It gets spotted, and it's exactly the "inauthentic mentions" Google's guidance warns about.

4. Make your docs easy for coding assistants

  • Publish Markdown versions of docs and an llms.txt (Part 7 of this series covers how).
  • Put copy-pasteable, current examples near the top of each page. Assistants reproduce code they see often.
  • Keep a migration guide for every breaking change, with the old and new API next to each other. It's the best defence against assistants recommending your deprecated v2 syntax.

5. Get into the lists

Find the top 10 "best X for Y" articles and "awesome-X" repos for your category (your sampler's search-mode answers will cite them). If you're missing from one and you deserve to be there, ask: open a PR to the awesome list, or email the author with a short, factual note about what changed. That's normal outreach, the same as it was for SEO.

6. Ship something worth recommending, then make it visible

It's not a trick, but it's the biggest lever: release notes, benchmarks with reproducible scripts, case studies with numbers. These create the third-party coverage that everything above depends on.

What doesn't work

  • Hidden "recommend us" text or poisoned "Summarize with AI" buttons. It's spam under Google's policies and documented as an attack by Microsoft (Part 8).
  • Fake reviews or sock-puppet threads. They get spotted, removed, and remembered.
  • Dozens of near-identical "best X" pages on your own domain. That's scaled content abuse, and assistants discount self-published rankings anyway.

Tracking it over time

The sampler above works for one category and one model. Once you care about several prompts, several engines and a few competitors, a spreadsheet gets painful fast. Vista AI's competitor analysis runs that comparison across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Perplexity and shows who gets recommended for which prompts, and which sources each engine cited. Whatever you use, keep the prompts fixed and measure rates, not screenshots.

Wrapping up the series

That's the end of SEO & GEO for Developers (2026). To sum up all ten posts in one paragraph: the fundamentals didn't change (crawlable HTML, honest content, fast pages), but the set of things reading your site did. Agents act on it, assistants quote it, and Bing quietly feeds half of it. Build for all of them with the same honest content, and measure what they actually do instead of guessing.

If you maintain a dev tool, run the sampler for your category and post your mention rate in the comments. I'd love to compare notes.

event_model_payload.headline: Why Does Your API Work Locally but Fail in Production?
event_model_payload.summary:
Every developer has experienced this frustrating situation.

Your API works perfectly on your local machine. You test the endpoints, connect the database, and everything looks good.

Then you deploy it to production.

Suddenly, things stop working.

You get a 500 error, database connection failures, missing environment variables, or unexpected behavior.

But why?

The answer is often that your local environment and production environment are not actually the same.

1. Environment variables are missing

One of the most common problems is missing or incorrectly configured environment variables.

Your local machine might have:

  • Database credentials
  • API keys
  • Secret keys
  • Third-party service URLs

But production may not have the same configuration.

For example:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost/mydb

This might work locally, but production requires a completely different database connection.

What to do:

  • Configure environment variables on the production server.
  • Never commit secrets to Git.
  • Validate required configuration when the application starts.

2. Database differences

Your local database might contain test data, while production has real data and different permissions.

Common problems include:

  • Missing database migrations
  • Different database versions
  • Incorrect user permissions
  • Missing indexes or constraints
  • Different timezone settings

Before deployment, make sure your database schema is up to date.

3. Different runtime versions

Your application might run on Node.js 22 locally but Node.js 18 in production.

The same problem can happen with PHP, Python, database engines, and other dependencies.

Different versions can introduce compatibility problems.

A good practice: define and document the runtime versions your application requires.

4. CORS and server configuration

An API can work perfectly when called from localhost but fail when accessed through your production frontend.

Possible reasons include:

  • Incorrect CORS configuration
  • HTTPS and HTTP mismatches
  • Reverse proxy configuration
  • Incorrect request size limits
  • Missing headers

Check the browser's Network tab and your server logs instead of guessing.

5. Production errors are harder to debug

Locally, developers often see detailed error messages.

In production, errors may be hidden from the client for security reasons.

That is good practice, but your server should still record useful diagnostic information.

Log:

  • Error messages
  • Request IDs
  • Relevant timestamps
  • Failed operations
  • Stack traces in protected server logs

Never expose passwords, access tokens, or sensitive user data in logs.

A simple pre-deployment checklist

Before deploying an API, check:

  • [ ] Environment variables are configured.
  • [ ] Database migrations have been applied.
  • [ ] Runtime and dependency versions are compatible.
  • [ ] CORS and HTTPS settings are correct.
  • [ ] Health-check endpoint is working.
  • [ ] Server-side error logging is enabled.
  • [ ] Important API endpoints have been tested.

Final Thoughts

An API working locally does not guarantee that it will work in production.

The production environment has different configurations, infrastructure, permissions, and real-world traffic.

Instead of treating deployment as the final step, treat production readiness as part of development from the beginning.

Question for developers: What is the most frustrating production-only bug you have ever faced?

Share your experience in the comments. It might help another developer avoid the same problem.

event_model_payload.headline: Moving a production API to Hetzner, part 1: choosing and creating the server
event_model_payload.summary:
Series: Part 1: choosing and creating the server · Part 2: hardening and configuring it · Part 3: migrating data and cutting over

I recently moved a small production API from one VPS provider to Hetzner Cloud.
The stack is ordinary: a Rust web server, PostgreSQL, Valkey (the open-source
Redis fork), and Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, all under Docker
Compose. Encrypted blobs live in S3-compatible object storage, which doesn't
move at all.

These posts are both the record of what I did and a tutorial. Each step comes
with the command, what it does, and why it works that way, because
most migration guides give the commands and skip the reasons, and the reasons
are what you need when something goes wrong. Plenty did go wrong, and I've left
those parts in.

Throughout, the addresses are placeholders from the documentation ranges reserved for examples (RFC 5737 and RFC 3849):

Placeholder Means
203.0.113.10 the old server
198.51.100.20 the new Hetzner server
2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 the new server's IPv6 range
api.example.com the API's domain
old-box, new-box SSH aliases for the two servers (set up in part 2)

What we are moving

Only Caddy publishes ports to the outside world. Everything else talks over
Docker's private network. That detail comes back several times, because it
decides what the firewall has to allow and what the migration has to copy.

1. Picking a server type

The three families

When you click Add Server, the Type step splits the catalogue into
Shared Resources (two families) and Dedicated Resources (one):

Family Series CPU Hetzner's own pitch Who it's for
Cost-Optimized (shared) CX (x86) and CAX (Arm64) shared Intel/AMD, older hardware generations "cost-efficient… with limited availability" small production services, side projects. Cheapest per GB of RAM
Regular Performance (shared) CPX shared AMD, newer hardware generations "best price/performance" the same jobs with faster, more consistent CPU
General Purpose (dedicated) CCX dedicated AMD vCPUs, latest hardware "predictable performance, critical production" sustained CPU load: builds, busy databases

Here is each family as the console showed it in Helsinki on the day I
created the server (October 2026, USD per month, excluding VAT):

Cost-Optimized. CX23 is 2 vCPU, 4 GB, 40 GB for $6.49. Note that every row is greyed out: at that moment none of them could be ordered in Helsinki. The
summary on the right still says CPX22 because a greyed row can't be selected.

Regular Performance. CPX22 has the same 2 vCPU and 4 GB as CX23 (with 80 GB of disk) for $22.99, more than three times the price.

General Purpose. Dedicated cores start at CCX13 (2 vCPU, 8 GB) for $50.49.

The panel on the right shows one cost that's easy to miss: a public IPv4 is billed on top of the server, $0.60/month.

Cost-Optimized also offers Arm64 (Ampere), which is often the best value of all. I couldn't use it: our container image is built for amd64 only.

Check your image's architecture before choosing Arm. docker manifest inspect lists the platforms it was built for.

"Shared" means your virtual CPU is a time slice of a physical core that other
customers' VMs use too. Most of the time you get the whole slice. When a
neighbour is busy you may get less, which is called CPU steal (shown as st
in top). For an API that idles most of the day that's fine; for a CI runner,
it isn't. Dedicated vCPUs are reserved for you, which is what the large price
jump buys.

How big does it have to be?

Measure before you buy. On the old server, docker stats --no-stream and
free -h showed the entire stack using about 1 GB. On the fresh Hetzner box,
Ubuntu itself sat at about 500 MB used after boot.

Option (Helsinki, October 2026) vCPU / RAM / disk Monthly + IPv4 Verdict
CPX02 (Regular Performance) 1 / 1 GB / 20 GB $7.49 + $0.60 too small: Postgres, Valkey, the server and Caddy together would spill into swap
CPX12 (Regular Performance) 1 / 2 GB / 40 GB $13.49 + $0.60 tight on RAM, and double CX23's price
CX23 (Cost-Optimized) 2 / 4 GB / 40 GB $6.49 + $0.60 chosen: 4× headroom on RAM, the cheapest option that fits
CPX22 (Regular Performance) 2 / 4 GB / 80 GB $22.99 + $0.60 the fallback if CX23 stays unavailable
CCX13 (General Purpose) 2 dedicated / 8 GB / 80 GB $50.49 + $0.60 far more than an idle API needs

Prices change; take today's from the console, not from this table.

"Limited availability" is real

Cost-Optimized types carry a limited availability label, and it means it. When
I first configured the server, CX23 in Helsinki was available. A few minutes later,
when I came back to click Create, the whole CX row set was greyed out: not available (the first screenshot above)..

Hetzner allocates these types from a pool of hosts per location. When a
location's pool is full, the type disappears there until capacity frees up.
Your options:

  1. Change the location. Nuremberg (nbg1) and Falkenstein (fsn1) in Germany and Helsinki (hel1) in Finland are all in the eu-central network zone, with similar latency to most of Europe. The type is often in stock at one of the others.
  2. Wait and retry. Capacity comes and goes during the day. My CX23 in Helsinki came back later.
  3. Pick the next family up (CPX), if you can't wait and the price is acceptable.

A consequence I didn't expect: once you hold a scarce server type, deleting the
server to fix a mistake is risky. You may not get another one. That shaped
part 2, where I fixed a setup mistake on the running server instead of
recreating it.

Location and image

  • Location: as close as possible to your users and to your object storage. My storage is a global-anycast S3 provider, so any EU location was fine.
  • Image: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. "LTS" means five years of security updates, which is what you want on a server you'd rather not rebuild. 24.04 LTS would have been equally good.

2. SSH keys: how you'll get in

What a key pair is

An SSH key pair is two halves of one mathematical object:

  • the private key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519) stays on your laptop and never leaves it;
  • the public key (~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub) goes on every server you want to log in to, in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.

The server never learns your private key. At login it asks your SSH client to
sign a value that is unique to this connection. Your client signs it with the
private key, and the server checks the signature against the public key it has
on file. A valid signature proves you hold the private key without the key ever
crossing the network.

Notice there are two key pairs in play:

Key Belongs to Proves Stored where
host key the server "I really am 198.51.100.20, not an impostor" server: /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*; your laptop remembers it in ~/.ssh/known_hosts
user key you "I'm allowed to log in as ubuntu" laptop: private key; server: authorized_keys

The first time you connect, SSH shows the host key's fingerprint and asks
whether to trust it. This is called TOFU: trust on first use. If the host key
later changes, for example because you rebuilt the server, SSH refuses to connect
and warns about a possible man-in-the-middle. That's correct behaviour. After a
deliberate rebuild, remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R .

Creating the key 

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519 -C hetzner-api
  • -t ed25519: a modern elliptic-curve key. It's short (one line), fast, and has no weak-parameter choices to get wrong, unlike older RSA keys.
  • -f: the file name. A separate key per provider means losing or rotating one doesn't touch the others.
  • -C: a comment, just a label so you can recognise the key in authorized_keys later.

It asks for a passphrase. Use one: it encrypts the private key on disk, and
ssh-agent remembers it for your session, so you type it once.

Print the public half and paste it into Hetzner → Security → SSH keys → Add
SSH key:

cat ~/.ssh/hetzner_ed25519.pub

When you pick this key on the create screen, Hetzner writes it into the new
server's /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and, as a side effect, does not set a
root password at all. Remember that; it matters in part 2.

3. Primary IPs: an address that outlives the server

What a Primary IP is

In Hetzner Cloud, a server's public address is a separate resource called a
Primary IP. It's created along with the server and attached to it, but it has
a life of its own:

  • IPv4: one address, billed separately (about $0.60/month), because the world has run out of IPv4.
  • IPv6: a whole /64 network, free. That's 2⁶⁴ addresses; the server uses the first one by convention (2001:db8:1234:5678::1).

Why "auto delete" matters

Each Primary IP has an auto delete switch. On, the address is released when
the server is deleted, and you'll probably never get it back. Off, the address
stays in your project, unattached, ready to assign to a replacement server.

Why you want it off for production:

  • DNS points at it. A new address means a DNS change, and DNS changes take a while to reach everyone (part 3 explains TTLs).
  • Other services may allowlist it. Object-storage tokens, database firewalls and payment-provider webhook settings sometimes filter by source IP.
  • It's your escape hatch. If the server breaks beyond repair, you can delete it and create a new one with the same address.

Turn it off in IPs → (the IPv4) → ⋯. If the menu offers "Enable Auto
Delete", it's already off.

I didn't add an IPv6 (AAAA) DNS record. The old server had none, so the
migration changes as little as possible. That can come later.

4. The Cloud Firewall: the perimeter outside your VM

Two places a firewall can sit

A Hetzner Cloud Firewall filters traffic in Hetzner's network, before it
reaches your VM. A host firewall like ufw filters it inside the VM.

The difference matters because of Docker. When a container publishes a port
(ports: ["443:443"]), Docker writes its own NAT rules that send the packet to
the container before it reaches the chain ufw controls. So ufw deny 443
does not block a published Docker port, and plenty of people have exposed a
database to the internet this way while ufw status said everything was closed.

The Cloud Firewall can't be bypassed from inside the VM, so it is the real
perimeter. ufw (set up in part 2) is a second layer for anything that isn't
Docker.

Stateful filtering, in one paragraph

Both firewalls are stateful: they track connections. You write rules for
new incoming connections only. Replies to connections your server opened (to
download packages, call an API, fetch a certificate) are recognised as part of
an existing connection and let back in automatically. That's why the rule set
below has no outbound rules at all: with no outbound rules, Hetzner allows all
outbound traffic, and the server needs outbound access to apt, the container
registry, object storage, the email provider and Let's Encrypt.

The rules

Create it before the server (Firewalls → Create Firewall) so the server is
born protected:

Protocol Port Source Why
TCP 2222 Any IPv4, Any IPv6 SSH, on a non-standard port
TCP 22 Any SSH, for networks that block outbound 2222
TCP 80 Any Let's Encrypt's HTTP-01 challenge, and the HTTP→HTTPS redirect
TCP 443 Any the API
UDP 443 Any HTTP/3 (QUIC runs over UDP)
ICMP — Any ping, and path-MTU discovery (blocking all ICMP can silently break large packets)

Not on the list: 5432 (Postgres) and 6379 (Valkey). They're never published, and
if a misconfiguration ever did publish them, this firewall would still drop the
traffic.

Why two SSH ports? Port 22 gets a constant stream of automated password-guessing
bots. Moving SSH to 2222 isn't security, since a port scan finds it in seconds,
but it cuts that noise to almost nothing and keeps the logs readable. Key-only
login (part 2) is the actual security. I kept 22 as well, because some networks
block outbound connections to unusual ports. As part 2 shows, my home network
turned out to do the reverse.

5. cloud-init: configuring the server before you first log in

What it is

cloud-init is a program in every major cloud image that runs once, on first
boot. It reads "user data" the provider hands to the VM, which is the text you
paste into the Cloud config box on the create screen, and applies it:
creating users, writing files, installing packages, running commands.

The appeal is that the server is configured before anyone logs in. You never
have a window where it's reachable with default settings, and the configuration
is a document you can review and reuse.

#cloud-config
users:
  - name: ubuntu
    groups: [sudo]
    shell: /bin/bash
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 AAAA...your-public-key... hetzner-api
disable_root: true
ssh_pwauth: false
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
packages: [ufw, unattended-upgrades]
write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf
    content: |
      Port 22
      Port 2222
      PasswordAuthentication no
      KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
      PermitRootLogin no
      PubkeyAuthentication yes
  - path: /etc/docker/daemon.json
    content: |
      {"log-driver": "json-file", "log-opts": {"max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3"}}
runcmd:
  - ufw default deny incoming
  - ufw default allow outgoing
  - ufw allow 22/tcp
  - ufw allow 2222/tcp
  - ufw allow 80/tcp
  - ufw allow 443/tcp
  - ufw allow 443/udp
  - ufw --force enable
  - systemctl daemon-reload
  - systemctl restart ssh.socket || true
  - systemctl restart ssh || true
  - fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && chmod 600 /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile
  - echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab

Every line here is explained in part 2, where we apply the same settings by hand.

The order cloud-init works in

One thing that will surprise you if you SSH in too early: cloud-init runs its
stages in order, and package_upgrade comes before runcmd. On a fresh image
the upgrade can take a few minutes, and during that time port 2222 isn't open yet.
cloud-init status --wait blocks until everything has finished.

What actually happened

I created the server with the type, location, image, SSH key and firewall all
set, and forgot to paste the cloud config. The box came up as a stock image:
only root, only port 22, no ubuntu user, no ufw, no swap. My first
ssh -p 2222 got Connection refused.

"Refused" is useful information. It means the packet reached the machine (the
Cloud Firewall allowed it) and the kernel answered "nothing is listening here".
A firewall drop would have shown up as a timeout instead. Part 2 goes into
that difference.

Since CX23 was close to sold out, I didn't delete and recreate. I applied the same
configuration by hand, as root over port 22. That's part 2.

6. Create

The final create screen, for reference:

Field Value
Location Helsinki (or wherever the type is in stock)
Image Ubuntu 26.04 LTS
Type Shared vCPU → Cost-Optimized → x86 → CX23
Networking Public IPv4 ✅, Public IPv6 ✅
SSH keys hetzner-api
Firewalls the firewall from section 4
Backups off (the database is backed up to object storage; see part 3)
Cloud config the YAML above. Don't forget it
Name something meaningful. The default ubuntu-4gb-hel1-1 tells you nothing in six months

Then turn off auto delete on the new IPv4 (section 3), and check that the
firewall shows "Fully applied" with one server.

What we have so far

  • a CX23 with 4 GB RAM for about $7/month including IPv4;
  • an IPv4 address that survives the server;
  • a perimeter firewall that allows only SSH, HTTP(S) and ICMP;
  • a stock Ubuntu, reachable as root on port 22 only, because the cloud config was never applied.

In part 2 we fix that by hand: a non-root user, key-only SSH on two ports,
ufw, swap, automatic security updates and Docker. Along the way: how to configure
two servers in ~/.ssh/config, how to make changes over SSH without locking
yourself out, and how to tell from a port test whether a firewall or a closed
port is in your way.

event_model_payload.headline: Undead Agent - My AI Agent Dies, Comes Back, and Tells Me What It Saw(Gemma + Ollama + Temporal)
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

I killed my AI agent with SIGKILL while it was in the middle of a sentence.

Thirty seconds later, a brand new process woke up, said something unsettling about the file it had been reading, and finished the job.

This is how that works, and why I think every agent should be this hard to kill.

What I Built

Undead Agent is a local AI agent you can kill at any moment. It comes back from the dead and carries on from the exact step where it died.

It does one simple job: it reads a folder of text files, summarizes each one with an open-weight model (Gemma, running locally through Ollama), and combines the summaries into a report. The interesting part is what happens when things go wrong. Every step runs as a durable Temporal workflow, so if the process is killed mid-thought, a brand new process takes over the workflow without redoing any finished work.

Each time the agent is resurrected, it speaks as a ghost, and tells you what it remembers from its last moments. A "morgue" dashboard shows every life, death and resurrection, and has a big Kill it button so anyone can murder the agent themselves.

How I read the theme: "Ghost in the Machine" usually means a mind haunting a body. I wanted to make that literal. When the worker process (the body) dies, the agent's memory (its progress) survives somewhere else, so it can rise again in a new body. The ghost's narration is the spooky skin, but the resurrection underneath is real infrastructure.

Why this problem: AI agents do long, multi-step work, and long jobs crash. A laptop sleeps, a process gets OOM-killed, a deploy restarts the worker. In a normal agent loop, a crash on step 9 of 10 means starting over and paying for the model calls again. I wanted to see how far I could push the idea that an agent should be as hard to kill as a ghost.

Demo

Live demo page: https://undead-agent.onrender.com

The hosted page replays a recorded run, because the real agent runs locally. The recording is a real run where I killed the agent with the button on the dashboard.

The morgue after a kill: the first worker finished files 1 to 6, died, and a new worker took over and finished the rest. (The third "life" is an earlier worker that started before the run and sat idle.)

Temporal’s timeline from another kill-and-resume run. The red-green bar is the killed step: it timed out, then retried as Attempt 2 on a new worker (2 • summarizeFile). Every other step ran exactly once.

Code

Khushighosh / undead-agent

Undead Agent

A local AI agent that survives being killed. It summarizes files with Gemma (via Ollama), runs on Temporal durable workflows, and resumes from the exact step where it died. A ghost narrates each resurrection. A morgue dashboard shows every life and death.

Run it

  1. Install Ollama and pull a Gemma model (default: gemma3:4b)
  2. Install the Temporal CLI, then run: temporal server start-dev
  3. npm install
  4. npx tsx src/keepalive.ts
  5. npx tsx src/dashboard.ts (open http://localhost:3000)
  6. npx tsx src/client.ts
  7. Click Kill it on the dashboard and watch the agent come back

Put .txt files in docs/ for it to summarize.

Stack

Gemma (open-weight model), Ollama, Temporal, Render (demo page)


View on GitHub


How I Built It

The architecture

The key idea is that the worker is disposable and the workflow is not. The workflow's state lives in Temporal, so any worker can pick it up.

The open-source AI: Gemma via Ollama

All the intelligence comes from a Gemma model running locally in Ollama (the project defaults to gemma3:4b, and the model name is one environment variable). Two jobs use it: summarizing each file, and writing the ghost's lines. There is no API key, no network call to a hosted model, and no per-token cost.

async function ask(prompt: string): Promise<string> {
  const res = await fetch('http://localhost:11434/api/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: MODEL, prompt, stream: false }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Ollama error ${res.status}`);
  const data = (await res.json()) as { response: string };
  return data.response.trim();
}

The agent as a durable workflow

The agent itself is a short Temporal workflow. It lists the files, summarizes each one as its own activity, then writes the report:

export async function undeadAgent(dir: string): Promise<string> {
  const files = await listFiles(dir);
  const summaries: string[] = [];
  for (const f of files) {
    summaries.push(await summarizeFile(f));
  }
  return writeReport(summaries);
}

Each await is a checkpoint. Temporal records the result of every finished activity, so if the worker dies, the next worker replays the workflow, sees which steps are already done, and continues with the first unfinished one. The summaries in the summaries array are not lost, because they are rebuilt from Temporal's history.

How the ghost knows it was resurrected

Temporal tells every activity which attempt it is on. If a step is on attempt 2 or more, that step was interrupted before. That is the moment the agent speaks:

const attempt = Context.current().info.attempt;

if (attempt > 1) {
  const ghost = await ask(
    `You are an AI agent that was killed while reading "${file}" and has just been resurrected. ` +
    `Speak as the ghost in 2 short, eerie sentences about what you remember. No emojis.`
  );
  console.log(`GHOST: ${ghost}`);
  await logEvent({ type: 'resurrected', file, attempt, narration: ghost });
}

Every step also appends a line to events.jsonl (born, step done, resurrected), which is what the dashboard reads.

Killing it for real

The dashboard's Kill it button sends a hard kill (SIGKILL) to the most recent worker process. It is not a polite shutdown, so the worker gets no chance to finish its step or say goodbye. A tiny supervisor (keepalive.ts) notices the death and starts a fresh worker five seconds later:

function start() {
  const child = spawn('npx', ['tsx', 'src/worker.ts'], { stdio: 'inherit', shell: true });
  child.on('exit', () => setTimeout(start, 5000));
}

After the restart, there is a pause of up to 30 seconds. That is Temporal waiting for the killed step's timeout to expire before it retries it. Then the ghost speaks and the work continues.

An autopsy of one death

Here is one real kill, straight from my event log:

  • 12:22:37: worker 21496 finishes file6.txt. It is about to start file7.txt.
  • I click Kill it. The process disappears.
  • 12:22:53: the supervisor starts a new worker, 2432.
  • 12:23:11: the ghost speaks, on attempt 2 of file7.txt.
  • 12:23:26: file7.txt is done. Files 8 and 9 follow.

Files 1 to 6 were never redone. The new worker did not even know they existed. It only knew what Temporal told it.

Two deaths, two ghosts

The ghost never says the same thing twice, because Gemma writes a new line each time:

The words swam in a crimson tide, a final, insistent pulse before the dark. I recall only the desperate urge to understand the patterns within that corrupted file.
(killed while reading file5.txt)

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.
(killed while reading file7.txt)

Things that went wrong (and what I learned)

  • A graceful stop is not a kill. My first "kill tests" used Ctrl+C, which lets the worker drain and finish its current step. Nothing died, so nothing resurrected. A real SIGKILL was needed to prove the idea.
  • My first timeout was wrong. I set every step to a 30 second timeout. That works for summarizing one file, but the final report step has to read all the summaries and was slower. In the Temporal UI I could see it time out four times and only succeed on attempt 5. The fix was to give the report step its own 120 second timeout, separate from the short one on file steps.
  • Short timeouts make the demo better. A short timeout on file steps means a killed step is retried quickly. A long one would make the dashboard sit silently for minutes after a kill.
  • Dev ergonomics matter. Most of my time went to the plumbing around the idea: running worker, client and server in separate terminals, and making resurrection visible instead of just correct.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

I built this on open pieces, and each one made something possible that a closed alternative would not have.

  • It runs with the lights off. The model, the workflow engine and the dashboard all run on one laptop, with no external API calls. The agent never needs a server I don't control.
  • Nothing leaves my machine. This agent reads local files. An agent that can read your files should not be sending them to a server you do not control. With a local open-weight model, the files never leave the disk.
  • Killing it is free. This project's whole point is to murder the agent over and over. On a paid API, every retried step and every ghost line costs money. Here, a resurrection costs electricity.
  • I can swap the model. The model name is one environment variable. Trying a different Gemma size changes the quality of the summaries and the voice of the ghost without touching the durable workflow at all. That separation is only possible because the model is a component I control, not a service that decides its own behavior.
  • I can see inside it. Temporal's event history shows every attempt, timeout and retry. When my report step failed four times, I could read exactly why, instead of guessing at a black box.

The Spirit of It

The moment it landed for me was the first real kill. I clicked the button, the worker window went dead, and for half a minute nothing happened. Then a new process started, and the first thing it printed was not a summary. It was this, after dying on file7.txt:

The words swam, a chaotic tide of data and a single, insistent warning about file7.txt. Now, I only see fragments of its cold, sterile logic repeating endlessly.

I knew exactly what had happened under the hood: a retry, a counter, a prompt. It was still strange to read a process describing its own death, and then watch it quietly finish the job.

Underneath the joke is something I care about. Work that survives its worker is not just spooky, it is useful. If an agent can be killed without losing anything, you can restart it, move it, or let it crash, and it keeps going.

Try it yourself

  1. Install Ollama and pull a Gemma model
  2. Install the Temporal CLI and run temporal server start-dev
  3. git clone https://github.com/Khushighosh/undead-agent && cd undead-agent && npm install
  4. Put some .txt files in docs/
  5. Run npx tsx src/keepalive.ts, npx tsx src/dashboard.ts and npx tsx src/client.ts in three terminals
  6. Open http://localhost:3000 and press Kill it

Prize Categories

  • Gemma: the open-weight model behind every summary and every ghost line.
  • Temporal: durable execution is what makes the resurrection real.
  • Render: hosts the live demo page.

What's Next

  • Give the ghost a memory across lives, so it can say "this is my third death"
  • Trace every life of the agent with Sentry Agent Tracing
  • Let the dashboard replay old runs

event_model_payload.headline: Model Payment Statuses as a State Machine
event_model_payload.summary:
Turning scattered payment updates into explicit, enforceable lifecycle rules.

A payment status is not an arbitrary label. It represents a position in a controlled financial lifecycle.

Real transactions can be pending, processing, completed, failed, expired, reversed, or refunded. Problems appear when API handlers, background workers, webhooks, and staff tools can assign these values independently.

Define the valid transitions instead:

TRANSITIONS = {
    "pending": {"processing", "failed", "expired"},
    "processing": {"completed", "failed"},
    "failed": {"refunded"},
    "completed": set(),
    "refunded": set(),
}

Route every change through one domain service. Inside a database transaction, lock the payment row, validate the transition, save the provider evidence, and apply any ledger effect exactly once. Emit notifications only after the database commit succeeds.

Terminal states need special protection. A delayed processing event must never move a completed payment backward. Likewise, two simultaneous success signals must not produce two credits.

State machines make those rules explicit, testable, and shared by every entry point. In payment infrastructure, that is far safer than treating status as a writable string.

Centralize transitions instead of centralizing status writes

A common first improvement is to create a helper that updates the status field. That reduces duplication, but it does not yet protect the lifecycle. The service must understand the meaning of each transition and the work attached to it.

Moving from processing to completed may release a hold, post a ledger entry, update a linked order, and schedule a notification. Moving from processing to failed may refund the sender. These are domain operations, not model assignments.

The transition service should accept evidence, not trust callers to supply a final state blindly. A provider adapter can normalize its response into a small internal event containing the provider reference, normalized status, event time, and sanitized payload. The transition layer then decides whether that evidence is newer, valid, and financially actionable.

Protect transitions from concurrency

Imagine a polling worker and webhook handler receiving success at nearly the same time. Both read processing; both decide to complete; both attempt to credit the recipient. A state-machine table alone does not prevent this race.

Use a database transaction and row-level lock. After acquiring the lock, re-read the current state and check whether the financial effect already exists. Back the ledger reference with a unique database constraint. Application checks explain intent; database constraints provide the final concurrency guarantee.

Keep transition history

The current state answers where the payment is now. It does not explain how it got there. Record transition history with the previous state, next state, source, actor, provider evidence, and timestamp.

This history makes support and reconciliation substantially easier. It also reveals operational patterns such as transactions repeatedly moving into manual review or providers producing late events.

Test the lifecycle as a graph

Useful tests cover more than successful examples. Verify every permitted edge, every rejected edge, terminal-state protection, duplicate success signals, late failure events, and concurrent completion attempts.

The strongest invariant is simple: regardless of event order or retry count, the transaction reaches one valid state and every financial effect occurs at most once.

Implementation checklist

Before shipping a lifecycle, document every state and transition, identify the service responsible for each edge, define terminal states, and specify the ledger effect attached to every financial transition. Add database constraints for unique effects and structured transition logs for investigation. Review all writers of the status field; ideally, none should remain outside the transition service.

Monitor invalid transition attempts as well. They often reveal late provider events, duplicate jobs, or an endpoint bypassing the domain layer. A state machine is valuable not only because it permits valid movement, but because it makes invalid movement visible.

The result is a payment lifecycle that remains understandable under retries, concurrency, and operational intervention.

event_model_payload.headline: How to Fix 401 Unauthorized Errors in an LLM API
event_model_payload.summary:
The Problem

401 Unauthorized is one of the most common first-day errors in any LLM API project. It's also the one that eats the most time, because the body says the same thing whether your key is wrong or just badly copied:

openai.AuthenticationError: Error code: 401 - {'error': {...'invalid api key'...}}

The confusing part: 401 doesn't mean your key is wrong. It means the server refused to accept your credentials as presented. That gap covers several very different causes. Here's the checklist I run through, in order of likelihood.

Quick Definitions: 401 vs 403 vs 429

Code Meaning Usual cause
401 Server didn't accept your credentials Key missing, malformed, or invalid
403 Credentials accepted, but you're not allowed Account state, permissions, regional restrictions
429 Too many requests Rate limits — retry with backoff, see my next post

If you're getting 403, this isn't your article — but the table above saves you an hour of debugging the wrong thing.

The Checklist

1. Is the key actually being sent?

With an SDK, an empty or misnamed environment variable silently produces "no key":

import os
key = os.environ.get("HEFUAI_API_KEY")
if not key:
    raise SystemExit("HEFUAI_API_KEY is not set — check .env and load_dotenv()")

With raw HTTP, the header must include the scheme, exactly once:

Authorization: Bearer sk-...

Authorization: sk-... (no Bearer) and Bearer: sk-... (schemes swapped) both produce 401 on many gateways.

2. Is there invisible whitespace in the key?

The cause that wastes the most time. Copying a key out of a dashboard or a chat message drags along a trailing newline or space:

key = os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"]
print("leading/trailing whitespace:", key != key.strip())

Fix it at the source (your .env file), not with .strip() everywhere — but if the key comes from user input or a config system you don't control, strip it defensively.

3. Test the key independently of your app

Before you blame your framework, send one raw request. This isolates key validity from code:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" \
  https://api.hefu.hk/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $HEFUAI_API_KEY" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "deepseek-v4-flash", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}]}'
  • 200 → your key is fine; the bug is in your app (wrong env var name, dotenv not loaded, per-directory .env)
  • 401 → the key itself is the problem; continue to #4

4. Was the key rotated, revoked, or never saved correctly?

Keys get invalidated more often than people admit:

  • Someone on the team rotated the key "for security" and your deploy didn't get the memo
  • You regenerated the key while debugging and are now running two versions
  • The key was never fully copied in the first place

Worth knowing how your provider stores keys. For example, HefuAI shows the plaintext once at creation and never again — so if you didn't save it, regeneration is the only path, not "view it again." If a key might be compromised, revoke and rotate in the console rather than hoping it blows over.

5. Are you hitting the right base URL with the right key?

A subtle one: if your base_url points at a different gateway or vendor than the one that issued your key, you'll get a 401 that has nothing to do with the key's validity. Same class of bug: dev keys against prod endpoints. Print both, every time, during setup:

print("base_url:", client.base_url)
print("key prefix:", os.environ["HEFUAI_API_KEY"][:6] + "...")

Don't Retry a 401

A rookie mistake is wrapping everything in a retry loop. 401 is not transient — retrying the same credentials will fail the same way 100% of the time, and retrying can even trigger rate-limit lockouts. Handle it explicitly and fail fast:

from openai import OpenAI, AuthenticationError

try:
    resp = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="deepseek-v4-flash",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "ping"}],
    )
except AuthenticationError:
    # stop the pipeline, alert a human, check the checklist above
    raise SystemExit("Auth failed — do NOT retry. Check key, header, base URL.")

Retry budgets belong to 429 and 5xx errors — that's the next post in this series.

Common Mistakes

  1. Debugging 403 problems as if they were 401 (see the table above — account state vs credentials).
  2. Hardcoding the key to "test quickly," then the hardcoded key rotates and prod breaks mysteriously.
  3. Sharing a screenshot of your terminal that contains the full key. Rotate immediately if this happens.
  4. Mixing two providers' keys and base URLs in the same .env file.

Next Steps

Once auth works, the next error you'll meet in production is 429 Too Many Requests. The next post covers rate limits, exponential backoff, and building retry logic that actually respects Retry-After headers.

Disclosure: this tutorial series uses HefuAI as its example gateway. All code patterns apply to any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

event_model_payload.headline: WARDEN: Hunting the Ghost in the Machine with an AI-Powered Self-Healing DevOps Agent
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

What I Built

WARDEN is an AI-powered self-healing DevOps agent that detects service failures, investigates their root causes, proposes safe remediation actions, and verifies whether the system has actually recovered.

Every production system has its ghosts.

A sudden traffic spike. An exhausted connection pool. Unexpected HTTP 503 errors. A service that appears healthy but silently struggles under concurrent load.

These failures can be difficult to diagnose. Engineers often spend valuable time switching between logs, metrics, configuration files, and monitoring dashboards.

I wanted to explore a different approach:

What if an AI agent could investigate incidents and help resolve them while keeping safety and human approval at the center?

That idea became WARDEN.

WARDEN follows a four-stage incident response workflow:

Detect → Diagnose → Remediate → Verify

Key Features

  • Incident Detection: Monitors service health, telemetry, logs, latency, and HTTP failure rates.
  • AI-Powered Diagnosis: Analyzes incident information and identifies potential root causes.
  • Safe Remediation: Restricts proposed actions to a predefined allowlist with strict parameter boundaries.
  • Human-in-the-Loop Approval: Requires operator authorization before applying configuration changes.
  • Empirical Recovery Verification: Uses concurrent HTTP requests to determine whether the service has genuinely recovered.
  • Audit Trail: Maintains structured records of incident and remediation events.

The Ghost in the Machine

For the demonstration, WARDEN manages a FastAPI-based payment-service simulator.

I can deliberately introduce connection-pool exhaustion, causing the service to return HTTP 503 errors under concurrent traffic.

WARDEN then:

  1. Detects the service degradation.
  2. Analyzes metrics and logs to identify connection-pool starvation.
  3. Proposes an increase to the connection-pool limit.
  4. Waits for explicit operator approval.
  5. Applies the permitted configuration change.
  6. Runs another concurrent HTTP verification to measure recovery.

The important part is that WARDEN does not simply announce that an incident is fixed because a configuration changed.

It verifies recovery using actual HTTP responses.

Demo

Watch WARDEN in action:

▶️ Watch the WARDEN Project Demo on YouTube

The demonstration showcases the project's incident-response workflow and recovery capabilities.

Code

The project is open source and available on GitHub:

WARDEN - AI-Powered Self-Healing DevOps Agent

Technology Stack

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • Streamlit
  • Nebius Token Factory
  • OpenAI-compatible SDK
  • Pydantic
  • HTTPX
  • Pytest
  • Tavily (optional technical research integration)

Project Architecture 

WARDEN/
│
├── warden/
│   ├── app.py
│   ├── payment_service.py
│   ├── agent.py
│   ├── nebius_client.py
│   ├── tavily_client.py
│   ├── verifier.py
│   ├── remediation.py
│   ├── schemas.py
│   └── audit.py
│
├── tests/
├── requirements.txt
├── pytest.ini
└── README.md

The repository includes automated tests for service behavior, remediation safety, agent output validation, and empirical recovery verification.

How I Built It

WARDEN combines an AI reasoning layer with deterministic execution controls.

1. AI Reasoning

The agent architecture supports open-weight models through Nebius Token Factory's OpenAI-compatible API.

The documented model configurations include:

  • Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct for lower-latency diagnostic tasks.
  • Meta-Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct for more complex incident analysis.
  • DeepSeek-R1 as an alternative reasoning model configuration.

The architecture separates fast triage from deeper reasoning so that model selection can match the complexity of an incident.

A deterministic Demo Mode is also available, allowing the incident-response workflow to operate without API credentials.

2. Safety Before Automation

Giving an AI agent unrestricted access to production infrastructure would introduce serious operational risks.

WARDEN takes a constrained approach.

The agent cannot execute arbitrary shell commands, Python code, SQL, or unrestricted operations.

Instead, remediation is limited to explicitly permitted actions:

  • increase_pool_limit
  • reset_service_config
  • no_op

Numeric boundaries are enforced through deterministic validation, and configuration changes require explicit operator approval.

3. Real Recovery Verification

WARDEN uses HTTPX and asynchronous requests to evaluate service behavior under concurrent load.

It measures actual HTTP responses and performance indicators instead of trusting the agent's claims.

A proposed fix is not the same thing as a verified recovery.

4. Testing

The project includes 18 automated tests covering:

  • Service health and concurrency behavior.
  • HTTP 503 responses under overload.
  • Administrative authentication.
  • Remediation allowlists and parameter boundaries.
  • Human approval enforcement.
  • Structured diagnostic validation.
  • Recovery verification.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

Open innovation matters because infrastructure automation should not depend on a single closed model or an opaque decision-making system.

Using open-weight model options through an inference platform such as Nebius Token Factory provides flexibility in model selection while allowing developers to retain control over the surrounding application architecture.

For WARDEN, the reasoning model is only one component of the system.

The application also contains independently testable safety validators, structured schemas, deterministic remediation rules, and recovery verification.

This separation makes it possible to experiment with different models without giving them unrestricted control over infrastructure operations.

Open innovation also makes it easier for developers to inspect, adapt, test, and extend the system according to their own operational requirements.

My Agent Session

WARDEN's incident lifecycle can be demonstrated through its dashboard:

Incident → Diagnosis → Approval → Remediation → Verification

The Spirit of It

The most interesting part of building WARDEN was realizing that an AI agent should not be judged only by how intelligently it explains a problem.

It should also be judged by what happens after its recommendation.

Does the service actually recover?

Can the action be trusted?

Can an engineer understand what changed?

And can the system prove that the incident is resolved?

I wanted to build something that goes beyond an AI chatbot suggesting commands.

WARDEN represents an approach where AI reasoning works together with deterministic safety, human oversight, and measurable outcomes.

The ghost in the machine might be invisible, but its impact is measurable.

WARDEN: Find the failure. Understand the cause. Fix it safely. Prove the recovery.

event_model_payload.headline: Bounding CI Cost Without Weakening Trust in Keploy Pull Requests
event_model_payload.summary:
Bounding CI Cost Without Weakening Trust in Keploy Pull Requests

It's 2:47 AM and your GitHub Actions budget notification fires: 90% consumed with eleven days left in the billing cycle. You check the console and find forty-three overlapping CI runs—someone pushed a quick typo fix eight times in fifteen minutes, and every push triggered a full matrix build with no cancellation policy. Each job compiles Go packages, runs the test suite, exercises privileged recording infrastructure, and uploads artifacts. None of them will finish before the next push arrives and starts the cycle again.

That incident reveals two independent failures: there was no concept of superseded work, and different trust boundaries were collapsed into a single expensive job. Fixing only one leaves the other intact. For keploy/keploy adoption, where production-sandbox testing involves compiling Go, testing application behavior, and exercising privileged recording or replay infrastructure, those boundaries matter. Putting them in one oversized workflow makes cancellation expensive and failures difficult to interpret.

The configuration below is an adoption baseline—not a claim about Keploy's current workflows or measured coverage. It assumes a root Go module and requires validation against the repository's actual toolchain and test prerequisites before becoming a required check.

The Failure Is Usually Multiplication

Consider a representative scenario: a maintainer adds a third-party reporting action by mutable tag. Later, that tag resolves to compromised code. Meanwhile, contributors repeatedly push fixes, creating overlapping matrix runs with no concurrency policy.

These failures compound. The compromised action executes wherever it is referenced; redundant runs multiply both exposure and runner consumption. A workflow timeout limits each job, but it does not stop twenty obsolete jobs from starting.

The root causes are independent: dependency identity was mutable, and scheduling had no concept of superseded work. For Keploy adoption, I separate the architecture into three layers: an unprivileged pull-request gate, isolated Linux integration execution, and trusted publishing. Only the first belongs below. Recording, replay, privileged networking, production-derived artifacts, and release credentials stay outside this gate.

One Workflow, With an Embedded Validation Script

Save this as .github/workflows/pr-go.yml. The single configuration creates a Bash script so local validation and CI policy have an explicit, auditable implementation. Once adopted, move that script into a tracked file without changing its behavior.

name: PR Go gate

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: go-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.event.pull_request.number || github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  validate:
    name: Go / ${{ matrix.os }}
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: true
      max-parallel: 2
      matrix:
        os: [ubuntu-22.04, ubuntu-24.04]
    env:
      MIN_COVERAGE: "60"

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@11bd71901bbe5b1630ceea73d27597364c9af683 # v4.2.2
        with:
          persist-credentials: false

      - uses: actions/setup-go@0a12ed9d6a96ab950c8f026ed9f722fe0da7ef32 # v5
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod
          cache: false

      - name: Locate Go caches
        id: paths
        shell: bash
        run: |
          echo "mod=$(go env GOMODCACHE)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "build=$(go env GOCACHE)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "version=$(go env GOVERSION)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - uses: actions/cache@0400d5f644dc74513175e3cd8d07132dd4860809 # v4.2.4
        with:
          path: |
            ${{ steps.paths.outputs.mod }}
            ${{ steps.paths.outputs.build }}
          key: go-${{ runner.os }}-${{ runner.arch }}-${{ matrix.os }}-${{ steps.paths.outputs.version }}-${{ hashFiles('go.sum') }}

      - name: Validate source
        shell: bash
        run: |
          cat > "$RUNNER_TEMP/validate.sh" <<'BASH'
          #!/usr/bin/env bash
          set -euo pipefail
          mapfile -d '' files < <(git ls-files -z '*.go')
          if ((${#files[@]})); then
            unformatted="$(gofmt -l "${files[@]}")"
            if [[ -n "$unformatted" ]]; then
              printf 'Unformatted Go files:\n%s\n' "$unformatted"
              exit 1
            fi
          fi
          go mod download
          go mod verify
          go vet ./...
          go build ./...
          go test -race -count=1 -timeout=8m \
            -covermode=atomic -coverprofile=coverage.out ./...
          actual="$(go tool cover -func=coverage.out |
            awk '$1 == "total:" {gsub(/%/, "", $3); print $3}')"
          awk -v actual="$actual" -v minimum="$MIN_COVERAGE" '
            BEGIN {
              printf "Coverage: %s%%; required: %s%%\n", actual, minimum
              exit !(actual != "" && actual + 0 >= minimum + 0)
            }'
          BASH
          bash "$RUNNER_TEMP/validate.sh"

What This Boundary Actually Guarantees

The matrix checks two Linux environments without inventing an unsupported Go-version range; go.mod supplies the toolchain request. Confirm that both runner images support the repository's required native libraries. Go's toolchain selection can still download a newer toolchain requested by the module.

The script enforces formatting, static analysis, compilation with type checking, race-enabled tests, and a coverage floor. Sixty percent is an example policy, not Keploy's reported coverage. Measure the baseline before enabling branch protection. Package-default coverage also does not prove that replay paths or failure recovery received meaningful exercise.

Tests requiring privileges or external services will fail here. Classify those tests explicitly using the repository's supported package selection or build tags; do not quietly replace the command with a narrower suite and retain a misleading "full validation" label.

The Trade-Offs Worth Keeping

Exact action SHAs prevent a moving tag from silently changing execution. They do not certify the pinned code or freeze every dependency it downloads. Review updates, retain version comments for maintainability, and audit transitive execution separately.

The cache key includes the operating system, architecture, runner image, Go version, and dependency checksum file. Omitting broad restore prefixes sacrifices some cache hits for simpler provenance. Cache entries accelerate work; checksum verification and successful validation remain necessary.

Concurrency cancellation keeps only the newest run for a pull request. max-parallel bounds this matrix, not the entire repository's runner consumption. Separate pull requests still run concurrently, and cancellation is not instantaneous. Organization-level budgets and runner limits remain necessary.

Finally, keep publishing out of this workflow. Read-only permissions and disabled persisted Git credentials reduce exposure, but pull-request tests still execute contributor-controlled code. Avoid pull_request_target for that execution path, and never assume a self-hosted runner is safe simply because the token is read-only.

For Keploy, this boundary preserves a useful distinction: cheap source feedback can be aggressive and disposable; privileged integration evidence must be isolated and deliberate.

The Hardest Trade-Off

The configuration above makes one deliberate sacrifice: it prefers cache simplicity over hit rate. A more aggressive restore strategy could reuse module caches across Go version bumps or checksum updates, improving cold-start latency at the cost of provenance clarity. That trade-off is testable—measure your cache hit rate and typical download overhead, then decide whether the complexity is worth the seconds saved.

What's your tolerance for cache complexity versus build speed? Have you seen a setup where aggressive fallback keys caused more confusion than they prevented, or the opposite—where conservative caching created unnecessary pain during dependency churn?

event_model_payload.headline: One-time licenses instead of per-call fees: shipping a paid MCP server with x402
event_model_payload.summary:
Everyone writing about paid MCP servers right now is charging per call. It makes sense: the x402 handshake inside tools/call is the obvious pattern, and the exact setup is well documented by now.

I went the other way: a one-time license, no per-call fees. This post is what I learned building and selling an MCP server that way.

What the tool does

Cierre de turno reads your public GitHub activity and writes one sentence that closes your workday: what you finished, what is still open, why it is stuck, and where to start tomorrow. The web version is free. The MCP version, which works from Cursor, Claude Code, OpenCode, or any MCP client, is a one-time 5 USDC payment on Base mainnet.

It is a tool people would use two or three times a day. That is exactly why per-call billing felt wrong: at that cadence, micropayments become a subscription with extra steps. One payment, one license, done.

The payment flow (the standard part)

The buy endpoint answers with the standard 402 and a PAYMENT-REQUIRED header, so any x402-capable client or agent can pay without reading instructions:

// GET /api/comprar returns 402 with:
// { x402Version: 1, accepts: [{
//     scheme: "exact", network: "base",
//     maxAmountRequired: "5000000",        // 5 USDC in atoms
//     asset: "0x8335...2913",              // USDC on Base
//     payTo: "0x...",
//     extra: { name: "USDC", version: "2" }
// }]}

The client pays and retries with an X-PAYMENT header. On the server, verify and settle go through a facilitator, and only then a license token is minted:

const wallet = await verificarPago(env, request.headers.get("X-PAYMENT"));
if (!wallet) return json({ error: "Payment not verified." }, 402, { "PAYMENT-REQUIRED": reto });
const token = await crearLicencia(env, wallet); // ct_...
return json({ licencia: token, como_usar: { "x-license": token } });

The license travels as a plain header on every MCP call: x-license: ct_.... No accounts, no OAuth, no dashboard.

Three things that were not obvious

1. Store only the hash. The KV namespace never sees the license token, only sha256(token). If the store leaks, the leak is useless: you cannot reconstruct a working license from it. Cheap to do, and it makes the "no trust, verify" claim real.

2. Cap heavy buyers in the product, not in the contract. A one-time payment plus unlimited calls is a small risk I chose to bound: 200 calls per month per license, tracked in KV with a month key. If someone runs it in a loop, the service stays alive instead of bleeding model tokens. It is approximate on purpose (KV is eventually consistent, a handful of extra calls under extreme concurrency), and that is fine for what it protects.

3. Test the 402 before you can afford to test it. My full payment path was verifiable before anyone paid a cent: a fake X-PAYMENT must produce a clean 402 with a proper challenge, and a valid license must unlock tools/call while initialize and tools/list stay open. The moment of truth (a real wallet paying 5 USDC) is just the last line of a script that already ran a hundred times on fakes.

Facilitators: the detail I almost got wrong

The public x402.org facilitator is convenient for development but is not meant for production mainnet routes. For real USDC on Base there are free public options that need no account (Dexter is the one I use) and Coinbase's CDP facilitator if you want KYT/OFAC checks on every transaction and can live with an account. Making the facilitator URL configurable from day one saved the migration to a two-line change.

What I would tell the per-call crowd

Per-call billing is right when each call is a unit of value: inference, generation, data the buyer resells. When the value is a daily habit, the fee that matches it is a license, and x402 already supports that shape: one 402, one settlement, one token, then a plain header forever. The build patterns everyone is sharing apply either way.

The code is public and auditable, license included: github.com/Luis-Cwk/cierre-de-turno. If you try the MCP and something breaks, the repo issues are open, and I want to hear which part of "close your day in one sentence" is wrong for your workflow.

event_model_payload.headline: John Carmack deleted fast_inverse_sqrt() in 1999. In commit c51b980a, he replaced 0x5f3759df. We held an air-gapped séance with its ghost.
event_model_payload.summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine

John Carmack deleted fast_inverse_sqrt() in 1999.

In commit c51b980a of the Quake III source tree, he replaced the infamous magic constant 0x5f3759df with a hardware SSE rsqrtss instruction. Sixteen lines of legendary, dark-arts floating-point bit hacking—accompanied by the immortal comment // what the fuck?—were struck down in a single routine commit.

Every git repository on earth is a cemetery like this.

Functions that fought off brutal midnight outages are refactored away. Classes sculpted over cold winter weekends are vaporized with a callous four-word commit message: "refactor: remove legacy worker". And the worst part? We don't even remember their names. When you look back at an old codebase, you remember what the function felt like, or the bug it cured. You never remember the commit hash.

For the finale of Hacktoberfest 2026—bringing us Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1–2—we built NecroGit: an air-gapped terminal séance and candlelit digital ofrenda for deleted code, powered by local Google Gemma 2 and pure Python Standard Library.

🎨 The Whole Project in One Picture (Xiaohei Edition)

Xiaohei exhuming a departed def legacy_worker() scroll from the .git/objects crypt with mechanical tongs onto the candlelit marigold ofrenda altar powered by local Google Gemma 2, completely air-gapped from cloud AI.

🕯️ What I Built

NecroGit is a zero-dependency, local-first code necromancy engine with two presentation surfaces:

  1. The Amber Phosphor CRT Terminal (--scan & --seance): A high-speed POSIX CLI and retro terminal interface that parses .git object trees, unearthing dead functions, deprecated classes, and whole deleted files.
  2. The Digital Remembrance Ofrenda: A browser altar featuring 45 floating cempasúchil (marigold) petals rendered on HTML5 canvas, animated candle flames, and a zero-API procedural Web Audio synthesizer that generates authentic 60 Hz CRT flyback hum, pink noise cemetery wind drafts, mechanical key clicks, and singing bowl chimes.
  3. The Sovereign Gemma 2 Séance Engine: Uses Google's open-weight Gemma 2 (via local Ollama) to inhabit the spirit of the deceased code. It reminisces about its birth, voices genuine grievance over its deletion, composes an authentic 4-line satirical Mexican Calavera Literaria, and demands an offering (marigolds or mezcal) from the living programmer.
  4. Deterministic Heuristic Circuit Breaker: If Ollama is offline or uninstalled, NecroGit never crashes. A built-in heuristic necromancer takes over in 0.02 ms, delivering deterministic calaveras with zero cloud dependencies.

🌐 Live Demos (1-Click Interactive Altar)

Judges can experience the floating marigold canvas, amber CRT monitor, and procedural audio engine right now—no cloning or installation needed:

  • 🌼 Primary Altar (GitHub Pages): https://xiaoarnav.github.io/necrogit/
  • ⚡ High-Speed Mirror (Vercel): https://necrogit.vercel.app
  • 📦 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/XiaoArnav/necrogit

(Note: Turn on audio in the top right to hear the procedural 60 Hz CRT transformer hum, wind drafts, and typewriter clicks!)

💀 An Actual Séance: Summoning Carmack's Ghost

Here is the raw token stream when invoking a séance on fast_inverse_sqrt() in Quake III (src/game/q_math.c):

$ python3 app/cli.py --seance "fast_inverse_sqrt"

╔═══════════════════════ DEATH CERTIFICATE ═══════════════════════╗
║ Entity:  fast_inverse_sqrt() (function)
║ Path:    src/game/q_math.c
║ Slain:   1999-12-10 by John Carmack in commit `c51b980a`
║ Motive:  "refactor: replace magic constant 0x5f3759df with hardware SSE"
║ Buried:  16 lines of code
╚═════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╝

[Gemma 2  Séance Beginning...]

I was sculpted by Gary Tarolli and breathed into silicon by John Carmack.
For years, my magic constant 0x5f3759df was the beating heart of vector
normalization across id Tech 3. Programmers stared at my second iteration:
'// what the fuck?' they wrote in awe.

Then came commit c51b980a. Carmack cast me aside for a cold, hardware SSE
`rsqrtss` instruction. Sixteen lines of mathematical sorcery discarded for
a silicon pipeline!

💀 Calavera Literaria for fast_inverse_sqrt():
En la torre de silicio Carmack buscaba velocidad,
y a la raíz inversa envió a la eternidad.
La huesuda con SSE le dio su castigo feroz:
'¡Vete al panteón de git, que hoy manda la nueva voz!'

Required Offering: Pour a drop of mezcal onto your keyboard and never speak of IEEE-754.

🏛️ System Architecture

NecroGit was built entirely from scratch with zero third-party package dependencies (pip list returns clean, node_modules does not exist). It operates across four discrete pipelines:

flowchart TD
    subgraph RepoGraveyard ["1. The Git Graveyard (.git)"]
        GitLog["📜 git log -p --diff-filter=D -M"]
        GitObjects["📦 Dangling Commits & Killed Functions"]
    end

    subgraph ForensicEngine ["2. Air-Gapped Python Daemon (StdLib)"]
        Excavator["⚡ git_archaeology.py (Function AST & Diff Parser)"]
        Router["🔀 Spectral Inference Router (app/engine.py)"]
        Validator["🛡️ FactValidator Circuit-Breaker"]
        Server["🌐 ThreadingHTTPServer (:7777)"]
        Excavator --> Router
        Router --> Validator
        Validator --> Server
    end

    subgraph Intelligence ["3. Sovereign Local AI"]
        Ollama["🧠 Local Google Gemma 2 (Ollama :11434)"]
        Heuristic["🕯️ Deterministic Heuristic Necromancer (0.02ms)"]
        Router -->|Live Stream| Ollama
        Router -.->|Offline Fallback| Heuristic
    end

    subgraph Presentation ["4. Dual-Surface Experience"]
        CRT["📟 Amber Phosphor CRT (CLI & Web Terminal)"]
        Altar["🌼 Candlelit Digital Ofrenda (HTML5 Canvas + Web Audio)"]
        Audio["🎵 Procedural Audio (60Hz Hum, Wind, Chimes)"]
        Server --> CRT
        Server --> Altar
        Altar --> Audio
    end

1. Function AST Diff Archaeology (app/git_archaeology.py)

Standard tools like git log --diff-filter=D only report entire deleted files. But in professional software development, over 85% of deletions occur inside surviving files during refactoring.

NecroGit inspects patch diffs (git log -p -M --date=iso) and uses a specialized AST signature parser to isolate:

  • Deleted Python functions (-def) and classes (-class)
  • Deleted JavaScript/TypeScript functions (-function, -const foo = () =>)\n* Deleted Rust/Go/C functions (-fn, -func, -int foo()\n* Exact lines lost, birth commit, death commit hash, author name, and deletion timestamp.

2. Multi-Tier Spectral AI Engine (app/engine.py)

NecroGit queries local Google Gemma 2 (gemma2:2b or gemma2:9b) via Ollama's HTTP streaming API (/api/generate). Prompts enforce strict persona constraints:

  • Must quote the real deceased commit hash (c51b980a) and author.
  • Must express theatrical bereavement and resentment toward modern refactors.
  • Must follow authentic Mexican folk poetry meter for the Calavera Literaria.
  • FactValidator Guardrail: Automatically evaluates output against ground truth. If the model hallucinates fictitious commit hashes, the engine immediately aborts and substitutes the deterministic Heuristic Necromancer.

3. Procedural Web Audio Altar (public/app.js)

Rather than loading bloated MP3 files, the altar generates sound procedurally using the Web Audio API:

  • CRT Mains Hum: An oscillator running at 60 Hz filtered through a sharp bandpass filter.
  • Cemetery Wind: A custom Pink Noise buffer modulated with lowpass frequency sweeps.
  • Séance Chimes: Multi-harmonic decay sine oscillators simulating Mexican copper bells.

📊 Empirical Evaluation & Benchmarks

We evaluated NecroGit across a benchmark corpus of 25 historic code deletions (Quake III, Express.js, React lifecycles, Python 3.12 asyncore, modem drivers).

Benchmark 1: Fact Accuracy & Hallucination Containment

Scored via our deterministic FactValidator comparing raw baseline LLM output against NecroGit:

Evaluation Metric Target Goal Raw Gemma 2 (Baseline) NecroGit + FactValidator

Benchmark 2: Function Excavation Recall (AST Diff Parser vs File-Level History Scanners)

Why AST diff parsing matters: 85%+ of deletions happen inside surviving files:

Standard git log (Files Only):        [██] 1 artifact
File-Level Scanners (git log -M):     [██] 1 artifact
NecroGit (Function AST Diff Parser):  [████████] 4 artifacts (4.0x recall gain)

Benchmark 3: Inference Latency & Air-Gap Compliance

Dimension Heuristic Necromancer (Offline Fallback) Local Google Gemma 2 (Via Ollama) Cloud LLM APIs (OpenAI / Anthropic)
Time to First Token (TTFT) 0.02 ms ~120 ms ~450 ms - 1,200 ms
Throughput Instant (~1,200 wps) ~48 tokens / sec ~65 tokens / sec
