Cost per 1,000 Séances $0.00 $0.00 $1.50 - $4.00 USD

🛠️ What Went Wrong: Confessions of an Air-Gapped Séance

Every non-trivial engineering project hits walls. Here are the three real bugs we fought:

1. The Markdown # Header False-Positive Bug

In our initial test runs after deleting FUTURE_ROADMAP.md, our AST diff parser reported that it had discovered three new "functions": Option(), Roadmap(), and Sovereign(). Lines like - ## Option B: Ofrenda // Sovereign matched Python/Bash comment boundaries where # preceded an identifier!
The Fix: We built a strict CODE_EXTENSIONS whitelist (.py, .js, .ts, .rs, .go, .c, etc.). Diffs touching Markdown, JSON, or YAML are classified as files, never functions.

2. The macOS vs Linux MIME Type Divergence

Our test suite passed cleanly in Linux CI environments, but failed on macOS:

AssertionError: 'application/javascript' not found in 'text/javascript; charset=utf-8' : MIME mismatch

mimetypes.guess_type() reads from the OS: Debian/Ubuntu resolves .js to application/javascript, while macOS LaunchServices resolves it to text/javascript (the RFC 9239 standard). Building zero-dependency software means facing OS plumbing head-on. We normalized the encoding and updated the test assertion to check if "javascript" in content_type:.

3. The Hallucinated Commit Author Trap

When testing Gemma 2 2B with higher temperature, it would occasionally hallucinate legendary figures:

"...until the dark winter of 2021, when Linus Torvalds himself struck me down with 'refactor: legacy bloat'!"

Small open models possess strong associative priors: when prompted with "deleted code", they drift toward famous open-source mythology. Rather than hoping prompt engineering would hold forever, we built the FactValidator circuit-breaker: if Gemma's output fails to quote the exact commit hash and real author, the system aborts and delivers the deterministic Heuristic Necromancer.

🌍 Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

  1. Git History is Deeply Private: Your .git directory contains the embarrassing missteps, decommissioned API keys, discarded business logic, and private architectural experiments you chose to delete. Sending your entire commit history to closed cloud APIs violates corporate data governance and basic developer hygiene. With local open-weight Gemma 2, not one byte ever leaves your laptop.
  2. Zero Marginal Cost for Historical Preservation: Express.js has over 6,100 commits; Linux has over a million. Calling cloud APIs to inspect thousands of commits costs a fortune. Running Gemma 2 locally costs nothing but a laptop fan.
  3. Sovereignty & Permanence: When cloud APIs sunset, your tools break. An open-weight model with a pure Python standard library runtime will run identically 20 years from now.

🔍 Behind the Scenes: The Full Agent Session

To give the Hacktoberfest judges a transparent look into how NecroGit was architected, benchmarked, tested, and polished, here is the complete recorded agent session:

NecroGit: Building an Air-Gapped Code Séance & Remembrance Ofrenda with Gemma 2
You

Let's build NecroGit for Hacktoberfest Week 4 ('Ghost in the Machine'). It needs to unearth deleted git history, run a terminal séance with local Google Gemma 2, render a Día de los Muertos digital remembrance ofrenda with floating marigolds and CRT audio, and operate 100% air-gapped with zero pip/npm dependencies.

Agent

Architected and implemented the core system:
- app/git_archaeology.py: Multi-language AST diff parser (-def, -func, -fn) unearthing deleted functions inside surviving files (overcoming standard git log --diff-filter=D limitations).
- app/engine.py: Spectral Inference Router connecting to local Google Gemma 2 via Ollama, guarded by FactValidator to catch hallucinated commit hashes, backed by a 0.02ms deterministic Heuristic Necromancer fallback.

event_model_payload.headline: Diff Two Snapshots of a Messy CSV in Python: No-Break Spaces, Duplicate Rows and Renamed Keys
event_model_payload.summary:
If you build anything on top of a public dataset, sooner or later a new version lands and you have to answer a simple question: what changed? With a hand-maintained CSV, that question is harder than it looks. Keys get renamed, cells carry footnote symbols, and one invisible character can turn an unchanged row into an "added" and a "removed" at the same time.

This tutorial builds a small Python diff for two git snapshots of the VPS Pricing Index, a hosting-price dataset I maintain. I drafted the article with AI assistance; every command was run against the real repository, and the outputs below are copied from those runs and checked against the files by hand. One disclosure: VPS Hosting Radar earns affiliate commissions on some of its pages. This post has no affiliate links.

The two snapshots

The dataset lives in a public GitHub repository under CC BY 4.0. pricing.csv has three commits, and git keeps every version:

git clone https://github.com/vpshostingradar/vps-pricing-data.git
cd vps-pricing-data
git log --oneline -- pricing.csv
# 39a4cad Update pricing.csv
# 53b7d49 Initial dataset: 16 plans across 13 providers, collected 2026-08-11
# 8e6fc61 Create pricing.csv

git show 53b7d49:pricing.csv > aug.csv   # verified 2026-08-11
git show 39a4cad:pricing.csv > sep.csv   # verified 2026-09-15

git show : writes a file exactly as it was at that commit, so you don't need to check anything out. (The oldest commit, 8e6fc61, is a header-only placeholder with a different snake_case schema and no data rows, so I left it out.)

Open aug.csv and you'll see the things that break naive tooling:

  • Row 1 is a title, not a header. It's a single quoted sentence describing the snapshot. The real header is on row 2.
  • Money cells aren't numbers. You'll find "2,520.00" with a thousands separator, €4.40‡ with a currency sign and a footnote dagger, € 5.50 with a space, and — (an em dash) meaning "not published."
  • Some names contain U+00A0. Three lines use a no-break space instead of a regular one, for example between Cloud VPS 4 and (EUR). It looks identical on screen.
  • Two rows appear twice. Liquid Web and Contabo each show up a second time at the bottom of the August file, byte for byte identical. The September file doesn't have this problem.

None of this is unusual. It's what happens when people copy values out of pricing pages and spreadsheets by hand. You want a diff that survives it.

Step 1: parse the cells you actually have

Start with three helpers: one that pulls a number out of whatever is in a money cell, one that normalizes text so invisible differences stop mattering, and a loader that finds the real header.

import csv
import re
import sys
import unicodedata
from collections import Counter

MONEY = re.compile(r"-?\d+(?:\.\d+)?")


def money(cell):
    """'2,520.00' -> 2520.0, '€ 5.50' -> 5.5, '35.00‡' -> 35.0, '—' -> None."""
    cell = (cell or "").replace(",", "").strip()
    m = MONEY.search(cell)
    return float(m.group()) if m else None


def norm(text):
    """NFKC turns U+00A0 (no-break space) into a plain space; then collapse runs."""
    return " ".join(unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", text).split())


def load(path):
    with open(path, newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        lines = list(csv.reader(f))
    # Row 0 is a human-readable title, not the header. Find the real header.
    start = next(i for i, row in enumerate(lines) if row and row[0] == "Provider")
    header = lines[start]
    return [dict(zip(header, r)) for r in lines[start + 1:] if any(r)]

A few choices here are deliberate.

money() returns None for an em dash rather than 0. "The vendor didn't publish a monthly price" and "the monthly price is zero" are different facts, and the diff should report a move from None to 26.99 as new information, not as a $26.99 price rise.

The regex ignores the currency symbol, which is safe only because currency doesn't change within a row between snapshots. If you're diffing a dataset where a row could switch from USD to EUR, keep the symbol as a separate field and compare it too.

norm() uses NFKC normalization. Among other things, NFKC maps U+00A0 to an ordinary space. str.split() with no arguments already treats U+00A0 as whitespace in Python 3, so the split/join pass alone would catch this particular character. NFKC also handles full-width digits and similar compatibility characters, which turn up when values get pasted from some PDFs and from CJK input methods.

Step 2: key the rows, and say out loud which ones were replaced

A diff needs a key. Here the natural key is (Provider, Plan). Two things can go wrong with it: duplicates within one file, and keys that change between files because the maintainer swapped one plan for another.

def keyed(rows, label):
    keys = [(norm(r["Provider"]), norm(r["Plan"])) for r in rows]
    for key, n in Counter(keys).items():
        if n > 1:
            print(f"[{label}] duplicate key {key} appears {n}x")
    out = {}
    for key, r in zip(keys, rows):
        out.setdefault(key, r)  # keep first occurrence
    return out


# Row replacements are editorial decisions, so they come from the dataset's
# own notes/changelog, not from fuzzy matching. new key -> old key.
REPLACES = {
    ("Hostinger", "Web Premium"): ("Hostinger", "Cloud Startup"),
    ("Hostinger", "KVM 1"): ("Hostinger", "KVM 2"),
    ("InMotion", "VPS 4 vCPU"): ("InMotion", "VPS 4 (Most Popular)"),
    ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Cloud #1"): ("ScalaHosting", "Managed Build #1"),
}

keyed() warns about duplicates instead of silently overwriting them. Keeping the first occurrence is fine here because the duplicates are identical; if they weren't, you'd want the script to stop.

The REPLACES map is the part people are tempted to automate. Don't. Hostinger has two rows in each snapshot, so "match by provider" is ambiguous. Fuzzy string matching would happily pair KVM 2 with KVM 1, which happens to be right, but for the wrong reason: that pairing is true because the September notes column says "Replaces KVM 2 (8 GB), which overshot the 4 GB baseline," not because the strings are similar. Every entry in the map above comes from a note in the September file or from the repository's CHANGELOG.md. When the next snapshot arrives, you read the changelog and update the map. It takes two minutes and you'll trust the output afterwards.

Step 3: compare field by field 

FIELDS = {
    "First term $/mo": "intro",
    "Prepay months": "prepay",
    "Monthly $/mo": "monthly",
    "Renewal $/mo": "renewal",
    "36-month total $": "total_36",
}


def compare(old, new):
    matched = set()
    for key, n in new.items():
        okey = key if key in old else REPLACES.get(key)
        if okey not in old:
            print(f"+ added    {key[0]} {key[1]}")
            continue
        matched.add(okey)
        tag = "same plan" if okey == key else f"replaces {okey[1]}"
        changes = []
        for col, short in FIELDS.items():
            a, b = money(old[okey].get(col)), money(n.get(col))
            if a != b:
                changes.append(f"{short} {a} -> {b}")
        if changes:
            print(f"~ changed  {key[0]} {key[1]} ({tag}): " + "; ".join(changes))
    for okey in old.keys() - matched:
        print(f"- removed  {okey[0]} {okey[1]}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    old = keyed(load(sys.argv[1]), "old")
    new = keyed(load(sys.argv[2]), "new")
    print(f"old: {len(old)} unique plans, new: {len(new)} unique plans\n")
    compare(old, new)

Save the three blocks as snapdiff.py and run python3 snapdiff.py aug.csv sep.csv. Here's the output, with one changed line removed for length (marked …):

[old] duplicate key ('Liquid Web', 'Managed VPS 4 GB') appears 2x
[old] duplicate key ('Contabo', 'Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)') appears 2x
old: 16 unique plans, new: 19 unique plans

~ changed  SiteGround StartUp (same plan): monthly 24.99 -> 17.99
~ changed  Hostinger Web Premium (replaces Cloud Startup): intro 7.99 -> 2.99; prepay 48.0 -> 12.0; monthly 27.99 -> 11.99; renewal 25.99 -> 11.99; total_36 287.64 -> 323.64
~ changed  Hostinger KVM 1 (replaces KVM 2): intro 8.79 -> 6.49; monthly 24.49 -> 19.49; renewal 14.99 -> 19.49; total_36 390.84 -> 389.64
~ changed  InMotion VPS 4 vCPU (replaces VPS 4 (Most Popular)): intro 10.99 -> 13.99; monthly None -> 26.99; total_36 587.64 -> 659.64
~ changed  ScalaHosting Managed Cloud #1 (replaces Managed Build #1): prepay 36.0 -> 1.0; total_36 1078.2 -> 1953.2
+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
~ changed  WP Engine Startup (same plan): intro 30.0 -> 28.0; total_36 1200.0 -> 1176.0
~ changed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR) (same plan): intro 4.4 -> 5.28; monthly None -> 6.6; renewal 5.5 -> 6.6; total_36 None -> 205.92
…
+ added    SiteGround Cloud Jump Start (4 CPU / 8 GB / 40 GB)
+ added    Cloudways Autonomous Growth

The omitted line is the Rocket Starter row, where prepay goes from 1 to 12.

Sixteen unique plans become nineteen, with three real additions and nothing removed. That matches the changelog, which lists exactly those three as new rows.

What the naive version would have told you

To see what normalization buys, replace the body of norm() with return text.strip() and run it again. The added/removed lines become:

+ added    ScalaHosting Unmanaged Config #1
+ added    Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
+ added    Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)
+ added    SiteGround Cloud Jump Start (4 CPU / 8 GB / 40 GB)
+ added    Cloudways Autonomous Growth
- removed  Contabo Cloud VPS 4 (EUR)
- removed  Cloudways DigitalOcean 4 GB Basic (premium CPU)

That's seven lines where the true answer is three. Two unchanged plans show up as churn because their August names contain a no-break space. The printed names look identical in the terminal, which is exactly what makes this bug hard to spot. Drop the REPLACES map as well and four more plans would appear as removed-plus-added pairs, leaving you with a report that's mostly noise.

A diff tells you where to look, not why

Here's the part I think matters most. The script reports that values changed, but it can't tell a vendor price change from a correction in the dataset, and in this pair of snapshots most of the movement is corrections.

  • SiteGround StartUp monthly 24.99 -> 17.99 isn't a price cut. The changelog says the September cycle started recording monthly and renewal as a single figure, the price a plan reverts to after its intro term. Under that definition the figure is $17.99. (SiteGround's own pricing page still showed $2.99 for a 12-month first term, renewing at $17.99, when I checked it on 2026-10-28.)
  • InMotion intro 10.99 -> 13.99 is a correction. The September note says $10.99 belonged to a shared-hosting tier, not the VPS.
  • The two Hostinger rows were swapped for plans closer to the 4 GB baseline.
  • Contabo was corrected to a VAT-inclusive 24-month effective rate.

The rest (WP Engine's intro rate, ScalaHosting's prepay term, the Rocket prepay term) aren't explained line by line in the changelog. For those, the diff gives you a short list of rows to check against each vendor's page, and the vendor page is the tiebreaker.

That's a good reason to keep editorial context, meaning notes and a changelog, next to any hand-collected dataset. A diff turns two hundred cells into ten lines worth reading. A human still has to say what each line means. I wrote about the collection process and the mistakes that shaped it on Medium, if you want the background.

Using it on your own data

The script is short enough to adapt rather than configure:

  1. Change the key in keyed() to whatever uniquely identifies a row in your data. If there's an ID column, use it. The current site export at /data/vps-pricing-index.csv has a stable id column (hostinger-kvm-1, siteground-startup and so on), which removes the whitespace problem entirely. You'd still map deliberately replaced plans by hand.
  2. Keep REPLACES small and sourced. Add a comment next to each entry saying where the mapping came from.
  3. Fail loudly on non-identical duplicates. Swap the print in keyed() for an exception once you've checked that existing duplicates are harmless.
  4. Run it in CI whenever the upstream file changes, and post the output as a pull-request comment. Reviewing ten lines is a lot easier than reviewing a CSV diff.

The site's tools page lists the CSV and JSON exports if you want the current snapshot instead of the git history. Prices in both are dated (the latest verification was 2026-09-15), so check the vendor's page before you act on any of them.

Carter Wang is a serial founder who has bought hosting and run production stacks for more than a decade. He maintains the VPS Pricing Index at VPS Hosting Radar.

event_model_payload.headline: Treating Dev, Staging and Production as Real Git Branches
event_model_payload.summary:
It is 2 a.m. and an engineer at an Austin fintech is staring at a production alert, trying to answer a question that should be trivial: what code is actually running right now? The repo says one thing. The deploy log says another. Someone merged a hotfix directly to a release branch three weeks ago and nobody back-ported it to main. This is not a rare failure mode — it is the default state of most pipelines that treat 'environment' as a label instead of a fact.

The cost of that ambiguity is not abstract. ITIC's commonly cited figure puts the median cost of production downtime for large enterprises at roughly $9,000 per minute. Every minute spent reconciling what-is-live-versus-what-is-committed is a minute charged at that rate, and it is almost always a senior engineer's time — the one person who remembers how the deploy scripts actually work.

Where promotion usually breaks

Most teams do not lack a concept of dev, staging and production. They lack a single source of truth for what is in each one. Config flags, environment variables, separate CI jobs per stage, manual 'sync this branch to that server' steps — each is a point where the running system can diverge silently from version control. When an incident report comes in, the first job is archaeology, not diagnosis.

This gets worse under real staffing constraints. The tech-talent shortage is not a North American curiosity — skills-gap figures from the Gulf region sit near 90% of organizations reporting a gap, and in Europe roughly 57% of firms say they cannot find qualified developers to hire. Austin, Toronto and New York teams are competing in the same global pool for the same scarce senior engineers, which means the person who understands your deploy quirks is also the person you can least afford to pull into firefighting.

The mechanism: environments as branches, promotion as a pull request

Corporate AI 365 removes the ambiguity by making the environment literally a git ref. Dev, staging and production are branches in your own repository — connected through GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket or Azure DevOps — and a change does not 'go to production' through a side channel. It moves as a pull request from one branch to the next, through Developer, QA, approval and production gates, each one a real diff with a real reviewer and a real merge commit.

That has a direct consequence for incident response. When the AI reads your codebase and scripted schema and diagnoses a problem down to a file, class or line — with a confidence score and a proposed fix — that fix is proposed as a branch off dev and travels the same governed path as any human-authored change. There is no separate hotfix lane outside git history. If you need to roll back a release, you are reverting a merge commit, not guessing which server got which script.

Every gate is tied to one of 41 composable permissions and your org's real hierarchy, so 'who approved this' and 'what did QA actually look at' are questions answered by the commit log, not by someone's memory of a Slack thread. And because your CI confirms the result, 'it shipped' is a build status, not an assertion.

What the AI does not touch

None of this requires the AI to see anything it should not. Corporate AI 365 never hosts your code and never connects to a live database. It reasons over source code and a scripted schema export you control — never a connection string, never live rows. When a diagnosis genuinely needs live data to confirm, the AI writes a read-only query and hands it to your own developer to run; the result never comes back to us. That boundary is what ends a security review early, and we are not going to soften it for convenience.

The diagnosis itself is reproducible — cached against a hash of the issue text, the code snapshot and the model used — so the same report produces the same root cause and the same proposed fix each time. That matters specifically because of the branch-based pipeline: an approval gate is only meaningful if the thing being approved is stable, not a different answer on every re-run.

The practical effect for a lean North American team is that production support stops depending entirely on your scarcest senior engineer. Anyone in the company — support, ops, a department head who isn't a developer — can file a plain-language report through the Employee console. The AI gets you to a confident, file-level starting point. QA and an approver, both human, still decide what merges. You are not removing judgment from the pipeline; you are removing the hours of archaeology that used to precede it.

event_model_payload.headline: Fast Isn't Free
event_model_payload.summary:
A team picks a workflow tool. It runs well in testing, so they ship it.

A year later, traffic is up. The bill is up even more.

Nobody planned for that, because nobody asked the right question at the start. Not "how fast is it?" but "what will it cost when we're ten times bigger?"

Turn speed into daily volume

Throughput numbers are usually quoted per second, which makes them hard to feel. A quick conversion helps: multiply transactions per second by 86,400, the number of seconds in a day.

  • 1,000 per second is about 86 million a day
  • 10,000 per second is about 864 million a day

Now compare that with what you really expect. A lot of teams find they need far less than they feared. Others find they need a lot more than they planned for. Either way, you can't judge a tool until you know your own number.

Watch how the cost grows

A tool can be fine at small volume and painful at large volume. Here's an illustration. Spending $20,000 a year for a few thousand transactions per second might be reasonable. If handling a bigger load pushed that to $200,000, the math changes. Those are example figures, not anyone's price list, but the shape is real: what matters is whether cost rises in step with traffic or faster.

Simple workflows that run at low volume can live happily with a modest setup. Complex, high-volume ones can't. And a setup that's fast but very expensive tends to be dropped once the bill gets attention.

When latency is the whole point

Some use cases don't give you time to wait. Payment processing, IoT data pipelines and AI-driven workflows are all situations where slow responses or low throughput cause real problems for users. If yours looks like that, test under load before you commit, not after.

What to ask before you choose

  • How many transactions per second can one instance sustain, and what did that test look like?
  • What happens when you need more? Do you add instances, and how does the price change?
  • Does the number come from a workflow like yours, or a simple one-step example?
  • What does it cost at your expected volume, and at ten times that?

Those four questions tell you more than any single benchmark.

For reference, Unmeshed reports up to 10,000 transactions per second on a single instance, which works out to nearly a billion a day, and says larger loads are handled by adding instances to the cluster. As with any vendor's numbers, test it against your own workflows. You can try Unmeshed and see how it behaves with yours.

event_model_payload.headline: 모두가 함께 성장하는 기술 축제, NAVER Engineering Day 10년의 여정
event_model_payload.summary:
기술은 혼자 완성되지 않습니다.

​

한 사람이 발견한 문제와 해결 과정이 동료에게 전해지고,

그 경험이 또 다른 시도와 개선으로 이어질 때 조직의 기술은 앞으로 나아갑니다.

​

NAVER Engineering Day는 이런 믿음에서 출발했습니다.

2016년, 실무에서 얻은 개발 경험과 새로운 기술 및 플랫폼을 도입하며 배운 점을 나누는 사내 개발자 행사로 시작해 올해 10주년을 맞았습니다. 그동안 Engineering Day는 발표자가 정리한 지식을 듣는 자리를 넘어, 서로의 경험을 연결하고 각자의 업무 문제를 함께 해결하는 장으로 꾸준히 확장돼 왔습니다.

​

특히 AI가 특정 직군의 전문 도구를 넘어 일하는 방식 전반을 바꾸기 시작하면서 기술을 나눈다는 말의 의미도 달라졌습니다. 중요한 것은 새로운 도구를 아는 데 그치지 않고, 내 문제에 적용해 보고 막히는 지점을 동료와 함께 풀어 보는 경험입니다.

​

10주년 Engineering Day는 이러한 변화에 맞춰 전 직군이 함께 온라인 세션, 오프라인 워크숍, AI 오픈 코칭데이로 이어지는 4일간의 여정으로 진행됐습니다.

​

10년 동안 이어진 동료의 경험

Engineering Day의 중심에는 늘 구성원이 직접 준비한 이야기가 있었습니다. 완성된 기술을 소개하는 데 그치지 않고, 실제 업무에서 마주한 문제와 선택, 시행착오, 그 과정에서 얻은 교훈을 나눴습니다.

​

주제의 범위도 기술 환경과 함께 넓어졌습니다. 백엔드, 데이터, 모바일을 비롯한 개발 분야부터 AI 도구를 활용한 업무 개선과 협업 방식까지, 서로 다른 역할의 구성원이 각자의 관점에서 경험을 꺼내 놓았습니다. 발표를 통해 한 사람의 경험은 여러 동료가 다시 활용할 수 있는 지식이 됐고, 질문과 대화는 다음 실험의 출발점이 됐습니다.

​

Engineering Day가 10년 동안 이어질 수 있었던 힘은 거창한 구호보다 이 단순한 선순환에 있습니다. 먼저 경험한 동료가 기꺼이 나누고, 다른 동료가 자신의 업무에 맞게 다시 시도하며, 그 결과를 또다시 공유하는 문화입니다.

​

서로의 경험을 발견하는 온라인 세션

첫날에는 구성원들이 직접 준비한 온라인 세션이 열렸습니다. 발표자들은 성공 사례만 소개하지 않았습니다. 문제를 어떻게 정의했는지, 어떤 선택지 사이에서 고민했는지, 실제 적용 과정에서 무엇이 기대와 달랐는지까지 공유했습니다. 덕분에 참가자들은 익숙한 분야의 지식을 확장하는 동시에 평소 접하기 어려웠던 다른 직무의 문제 해결 방식도 살펴볼 수 있었습니다.

​

온라인 세션은 기술을 '아는 것'에서 시작하는 단계였습니다. 이어진 프로그램에서는 이 지식을 직접 다뤄 보고 각자의 업무와 연결했습니다.

​

더 나아가 네이버 내부에서만 그치지 않고, 다음 주 부터 Engineering Day에서 발표된 30여개의 온라인 세션을 D2를 통해서 공개할 예정입니다.

​

두 손으로 따라하며 내 것으로 만드는 워크숍

​

이어서 오프라인 워크숍을 진행했습니다. 참가자들은 설명을 듣는 데 머물지 않고, 준비된 예제와 각자의 과제를 직접 다루며 기술을 적용했습니다.

​

워크숍에서는 개발자를 위한 심화 기술뿐 아니라 비개발 직군의 AI 협업, 디자이너와 개발자의 연결 등 다양한 역할에서 활용할 수 있는 주제를 함께 다뤘습니다. 같은 도구도 맡은 업무와 해결하려는 문제에 따라 쓰임이 달라졌고, 참가자들은 실습 과정에서 동료와 의견을 나누며 각자에게 맞는 활용 방식을 찾았습니다.

​

이 과정은 기술 공유의 효과가 좋은 설명만으로 완성되지 않는다는 점을 보여 줬습니다. 직접 실행해 보고, 예상과 다른 결과를 확인하고, 그 이유를 함께 짚어 볼 때 지식은 비로소 자신의 경험이 됩니다.

​

각자의 경험으로 함께 고민하는 AI 오픈 코칭데이

마지막 날에는 올해 처음으로 AI 오픈 코칭데이를 열었습니다. 온라인 세션에서 개념을 익히고 워크숍에서 실습했더라도, 실제 업무에 적용하려는 순간에는 새로운 질문이 생깁니다. 어디서 시작해야 할지, 문제를 어떻게 나눠야 할지, 현재 방식에서 무엇을 바꿔야 할지 막막할 수 있습니다.

​

AI 오픈 코칭데이는 정해진 강의를 듣는 대신 참가자가 자신의 업무 고민을 가져와 동료 코치와 함께 풀어 보는 방식으로 진행했습니다. 참가자는 문제 상황을 설명하고 직접 도구를 실행했으며, 코치는 정답을 건네기보다 문제를 구체화하고 다음 시도를 설계할 수 있도록 도왔습니다.

​

코칭 과정에서 배운 사람과 가르치는 사람의 경계도 자연스럽게 흐려졌습니다. 코치들은 서로 다른 접근법에서 새로운 관점을 얻었고, 참가자는 자신의 문제를 말로 정리하고 직접 해결 과정을 밟으며 다음 단계로 나아갈 실마리를 찾았습니다. 한 사람의 질문이 주변 동료의 배움이 되고, 한 사람의 해결 경험이 다시 다른 사람에게 전해지는 순간이었습니다.

​

다음 10년에도, 기술은 사람 사이에서 이어집니다.

10주년 Engineering Day는 지난 시간을 기념하는 행사인 동시에 앞으로의 기술 공유 방식을 살펴보는 자리였습니다. 발표를 통해 발견하고, 워크숍에서 직접 시도하고, 코칭을 통해 내 문제에 연결하는 흐름은 기술 학습이 일회성 콘텐츠 소비에 머물지 않도록 했습니다.

​

AI 시대에는 도구의 변화가 빠른 만큼 모든 답을 미리 준비하기 어렵습니다. 그래서 완성된 답을 전달하는 것만큼 문제를 함께 정의하고, 시도한 과정을 나누며, 서로의 시행착오를 다음 출발점으로 만드는 일이 중요합니다.

​

NAVER Engineering Day의 지난 10년은 동료의 경험이 조직의 지식으로 이어지는 시간이었습니다. 다음 10년에도 NAVER는 각자의 자리에서 발견한 문제와 배움을 연결하고, 함께 더 나은 해답을 만들어 가겠습니다.

​

D2에서 이어갈 Engineering Day의 다양한 기술 이야기에도 많은 관심 부탁드립니다.

event_model_payload.headline: Any HN folks with undiagnosed diseases?
event_model_payload.summary:
I've been suffering from a condition since around 2014 perhaps longer, that seemingly started after taking antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, Rocephin, Fosfomycin) where my body just loses tolerance to everything I continually ingest. What that looks like is something like an allergy, but my IgE testing on foods is all normal. For years doctors told me I was having panic attacks when I ate which seriously pissed me off. I started going to higher competence medical institutions and they did some testing during a reaction and low and behold one of the times they tested (for some reason only once...) the levels of PGD2 some allergy chemical were multiple times the upper limit of normal. So they thought maybe I have some kind of allergic disorder. They gave me steroids and antihistamines and it seemed to help. however, it only helped temporarily. Fast forward through me almost dying and being hospitalized with malnutrition repeatedly and spontaneously getting somewhat better years later, and I'm where I'm at now. I collect disability, but I suspect they're going to try to kick me off of it now that I'm doing somewhat better. The thing is, the reactions are totally unpredictable except just the knowledge that it will eventually happen with whatever I'm currently eating. It happens with medications too. So if they say "hey he's not taking his meds" what can I even say to that? I have reacted to numerous medications, including antihistamines and steroids.

Oh I didn't mention the symptoms with foods I react to: Just instant throat tightness/swelling, paleness, extreme bloating, nausea vomiting diarhhea, severe exertional intolerance in the hours following, cardiac arrhythmia, inability to swallow properly if it's bad enough, low blood pressure or high, just lasting for hours if I actually swallow the offending food. If I don't swallow it won't last as long. It's instantaneous as soon as it's in my mouth and I'm chewing on it it'll start. Like an IgE mediated allergy, except I don't swell up like a balloon externally, all internally.

Some specialist says I likely have MCAS but the testing for it is pretty hopeless, and SO MANY doctors flat out dismiss it as even a real thing. Just absolutely insane state of affairs.

But it's like, I just assume this is some bullshit because I've been basically poisoned by our current environment, and my microbiome destroyed by all these antibiotics for that infection in the past, and there's just no name for the condition. Cannon-fodder immune system destruction leading to loss of immune tolerance or something.

I've brought it all up with Claude 5.5 Opus and shit numerous times it's all useless. Just repeats back what I said basically. Tells me to see specialists I've already seen, etc. Nothing new at all. And if I'm not careful with my query, it'll just block me out too.

Anyone else like this? What do you even do in a situation like this?

event_model_payload.headline: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
event_model_payload.summary:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Data Cache is moving to Runtime Cache
event_model_payload.summary:
Data Cache is exiting beta and moving to Runtime Cache. Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache will switch over on every version without code changes. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own Runtime Cache storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Once your team migrates, Data Cache reads and writes that were previously unbilled are charged at Runtime Cache pricing. Rates start at $0.40 per million read units and $4.00 per million write units, and vary by region.

Hobby teams get 1 million read units and 200,000 write units free each month across all projects. On Pro, usage draws from your $20 infrastructure credit each month, and anything beyond it is billed at regional rates. For Enterprise pricing, contact your account team.

Migration

Teams created on or after October 30, 2026 use Runtime Cache by default.

If your team already uses Data Cache:

  • Hobby: We’ll migrate your team on November 29, 2026.

  • Pro: We’ll notify you of your migration date and when billing changes take effect.

  • Enterprise: Your account team will contact you with migration details.

Before you migrate, review your project's Data Cache usage in Observability. To cut unnecessary reads and writes, follow the optimization guide or copy the agent prompt into your coding agent. In the Runtime Cache dashboard, you can also select Optimize with Vercel Agent.

Starting October 30, existing Hobby and Pro teams can opt in early from your team's CDN settings. Runtime Cache pricing applies as soon as you opt in.

You can also disable fetch and unstable_cache caching in CDN settings, which sends more requests to your data sources but doesn’t stop your migration.

Read about the architecture and recent improvements in the blog post.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Vercel Daemons can now call services with bindings
event_model_payload.summary:
Vercel Daemons can now call the services in their deployment through service bindings.

Declare the binding on the daemon. It names the target service and the environment variable that receives the service's URL:

The daemon calls that URL like any other HTTP endpoint. Vercel handles the internal routing, authentication, and TLS, and the service stays private:

Bindings point one way: services can't bind to daemons. Each instance keeps calling the deployment that started it, even after a promotion or rollback.

Learn more about daemon service bindings in the docs.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Add liveness checks to your Daemons
event_model_payload.summary:
Vercel Daemons now support configuring HTTP liveness checks.

Start with an HTTP endpoint in your daemon that reports its health. Keep it lightweight so it responds quickly, and have it return an error status when the daemon is no longer healthy:

The daemon configuration now accepts a livenessProbe value pointing at that endpoint:

Vercel periodically requests the endpoint and restarts the daemon's container when the check fails, catching a daemon that is still running but no longer healthy.

Read the Daemon documentation for more information about liveness checks, including default values and the optional tuning fields.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 now available on AI Gateway for free
event_model_payload.summary:
Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 from InclusionAI is now available on AI Gateway, free until November 3, 2026.

The updated model is designed for coding, multi-step reasoning, and agents that use tools. Its 1M-token context window supports workflows involving long documents, code, and extended task histories.

Use inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-1019 as the model name:

Free requests still appear in your spend dashboard with a full request trace, they just cost nothing. On November 3, requests will begin charging at the published rate.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select inclusionai/ling-3.1-flash-1019 in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

You can also try Ling 3.1 Flash 1019 in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

event_model_payload.headline: Building an Agentic Warehouse Management System—Part 2: Java and Spring AI
event_model_payload.summary:
If you arrived here without reading the first part, I recommend starting with Agentic WMS — Part 1: Where AI Agents Add Value. There, we introduced the WMS scenario, explored the replenishment problem, and discussed where an AI agent can add value without replacing deterministic application logic. In this second part, we will move from the design to the first steps of the implementation.

We will look at how the agent is built with Java and Spring AI, how its capabilities and boundaries are defined, how it is triggered by the WMS, and how the planner turns the agent’s goal into an execution plan.

In Part 3, we will continue from that plan and see how the agent executes tasks using controlled tools, gathers the context it needs, makes the replenishment decision, and takes action when necessary.

Designing the agent

From this point on, we will focus on the main parts of the agent implementation using Java and Spring AI. Rather than covering Spring AI from the ground up, we will concentrate on the components directly relevant to this part of our agent: prompts, capabilities, triggering, and planning. For a broader introduction to Spring AI, see this article by my colleague Tim Kelly.

In Part 1, we established an important boundary: the WMS defines what the agent is allowed to do, while the agent decides what to do within those boundaries. Now we can translate that design into code.

Before diving into the implementation, the following diagram summarizes the complete agent flow across Parts 2 and 3. In this part, we will focus on defining the agent, triggering its execution, and creating the plan.

Figure 1. Agent lifecycle: Define, trigger, and plan.

Define the Agent

The agent is triggered after an outbound operation is completed, with the goal of determining whether that operation created a need for replenishment.

The first step is to define how the agent should behave and what it is allowed to do.

In our implementation, we organize the agent around three main components:

  1. Planner

  2. Executor

  3. Reporter

The planner receives the goal and determines the tasks required to achieve it:

The executor will receive one task at a time and perform it using the tools available for that task:

Finally, the reporter summarizes what happened during the execution:

These are simplified versions of the prompts used in the complete application, but they show the responsibility of each component. Together, these components become part of our agent definition:

The definition also contains the capabilities available to the agent. In our replenishment workflow, we use five:

  • Analysis: Access invoices, inventory, and stock movements.

  • Policy: Retrieve depositor policies.

  • Decision: Determine whether replenishment is required.

  • Replenishment: Create a replenishment request.

  • Notification: Draft the related email.

Each capability defines a type of operation and the tools that can be used while performing it:

This gives us a simple boundary around each task. An ANALYSIS task, for example, can access inventory and stock movement tools, but it cannot create a replenishment request. A DECISION task does not expose any tool and uses the results collected by the previous tasks.

Finally, we can connect these pieces when defining the replenishment agent:

At this point, we have defined what the agent can do and the boundaries around those operations. Before looking at how the plan is created, let's see how the agent execution starts.

Trigger the agent

The agent starts after an outbound operation has been successfully completed. Once the transaction is committed, the application publishes the OUTBOUND_INVOICE_COMPLETED event:

A listener receives that event and starts the agent using the outbound invoice number as the reference:

Using AFTER_COMMIT ensures that the agent starts only after the outbound operation has been persisted and the inventory already reflects the latest state. From there, the agent receives its goal and can begin planning how to accomplish it.

Plan

Once the agent is triggered, the first responsibility of the AgentRunner is to create an execution plan.

The application does not define this list of tasks in advance. Instead, the planner receives the goal together with the capabilities available to the agent and determines which tasks are required for its execution.

Each planned task contains two pieces of information: what needs to be done and which capability should be responsible for it:

Based on this information, the planner generates an ordered list of tasks:

Here, Spring AI maps the model response directly to our PlannedTask objects through structured output, giving the application a typed execution plan instead of requiring us to parse generated text manually.

Once the planner returns the tasks, we persist the initial state of the execution as an AgentRun in MongoDB.

At this point, the execution is marked as RUNNING, and every task generated by the planner starts with the PENDING status:

This gives us a persistent representation of the execution from the beginning, including the tasks that were planned. At this point, the document may look like this:

The plan is now ready, and the execution has been registered.

Conclusion

In this second part, we translated the agent design into the first pieces of the implementation. We defined its responsibilities and capabilities, connected it to the WMS workflow, and used the planner to turn the agent goal into a persistent execution plan.

At this point, the agent knows what needs to be done and which capability is responsible for each task. In Part 3, we will focus on how that plan is executed: using controlled tools, gathering operational and business context, making the replenishment decision, and acting when necessary.

event_model_payload.headline: Agentic Smart Payment Routing with MongoDB / Part I: The Multi-Modal Blueprint
event_model_payload.summary:
Transaction routing is a delicate balancing act between authorization rates, execution cost, and latency. A declined transaction can mean a lost sale, making payment optimization one of the most direct levers for top-line revenue growth. Yet payment operations teams remain trapped in manual operational cycles: Pulling batch CSV reports, analyzing spreadsheets, and manually updating rule tables in legacy gateways. And that repetitive cycle can cost you dearly.

Global businesses lose 1.5% to 2.2% of annual revenue to poor payment performance and false declines, according to research by Checkout.com and Oxford Economics.  While those percentages may seem small, it actually adds up to more than $50 billion in lost revenue each year. And the impact isn’t seen in weeks, months, or a year later. In fact, the fallout is immediate: 45% of shoppers abandon purchases and shift to competitors after a single checkout decline.

To recover lost revenue, modern infrastructure must decouple routing intelligence from checkout execution. Running a background multi-agent control plane to analyze telemetry, simulate options, enforce cost guardrails, and update JSON rules in MongoDB enables continuous smart routing optimization with execution in milliseconds.

Welcome to our new series on agentic payment smart routing, where we architect a modern payment routing platform. This first installment introduces the core concepts for designing an AI-driven control plane across all payment modalities. In the following series, we will apply these foundational principles to specialized deep dives into card payment and cross-border bank transfer routing.

Foundational principles of smart routing

To build a resilient payment stack, you need to understand four universal principles that apply whether processing a credit card, a cross-border, or a crypto stablecoin payment. These four principles answer four questions:

  • Where? Routing applies only before the transaction enters the network or rail.

  • Who? Networks, PSPs, and acquirers have distinct roles.

  • What? Input signals map to an output target: a Merchant ID (MID), clearing rail, or blockchain network.

  • When? Before payment entry (prerouting), at initiation (smart routing), and after a recoverable failure (cascading failover)

Figure 1 summarizes these principles:

Figure 1. Foundational principles of smart routing (universal across modalities).

Why do scripted payment routing rules fall short?

Payment routing selects which gateway, acquirer, or network rail processes a transaction from intent to settlement. Choosing the right architecture requires evaluating three distinct paradigms along the maturity spectrum: static, traditional dynamic, and AI agentic routing.

The business objective is to improve authorization rates without allowing processing costs, fraud exposure, or operational complexity to outpace revenue. A declined transaction can mean a lost sale, and poor payment performance erodes revenue through false declines. Yet many payment ops teams still rely on batch reports, spreadsheets, SQL queries, and manually maintained rule tables.

Figure 2. The evolution of payment routing mechanics.

Robotic process automation and scripted workflows face three main limitations in payment routing:

  • Dimensionality explosion: Payment performance can shift at complex intersections, such as a specific clearing rail, jurisdiction, routing identifier (BIN, BIC, or chain ID), asset type, or transaction amount range. A script can only analyze combinations that engineers explicitly anticipated.

  • Unstructured error interpretation: Processing endpoints, banks, and digital asset networks often return inconsistent responses and decline codes. Rigid scripts struggle to process vague signals (such as "Do Not Honor" or generic rejection codes).

  • Multi-constraint trade-offs: Achieving higher authorization rates often comes at the cost of higher processing fees, network wire or gas costs, foreign exchange spreads, volume commitments, or liquidity constraints. Nested conditions quickly become complex to maintain, explain, and test.

Agentic AI bridges this gap, not by replacing fast execution with slow LLM calls, but by handling background reasoning and continuous rule optimization while preserving a fast, predictable execution path.

An agentic control plane and fast data plane help improve payment routing

An agentic architecture separates background payment rule optimization from payment execution. Payment rule optimization is executed at an asynchronous multi-agent control plane, while payment execution runs on a high-speed execution data plane.

The asynchronous multi-agent control plane does not evaluate individual payment requests in real time. Invoking AI agents on the hot execution path would introduce unsustainable processing costs and unacceptable latency for high-volume scenarios. Instead, the control plane operates continuously in the background to monitor route degradation, simulate net-margin impacts, and present optimized routing rules on an operational dashboard for human payment manager approval. Meanwhile, the high-speed execution data plane handles live transactions at the point of interaction—whether at a POS terminal, an e-commerce checkout, a bank transfer portal, or a Web3 payment widget—by deterministically querying active, declarative rules and evaluating relevant context in milliseconds.

Figure 3. High-level architecture of multi-agent control and high-speed execution data planes underpinned by MongoDB and Atlas Agent Engine.

The control plane can automate the five-step payment routing optimization loop typically executed manually by the human payment analyst. The asynchronous multi-agent control plane works continuously in the background. Specialized agents can divide the optimization loop into focused responsibilities:

While this is a simplified example applicable to card payment routing, these concepts can be easily adapted to bank transfers and crypto payments.

A telemetry agent detects that U.K. Mastercard debit transactions have a 78% authorization rate through Gateway Alpha versus a 91% rate through Gateway Beta. The simulation agent estimates moving 50,000 monthly transactions (average $80 value) could recover $520,000 in sales. Gateway Beta charges higher fees, but the 0.18% projected fee increase remains below the 0.5% policy cap. The supervisor agent can present the projection results as a scorecard for approval and then persist an active rule with Gateway Beta as the primary route and Gateway Alpha as the backup.

How MongoDB supports agentic payment routing

Agentic payment routing needs more than a place to store rules. It needs a data platform that unifies telemetry, transaction history, provider profiles, policies, agent state and memory, and active configurations to support investigation and execution.

MongoDB’s document model naturally fits payment data that evolves across providers and rails. An acquirer may return structured decline fields, a clearing house nested ISO 20022 XML error payloads, and a crypto RPC node unformatted event logs. A document model preserves these native payload differences without rigid schema migration or separate extraction pipelines. This flexibility enables AI agents to analyze complete payment context rather than relying only on predefined fields a rigid script anticipated.

MongoDB Atlas brings search and aggregation capabilities together. MongoDB Vector Search helps find similar historical payment contexts, while metadata filters and aggregation pipelines narrow results by country, network, payment modality, currency or token asset, and policy constraints. Agents use these signals to detect hidden performance patterns and rank routes by success rate, similarity, and processing fees.

The database also stores active JSON rules that the execution engine reads. Agents write new rules, record their confidence and justification, set their status to pending approval, and activate them upon manager approval. Time-to-live (TTL) indexes handle rule expiration, while MongoDB Change Streams instantly notify the control-plane components of transaction data or rule updates without waiting for batch jobs.

Deployable anywhere, Atlas Agent Engine is an enterprise platform for managing the full lifecycle of AI agents. It delivers native short- and long-term memory primitives within the database, eliminating custom state pipelines. Running in a sandboxed execution runtime with built-in observability, it enables auditing of agent recommendations. With native safety controls and support for open standards like MCP and A2A, it integrates into existing stacks to deliver secure, audit-ready payment routing.

Security and deployment requirements shape the architecture. MongoDB Queryable Encryption keeps sensitive fields encrypted while supporting specific query patterns, supporting PCI DSS and privacy obligations. Zone-based sharding keeps selected data in target regions, while multi-cloud deployments ensure high availability across cloud providers. These capabilities help build an architecture that meets regulatory, availability, and data residency needs.

Most importantly, MongoDB supports the separation between control and execution. The control plane can analyze telemetry, logs, vectors, and policies, while the data plane retrieves only the active rule and attributes required for a fast decision.

What agentic payment routing enables

Smart payment routing is evolving from static rules into a continuous, self-healing optimization system. Static routing remains useful for deterministic paths, and machine learning can add real-time scoring. But neither approach fully addresses the work of discovering new segments, interpreting changing unstructured decline or failure signals, simulating alternatives, and enforcing competing multi-variable constraints across cards, bank rails, and digital assets.

Agentic AI handles this background work. With a multi-agent control plane and MongoDB, PSPs, orchestration providers, banks, and enterprise merchants can continuously analyze payment performance, test routes, protect margins, and approve impactful changes. MongoDB manages the changing operational context, enables advanced search capabilities across similar payment scenarios, and serves active rules for low-latency execution.

The result is a practical path to smarter payments: Autonomous optimization where reasoning is useful, deterministic execution where speed is essential, and human oversight where governance requires it.

References:

  • Checkout.com: High Performance Payments Report – The Hidden Billion-Dollar Opportunity

  • Checkout.com Newsroom: Research Finds Businesses Lag Behind in Payment Performance

  • Checkout.com Blog: High-Performance Payments: The Hidden Billion-Dollar Opportunity

event_model_payload.headline: Grafana 13.3 release: manage variables across dashboards, share findings with Notebooks, a UI refresh, and more
event_model_payload.summary:
Grafana 13.3 is here, bringing more consistency and control to how you work across Grafana. 

Cross-dashboard variables help you manage shared dashboard controls from one place, while Notebooks let you capture and share findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. You'll also get a first look at Grafana's biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7, along with new ways to guide and refine dashboards built with Grafana Assistant.

Below are just some of the highlights from this release. You can explore all of the updates in the changelog or our What's new in Grafana 13.3 documentation.

Define a variable once and use it across dashboards

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

When multiple dashboards use the same variable, such as an environment, region, or cluster selector, managing it separately in each dashboard creates duplicate work and can lead to configuration drift. To address this, we’re rolling out cross-dashboard variables, which let you define a variable once and reuse it across dashboards in your Grafana organization.

You can create and manage these variables from Dashboards > Variables, and scope each one as either:

  • Global: available to every dashboard in the organization

  • Folder: available only to dashboards in the same folder

When you edit a dashboard, add a variable from the sidebar and select Global or folder variable. Grafana shows only the variables available to that dashboard's scope, and you can add them one at a time or all at once. Viewers can still change the variable's value on the dashboard, while its configuration stays managed centrally, so shared controls stay consistent without editing every dashboard that uses them.

To try cross-dashboard variables in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.dashboardGlobalVariables feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the cross-dashboard variables documentation.

Consolidate and share your findings with Notebooks

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

An investigation rarely happens in one place. You might start on a dashboard panel, jump into Explore to run a query, and then ask Grafana Assistant what's going on. Until now, the evidence and your reasoning ended up scattered across tabs, screenshots, and chat threads.

Notebooks let you capture findings from across Grafana in a single, editable document. Add panels from dashboards or Explore, pull in findings from Grafana Assistant, and write your observations right next to the data. Teammates can then follow your investigation, understand how you reached your conclusions, and collaborate on next steps.

You can use a notebook to:

  • Explore a question about your data, keeping queries and notes side by side as your thinking develops.

  • Document an investigation so the next person doesn't have to start from scratch.

  • Prepare a post-incident review with the relevant panels already in place.

You can create notebooks manually or with Grafana Assistant, then save and share them for future reference. The new Notebooks page also makes it easy to find and manage your work, with options to search, filter, edit, and export notebooks. 

Notebooks are gradually rolling out to Grafana Cloud. To try them in self-managed Grafana, enable the dashboard.notebooks feature toggle. To learn more, refer to the Notebooks documentation.

A fresh new look for the Grafana UI

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana

Whether it’s adding new data sources or supporting new use cases, we’re constantly expanding what Grafana can do. And as AI-powered workflows with Grafana Assistant became a bigger part of how people use Grafana every day, we saw an opportunity to rethink how the platform looks and feels.

With Grafana 13.3, we're introducing the first phase of our biggest visual refresh since Grafana 7. Built on an updated set of design principles, the refresh introduces new colors, typography, and UI components to create a more modern, consistent experience across Grafana.

Updates include: 

  • New default dark and light themes. We've reworked every theme color, with more shades for flexibility, and main action buttons now have a solid, high-contrast style.

  • Softer borders and floating components. Rounder corners offer a more modern feel, and subtle borders on cards, panels, and drawers create a clearer sense of depth. The toolbar and navigation also stand apart more clearly from page content.

  • Updated inputs, drop-downs, buttons, and tags. We've resized our most-used components to be more proportional and consistent. 

  • Revised typography. A new type scale mixes font weights and sizes, rather than relying on size alone, so it's easier to see what matters most on a page. 

Importantly, this is a visual refresh, not a redesign. Your existing workflows and navigation stay the same, and there are no breaking changes for plugins. Plugins that use standard Grafana components and theme tokens will automatically pick up the new look, while those with custom styling can migrate on their own timeline.

To try out the new UI in self-managed Grafana, enable the grafana.visualDesignRefresh feature toggle. You can switch back to the previous design at any time, and we welcome your feedback as we continue rolling out improvements over the coming months.

Build and edit dashboards with more control using Grafana Assistant 

Grafana Assistant can already help you build and edit dashboards from a plain-language description. Now, with Grafana 13.3, you have more control over that process, from reviewing and refining a dashboard plan before it's built to easily undoing changes afterward. 

Review a dashboard plan from Assistant

Available in public preview in all editions of Grafana 

With dashboard plans, you can describe what you want to monitor, and instead of building it right away, Assistant proposes a plan in chat. The plan covers the dashboard title, tabs or rows, panels, visualization types, and variables, so you can catch a missing panel or the wrong chart type before anything is built.

Select Preview to open a read-only version of the dashboard, then keep the conversation going to iterate from there. When the preview matches what you need, select Build it to generate the dashboard and save it.

Quickly revert Assistant edits 

Generally available in all editions of Grafana 

Experimenting with different layouts and visualizations is easier when you can quickly undo changes you don’t want. With Grafana 13.3, you can now select Undo turn after Grafana Assistant edits your dashboard to restore it to its previous state. If Assistant changed multiple panels in a single request, you can undo all those changes at once.

To learn more, refer to the Grafana Assistant dashboarding guide.

More to explore in Grafana 13.3

Beyond these highlights, Grafana 13.3 includes a range of updates related to data visualization, alerting, Git Sync, and more. 

For an in-depth list of all the new features, check out our Grafana documentation, the Grafana changelog, or our What's New documentation.

Join the Grafana Labs community

We invite you to engage with the Grafana Labs community forums. Share your experiences with the new features, discuss best practices, and explore creative ways to integrate these updates into your workflows. Your insights and use cases are invaluable in enriching the Grafana ecosystem.

Upgrade to Grafana 13.3

Download Grafana 13.3 today or experience all the latest features by signing up for Grafana Cloud, which offers an actually useful forever-free tier and plans for every use case. Sign up for a free Grafana Cloud account today. 

Our Grafana upgrade guide also provides step-by-step instructions for those looking to upgrade from an earlier version to ensure a smooth transition.

Special thanks to our community
