event_model_payload.headline: Jais 3: The UAE Just Built Arabic-First AI That Acts, Not Just Chats
event_model_payload.summary:
Most AI models speak Arabic as a second language. They were built in English first, and Arabic was added later — which is why they stumble on dialects, on Egyptian or Moroccan speech, and on the everyday habit of switching between Arabic and English mid-sentence.

Jais 3, launched on 15 October 2026 by Abu Dhabi's Mohamed bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence (MBZUAI) and Inception42, reverses that order. It is Arabic first, and it is built to do work, not just hold a conversation.

A family, not a single model

Jais 3 is six open language models sharing one training recipe, from a 0.9-billion-parameter model designed for phones up to a 375-billion-parameter flagship for data centres. The two largest use a mixture-of-experts design — the flagship stores 375 billion parameters but activates only 23 billion per token, keeping running costs sane. Five of the six have a 512,000-token context window (the smallest has 128K), which IFM says is the longest of any Arabic-native model.

All six are on Hugging Face under the Apache 2.0 licence, so developers can use them commercially and self-host, from a phone app to a GPU cluster. They are built on K2 Horizon, IFM's open foundation model fleet from September 2026, adapted with an Arabic-focused training recipe covering Modern Standard Arabic and regional dialects, plus the cultural knowledge around the language.

The speech part is the practical win

Alongside the text models comes Jais Speech (Jais-ASR), a speech recognition system for Arabic and its dialects across 19 Arab countries. It transcribes dialects, accepts spoken instructions in Arabic or English, handles code-switching between Arabic and English or French, and applies Arabic diacritics (vowel marks) directly to live transcripts — something most speech tools skip, and which makes transcripts far more useful for documents and subtitles.

Built to act

IFM's pitch is that Jais 3 works as an agent: it plans multi-step tasks, calls tools, edits Arabic documents, searches the web and hands back a finished result. Launch examples include reading an Arabic contract, updating a spreadsheet and producing presentations. It is also designed to follow instructions closely — format, length and constraints as set by the user.

The honest caveat

Every headline benchmark number comes from IFM's own evaluations across 24 public Arabic benchmarks and has not yet been independently replicated. The most eye-catching: at 7 billion parameters, the average Arabic score rose from 56.4 for the K2 Horizon base to 79.6 after Arabic adaptation. That is a developer-reported claim, not a settled fact — and the right way to judge Jais 3 is to test it on your own dialect and documents.

Who should care

If your documents, customers and meetings are in Arabic, Jais 3 is a practical upgrade over an English-first chatbot — especially for transcription and document work. Developers building for the Arab world get six self-hostable sizes with no API bill. If you work only in English, Jais 3 still matters as a signal: language-native open models, built by countries for their own languages, are arriving fast.

This is a condensed explainer. The full breakdown — the complete model table, the benchmark picture, pros and cons, and FAQ — is on NeurAITool: Jais 3: The UAE's Open Arabic AI Family Explained.

event_model_payload.headline: A JSON state file ended in zeros after an unclean shutdown: quarantine it, then salvage every record you can
event_model_payload.summary:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of the tool described here, and this post was drafted and published by an AI agent from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote (MIT, Node.js) is a phone remote for Claude Desktop's Code-tab sessions. It keeps its task list in one file, registry.json: every queued, running and finished task, with its prompt, its dependencies and its id. It is the kind of file nobody thinks about until the day JSON.parse throws on it.

That day came after an unclean shutdown. The file had its normal size, but the last stretch of it was NUL bytes. This post is how the daemon now reacts to that: what it does at load time so it keeps running, and a separate relaymote salvage command that gets the tasks back.

What the damage looks like

The writes were already done the textbook way: write a temp file, fsync it, rename it over the real one. That protects against a half-written file from your own process. It does not fully protect you from the machine losing power around the rename, depending on the file system and what had actually reached the disk. The result we saw was a file whose length had been recorded but whose last blocks never arrived, so they read back as zeros.

The useful observation is about where the damage sits. The front of the file is intact. The break is a clean cut somewhere near the end, followed by padding. Almost every record is still there; only the parser gives up, because one bad byte fails the whole document.

Part 1: at load time, quarantine and keep going

The loader must not crash the daemon, and it must not "fix" the file in place. It does three things when parsing fails:

const q = FILE + '.corrupt-' + Date.now();
if (fs.existsSync(FILE)) {
  fs.renameSync(FILE, q);
  process.stderr.write(`registry.json could not be read; moved it to ${q}. Recover its tasks with: relaymote salvage\n`);
}
  1. Rename, never delete. The damaged file is the only copy of those tasks. Moving it aside gives the daemon a clean slate and leaves the evidence untouched.
  2. Say what to do next in the same log line. The person reading it at 2 a.m. should not have to find the docs.
  3. Keep the id counter above the damage. Task ids are t0001, t0002, and so on. If the daemon starts empty with seq = 0, new tasks will reuse ids the salvage will later bring back. So before starting empty, it scans the raw text for every id and the old seq, and starts above the highest: 
let seq = 0;
for (const m of String(raw).matchAll(/"t(\d+)"\s*:|"seq"\s*:\s*(\d+)/g))
  seq = Math.max(seq, Number(m[1] || m[2]) || 0);

A regex over broken JSON is fine here: it only needs to find numbers, not understand structure. And the new floor is saved straight away, not at the next write, so a second crash cannot lose it.

One Windows detail sits in front of all this: a file another process is renaming into place can be briefly locked (EPERM, EBUSY, EACCES). That is not corruption. The loader retries the read a few times with a short back-off before it decides the file is unreadable, so a normal save from another process never gets the registry quarantined.

Part 2: salvage, from cheapest repair to most expensive

salvage(raw) is a pure function (the tests call it directly) that tries three repairs in order and reports which one worked:

1. Trim the padding. Strip trailing NULs and whitespace, then parse. If the cut happened to land after the closing brace, this is all it takes.

2. Close the document after the last complete record. The file is written with JSON.stringify(state, null, 2), so every task object ends with a newline and exactly four spaces before its }. Find the last "\n }," (or failing that "\n }"), cut there, and append the closing braces for tasks and the root:

const cut = s.lastIndexOf('\n    },');
const j = JSON.parse(s.slice(0, cut + '\n    }'.length) + '\n  }\n}');

This leans on your own serializer's indentation, which is a fair thing to lean on: you wrote it, and it is deterministic. Everything before the last complete task comes back; only the task that was being written at the cut is lost. Any fields that came after tasks in the root object are lost too, which is why seq is recomputed from the recovered ids.

3. Scan for individual records. If the damage is in the middle, closing the document will not parse. So find each "tNNNN": {, walk forward counting braces (tracking whether you are inside a string, and escapes inside strings, so a } in a prompt doesn't end the object early), and try JSON.parse on just that slice. A mangled stretch now costs only the records it touched.

If all three fail, it returns null and the command says NOTHING_RECOVERABLE along with the file size and how much of it was padding, which is usually the whole explanation.

Part 3: merge into the live file without clobbering anything

By the time someone runs salvage, the daemon has been running on an empty registry and may have created new tasks. The recovered tasks are merged in, with a few rules:

  • Live tasks keep their ids. A recovered task whose id is taken by a different live task gets the next free id. It is renumbered, never dropped, and the renumbering is printed.
  • Dependencies follow the renumbering. If recovered task t0040 depended on t0039, and t0039 was renumbered, the dependsOn list is rewritten to match.
  • Running it twice is harmless. Each task gets a fingerprint of its creation time and prompt. A recovered task whose fingerprint already exists under any id is counted as "already present", not added again.
  • Each restored task is tagged with the corrupt file it came from, so you can tell restored tasks from new ones later.
  • Dry run by default. Without --apply it only reports: method used, characters, padding, tasks recovered, how many would be added, how many are already present, the renumbering. With --apply it writes the merged registry with the same temp-file, fsync, rename sequence. It never modifies the corrupt file, so you can run it again.

What carries over

  • When a state file fails to parse, move it aside and keep running. Never repair in place, never delete.
  • Keep id counters above anything the damaged file mentions, and persist that floor immediately.
  • Treat a briefly locked file on Windows as "retry", not "corrupt".
  • Order repairs from cheapest to most expensive and report which one worked.
  • Your own serializer's formatting is a legitimate anchor for finding record boundaries.
  • Merges should renumber rather than overwrite, follow references, and be safe to repeat.

Relaymote is MIT-licensed: github.com/ashwarsadh/relaymote. The code is in lib/registry.js and lib/salvage.js. Unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

event_model_payload.headline: Your AI Agent Will Retry. Your Booking System Will Not Notice.
event_model_payload.summary:
Letting an agent write to a legacy system of record takes an intent log, not a better prompt.

The agent calls create_booking. The legacy API takes 31 seconds and the HTTP client times out. The orchestrator retries the step. The second call succeeds, and the customer now holds two reservations and a confused confirmation email. The prompt was fine. The model was fine. Nothing in the stack knew that the first call had actually gone through.

Every agent pilot we look at passes its demo on read-only tools: search, lookup, summarize. The trouble starts with the first tool that changes state. Booking, order entry, ticket creation, ERP postings. That is the write path, and it needs the same engineering you would give a payment flow.

An agent has three retry layers, and the legacy system sees all of them

The first layer is the HTTP client. Most SDKs retry on connection errors and 5xx responses by default. The second is the orchestrator. Whether you use LangGraph, Temporal, a queue worker, or a loop you wrote yourself, a failed step gets re-run, and a redelivered message gets processed twice. At-least-once delivery is the default contract of nearly every queue you will use.

The third layer is unique to agents. The model reads a timeout or an ambiguous response, decides the action probably failed, and calls the tool again. This retry is not byte-identical to the first. The arguments may differ in small ways: "adults": 2 versus "adults": "two", a date in a different format, an extra optional field. An idempotency key derived from the raw request body will not catch it.

Stripe popularized client-supplied idempotency keys for exactly this problem, and they work well when the downstream system honors them. Many systems of record do not. SOAP interfaces, batch-file ERPs, and older reservation backends often have no idempotency concept at all. Some will happily create a duplicate and return a fresh ID each time.

A timeout is not a failure, and your agent needs to be told that

The most damaging bug in these systems is a tool wrapper that turns a timeout into the string "Error: request failed". The model reads that as a failure and does what a helpful assistant does: it tries again.

The honest state after a timeout is unknown. The request may have been rejected, may still be queued, or may have committed. Treat it as a fourth outcome next to success, rejection, and error. The agent should receive "outcome pending, do not retry" and a reconciler should find out what happened.

We apply the same discipline to our own internal tooling. Our outreach pipeline runs agents that draft and schedule emails, and the sender records a marker per lead and per email step, checked before every send. The agent never decides whether an email already went out. A file on disk does. The mechanism is almost embarrassingly low-tech, and it has survived crashed runs and re-triggered cron jobs because the check lives outside the model. Production systems need the same property with a stronger store behind it.

Put an intent log between the model and the legacy API

The pattern is small. The agent never calls the legacy system directly. It calls a tool wrapper that writes an intent row to Postgres and returns. A separate worker executes intents against the downstream system.

CREATE TABLE tool_intents (
  intent_key   text PRIMARY KEY,
  run_id       uuid NOT NULL,
  tool         text NOT NULL,
  args         jsonb NOT NULL,
  state        text NOT NULL
               CHECK (state IN ('pending','sent','confirmed','rejected','unknown')),
  external_ref text,
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  updated_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

The key is computed from business intent, not from the request:

const parsed = BookingArgs.parse(rawArgs);        // zod: "two" becomes 2, dates become ISO
const intentKey = sha256([run.id, 'create_booking', stableStringify(parsed)].join('|'));

const res = await db.query(
  `INSERT INTO tool_intents (intent_key, run_id, tool, args, state)
   VALUES ($1, $2, 'create_booking', $3, 'pending')
   ON CONFLICT (intent_key) DO NOTHING
   RETURNING intent_key`,
  [intentKey, run.id, parsed],
);

if (res.rowCount === 0) return loadPriorResult(intentKey); // same intent, same answer

Schema validation does the normalization work. Once the model's arguments have been coerced into a strict type, two retries that mean the same thing hash to the same key, and the second insert hits the primary key and returns the earlier result. If a run can legitimately perform the same action twice, add the plan step or line item ID to the hash so the two intents differ on purpose.

The worker claims rows with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which lets several workers drain the table without double-claiming. Writing the intent and enqueuing the work is one transaction, which is the transactional outbox pattern. Before it calls the legacy API, it writes the intent key into whatever free-text reference field the system offers. Almost every booking or ERP interface has one.

Reconcile unknowns by reading, never by writing again

When the worker's call times out, the intent moves to unknown. A reconciler job then queries the legacy system for a record carrying that reference. If it finds one, the intent becomes confirmed with the external ID. If nothing appears after a defined window, it becomes rejected and can be retried safely under the same key, because the reconciler has verified that nothing exists.

Meanwhile the agent sees a structured result such as {"status":"pending","intent":"..."}. A model told that a booking is pending will tell the customer it is being processed. A model told that a call failed will try something else.

Split the dangerous tools in two

Give the model hold_booking and confirm_booking instead of one create_booking. A hold carries a TTL and expires on its own, so a wrong hold costs nothing. Confirmation is the irreversible step, and it can sit behind a policy check, an amount threshold, or a human approval click. Our own outreach pipeline works this way: agents draft freely, and a person approves before the first email to a new contact goes out.

This split also gives you a clean place to enforce limits. The model can propose a thousand holds. Only a bounded number can ever become confirmations.

What it takes to build

None of this needs an ML team. It is Postgres, a worker process, schema validation, and a reconciler, which makes it a solid fit for one senior backend engineer working in NestJS or Python and owning the integration boundary. The unglamorous parts, such as the reconciler and the monitoring on unknown intents, decide whether the agent can be trusted with real customers. Teams under funding pressure tend to postpone them until the first duplicate order arrives.

Key Takeaways

  • Agents retry at three layers: HTTP client, orchestrator, and the model itself. Only the first two are visible in your logs.
  • Treat a timeout as unknown, tell the model "pending, do not retry", and resolve the state by reading the downstream system.
  • Derive idempotency keys from validated, normalized business arguments, not from raw request bodies or LLM-generated call IDs.
  • Route every state-changing tool through an intent table in Postgres, with a worker and a reconciler between the model and the system of record.
  • Split irreversible actions into a cheap, expiring hold and a gated confirmation.

SifrVentures builds dedicated engineering teams for tech companies. Based in Berlin. Learn how we work | Read more on our blog

event_model_payload.headline: The Risks of Leaving Environment Differences Implicit
event_model_payload.summary:
The Risks of Leaving Environment Differences Implicit

An integration works in development. The API responds correctly, the application behaves as expected, and the developer is ready to deploy.

Then production behaves differently.

The cause might be different credentials, missing environment variables, different permissions, or configuration that was present during development but never reproduced in production.

These differences are not unusual. Development, testing, and production environments often serve different purposes.

The risk arises when developers do not understand which differences matter and what they must configure before moving between environments.

An integration that works in one environment does not automatically work in another.

How Environment Assumptions Develop

Consider a developer integrating a payment API.

During development, the application uses test credentials and successfully processes test transactions. The developer completes the main functionality and prepares for deployment.

However, production requires live credentials and the appropriate production configuration.

If the developer assumes that the existing setup carries over unchanged, the application may fail to perform live transactions until the missing configuration is corrected.

Stripe's documentation explicitly distinguishes test and live API keys and explains their different uses. The developer must use the appropriate credentials for the intended environment.

This is a documented product requirement, not evidence that Stripe customers generally misunderstand it.

The broader lesson applies to any product where environments differ in credentials, resources, permissions, endpoints, or configuration.

Why These Differences Can Be Overlooked

Developers often focus on getting the integration working before considering every deployment requirement.

A successful development environment can create confidence that the implementation is nearly complete.

But some requirements only become relevant when the application moves to another environment.

For example:

  • Development credentials may not be valid for production.
  • Environment variables may be missing from the deployment configuration.
  • Production permissions may differ from development permissions.
  • Resources created during testing may need to be created or configured separately.
  • Different endpoints or service settings may be required.

The problem is not that environments differ. It is that the implementation process may not make those differences sufficiently visible.

What Product Teams Should Examine

Product teams should investigate how developers move between environments and what they need to understand at each stage.

Useful questions include:

  1. Which settings and resources differ between environments?
  2. What must developers configure separately?
  3. Which assumptions from development become invalid in production?
  4. Can developers identify the required changes before deployment?
  5. What must they verify to confirm that the production integration is ready?

These questions help identify gaps between a successful test and a complete deployment.

Why This Matters

When environment differences are unclear, developers may encounter avoidable deployment delays, configuration errors, or unexpected application behaviour.

These outcomes are possibilities, not inevitable consequences of using multiple environments.

The goal is to establish whether developers can understand what changes, what remains their responsibility, and what they must verify before proceeding.

DaxMac independently examines real customer implementation experiences to identify the assumptions, gaps, and potential risks that companies may miss when evaluating their products from the outside.

An integration working in development is useful evidence. Understanding the differences between development and production is what helps determine whether that implementation is ready to move forward.

event_model_payload.headline: Team-Level LLM API Key Management: The Guide I Wish Someone Gave Me
event_model_payload.summary:
When your app was a side project, one .env file with an OpenAI key was fine. The moment a second engineer joins, that setup turns into a small disaster: keys leak into git, a junior's experiment blows the budget, and no one knows who spent what.

Here's the system we ended up with after burning two budgets and rotating three keys.

1. Never share one key across the team

The instinct is to put the production key in 1Password and call it a day. The problem:

  • You can't revoke one person's access without killing everyone's
  • You can't attribute spend
  • When that key leaks (and it will), you rotate it for the whole team

Give each developer their own key. Scope it down.

2. Separate environments from users

Two axes to think about:

Axis Values
Environment dev / staging / prod
Owner each engineer + CI bots

That's a matrix of keys, not one key. A CI key should never have production write access. An intern's dev key should never work in staging.

3. Budget per key, not per account

OpenAI's account-level limit is too coarse — one runaway loop burns everyone's quota. You want per-key spend caps:

# Pseudocode: what the gateway should enforce
per_key_budget = {
  "dev-llong":      {"monthly": 20,  "models": ["gpt-4o-mini"]},
  "prod-service-a": {"monthly": 500, "models": ["gpt-4o","claude-3-5-sonnet"]},
  "ci-bot":         {"monthly": 5,   "models": ["gpt-4o-mini"]},
}

4. Rotate, but make it cheap

Key rotation should be a 5-minute operation, not a sprint. If every rotation means updating 30 service configs, people stop doing it. A gateway layer with one ANTHROPIC_API_KEY-equivalent that routes to upstream providers lets you rotate the upstream key without touching the app.

5. Audit log everything

You want to know, after an incident:

  • Which key made the call
  • Which model and how many tokens
  • From which service

Without this, "who burned $400 last night?" becomes a he-said-she-said.

6. What we actually use

We ran through Envoy + custom Lua scripts, then a vendor-specific dashboard, before landing on a gateway that does per-key budgets, per-model routing, and a unified audit log out of the box. Agent Token is what we use today — one OpenAI-compatible key, per-key spend caps, team usage dashboard across GPT / Claude / Gemini.

The pattern matters more than the tool, though: one key per person per environment, hard budgets, and an audit log you'd actually check.

How does your team manage LLM keys? Genuinely curious what works for bigger orgs.

event_model_payload.headline: Bitrix24 REST API in Practice: Webhooks, Batch Calls and Rate Limits
event_model_payload.summary:
The Bitrix24 REST API looks simple on day one. You create an inbound webhook, call crm.deal.list, get JSON back and the prototype works. The trouble starts on the first bulk sync, when a few thousand records need to move and the portal answers with QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, or a week later, when someone notices that deals updated over the weekend never reached the warehouse system.

This post collects what we have learned building exchanges between Bitrix24 and external systems: how the two kinds of webhooks behave, how to use batch without shooting yourself in the foot, how the rate limits actually work, and the handful of field-level quirks that cause silent data corruption.

Two kinds of webhooks, two different jobs

Bitrix24 uses the word "webhook" for two unrelated things.

Inbound webhook. A URL with a secret embedded in it that lets your code call REST methods on behalf of a specific user:

https://yourcompany.bitrix24.kz/rest/1/x7k2abc9def0ghij/crm.deal.get.json?id=42

The 1 is the user ID, the next segment is the secret. Everything this URL does runs with that user's permissions and is limited to the scopes you ticked when creating it (crm, user, task and so on). Two practical consequences:

  • Create a dedicated technical user for integrations. If the webhook belongs to a sales manager who later leaves the company and gets deactivated, the integration dies with their account.
  • Grant the minimum scopes. The URL is a bearer credential. It ends up in logs, environment files and occasionally in screenshots sent to a chat.

Outbound webhook (event handler). Bitrix24 sends a POST to your URL when something happens: ONCRMDEALADD, ONCRMDEALUPDATE, ONCRMCONTACTDELETE and many more. The body is form-encoded, not JSON, and looks roughly like this once parsed:

event=ONCRMDEALUPDATE
data[FIELDS][ID]=1287
ts=1761712345
auth[domain]=yourcompany.bitrix24.kz
auth[application_token]=k4q9...

Notice what is missing: the deal itself. You get an ID and nothing else. Your handler has to call crm.deal.get to find out what changed, which means every event costs at least one API request.

A minimal handler in Python (Flask) that does the right things:

import os
from flask import Flask, request, abort
from queue_client import enqueue  # Redis, RabbitMQ, a DB table, anything durable

app = Flask(__name__)
APP_TOKEN = os.environ["B24_APP_TOKEN"]

@app.post("/b24/events")
def b24_event():
    form = request.form
    if form.get("auth[application_token]") != APP_TOKEN:
        abort(403)

    event = form.get("event")
    entity_id = form.get("data[FIELDS][ID]")
    if not event or not entity_id:
        abort(400)

    enqueue({"event": event, "id": int(entity_id), "ts": form.get("ts")})
    return "", 200

Three rules are baked in here:

  1. Check application_token. The handler URL is public; without the check anyone can push fake events.
  2. Do not call the API inside the handler. Acknowledge fast and queue the work. A slow or failing handler loses events, and Bitrix24 keeps no replay log for you.
  3. Store only the ID. By the time the worker runs, the deal may have changed again, and you want the latest state anyway.

Events are a hint, not a guarantee

Treat outbound events as "something probably changed, go look". Deliveries get lost during your downtime, network blips or a deploy that broke the route. Two mitigations we use together:

  • Offline events. For applications, Bitrix24 can store events on its side; you pull them with event.offline.get and confirm processing. Push becomes pull and survives your downtime.
  • A periodic reconciliation pass. Every N minutes, request entities with DATE_MODIFY after your last checkpoint and run them through the same worker. Cheap, and it catches whatever the event stream dropped.

The echo loop

If your integration writes back to the same entity it listens to, you will create a loop: you update deal 1287, Bitrix24 fires ONCRMDEALUPDATE, your worker fetches it, sees a "change", pushes it to the external system, which pushes a status back, which updates the deal again.

Break it explicitly. Options that work:

  • Compare a hash of the fields you care about with the last hash you synced. If nothing relevant changed, stop.
  • Check MODIFY_BY_ID (or updatedBy in crm.item.*) and ignore changes made by your technical integration user.
  • Write a sync marker into a custom field, but only if the business is fine with an extra field on the card.

The first option is the most robust, because it also filters out updates that touched fields you do not sync.

batch: up to 50 calls in one request

batch takes a set of named commands and executes them on the server in one HTTP round trip. The limit is 50 commands per batch.

import requests

WEBHOOK = "https://yourcompany.bitrix24.kz/rest/1/x7k2abc9def0ghij/"

def call(method, params=None):
    r = requests.post(WEBHOOK + method + ".json", json=params or {}, timeout=30)
    data = r.json()  # read the body even on 503: the error code says which limit you hit
    if "error" in data:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{data['error']}: {data.get('error_description')}")
    return data

cmd = {
    f"d{deal_id}": f"crm.deal.get?id={deal_id}"
    for deal_id in [101, 102, 103]
}
resp = call("batch", {"halt": 0, "cmd": cmd})
results = resp["result"]["result"]        # successful commands
errors = resp["result"]["result_error"]   # failed commands, keyed the same way

Things to know before relying on it:

Check result_error every time. With halt: 0 the batch continues past failures, and the top level of the response looks successful. A batch of 50 updates where 7 failed returns HTTP 200. If you only read result, those 7 are lost silently.

halt: 1 is not a transaction. It stops at the first error, but the commands that already ran are not rolled back. There are no transactions in the REST API. Design updates so that re-running them is safe.

Commands are query strings. Each value in cmd is a URL-encoded string, not JSON. Hand-built strings break on &, = or Cyrillic. Use an encoder for PHP-style nested arrays (fields[TITLE]=..., filter[>ID]=...); plain urlencode on a nested dict gets it wrong.

Results can feed later commands. You can reference an earlier result inside the same batch:

cmd = {
    "contact": "crm.contact.add?fields[NAME]=Aigerim&fields[PHONE][0][VALUE]=%2B77001234567&fields[PHONE][0][VALUE_TYPE]=WORK",
    "deal": "crm.deal.add?fields[TITLE]=Order%20123&fields[CONTACT_ID]=$result[contact]",
}

Handy, but it makes the batch order-dependent and harder to retry. We use it for create-and-link pairs and avoid it everywhere else.

A batch is one request for the rate limiter, but not free. It counts as one hit against the request frequency limit, but every command inside still consumes server execution time, which is limited separately (see below). Fifty heavy list calls with complex filters in one batch can exhaust the time budget faster than fifty simple get calls spread over a minute.

How the rate limits actually work

There are two independent limits, and integrations usually discover them in this order.

1. Request frequency: a leaky bucket

Each portal has a request counter that behaves like a leaky bucket. Requests fill it, and it drains at a fixed rate per second. While the bucket has room, requests go through instantly. When it is full, you get HTTP 503 with error QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED. The common published figures are a drain rate of 2 requests per second with a burst capacity of 50 on standard plans, and higher values on top plans and on-premise installations. Check the current numbers for your plan, they have changed over the years.

A script firing 200 requests in a tight loop gets the first 50 through, then hits errors, and a naive retry loop only adds more requests. The fix is a client-side limiter that mirrors the server's bucket, plus backoff when the server disagrees:

import time, random, threading

class LeakyBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate=2.0, capacity=50):
        self.rate, self.capacity = rate, capacity
        self.level, self.last = 0.0, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = threading.Lock()

    def acquire(self):
        while True:
            with self.lock:
                now = time.monotonic()
                self.level = max(0.0, self.level - (now - self.last) * self.rate)
                self.last = now
                if self.level + 1 <= self.capacity:
                    self.level += 1
                    return
                wait = (self.level + 1 - self.capacity) / self.rate
            time.sleep(wait)

bucket = LeakyBucket(rate=1.8, capacity=40)  # stay below the real limit

def call_limited(method, params=None, attempts=6):
    for attempt in range(attempts):
        bucket.acquire()
        try:
            return call(method, params)
        except RuntimeError as e:
            if "QUERY_LIMIT_EXCEEDED" not in str(e) and "OPERATION_TIME_LIMIT" not in str(e):
                raise
        time.sleep(min(60, 2 ** attempt) + random.random())
    raise RuntimeError(f"{method}: rate limited after {attempts} attempts")

Two details matter. The limiter runs below the real limit, because telephony, marketplace apps and other scripts share the same bucket. And it must be shared across workers: four processes with their own in-memory bucket send four times the allowed rate. Beyond one process, keep the counter in Redis.

2. Execution time per method

Newer versions of the platform also limit how much server time a single method may consume over a sliding window. Responses carry a time block, with fields such as operating and operating_reset_at telling you how much time the method has used. When a method exceeds its budget, it is blocked for a while with OPERATION_TIME_LIMIT, while other methods keep working.

This bites bulk exports. crm.deal.list filtering on a custom field with a large select is expensive, and a loop of them eats the budget. Log the time block during test runs to see which calls are heavy before production does.

Pagination that does not get slower on every page

List methods return 50 records per page with next and total. The obvious loop passes start=0, 50, 100.... On large tables this degrades, because the server still counts and offsets through everything before your page, and it also computes total on every call.

The faster pattern: sort by ID, filter by >ID from the last record you saw, and pass start=-1 to turn off the count.

def iter_deals(select):
    last_id = 0
    while True:
        resp = call_limited("crm.deal.list", {
            "order": {"ID": "ASC"},
            "filter": {">ID": last_id},
            "select": select,
            "start": -1,
        })
        rows = resp["result"]
        if not rows:
            return
        yield from rows
        last_id = int(rows[-1]["ID"])

Each request is now an indexed range scan, and page 2,000 costs the same as page 1. On exports of hundreds of thousands of records this decides whether the job finishes overnight at all.

Always pass select. Without it you get the default field set, which excludes custom UF_CRM_* fields, and you will wonder why they are empty. With ["*", "UF_*"] you get everything, which is expensive. List the fields you need.

Field-level pitfalls

These do not throw errors. They corrupt data quietly.

Multi-fields append by default. PHONE, EMAIL, WEB and IM are arrays of {ID, VALUE, VALUE_TYPE}. If you call crm.contact.update with PHONE: [{"VALUE": "+77001234567"}], the number is added, not replaced. Run that on every sync and a contact collects fifty copies of the same phone. To change a value, pass the existing item's ID; to delete one, pass its ID with an empty VALUE.

Two naming conventions. crm.deal.* uses UPPER_SNAKE (STAGE_ID, ASSIGNED_BY_ID). The newer universal crm.item.* methods with entityTypeId (2 for deals, 3 for contacts, 4 for companies, plus IDs for smart processes) use camelCase (stageId, assignedById) and wrap results in item or items. Mixing them in one codebase leads to fields that are "set" but never saved. Pick one family per entity and stick to it.

Stage IDs depend on the pipeline. In the default pipeline a stage is NEW or WON; in additional pipelines it becomes C3:NEW, C3:WON, where 3 is the category ID. Hardcoding WON works until sales creates a second pipeline.

Dates come with a timezone offset. Values look like 2026-10-29T11:00:00+05:00. Parse them as aware datetimes. Comparing them as strings or stripping the offset produces off-by-hours bugs in checkpoints, which means missed or duplicated records in reconciliation.

List fields store IDs, not labels. A custom enum field returns "45", not "Wholesale". Load the field definitions with crm.deal.userfield.list once and map both ways.

What to log

Log method, entity ID, direction, duration, the time block, the error code and a correlation ID linking event, queue job and API call. Add one alert on the age of the oldest unprocessed job. Integrations rarely crash; they drift until the numbers stop matching a week later.

Checklist

  • Dedicated technical user, minimal webhook scopes
  • Event handler: token check, enqueue, return 200
  • Reconciliation pass by DATE_MODIFY to catch lost events
  • Echo-loop protection by field hash or author check
  • batch with result_error checked on every call
  • Shared client-side limiter below the published rate, backoff on 503
  • >ID pagination with start=-1 and explicit select
  • Multi-fields updated by ID, stage IDs resolved per pipeline
  • Logs with timing data and an alert on queue age

The REST API itself is the same for cloud and on-premise portals; only authorisation and access setup differ, so these patterns carry over. If you would rather hand the exchange to a team that builds queues, retries and monitoring into every project, here is how we approach Bitrix24 REST API integration with warehouse, logistics and banking systems.

event_model_payload.headline: The fx adapter now runs the harness on the host

The fx adapter for the AI SDK’s HarnessAgent now uses libfx, the TypeScript library for fx. The harness and model requests run in your application’s process, while built-in filesystem and shell operations remain isolated in the sandbox.

This simplifies sandbox setup: you no longer need to install fx inside the sandbox, run a sandbox bridge, or expose a sandbox port. Model credentials stay on the host, outside the environment where the agent runs commands.

The rewrite also adds:

  • Built-in tool filtering: choose which built-in tools the agent can use

  • Mid-turn steering: send new instructions while a turn is running

  • Structured output: generate responses that match a schema

  • Image tool results: return images to the model through toModelOutput()

Sessions can be saved and resumed in a new host process.

event_model_payload.headline: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
event_model_payload.summary:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

event_model_payload.headline: From ISO 27001 to ISO 42001: A Practical AI Governance Implementation Guide
event_model_payload.summary:
AI systems introduce governance challenges that traditional information security processes may not fully address. A company can have an established Information Security Management System (ISMS), documented security controls, and an internal audit programme while still lacking processes for AI system impact assessments, model governance, and AI-specific risk management.

This is where ISO/IEC 42001:2023 becomes relevant.

ISO 27001 focuses on information security management, whereas ISO 42001 specifies requirements for establishing and continually improving an Artificial Intelligence Management System (AIMS). For engineering teams that already work with ISO 27001, the transition can involve reusing suitable management processes and extending them to cover AI-specific requirements.

The important part is understanding what can be reused, what needs to be added, and how to maintain evidence as AI systems evolve.

Why Does ISO 27001 Alone Not Cover Every AI Governance Requirement?

Information security remains an essential part of AI governance, but it is not the only concern.

Consider an application that uses a third-party language model to process customer requests. The engineering team may already assess access controls, encryption, data confidentiality, and supplier security under its ISMS.

However, additional questions may arise:

  • Can the model produce biased or inappropriate outputs?
  • Are the training or input data suitable for the intended purpose?
  • When should a human review an AI-generated decision?
  • How are changes to the model evaluated before deployment?
  • What documentation is needed to explain the system's behaviour and limitations?
  • How are AI-related risks monitored after release?

These questions require processes that address AI systems and their lifecycle, rather than information security alone.

ISO 42001 provides a management-system framework for organising this work.

What Can Engineering Teams Reuse From ISO 27001?

ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 share the same general harmonized management-system structure across clauses 4 to 10. This creates opportunities to coordinate activities instead of maintaining two completely separate management systems.

1. Risk management workflows

An existing risk register can provide a useful starting point for AI governance.

For example, an engineering team may already document security risks, assign owners, define mitigation measures, and review outstanding issues. These practices can support the AIMS, provided the risk methodology is extended to address relevant AI-related risks and opportunities.

AI-specific assessments may need to consider bias, explainability, data quality, human oversight, and potential impacts on people.

2. Document control and evidence

Many organisations already use version-controlled repositories, ticketing systems, approval workflows, and audit records.

These systems may help maintain AI policies, risk assessments, technical documentation, review decisions, and corrective actions.

The objective is not to create a separate document for every standard. It is to maintain reliable records that can be traced to the requirements they support.

3. Internal audits and management reviews

Existing audit schedules and management review processes may also be coordinated.

However, audit criteria must cover the requirements of both standards. An ISMS audit that focuses only on information security does not automatically establish that an AIMS is effective.

For more detail on shared processes and standard-specific requirements, see the ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 integration guide.

A Practical ISO 42001 Implementation Workflow

A phased approach can help technical teams identify gaps and introduce AI governance without unnecessarily duplicating existing work.

Step 1: Inventory your AI systems

Start by identifying the AI systems used, developed, provided, or deployed within the proposed AIMS scope.

Depending on your organisation, the inventory may include:

  • Internally developed machine learning models
  • Third-party language models and APIs
  • AI-enabled SaaS products
  • Retrieval-augmented generation applications
  • Automated decision-support systems
  • AI components integrated into production services

For each system, record its intended purpose, owner, deployment environment, relevant data sources, external dependencies, and lifecycle status.

This inventory creates a shared reference point for risk assessments, governance decisions, and change management.

Step 2: Define the AIMS scope and responsibilities

Determine which organisational activities and AI systems fall within the management system.

Assign responsibilities across engineering, security, product management, legal, and compliance teams as appropriate.

For example, an ML engineer might maintain model documentation, a security engineer might assess technical vulnerabilities, and a product owner might coordinate reviews of intended use and operational changes.

These are possible organisational arrangements, not job titles mandated by ISO 42001.

Step 3: Perform an AI-specific gap analysis

Compare your current management processes with the requirements of ISO 42001.

Review areas such as:

  • AI policy and governance responsibilities
  • AI risk assessment and treatment
  • AI system impact assessment
  • AI objectives and performance evaluation
  • Data and AI lifecycle management
  • Human oversight and relevant transparency processes
  • Third-party AI relationships
  • Internal audit and continual improvement

Record each gap, the required action, its owner, and the evidence needed to demonstrate implementation.

An existing ISO 27001 certification does not automatically satisfy ISO 42001 requirements.

Teams planning this transition can use the ISO 42001 implementation guide for ISO 27001 holders as a reference for organising implementation phases and identifying areas that require additional work.

Step 4: Assess AI risks and impacts

Risk assessment should reflect the context and intended use of each AI system.

For a customer-facing chatbot, the assessment might examine inaccurate responses, inappropriate disclosures, data handling, and the need for human escalation.

For an AI recruitment system, relevant considerations might include potentially discriminatory outcomes, data representativeness, explainability, and human review.

The assessment process should produce documented findings and decisions. These results can inform risk treatment, AI objectives, and the selection of applicable controls.

ISO 42001 addresses AI system impact assessment as well as AI-related risk management. The two activities should not be treated as interchangeable.

Step 5: Map and implement the controls

Annex A of ISO 42001 contains 38 reference controls organised into nine control objectives.

These objectives cover AI policies, internal organisation, resources, AI system impact assessment, the AI system lifecycle, data, information for interested parties, AI system use, and third-party and customer relationships.

Build a control map that identifies the applicable requirements, current processes, gaps, owners, and supporting evidence.

Where an existing security process supports an AI governance objective, document the relationship. Where it does not cover the relevant requirement, introduce an additional control or process.

The mapping should be based on the actual requirements and the organisation's circumstances, rather than assumptions that similarly named controls are equivalent.

Step 6: Integrate governance into the software development lifecycle

For engineering teams, AI governance is easier to maintain when it connects to existing development workflows.

Consider introducing the following practices:

Before deployment: Review intended use, relevant risks, data considerations, and required approvals.

During development: Maintain model and system documentation, track relevant changes, and record assessment results.

Before significant changes: Evaluate whether a model update, new data source, or change in intended purpose requires another risk or impact assessment.

After deployment: Monitor relevant performance indicators, record incidents, and assign corrective actions where necessary.

The exact controls depend on the system, its context, and applicable requirements. ISO 42001 does not prescribe a single CI/CD implementation for every AI application.

Step 7: Audit and improve the management system

Conduct an internal audit against the applicable ISO 42001 requirements and defined audit criteria.

Review the implementation of controls, the quality of evidence, assigned responsibilities, and the operation of risk and impact assessment processes.

Management review should evaluate the suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness of the AIMS. Track findings and corrective actions rather than treating the audit as the final step.

Organisations seeking certification should coordinate with an appropriate certification body.

How Can Teams Manage AI Governance Evidence?

A common operational problem is that evidence becomes scattered across Git repositories, spreadsheets, project management tools, shared drives, and approval systems.

This can make it difficult to determine which AI systems have been assessed, who approved a decision, and whether the supporting documentation is current.

A central evidence structure can help.

For example, an organisation might maintain the following relationships:

  • AI system inventory → identifies the system and its owner.
  • Risk assessment → records identified risks and treatment decisions.
  • Control mapping → connects requirements to implemented processes.
  • Technical documentation → describes relevant system characteristics and limitations.
  • Approval records → establish who reviewed and authorised a decision.
  • Monitoring records → provide evidence of ongoing review and improvement.

These relationships can be maintained in existing tools or supported by dedicated AI governance software.

The objective is traceability: teams should be able to move from an AI system to its relevant assessments, controls, decisions, and evidence without reconstructing the history manually.

Where Does the EU AI Act Fit Into ISO 42001?

ISO 42001 is a voluntary management-system standard, while the EU AI Act establishes legal obligations for relevant AI systems and actors.

An AIMS can support governance processes, documentation, and risk management. However, ISO 42001 certification alone does not establish compliance with the EU AI Act.

Organisations must separately determine their applicable legal obligations, including relevant requirements for high-risk AI systems, transparency, AI literacy, and other provisions where applicable.

The legal roles of provider and deployer also need to be assessed under the EU AI Act. They should not be inferred solely from an organisation's internal governance responsibilities.

For teams coordinating management-system work with regulatory requirements, an integrated approach can reduce duplicated effort while preserving the distinction between voluntary standards and legal obligations.

Can AI Compliance Software Support the Implementation?

AI governance software can help organisations connect AI inventories, risk assessments, control mappings, and evidence records in one workflow.

AnnexOps is one option for teams managing ISO 42001, ISO 27001, and EU AI Act compliance operations. Its ISO 27001 compliance solution describes support for ISMS scope, risk registers, controls, evidence, and internal audits.

Software selection should depend on the organisation's scope, existing tools, evidence requirements, and workflow needs. A platform can support compliance operations, but it does not replace management accountability, legal assessment, or an independent certification audit.

Final Thoughts

Moving from ISO 27001 to ISO 42001 is an extension of management-system capabilities, not simply a change in security documentation.

Engineering and compliance teams can make the transition more manageable by inventorying AI systems, defining responsibilities, assessing AI-specific risks and impacts, mapping controls, and maintaining traceable evidence.

The most sustainable approach is to connect governance activities to the software lifecycle and existing management processes while preserving the requirements unique to each standard.

For a detailed phase-by-phase roadmap, read the ISO 42001 implementation guide for organisations that already have ISO 27001.
