event_model_payload.summary:
This article is about engineering an offline-first app for low-end devices based on our experience in Nigeria and India. The interesting problems in this space are storage, quota, cold start, and failure-path design. Our approach applies to any product whose users are on constrained devices and intermittent connections, when the assumption they have a laptop and broadband access do not hold.

By Chidi Nwaogu

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway
event_model_payload.summary:
Today, we are introducing Virtual Models on AI Gateway.

Virtual Models are an abstraction of the model string and configurations your apps and developers use. With a single virtual model ID, you can change and update models, configure fallbacks and priority, and enforce Zero Data Retention centrally. The virtual model configuration applies wherever the ID is used.

Assign a virtual model ID to an agent task, and pass it as the model string wherever that task is called. You can then change the model and settings behind the virtual model ID in AI Gateway, and your apps and agents will pick up the new configuration automatically, without code changes or redeploys.

New models use the same virtual model ID

In the last 90 days, 125 new models from more than 10 labs became available on AI Gateway. That adds up to about 10 a week. AI Gateway already makes switching a one-line change. You call any of those models by ID, and AI Gateway routes each request to a healthy provider and can fall back to others when one fails.

That one line still lives in your code, so switching usually means a redeploy.

Virtual Models move model selection and configuration to AI Gateway. You create an ID for a task, like vmc/coding-agent, and then configure the model and the settings it should use:

You can then use that virtual model ID as the model string wherever the task runs:

For coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, and others, connect them with vercel ai-gateway setup, then select your virtual model in each harness's model picker or configuration.

When a different model is available, including one from another provider, edit the virtual model. Every app and agent that calls vmc/coding-agent picks it up within a few minutes, with no code change or deployment needed:

Give each task its own model

An agent task like support ticket triage can run hundreds of times an hour and needs to be cheap. Other tasks, like legal contract review, may only run a few times a day, but require a high level of reasoning.

You can now give each task a purpose-built virtual model and easily evolve that model and configuration over time:

Settings such as fallbacks, Zero Data Retention, and tags stay with the virtual model when you switch models. Provider options apply per provider, so an Anthropic-specific setting stops applying when you point the virtual model at an OpenAI model. Review your provider options whenever you switch providers.

Before you switch a virtual model that serves production traffic, point a second one, like vmc/coding-agent-candidate, at the new model and run your evals against it. If quality drops after the switch, point the original back at the previous model.

Govern which models your team uses and how

Anyone on your team can call a virtual model, and team roles control who can make changes to it. Platform and security teams can centrally govern and test models and settings, while still easily giving teams access to new models as they are released.

Settings on a virtual model win over the same settings in a request, so callers can't override the provider order, fallbacks, or service tier you chose. For example, you can configure the fallback models for vmc/storefront-assistant centrally, and every app using that virtual model ID will use the same failover configuration, even if a request specifies different fallbacks.

If a virtual model requires Zero Data Retention or providers that don't train on request data, those configurations are enforced even if a request explicitly sets zeroDataRetention or disallowPromptTraining to false.

Tags on a virtual model replace any tags sent with the request, so spend lands on the task no matter how each app tags its calls. The Virtual Models page shows requests, spend, and success rate for each task.

Get started

Create a virtual model from your team dashboard or with the Vercel CLI.

About AI Gateway

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and doesn't charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

Virtual Models work with every model type on AI Gateway, including image, video, speech, embedding, and realtime models, and with the AI SDK and the OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible APIs. See the Virtual Models documentation for every setting.

Read more

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing AptMQL-Bench: A Text-to-MQL Benchmark
event_model_payload.summary:
Large language models increasingly sit between people and their data, whether answering questions in a chat interface or acting as agents that query databases directly. Either way, the model must reliably translate a request into the query language the database speaks.

For SQL, progress on this task has been driven by large benchmarks such as BIRD1 and Spider2. MQL, the query language of MongoDB, has received less attention despite the fact that MongoDB is one of the world’s most popular and widely used databases.

In this blog post, we introduce AptMQL-Bench (Access-Patterns-Based Text-to-MQL), a Text-to-MQL benchmark obtained by converting existing Text-to-SQL datasets. We also present the agent-driven conversion pipeline that produced it.

We're releasing:

  • AptMQL-Bench: the benchmark dataset. It consists of 21 new MongoDB databases along with 3,186 natural-language requests, migrated from BIRD1, spanning domains such as commerce, science, sports, and finance.

  • A technical report describing our proposed conversion pipeline for access-pattern schema design, data-preserving migration, and SQL-to-MQL translation.

  • Conversion pipeline prompts

  • Evaluation script, including our proposed soft execution accuracy (Soft-EX).

The challenges

Existing Text-to-MQL approaches take one of two routes. The NL-to-mongosh dataset3 starts from native MongoDB data, pairing 766 synthetically generated requests with the eight MongoDB Atlas sample databases. Other works convert existing Text-to-SQL datasets mechanically: DocSpider4 maps each relational table to its own collection one-to-one, while TEND-v25 and its multilingual extension MultiTEND6 embed tables along foreign keys (FK).

However, doing these conversions well is not trivial. Mechanical denormalizations along foreign keys, in particular, can be fragile. In our experiments, three out of 24 databases failed to migrate due to infinite recursion on self-referential keys, while another three produced individual documents so large that they didn't fit in MongoDB's 16 MB document limit. Additionally, on eight other databases, rows whose foreign keys resolved to no surviving parent were silently dropped, reaching 25.9% row loss in the worst case.

Finally, as we show below, these conversions also lead to schemas with poor scalability characteristics.

Our proposed conversion pipeline

As Figure 1 shows, we treat schema design as a first-class step and then revise that design while migrating the data. The pipeline is driven by coding agents (e.g., Claude Code) with human review at designated quality gates, and runs in three stages.

Figure 1. The conversion pipeline: document schema design, migration and validation, and SQL-to-MQL translation, each driven by a coding agent with human review at the quality gates.

1. Access-pattern schema design. Given the source SQLite database and its column descriptions, an agent first infers a real-world application the database would serve and the access patterns it would generate. The agent then designs a high-level conceptual schema (which collections exist and how they relate), and a low-level logical schema, specifying each collection’s fields, data types, and mappings from the source database. Both follow a design guidebook we curated from three MongoDB University courses. A reviewer then confirms each modeling choice and verifies that every source table remains retrievable from the design.

This approach ensures that the resulting schemas adhere to MongoDB's golden rule for schema design: data that is accessed together should be stored together.

2. Migration and validation. To catch errors or omissions in the schema design and migration code, the agent runs three automated checks after each migration: (1) queries over each MongoDB collection retrieve the same data as corresponding queries over the original SQL tables, (2) references between collections point to existing documents, and (3) nothing on the SQLite side was left behind. Anything that fails is surfaced to a human reviewer, who then works with the agent to fix the design or the migration code. We repeat this until every check passes.

3. SQL-to-MQL translation, then optimization. Each reference SQL query from the source benchmark is translated into MQL by an agent, which revises the translation until automated checks confirm that both queries return identical results. Translations that pass are correct but often still relational in shape. For instance, they'll contain redundant $lookup stages that fetch already-embedded documents. A second pass rewrites them to use embedded fields and precomputed aggregates directly; 1,444 MQL queries (45.32%) were optimized this way, and a reviewer confirmed each one is equivalent to the original translation. BIRD's external knowledge evidence is rewritten in the same spirit, so its field references point to MongoDB paths rather than SQL columns, and each rewritten evidence is checked by a reviewer against the ground-truth MQL.

The importance of schema design

We compare the characteristics of schemas produced by our access-pattern design approach against the two mechanical strategies on the same source data.

Table 1. DB migration results. 24 databases: the 21 BIRD databases in AptMQL-Bench plus 3 Spider databases used in the scaling experiments.

One-to-one is lossless by construction: every row becomes its own document, but the result merely mirrors the relational schema, at a cost we measure below. Foreign key embedding fails outright on six out of 24 DBs, while in 8 other cases the migration is lossy.

On execution time, we find that the performance of the three designs diverges as the size of the underlying DBs is increased. To measure this, we took three DBs from Spider (bike_1, car_1, and pets_1) and 11 DBs from BIRD. We then expanded each DB by appending synthetic rows (see our paper for more details on this procedure), obtaining different versions of these DBs with sizes up to ~200 MB.

Figure 2. Execution time of the ground-truth MQLs as database size grows (log-log, averaged across databases), for each conversion strategy.

Figure 2 shows the resulting execution times. At 200 MB, access-pattern MQLs run about 11× faster than foreign key embedding and roughly two orders of magnitude faster than a one-to-one migration on the Spider datasets. On BIRD, the speedup over one-to-one grows from around 40× on the original databases to 77× once they reach the largest sizes investigated.

These results demonstrate the advantages of the workload-driven schema design advocated in this work.

Benchmarking LLMs

We evaluated eight models in total (five open-weight, three proprietary), each with and without BIRD's external knowledge evidence.

Table 2. Soft execution accuracy (Soft-EX) on AptMQL-Bench. Full results, including execution success rate and Strict-EX, are in the paper.

The results show that the benchmark is challenging for every model. The strongest model, Claude Opus 4.5, reaches only 57.38% Soft-EX without external knowledge and 70.34% with it. External knowledge helps every model, adding 12–19 points.

Some of the latest models (Gemma 4 and the Claude family of models) produce executable MQL about 98–99% of the time, confirming that invalid MQL is more and more rare and that the remaining difficulty is semantic rather than syntactic.

Why we score with Soft-EX

In metrics borrowed from Text-to-SQL, strict execution accuracy (Strict-EX) requires the returned result to equal the gold result field-for-field, so a prediction that hands back the whole document instead of a single projected field is marked wrong, even though it contains the right answer, and even though returning the document is the idiomatic thing to do in MongoDB.

We therefore propose soft execution accuracy (Soft-EX): a prediction is correct if it returns the same rows as the gold result, with matching values for every ground-truth field. Extra fields are allowed, but extra or missing rows and incorrect values are not.

Table 3. The following examples illustrate the difference between Strict-EX and Soft-EX.

With external knowledge, Opus 4.5 scores 50.44% under Strict-EX but 70.34% under Soft-EX. To confirm that this gap is due only to extra fields, we manually reviewed all 634 queries where the two metrics disagree, which covers every prediction that Soft-EX accepts but Strict-EX rejects.

In every case, the prediction returned the same rows as the gold result, with matching values for every gold field, and differed only by including extra fields. Strict-EX therefore marks these predictions wrong even though they contain the complete gold answer.

Next steps

Try it and learn more!

  • Benchmark and databases: Hugging Face dataset

  • Conversion pipeline prompts and evaluation scripts are here

  • Technical report

References

  • 1 Jinyang Li et al. 2023. Can LLM Already Serve as A Database Interface? A BIg Bench for Large-Scale Database Grounded Text-to-SQLs. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 36:42330–42357.

  • 2 Tao Yu et al. 2018. Spider: A Large-Scale Human-Labeled Dataset for Complex and Cross-Domain Semantic Parsing and Text-to-SQL Task. In Proceedings of the 2018 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, pages 3911–3921, Brussels, Belgium. Association for Computational Linguistics.

  • 3 MongoDB Education AI. 2025. Natural Language to MongoDB Shell (mongosh) Benchmark. Hugging Face dataset. https://huggingface.co/datasets/mongodb-eai/natural-language-to-mongosh

  • 4 Arif Görkem Özer, Recep Firat Cekinel, Ismail Hakki Toroslu, and Pinar Karagoz. 2025. DocSpider: A Dataset of Cross-Domain Natural Language Querying for MongoDB. Natural Language Processing, 31(6):1367–1398.

  • 5 Jinwei Lu, Yuanfeng Song, Zhiqian Qin, Haodi Zhang, Chen Zhang, and Raymond Chi-Wing Wong. 2025. Bridging the Gap: Enabling Natural Language Queries for NoSQL Databases through Text-to-NoSQL Translation. Preprint, arXiv:2502.11201.

  • 6 Zhiqian Qin, Yuanfeng Song, Jinwei Lu, Yuanwei Song, Shuaimin Li, and Chen Jason Zhang. 2025. MultiTEND: A Multilingual Benchmark for Natural Language to NoSQL Query Translation. In Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025, pages 24632–24657, Vienna, Austria. Association for Computational Linguistics.

event_model_payload.headline: Getting Started With MongoDB and AWS CodeWhisperer
event_model_payload.summary:
Amazon CodeWhisperer is trained on billions of lines of code and can generate code suggestions — ranging from snippets to full functions — in real-time, based on your comments and existing code. AI code assistants have revolutionized developers’ coding experience, but what sets Amazon CodeWhisperer apart is that MongoDB has collaborated with the AWS Data Science team, enhancing its capabilities!

At MongoDB, we are always looking to enhance the developer experience, and we've fine-tuned the AWS CodeWhisperer Foundational Models to deliver top-notch code suggestions — trained on, and tailored for, MongoDB. This gives developers of all levels the best possible experience when using AWS CodeWhisperer for MongoDB functions.

This tutorial will help you get AWS CodeWhisperer up and running in VS Code, but CodeWhisperer also works with a number of other IDEs including AWS Cloud9, AWS Lambda console, JupyterLab, and Amazon SageMaker Studio. On the Amazon CodeWhisperer site, you can find tutorials that demonstrate how to set up AWS CodeWhisperer on different IDEs, as well as other documentation.

Note: Amazon CodeWhisperer allows users to start without an AWS account because, usually, creating an AWS account requires a credit card. Currently, CodeWhisperer is free for individual users. So it’s super easy to get up and running.

Installing Amazon CodeWhisperer for VS Code

CodeWhisperer doesn’t have its own VS Code extension. It is part of a larger extension for AWS services called AWS Toolkit. AWS Toolkit is available in the VS Code extensions store.

Step 1. Open VS Code and navigate to the extensions store (bottom icon on the left panel).

Step 2. Search for AWS CodeWhisperer, and it will show up as part of the AWS Toolkit.

Step 3. Once found, hit Install. Next, you’ll see the full AWS Toolkit Listing.

Step 4. Once installed, you’ll need to authorize Amazon CodeWhisperer via a Builder ID to connect to your AWS developer account (or set up a new account if you don’t already have one).

Using AWS CodeWhisperer

Navigating code suggestions

With Amazon CodeWhisperer installed and running, as you enter your prompt or code, CodeWhisperer will offer inline code suggestions. If you want to keep the suggestion, use TAB to accept it. AWS CodeWhisperer may provide multiple suggestions to choose from depending on your use case. To navigate between suggestions, use the left and right arrow keys to view them, and TAB to accept.

If you don’t like the suggestions you see, keep typing (or hit ESC). The suggestions will disappear, and Amazon CodeWhisperer will generate new ones at a later point based on the additional context.

Requesting suggestions manually

You can request suggestions at any time. Use Option-C on Mac or ALT-C on Windows. After you receive suggestions, use TAB to accept and the arrow keys to navigate.

Getting the best recommendations

For best results, follow these practices.

  • Give Amazon CodeWhisperer something to work with. The more code your file contains, the more context CodeWhisperer has for generating recommendations.
  • Write descriptive comments in natural language — for example.

Or

  • Specify the libraries you prefer at the start of your file by using import statements.

  • Use descriptive names for variables and functions.
  • Break down complex tasks into simpler tasks.

Provide feedback

As with all generative AI tools, they are forever learning and forever expanding their foundational knowledge base, and MongoDB is looking for feedback. If you are using Amazon CodeWhisperer in your MongoDB development, we’d love to hear from you.

We’ve created a special “codewhisperer” tag on our Developer Forums, and if you tag any post with this, it will be visible to our Amazon CodeWhisperer project team, and we will get right on it to help and provide feedback. If you want to see what others are doing with CodeWhisperer on our forums, the tag search link will jump you straight into all the action.

We can’t wait to see your thoughts and impressions of MongoDB and Amazon CodeWhisperer together.

event_model_payload.headline: DataGrip: a great database IDE to work with MongoDB Atlas
event_model_payload.summary:
JetBrains released a new version of DataGrip that includes support for MongoDB and ships with the MongoDB Shell out of the box.

A few months ago, JetBrains released the first version of DataGrip that supports MongoDB. DataGrip is a professional DataBase IDE and is a great tool for advanced data exploration and analytical queries for your data in MongoDB and Atlas.

If you use any of the other JetBrains commercial products for development (e.g. PhpStorm, PyCharm), you can install the Database Tools plugin and work with MongoDB right inside your IDE.

As we announced last week at MongoDB.live, the MongoDB plugin in DataGrip and in the other JetBrains IDE now includes a database console built on top of the MongoDB Shell. This is the result of a close collaboration between engineering teams at MongoDB and JetBrains and we are excited to finally release it to all our users.

With this integration, when you connect to MongoDB and Atlas with DataGrip, you get a console/shell experience that is 100% consistent with what you get in the terminal or in the other MongoDB’s developer tools.

DataGrip and Atlas

When your data is stored in Atlas, navigating through it with DataGrip is extremely easy.

For example, to connect to my free Atlas cluster, I can just grab a connection string from the Atlas UI, use it to add a new data source in DataGrip and I am connected and ready to explore my data.

Using Consoles

If you need to run queries, aggregations, or other database commands, consoles are a great way to do that.

The engineering teams at JetBrains and at MongoDB worked together to bring the new, embeddable MongoDB Shell to DataGrip and use it as the engine behind database consoles. This means the same commands that you can run in the MongoDB Shell are available in DataGrip and the other JetBrains IDEs and you can expect them to work exactly in the same way with the addition of the beautiful UI you are already used to on top.

A great fit for Atlas Data Lake

DataGrip works well MongoDB deployments, whether self-managed or in Atlas. You can also use it with Atlas Data Lake. If you have data is stored in Amazon S3 and you want to query and analyze it with MQL, you can create a Data Lake and start working with it right away.

DataGrip’s search capabilities give you a quick way to find the data you are interested in, and its powerful export tool makes it easy to extract it in the format you need to use it with other tools like Excel, for example.

Get started with MongoDB Atlas and DataGrip

We are really happy with the result of our collaboration with the team at JetBrains and we are looking forward to working more together to bring all the future capabilities of the MongoDB Shell to DataGrip and the other JetBrains IDEs.

You can experience for yourself how DataGrip is a perfect companion for MongoDB Atlas:

  1. Get a free MongoDB Atlas cluster;
  2. Deploy some sample datasets;
  3. Download DataGrip and start working with your data immediately.

event_model_payload.headline: Building an Agentic Warehouse Management System—Part 1: Where AI Agents Add Value
event_model_payload.summary:
I spent a large part of my career working in banking and logistics. In logistics, I spent more than eight years working across different stages of logistics systems, from development to implementation and production support.

That experience shaped the way I think about technology. Knowing a tool or framework is important, but what interests me most is understanding the business problem behind it and where technology can actually add value.

A few weeks ago, I returned as a speaker to a company where I had worked for many years. Being back there reminded me of several day-to-day logistical challenges and made me wonder how I would approach those problems today.

That is where the Agentic Warehouse Management System came from.

With this project, I am not trying to build a complete WMS. Instead, I want to use a logistics scenario I know well to explore how an AI agent can become part of a real business workflow and where it can add value.

In this first part, we will introduce the WMS scenario and identify where an AI agent can help. In Part 2, we will define and connect the agent using Java and Spring AI. Finally, in Part 3, we will execute the plan, gather context, make the replenishment decision, and act when necessary.

The Warehouse Management System

A Warehouse Management System, or simply WMS, is a software system used to manage and control the movement of products inside a warehouse. It typically handles processes such as receiving goods, tracking inventory, shipping products, replenishment, and many others. A warehouse may store products owned by the company operating it, but it may also store products for other companies. In this article, we will call these companies depositors:

Figure 1. Warehouse Operations Overview.

A depositor owns the products stored in the warehouse, while the warehouse is responsible for receiving, storing, managing, and shipping them. A single warehouse may serve multiple depositors at the same time. For example, products from Amazon, Nike, or Walmart could be stored and managed in the same warehouse, while the inventory of each depositor remains separated. A real WMS can support many more processes, but for our application, we will focus on a smaller part of this flow:

Figure 2. Inventory Flow and Replenishment Trigger.

An Inbound operation represents goods entering the warehouse and increases the available inventory for a depositor.  An Outbound operation represents goods leaving the warehouse and reduces that inventory.

We will also include a simple Replenishment Request process. When additional units are needed, the warehouse can create a request indicating which products should be replenished and in what quantities. The depositor can then arrange a new inbound shipment to the warehouse. Once a replenishment request is created, a Depositor Email Draft is also prepared for notification.

Modeling the WMS flow

In the flow above, a traditional implementation would involve a few basic entities such as Inbound, Outbound, Inventory, and Replenishment Request, along with products and depositors. An Inbound operation represents products owned by a depositor entering the warehouse. For example:

Once completed, those quantities are added to the Inventory:

An Outbound operation does the opposite. Products leave the warehouse, and their quantities are reduced from the inventory:

After this operation, the inventory for product BR01 belonging to the depositor Amazon would contain only 20 units. At this point, a Replenishment Request may be needed. In practical terms, the warehouse is essentially saying:

“Amazon, your product BR01 is down to only 20 units. Could you arrange a new inbound shipment before we run out of stock?”

In our WMS, this request can be represented by a document like the following:

Deciding when to replenish

Creating a Replenishment Request is straightforward. The more interesting question is deciding when one should be created. Consider the following stock movements for product BR01:

On August 18, Amazon sent 1,500 units of the product to the warehouse. Over the following days, the warehouse processed outbound operations of 300 units per day.

Figure 3. Inbound and Outbound Movements List.

After each outbound operation, the available inventory becomes:

1,500 → 1,200 → 900 → 600 → 300 → 0

If this consumption pattern continues, the warehouse will completely run out of BR01 on the fifth outbound operation.

A common way to automate this process is to define a minimum stock threshold. For example, whenever fewer than 500 units are available, a replenishment request could be created:

This is a perfectly reasonable rule. Once the inventory reaches 300 units, the WMS detects that the stock is below the threshold (500) and requests more products.

However, consider that the depositor takes, on average, 7 days to deliver new products to the warehouse. If we wait until the stock falls below 500 units, the request may come too late, and the warehouse may run out of BR01 before the new shipment arrives.

We can account for this by adding the remaining days of stock to the decision:

Now the WMS can react to  low stock while also anticipating replenishment when the remaining inventory is not enough to cover the depositor's delivery lead time.

These are deterministic rules, and they work well when the decision can be clearly expressed through known conditions and calculations. As the business evolves, however, new rules and exceptions may continue to appear.

At some point, the challenge is no longer just adding another condition.

When the decision becomes contextual

The problem becomes more interesting when deciding what to do requires more than evaluating a predefined condition. Let's go back to the same example.

Amazon sent 1,500 units of BR01, and the warehouse has been shipping 300 units per day. After three days, only 600 units remain.

Using the rule we created earlier, the calculation is straightforward:

  • Current inventory: 600 units

  • Recent consumption: 300 units per day

  • Remaining stock: 2 days

  • Amazon lead time: 7 days

Since two days of stock are not enough to cover a seven-day lead time, our code will create a replenishment request.

But consider two different situations:

  1. Scenario A: The recent consumption of 300 units per day is part of the normal demand range for BR01. There is no indication that it will slow down. In this case, creating a replenishment request makes sense.

  2. Scenario B: The same 300-unit outbound operations came from a short promotion that has already ended. Previous movements show that BR01 typically consumes only around 50 units per day. In this case, immediately requesting the same replenishment may not be necessary.

Our deterministic rule sees the same values in both situations: 600 units in stock, 300 units of recent daily consumption, and a seven-day lead time, so it produces the same result.

But the situations are not the same.

To make a better decision, the system needs more context. It may need to inspect previous stock movements, understand whether the recent consumption represents the normal behavior of the product, retrieve relevant depositor policies, and then decide whether action is actually necessary.

This is where an AI agent starts to add value.

The agent does not replace deterministic operations such as inventory calculations, validations, persistence, or the creation of a replenishment request. Those operations remain regular application logic.

Instead, the agent can use controlled tools to look beyond the values used by the fixed rule. It can inspect previous stock movements, check pending replenishments, retrieve depositor policies, and gather additional information that helps explain the current situation.

The question is no longer only: Is the inventory below 500 units, or is the remaining stock not enough to cover the depositor's lead time?

It becomes: What does this situation actually mean, and do we need to act now?

That is the role of the agent in our WMS: gather the relevant information, understand the current situation, decide whether replenishment is necessary, and determine what should happen next,  while keeping well-defined business operations in deterministic code.

Where does the agent fit?

In our application, the agent enters the flow after an outbound operation is successfully completed. At that point, the inventory has already been updated, and the agent receives a goal:

Determine whether this outbound operation created a need for replenishment.

Before looking at the flow, it is useful to clarify what we mean by an AI agent.

In simple terms, an AI agent receives a goal, follows a set of instructions, interacts with the application through tools, observes the information it retrieves, and decides what to do next.

In our WMS, these elements have clear responsibilities:

  1. Goal: defines what the agent needs to accomplish. In this case, determine whether the completed outbound operation created a need for replenishment.

  2. Instructions: define how the agent should behave, what it should consider, and the boundaries it must respect.

  3. Tools: provide controlled access to the WMS. The agent can use them to inspect inventory and stock movements, retrieve depositor policies, check pending replenishments, or perform actions such as creating a replenishment request.

The important point is that the agent does not replace the existing WMS services or take control of the entire application. Inbound processing, outbound processing, inventory updates, validations, and persistence continue to be handled by regular Java code.

Instead, the agent acts as an orchestrator, deciding which available tools to use based on the goal and the context it gathers.

The following diagram shows where the agent becomes part of the WMS flow:

Figure 4. AI agent architecture for automated replenishment.

The diagram may look like a sequence of steps, but this is not a traditional hard-coded workflow where the application defines every decision in advance.

The application defines the agent's configuration, instructions, boundaries, and available tools. Within those boundaries, the agent determines what information it needs, uses the results it collects as context, decides whether action is necessary, and determines what should happen next.

For one outbound operation, the agent may conclude that replenishment is required and create a request. For another, after analyzing the available context, it may decide that no action is necessary.

This is an important distinction: the WMS controls what the agent is allowed to do, while the agent is responsible for deciding what to do within those boundaries.

Once the outbound invoice is completed, the OUTBOUND_INVOICE_COMPLETED event triggers the agent. From there, the workflow can be summarized in four steps:

  1. Plan: Based on the goal, instructions, and available capabilities, the agent determines what information and actions may be required.

  2. Analyze: The agent uses read-only tools to inspect information such as inventory, stock movements, pending replenishments, and depositor policies.

  3. Decide: Using the information collected, the agent determines whether replenishment is actually necessary.

  4. Act: If action is required, the agent can use controlled tools to create the replenishment request and prepare the depositor notification. If no action is required, the workflow ends without changing anything.

Conclusion

In this first part, we focused on where an AI agent can add value inside a Warehouse Management System and, just as importantly, where it should not replace deterministic application logic.

In Part 2, we will translate this design into Java and Spring AI by defining the agent, connecting it to the WMS workflow, and creating its execution plan.

Then, in Part 3, we will see how the agent executes those tasks using controlled tools, gathers the necessary context, makes the replenishment decision, and acts when required.

The complete source code is available here.

event_model_payload.headline: Build AI-Powered Applications with MongoDB Atlas in Grok Build
event_model_payload.summary:
The rise of AI agents has fundamentally changed how software is built, with agentic platforms like Grok Build redefining the unit of software work. Instead of asking an AI assistant for a function, a developer or architect gives an autonomous agent a goal, constraints, a codebase, and a definition of done. The agent researches, proposes a plan, edits files, runs tests, and iterates. The goal is not human approval of every keystroke; it is human ownership at consequential decision points, with agents handling mechanical work and humans supplying judgment.

This tutorial shows how to combine that workflow with MongoDB Atlas as the operational database, memory layer, and retrieval engine for a small knowledge assistant.

The workflow is portable: usePlan Mode and Agent mode, or planning/build loop in Grok Build. Keep the application artifacts rules, specs, tests, seed data, and deployment files in Git so either builder (i.e., the human developer or the AI agent) can work from the same source of truth.

Why choose Grok Build for agentic development?

A modern coding agent can inspect a repository, find related files, propose multi-file changes, run terminal commands, and use external tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). That makes the developer less of a line-by-line typist and more of an architect, reviewer, and test designer.

Grok Build is compelling because it combines an IDE-native workflow with persistent project context. Its project rules live in .grok/rules, where teams can version-control conventions, commands, and architectural constraints. Its Plan Mode researches the codebase, asks clarifying questions, creates a reviewable implementation plan, and waits for approval before building. That separation is valuable for AI applications, where an apparently small feature can touch schemas, indexes, prompts, APIs, security, and deployment.

The practical reason to choose Grok Build is control. You can inspect diffs as the agent works, constrain the files it should touch, require tests before implementation, and connect MCP servers without leaving the editor. The agent supplies speed; Git, rules, plans, tests, and human approval supply the guardrails. 

See Grok Build (Cursor) Plan Mode and Grok Build (Cursor) Rules for the current workflow and configuration model.

How MongoDB Atlas powers today’s agentic AI applications

An agent needs more than an LLM. It needs durable conversation state, user and tenant boundaries, tool results, business records, documents, and fast retrieval. MongoDB Atlas brings those workloads together in a document model, so an application can keep operational data and AI context close to one another instead of synchronizing multiple specialized stores.

MongoDB Atlas Vector Search lets developers retrieve semantically related content from MongoDB collections. It can support retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), long-term memory, recommendations, and tool context, while ordinary MongoDB queries still handle exact filters and transactional reads. This combination matters: an agent can find “refund policy for annual plans” semantically, then apply an exact tenant or product filter before the LLM sees the result.

MongoDB Atlas is also designed for the realities of production: managed clusters, database access controls, indexes, backups, observability, and deployment across major clouds.

A particularly useful simplification is Automated Embedding. Atlas can generate and maintain embeddings for a configured text field using a Voyage AI model, including at index time and query time. That reduces custom embedding workers and synchronization code. Choose voyage-4 for a balanced general-purpose default, voyage-4-lite for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads, or a code-focused Voyage model for technical content when available in your Atlas configuration.

Read MongoDB Automated Embedding and MongoDB AI Integrations before selecting the exact model and index options exposed in your region and Atlas project.

The joint value proposition: MongoDB Atlas and Grok Build

Grok Build helps developers turn intent into a tested code change, MongoDB Atlas turns that code into a data-aware AI application with one place for documents, memory, metadata, and vector retrieval.

Figure 1. MongoDB Atlas connects SpaceXSI’s agentic coding workflow in use.

Together, they shorten the path from prompt to production: Grok Build can inspect the repository and call Atlas tools through MCP, while Atlas supplies managed data services, Vector Search, Automated Embedding, and access controls. The developer stays in a tight plan-build-test loop instead of stitching together a separate database, vector store, embedding pipeline, and infrastructure script.

The MongoDB Atlas Managed MCP Server and agent skills with Grok Build

The MongoDB Atlas Managed MCP Server functions as the critical integration layer, empowering Grok Build agents to move beyond speculative code generation and directly interact with your Atlas deployments.

This server equips coding agents with over 40 specialized tools categorized into three primary domains:

By default, the Atlas Managed MCP Server runs read-only; destructive or billable operations like insert/update/delete require an explicit opt-in. A self-managed (local) MCP Server is different — it allows writes by default, so set --readOnly (or MDB_MCP_READ_ONLY=true) if you want the same safety net. See MongoDB MCP Server Configuration Options for the full defaults.

The official MongoDB Grok Build Plugin bundles the MongoDB MCP Server and pre-built MongoDB agent skills. Install it from Grok Build’s Marketplace by opening the command palette or Settings, searching for “MongoDB,” and following the prompts. You can also install it from the Agent input with:

After installation, pick the right connection for your setup. Choose the MongoDB Atlas managed connection when the plugin offers it and authorize your Atlas organization and project — Atlas handles authentication for you. For a self-managed server, point Grok Build's MCP settings at your own instance and connection string (SCRAM-SHA-256 by default, with OIDC, LDAP, Kerberos, and X.509 also supported). Follow MongoDB MCP Server Get Started and MongoDB MCP Server Configuration Options for client- and auth-specific setup.

Authenticate your Atlas account by following the instructions below:

Every tool remains active initially; however, you can adjust these settings or refresh the environment to suit specific requirements.

Use a development project, least-privilege roles, and environment-managed secrets. A connection string supports database access; Atlas-specific cluster management requires appropriately scoped service-account credentials. The developer still approves billable, destructive, or production changes.

Start with discovery rather than guessing project IDs:

Upon confirming the configuration, this tutorial utilizes a dedicated M10 cluster as the primary deployment resource.

Query and interact with MongoDB Atlas using natural language

Configure or inspect Vector Search index:

To inspect or create the vector search index using Automated Embedding, run:

Run a vector search test:

This keeps Grok Build close to live Atlas context while preserving human approval for mutations and infrastructure.

The detailed steps to create your first agentic application with MongoDB Atlas and SpaceXAI models using Grok Build are available here.

Why build with Grok Build and MongoDB Atlas?

MongoDB Atlas and Grok Build complement each other at the exact point where AI projects become real software. Grok Build accelerates exploration, implementation, and testing. Atlas supplies the durable application state, semantic retrieval, and managed operational foundation.

The result is not “AI-generated code” as an end in itself. It is a repeatable delivery loop: specify the architecture, provision a controlled data layer, seed realistic fixtures, evaluate behavior, build in small slices, and deploy with evidence. That is a practical way to move from an idea in a prompt to an AI application you can operate.

event_model_payload.headline: MongoDB.local London 2024: Better Applications, Faster
event_model_payload.summary:
Since we kicked off MongoDB’s series of 2024 events in April, we’ve connected with thousands of customers, partners, and community members in cities around the world—from Mexico City to Mumbai. Yesterday marked the nineteenth stop of the 2024 MongoDB.local tour, and we had a blast welcoming folks across industries to MongoDB.local London, where we discussed the latest technology trends, celebrated customer innovations, and unveiled product updates that make it easier than ever for developers to build next-gen applications.

Over the past year, MongoDB’s more than 50,000 customers have been telling us that their needs are changing. They’re increasingly focused on three areas:

  1. Helping developers build faster and more efficiently

  2. Empowering teams to create AI-powered applications

  3. Moving from legacy systems to modern platforms

Across these areas, there’s a common need for a solid foundation: each requires a resilient, scalable, secure, and highly performant database.

The updates we shared at MongoDB.local London reflect these priorities. MongoDB is committed to ensuring that our products are built to exceed our customers’ most stringent requirements, and that they provide the strongest possible foundation for building a wide range of applications, now and in the future.

Indeed, during yesterday’s event, Sahir Azam, MongoDB’s Chief Product Officer, discussed the foundational role data plays in his keynote address. He also shared the latest advancement from our partner ecosystem, an AI solution powered by MongoDB, Amazon Web Services, and Anthropic that makes it easier for customers to deploy gen AI customer care applications.

MongoDB 8.0: The best version of MongoDB ever

The biggest news at .local London was the general availability of MongoDB 8.0, which provides significant performance improvements, reduced scaling costs, and adds additional scalability, resilience, and data security capabilities to the world’s most popular document database.

Architectural optimizations in MongoDB 8.0 have significantly reduced memory usage and query times, and MongoDB 8.0 has more efficient batch processing capabilities than previous versions. Specifically, MongoDB 8.0 features 36% better read throughput, 56% faster bulk writes, and 20% faster concurrent writes during data replication. In addition, MongoDB 8.0 can handle higher volumes of time series data and can perform complex aggregations more than 200% faster—with lower resource usage and costs. Last (but hardly least!), Queryable Encryption now supports range queries, ensuring data security while enabling powerful analytics.

For more on MongoDB.local London’s product announcements—which are designed to accelerate application development, simplify AI innovation, and speed developer upskilling—please read on!

Accelerating application development

Improved scaling and elasticity on MongoDB Atlas capabilities

New enhancements to MongoDB Atlas’s control plane allow customers to scale clusters faster, respond to resource demands in real-time, and optimize performance—all while reducing operational costs.

First, our new granular resource provisioning and scaling features—including independent shard scaling and extended storage and IOPS on Azure—allow customers to optimize resources precisely where needed. Second, Atlas customers will experience faster cluster scaling with up to 50% quicker scaling times by scaling clusters in parallel by node type.

Finally, MongoDB Atlas users will enjoy more responsive auto-scaling, with a 5X improvement in responsiveness thanks to enhancements in our scaling algorithms and infrastructure. These enhancements are being rolled out to all Atlas customers, who should start seeing benefits immediately.

MongoDB Copilot Participant for VS Code (Public Preview)

Now in public preview, the new MongoDB Participant for GitHub Copilot integrates domain-specific AI capabilities directly with a chat-like experience in the MongoDB Extension for VS Code.

The participant is deeply integrated with the MongoDB extension, allowing for the generation of accurate MongoDB queries (and exporting them to application code), describing collection schemas, and answering questions with up-to-date access to MongoDB documentation without requiring the developer to leave their coding environment. These capabilities significantly reduce the need for context switching between domains, enabling developers to stay in their flow and focus on building innovative applications.

Multicluster support for the MongoDB Enterprise Kubernetes Operator

Ensure high availability, resilience, and scale for MongoDB deployments running in Kubernetes through added support for deploying MongoDB and Ops Manager across multiple Kubernetes clusters.

Users now have the ability to deploy ReplicaSets, Sharded Clusters (in public preview), and Ops Manager across local or geographically distributed Kubernetes clusters for greater deployment resilience, flexibility, and disaster recovery. This approach enables multi-site availability, resilience, and scalability within Kubernetes, capabilities that were previously only available outside of Kubernetes for MongoDB. To learn more, check out the documentation.

MongoDB Atlas Search and Vector Search are now generally available via the Atlas CLI and Docker

The local development experience for MongoDB Atlas is now generally available. Use the MongoDB Atlas CLI and Docker to build with MongoDB Atlas in your preferred local environment, and easily access features like Atlas Search and Atlas Vector Search throughout the entire software development lifecycle. The Atlas CLI provides a unified and familiar terminal-based interface that allows you to deploy and build with MongoDB Atlas in your preferred development environment, locally or in the cloud.

If you build with Docker, you can also now use Docker and Docker Compose to easily integrate Atlas in your local and continuous integration environments with the Atlas CLI. Avoid repetitive work by automating the lifecycle of your development and testing environments and focus on building application features with full-text search, AI and semantic search, and more.

Simplifying AI innovation

Reduce costs and increase scale in Atlas Vector Search

We announced vector quantization capabilities in Atlas Vector Search. By reducing memory (by up to 96%) and making vectors faster to retrieve, vector quantization allows customers to build a wide range of AI and search applications at higher scale and lower cost.

Generally available now, support for scalar quantized vector ingestion lets customers seamlessly import and work with quantized vectors from their embedding model providers of choice—directly in Atlas Vector Search. Coming soon, additional vector quantization features, including automatic quantization, will equip customers with a comprehensive toolset for building and optimizing large-scale AI and search applications in Atlas Vector Search.

Additional integrations with popular AI frameworks

Ship your next AI-powered project faster with MongoDB, no matter your framework or LLM of choice. AI technologies are advancing rapidly, making it important to build and scale performant applications quickly, and to use your preferred stack as your requirements and available technologies evolve.

MongoDB’s enhanced suite of integrations with LangChain, LlamaIndex, Microsoft Semantic Kernel, AutoGen, Haystack, Spring AI, the ChatGPT Retrieval Plugin, and more make it easier than ever to build the next generation of applications on MongoDB.

Advancing developer upskilling

New MongoDB Learning Badges

Faster to achieve and more targeted than a certification, MongoDB's free Learning Badges show your commitment to continuous learning and to proving your knowledge about a specific topic. Follow the learning path, gain new skills, and get a digital badge to show off on LinkedIn.

Check out the two new gen AI learning badges!

  • Building gen AI Apps: Learn to create innovative gen AI apps with Atlas Vector Search, including retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) apps.

  • Deploying and Evaluating gen AI Apps: Take your apps from creation to full deployment, focusing on optimizing performance and evaluating results.

Learn more

To learn more about MongoDB’s recent product announcements and updates, check out our What’s New product announcements page and all of our blog posts about product updates. Happy building!

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter: Durable Session Storage for Agents
event_model_payload.summary:
The Claude Agent SDK is a package that lets you embed Claude Code's own agent loop directly into your application: web search, file search, file editing, MCP server connections, and more, all without having to define those tools or manage the agent loop yourself. The SDK also automatically persists session transcripts to the local file system by default. Claude calls it the Agent SessionStore.

Today, we are excited to announce the MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter, available in Python (with TypeScript coming in January 2027).

What is the Claude Agent SessionStore?

But first, let's understand what a SessionStore actually is. It is the extension point in the Claude Agent SDK for saving an agent's session outside the machine where it ran. Configure one, and the SDK mirrors every conversation turn and action as the agent works, so the session can pick back up exactly where it left off, on any instance that has access to that store.

That matters most once an agent stops running on a single, persistent machine. Say a team deploys their Claude agent as a Lambda function, callable as an internal service by teams across the company. Every invocation is a disposable instance; there's no local disk to store anything between calls. Without a SessionStore, each request is stateless by default; the agent has no memory of what came before. With a configured SessionStore, any invocation can pick up a session's full history, regardless of which instance handled the last turn.

That is the gap the MongoDB Session Adapter closes.

This is especially useful for enterprises that have multiple teams developing agents across many machines, who need session storage that survives host failures, scales as the agent fleet increases, and enforces the same access controls and retention rules as the rest of their data estate, not a bolt-on system built solely for agent memory.

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter

The MongoDB Claude SDK Session Adapter gives Claude agents durable session storage: a record of the conversation and its action history that lets an agent pick back up exactly where it left off, whether that's on the same laptop, a different server, or any server in a distributed deployment.

The adapter helps cover three crucial areas:

  • Cross-environment continuity: Whether a different backend instance picks up a conversation after a restart or a user resumes on a different device, session state doesn't live on the machine that started it. Because every step is mirrored to MongoDB as it happens, any instance in your deployment can resume exactly where the last one left off.

  • Resilience to failure: If a host crashes or a container gets rescheduled mid-conversation, nothing is lost. Entries are written to MongoDB as they occur, not batched or cached locally, so whichever instance picks the session back up sees the same state as the failed one, up to the last completed step.

  • Retention and auditability: Many teams need to retain agent transcripts to meet internal data-retention or audit requirements. Instead of standing up a separate system just for that, session data lives in the MongoDB cluster you're already operating, under the same access controls and backup policies as the rest of your data.

How it works

This adapter implements the Claude Agent SDK's session storage interface directly, so you can mirror session transcripts to MongoDB in a few lines in ClaudeAgentOptions:

That's it. Every session started with these options is stored in MongoDB and can be resumed across machines. Each agent writes locally; MongoDB makes the conversation portable between app instances.

Figure 1. How the adapter allows you to access agent session transcripts mirrored in MongoDB.
