event_model_payload.headline: Modernize Your Insurance Data Models With MongoDB Relational Migrator
event_model_payload.summary:
In the 70s and 80s, there were few commercial off-the-shelf solutions available for many core insurance functions, so insurers had to build their own applications. Such applications are often host-based, meaning that they are mainframe technologies. These legacy platforms include software languages such as COBOL and CICS. Many insurers are still struggling to replace these legacy technologies due to a confluence of variables such as a lack of developers with programming skills in these older technologies and complicated insurance products. This results in high maintenance costs and difficulty in making changes. In brief, legacy systems are a barrier to progress in the insurance industry.

Whether you’re looking to maintain and improve existing applications or push new products and features to market, the data trapped inside those systems is a drag on innovation.

This is particularly true when we think about the data models that sit at the core of application systems (e.g., underwriting), defining entities and relationships between them.

In this tutorial, we will demonstrate:

  • Why the document model simplifies the data model of a standard insurance system.

  • How MongoDB's Relational Migrator effortlessly transforms an unwieldy 21-table schema into a lean five-collection MongoDB model.

This will ultimately prove that with MongoDB, insurers will launch new products faster, swiftly adapt to regulatory changes, and enhance customer experiences.

To do this, we will focus on the Object Management Group’s Party Role model and how the model can be ported from a relational structure to MongoDB’s document model.

Figure 1. OMG Property and Casualty Data Model, representing the major entities and their relationships.

In particular, we will describe the refactoring of Party in the context of Policy and Claim & Litigation. For each of them, a short description, a simplified Hackolade model (Entity Relationship Diagrams - ERD), and the document refactoring using Relational Migrator are provided.

Relational Migrator is a tool that allows you to:

  • Design an effective MongoDB schema, derived from an existing relational schema.

  • Migrate data from Oracle, SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, or Sybase ASE to MongoDB, while transforming to the target schema.

  • Generate code artifacts to reduce the time required to update application code.

At the end of this tutorial, you will have learned how to use Relational Migrator to refactor the Party Role relational data model and migrate the data into MongoDB collections.

Connect to Postgres and set up Relational Migrator

Prerequisites

  • MongoDB Relational Migrator (version 1.4.3 or higher): MongoDB Relational Migrator is a powerful tool to help you migrate relational workloads to MongoDB. Download and install the latest version.

  • PostgreSQL (version 15 or higher): PostgreSQL is a relational database management system. It will serve as the source database for our migration task. Download the last version of PostgreSQL.

  • MongoDB (version 7.0 or higher): You will need access to a MongoDB instance with write permissions to create the new database where we are going to migrate the data. You can install the latest version of the MongoDB Community Server or simply deploy a free MongoDB Atlas cluster in less than three minutes!

In this tutorial, we will use PostgreSQL as the RDBMS to hold the original tabular schema that will be migrated to MongoDB. To follow it, you will need access to a PostgreSQL database server instance with permission to create a new database and user. The instance may be in the cloud, on-prem, or on your local machine. You just need to know the URL, port, username, and password for the PostgreSQL instance you choose.

We will also use two PostgreSQL Client Applications: psql and pg_restore. These terminal-based applications will allow us to interact with our PostgreSQL database server instance. The first application, psql, enables you to type in queries interactively, issue them to PostgreSQL, and see the query results. It will be useful to create the database and run queries to verify that the schema has been successfully replicated. On the other hand, we will use pg_restore to restore the PostgreSQL database from the archive file available in the GitHub repository. This archive file contains all the tables, relationships, and sample data from the Party Role model in a tabular format. It will serve as the starting point in our data migration journey.

The standard ready-to-use packages will already include both the server and these client tools. We recommend using version 15 or higher. You can download it from the official PostgreSQL Downloads site or, if you are a macOS user, just run the command below in your terminal.

Note: Verify that Postgres database tools have been successfully installed by running `psql --version` and `pg_restore --version`. If you see an error message, make sure the containing directory of the tools is added to your `PATH`.

Replicate the Party Role model in PostgreSQL

First, we need to connect to the PostgreSQL database.

If it’s a newly installed local instance with the default parameters, you can use `127.0.0.1` as your host, `5432` as the port, `postgres` as the database, and type `whoami` in your terminal to get your default username if no other has been specified during the installation of the PostgreSQL database server.

Once you are connected, we need to create a database to load the data.

Then, we will create the user that will have access to the new database, so we don’t need to use the root user in the relational migrator. Please remember to change the password in the command below.

Finally, we will populate the database with the Party Role model, a standard widely used in the insurance industry to define how people, organizations, and groups are involved in agreements, policies, claims, insurable objects, and other major entities. This will not only replicate the table structure, relationships, and ownership, but it will also load some sample data.

  1. First, download the .tar file that contains the backup of the database.

  2. Navigate to the folder where the file is downloaded using your terminal.

  3. Run the command below in your terminal to load the data. Please remember to change the host, port, and user before executing the command.

After a few seconds, our new database will be ready to use. Verify the successful restore by running the command below:

You should see a list of 21 tables similar to the one in the figure below.

Figure 2. List of tables in the Party Role model.

If all looks good, you are ready to connect your data to MongoDB Relational Migrator.

Connect to Relational Migrator

Open the Relational Migrator app and click on the “New Project” button. We will start a new project from scratch by connecting to the database we just created. Click on “Connect database,” select “PostgreSQL” as the database type, and fill in the connection details. Test the connection before proceeding, and if the connection test is successful, click “Connect.” If a “no encryption” error is thrown, click on SSL → enable SSL.

Figure 3. Database connection in Relational Migrator.

In the next screen, select all 21 tables from the OMG schema and click “Next.” On this new screen, you will need to define your initial schema. We will start with a MongoDB schema that matches your relational schema. Leave the other options as default. Next, give the project a name and click “Done.”

This will generate a schema that matches the original one. That is, we will have one collection per table in the original schema. This is a good starting point, but as we have seen, one of the advantages of the document model is that it is able to reduce this initial complexity. To do so, we will take an object-modeling approach. We will focus on four top-level objects that will serve as the starting point to define the entire schema: Party, Policy, Claim, and Litigation.

By default, you will see a horizontal split view of the Relational (upper part) and MongoDB (lower part) model. You can change the view model from the bottom-left corner “View” menu. Please note that all the following steps in the tutorial will be done in the MongoDB view (MDB). Feel free to change the view mode to “MDB” for a more spacious working view.

Party domain

The Party Subject Area (Figure 4) shows that all persons, organizations, and groups can be represented as “parties,” and parties can then be related to other major objects with specified roles. The Party design also provides a common approach to describing communication identifiers, relationships between parties, and legal identifiers.

Figure 4. Party Subject Area.

To illustrate the process in a simpler and clearer way, we reduced the number of objects and built a new ERD in Relational Migrator (Figure 5). Such models are most often implemented in run-time transactional systems. Their impact and dependencies can be found across multiple systems and domains. Additionally, they can result in very large physical database objects, and centralized storage and access patterns can be bottlenecks.

Figure 5. Party Model tables.

The key Party entities are:

  • Party — represents people, organizations, and groups

  • Party Role — defines the role a party plays within a context:

    • Policy

    • Claim

    • Agreement

    • Litigation

    • Insurable Object

  • Communication Identity — generic representation of things like:

    • Address

    • Phone

    • Email

Party represents people, organizations, and groups. In the original schema, this is represented through one-to-one relationships. Party holds the common attributes for all parties, while each of the other three tables stores the particularities of each party class. These differences result in distinct fields for each class, which forces tabular schemas to create new tables. The inherent flexibility of the document model allows embedding this information in a single document. To do this, follow the steps below:

  • Select the "party" collection in the MDB view of Relational Migrator. At the moment, this collection has the same fields as the original matched table.

  • On the right-hand side, you will see the mappings menu (Figure 6). Click on the “Add” button, select “Embedded documents,” and choose "person" in the “Source table” dropdown menu. Click “Save and close” and repeat this process for the "organization" and "grouping" tables.

  • After this, you can remove the "person," "organization," and "grouping" collections.

  • Right-click on them, select “Remove Entity,” and confirm “Remove from the MongoDB model.” You have already simplified your original model by three tables, and we’re just getting started.

Figure 6. Party mapping menu.

Looking at Figure 5, we can see that there is another entity that could be easily embedded in the party collection: location addresses. In this case, this table has a many-to-many relationship facilitated by the "party_location_address" table. As a party can have many location addresses, instead of an embedded document, we will use an embedded array. You can do it in the following way:

  • Select the collection "party" again, click the “Add” button, select “Embedded array,” and choose "party_location_address" in the “Source table” dropdown. Under the “All fields” checkbox, uncheck the `partyIdentifier` field. We are not going to need it. Addresses will be contained in the “party” document anyway. Leave the other fields as default and click the “Save and close” button.

  • We have now established the relationship, but we want to have the address details too. From the “party” mapping menu, click the “Add” button again. Then, select “Embedded documents,” choose “location_address,” and in the “Root path” section, check the box that says “Merge fields into the parent.” This will ensure that we don’t have more nested fields than necessary. Click “Save and close.”

  • You can now delete the “party_location_address” collection, but don’t delete “location_address” as it still has an existing relationship with “insurable_object.”

You are done. The “party” entity is ready to go. We have not only reduced six tables to just one, but the “person,” “organization,” and “grouping” embedded documents will only show up if that party is indeed a person, organization, or grouping. One collection can contain documents with different schemas for each of these classes.

Figure 7. Document representation of the Party entity.

At the beginning of the section, we also spoke about the “party role” entity. It represents the role a party plays in a specific context such as policy, claim, or litigation. In the original schema, this many-to-many relationship is facilitated via intermediate tables like “policy_party_role,” “claim_party_role,” and “litigation_party_role” respectively. These intermediate tables will be embedded in other collections, but the “party_role” table can be left out as a reference collection on its own. In this way, we avoid having to update one by one all policy, claim, and litigation documents if one of the attributes of “party role” changes.

Figure 8. Document representation of the PartyRole entity.

Let’s see next how we can model the “policy” entity.

Policy domain

The key entities of Policy are:

  • Insurable Object — an object insured by a policy agreement

  • Insurable Object Party Role — associative entity which links:

    • Party

    • The role the Party plays

    • Insurable Objects

  • Agreement Party role — associative entity which links:

    • Party

    • The role the Party plays

    • Agreement (which is related to a product and policy)

Figure 9. Party in the context of Policy tables.

From a top-level perspective, we can observe that the “policy” entity is composed of policy coverage parts and the agreements of each of the parties involved with their respective roles. A policy can have several parts to cover and several parties' agreements involved. Therefore, similarly to what happened with party location addresses, they will be matched to array embeddings.

Let’s start with the party agreements. A policy may have many parties involved, and each party may be part of many policies. This results in a many-to-many relationship facilitated by the “policy_party_role” table. This table also covers the relationships between roles and agreements, as each party will play a role and will have an agreement in a specific policy.

  • From the MDB view, select the “policy” collection. Click on the “Add” button, select “embedded array,” and choose “policy_party_role” in the source table dropdown. Uncheck the `policyIdentifier` field, leave the other fields as default, and click “Save and close.”

  • We will leave the party as a referenced object to the “party” collection we created earlier, so we don’t need to take any further action on this. The relationship remains in the new model through the `partyIdentifier` field acting as a foreign key. However, we need to include the agreements. From the “policy” mapping menu, click “Add,” select “Embedded document,” pick “agreement” as the source table, leave the other options as default, and click “Save and close.” 

  • At this point, we can remove the collections “policy_party_role” and “agreement.” Remember that we have defined “party_role” as a separate reference collection, so just having `partyRoleCode` as an identifier in the destination table will be enough.

Next, we will include the policy coverage parts.

  • From the “policy” mapping menu, click “Add,” select “Embedded array,” pick “policy_coverage_part” as the source table, uncheck the `policyIdentifier` field, leave the other options as default, and click “Save and close.”

  • Each coverage part has details included in the “policy_coverage_detail”. We will add this as an embedded array inside of each coverage part. In the “policy” mapping menu, click “Add,” select “Embedded array,” pick “policy_coverage_detail,” and make sure that the prefix selected in the “Root path” section is `policyCoverageParts`. Remove `policyIdentifier` and `coveragePartCode` fields and click “Save and close.”

  • Coverage details include “limits,” “deductibles,” and “insurableObjects.” Let’s add them in! Click “Add” in the “policy” mapping menu, “Embedded Array,” pick “policy_limit,” remove the `policyCoverageDetailIdentifier`, and click “Save and close.” Repeat the process for “policy_deductible.” For “insurable_object,” repeat the process but select “Embedded document” instead of “Embedded array.”

  • As you can see in Figure 9, insurable objects have additional relationships to specify the address and roles played by the different parties. To add them, we just need to embed them in the same fashion we have done so far. Click “Add” in the “policy” mapping menu, select “Embedded array,” and pick “insurable_object_party_role.” This is the table used to facilitate the many-to-many relationship between insurable objects and party roles. Uncheck `insurableObjectIdentifier` and click “Save and close.” Party will be referenced by the `partyIdentifier` field. For the sake of simplicity, we won’t embed address details here, but remember in a production environment, you would need to add it in a similar way as we did before in the “party” collection.

  • After this, we can safely remove the collections “policy_coverage_part,” “policy_coverage_detail,” “policy_deductible,” and “policy_limit.”

By now, we should have a collection similar to the one below and five fewer tables than in our original model.

Figure 10. Document representation of the Policy entity.

Claim & litigation domain

Figure 11. Party in context of Claim & Litigation Hackolade model.

The key entities of Claim and Litigation are:

  • Claim — claim for coverage or compensation

  • Litigation — claim litigation 

  • Claim Party Role — associative entity which links:

    • Party

    • The role the Party plays

    • Insurable Objects

  • Litigation Party Role - associative entity which links:

    • Claim

    • The role the Party plays

    • Insurable Objects

  • Insurable Object Party Role - associative entity which links:

    • Party

    • The role the Party plays

    • Insurable Objects

In this domain, we have already identified the two main entities: claim and litigation. We will use them as top-level documents to refactor the relationships shown in Figure 10 in a more intuitive way. Let’s see how you can model claims first.

  • We’ll begin embedding the parties involved in a claim with their respective roles. Select “claim” collection, click “Add” in the mapping menu, select “Embedded array,” and pick “claim_party_role” as the source table. You can uncheck `claimIdentifier` from the field list. Lastly, click the “Save and close” button.

  • Next, we will integrate the insurable object that is part of the claim. Repeat the previous step, but choose “Embedded documents” as the table migration option and “insurable_object” as the source table. Again, we will not embed the “location_address” entity to keep it simple.

  • Within insurableObject, we will include the policy coverage details establishing the link between claims and policies. Add a new mapping, select “Embedded array,” choose “policy_coverage_detail” as the source table, and uncheck the field insurableObjectIdentifier. Leave the other options as default.

  • Lastly, we will recreate the many-to-many relationship between litigation and claim. As we will have a separate litigation entity, we just need to reference that entity from the claims document, which means that just having an array of litigation identifiers will be enough. Repeat the previous step by selecting “Embedded array,” “litigation_party_role,” and unchecking all fields except `litigationIdentifier` in the field list.

Figure 12. Document representation of the Claim entity.

The claim model is ready to go. We can now remove the collection “claimPartyRole.”

Let’s continue with the litigation entity. Litigations may have several parties involved, each playing a specific role and with a particular associated claim. This relationship is facilitated through the “litigation_party_role” collection. We will represent it using an embedded array. Additionally, we will include some fields in the claim domain apart from its identifier. This is necessary so we can have a snapshot of the claim details at the time the litigation was made, so even if the claim details change, we won’t lose the original claim data associated with the litigation. To do so, follow the steps below:

  • From the “litigation” mapping menu, click on the “Add” button, select “Embedded array,” and pick “litigation_party_role” as the source table. Remove `litigationIdentifier` from the field list and click “Save and Close.” 

  • In a similar way, add claim details by adding “claim” as an “Embedded document.” 

  • Repeat the process again, but choose “insurable_object” as the source table for the embedded document. Make sure the root path prefix is set to `litigationPartyRoles.claim`.

  • Finally, add “insurable_object_party_role” as an “Embedded array.” The root path prefix should be `litigationPartyRoles.claim.insurableObject`.

Figure 13. Document representation of the Litigation entity.

And that’s it. We have modeled the entire relationship schema in just five collections: “party,” “partyRole,” “policy,” “claim,” and “litigation.” You can remove the rest of the collections and compare the original tabular schema composed of 21 tables to the resulting five collections.

Migrate your data to MongoDB

Now that our model is complete, we just need to migrate the data to our MongoDB instance. First, verify that you have “dbAdmin” permissions in the destination OMG database. You can check and update permissions from the Atlas left-side security menu in the “Database Access” section.

Figure 14. New Migration Job, Connect Source DB menu.

Once this is done, navigate to the “Data Migration” tab in the top navigation bar and click “Create sync job.” You will be prompted to add the source and destination database details. In our case, these are PostgreSQL and MongoDB, respectively. Fill in the details and click “Connect” in both steps until you get to the “Migration Options” step. In this menu, we will leave all options as default. This will migrate our data in snapshot mode, which means it will load all our data at once. Feel free to check our documentation for more sync job alternatives.

Figure 15. New migration job, migration options menu.

Finally, click the “Start” button and wait until the migration is complete. This can take a couple of minutes. Once ready, you will see the “Completed” tag in the snapshot state card. You can now connect to your database in MongoDB Atlas or Compass and check how all your data is now loaded in MongoDB, ready to leverage all the advantages of the document model.

Figure 16. Successful migration job message.

Additional resources

Congratulations, you’ve just completed your data migration! We've not just simplified the data model of a standard insurance system; we've significantly modernized how information flows in the industry.

On the technical side, MongoDB's Relational Migrator truly is a game-changer, effortlessly transforming an unwieldy 21-table schema into a lean five-collection MongoDB model. This translates to quicker, more efficient data operations, making it a dream for developers and administrators alike.

On the business side, imagine the agility gained—faster time-to-market for new insurance products, swift adaptation to regulatory changes, and enhanced customer experiences.

The bottom line? MongoDB's document model and Relational Migrator aren't just tools; they're the catalysts for a future-ready, nimble insurance landscape.

event_model_payload.headline: How MongoDB Fits into the EU Sovereign Cloud Ecosystem
event_model_payload.summary:
The question of what the term “sovereign cloud” means in Europe has moved from policy debates to formal European Commission (EC) procurement frameworks and industrial investments. The Cloud Sovereignty Framework (CSF), Sovereignty Effectiveness Assurance Levels (SEAL), and the developing EU Cybersecurity Certification Scheme for Cloud Services (EUCS) are separate initiatives that provide distinct reference points. Alongside strategic capital mobilization under the Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform (STEP), they establish a clearer direction for critical cloud infrastructure. While specific to EU institutional tenders and funding programs rather than acting as universal mandates, this combined momentum offers IT leaders and enterprise architects across regulated sectors a concrete reference point for how sovereignty criteria shape long-term architectural thinking. These developments help illustrate that operating in a regulated market does not mean every workload must remain on-premises; instead, they demonstrate that sovereignty is a spectrum, helping organizations evaluate the specific level of data control their architecture truly requires.

As organizations evaluate these models, the critical question is not just which infrastructure provider can meet tech sovereignty expectations, but whether the rest of the technology stack upholds that sovereignty posture once workloads are deployed. This is where the database layer becomes a critical consideration, and where MongoDB provides key capabilities to define who has operational custody of data and how seamlessly workloads adapt to evolving governance requirements.

In April 2026, the European Commission awarded sovereign-cloud contracts under the Cloud III Dynamic Purchasing System and used SEAL-2 and SEAL-3 as practical reference points in its CSF for that procurement. This provides a concrete example of how sovereignty-related criteria can be evaluated in an EC-level procurement context. It also raises a practical architectural question: if sovereign-cloud requirements are being evaluated against the CSF as a benchmark, what does that mean for the rest of the technology stack, and especially for the database tier?

This overview examines the potential implications of the awarded landscape, the operational relevance of SEAL-2 and SEAL-3*, and how MongoDB deployment models can support different architectural approaches for organizations to evaluate against their own requirements.

Why the new procurement benchmark matters

The Commission selected several European provider groups for this initiative. These included:

  1. Post Telecom (headquartered in Luxembourg), working alongside OVHcloud and CleverCloud (both based in France).

  2. STACKIT, the cloud division of Schwarz Group, based in Germany.

  3. Scaleway, the cloud arm of Iliad Group, based in France.

  4. Proximus, based in Belgium, partnered with S3NS (a joint venture of Thales and Google Cloud in France), Clarence (Luxembourg), and Mistral (France).

As published in the European Commission’s report under reference IP/26/833, three of the four awarded groups achieved the reported assessment level of SEAL-3, while the Proximus consortium attained SEAL-2. The Proximus result of SEAL-2 is an assessed level within the CSF, not a failed outcome; the consortium’s remaining non-EU dependencies distinguished it from the groups assessed at SEAL-3. Together, these results show that the procurement considered a range of sovereignty postures rather than a simple pass-or-fail threshold, and may help inform future market expectations around sovereignty-driven infrastructure and digital resilience.

In environments governed by frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), and the Network and Information Systems Directive 2 (NIS2), where requirements vary by organization and industry, engineering teams face concrete design priorities: mitigating ICT third-party concentration risk, establishing tested exit strategies, or enforcing granular boundaries over data access and telemetry. The CSF evaluation offers technical leaders a reference point for examining these operational dependencies, informing technical due diligence across database tiers and multi-cloud strategies without prescribing a single deployment model or replacing organization-specific legal analysis.

The challenge: infrastructure certification does not cover the full stack

Using cloud infrastructure assessed in the European Commission’s procurement event addresses only part of the broader sovereignty discussion and does not automatically answer questions about every layer of the technology stack. The relevant considerations can include data residency, service operation, metadata flows, external control-plane dependencies, encryption, access controls, and workload portability if requirements or risk posture change.

The database tier is particularly important in a broader data-sovereignty assessment because it stores, processes, and governs access to the data itself. An infrastructure-focused assessment such as the CSF evaluation can provide useful information about the underlying cloud environment, but it does not by itself characterize the database service’s data paths, plaintext exposure, key management, backups, logs and metadata, support and control-plane dependencies, or workload portability.

Regulatory frameworks such as the US CLOUD Act (Clarifying Lawful Overseas Use of Data Act, enacted in 2018) have heightened enterprise sovereignty concerns over access to data held by providers subject to foreign jurisdiction under applicable legal processes, illustrating why physical data residency alone does not establish operational or jurisdictional control. One practical question is therefore not whether a platform carries a universal “sovereignty” label, but which controls and operating boundaries an organization must evaluate for its own environment. Variables such as control-plane dependencies, cross-region support access, cloud provider corporate jurisdiction, and cryptographic key custody must be individually assessed based on the organization's unique requirements. An organization may adopt cloud infrastructure aligned with SEAL-3 expectations and still find that database-layer telemetry, external support paths, or unencrypted metadata introduce unintended exposures. The infrastructure assessment and the database governance posture remain separate engineering challenges that require independent validation.

MongoDB's three roles in the European sovereign cloud ecosystem

MongoDB serves three distinct roles in the European sovereign cloud ecosystem when viewed through the lens of the European Commission’s CSF. MongoDB’s flexible document model and query API can remain consistent across deployment models, while the operating model, responsibilities, data flows, access controls, and contractual arrangements may differ.

Figure 1. MongoDB deployment modes.

Role one: DBaaS on SEAL-3 sovereign clouds

In this model, a European cloud provider—such as STACKIT, OVHcloud, or Scaleway—operates a MongoDB database service under its own brand, infrastructure, and legal entity. MongoDB supplies the database engine, compatibility guarantees, and technical support framework, while responsibility for operating the service remains with the European provider.

Because the European provider operates the service, it is the entity with operational custody of customer data in this model. MongoDB is a software supplier and does not have operational custody of customer data on the European-operated service. All three provider groups that achieved SEAL 3 for the purposes of the April 2026 EC procurement event include a MongoDB Certified DBaaS partner. For organizations seeking sovereign cloud environments aligned with SEAL-3-style expectations, MongoDB is already available through those partnerships, without workarounds, unsupported deployments, or vendor substitution.

However, architecture teams must carefully evaluate the specific database edition offered by each sovereign cloud provider. Managed offerings in the European ecosystem typically fall into two categories: DBaaS based on MongoDB Community Server and DBaaS powered by MongoDB Enterprise Server, which is the engine underlying Enterprise Advanced. While both editions share the same flexible document model and core query API, they differ significantly in built-in operational capabilities. Community Server provides core database functionality, but achieving enterprise-grade security and operational maturity requires teams to build and manage custom configurations for auditing, access controls, and maintenance. In contrast, DBaaS powered by Enterprise Server delivers turnkey features, including native enterprise auditing, advanced authentication integration, and enhanced operational tooling, representing the closest functional equivalent to MongoDB Atlas in a self-contained or sovereign environment.

Availability of these editions varies across the European market. Currently, European providers like STACKIT and OVHcloud, alongside providers like IONOS, offer DBaaS backed by Enterprise Server, whereas Scaleway provides managed Community Server with enterprise-grade offerings currently in development. Selecting the appropriate provider therefore depends on whether a given workload requires these out-of-the-box enterprise capabilities or can be supported through community-tier deployments.

Role two: MongoDB Atlas with sovereignty controls

MongoDB Atlas is a multi-cloud intelligent data platform with availability across Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Atlas provides data placement controls; Resource Policies can restrict cluster creation to approved EU regions, and zone-based sharding can support regional data placement, subject to the workload’s shard key and application design.

For encryption, MongoDB Atlas supports Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) integration with cloud provider key management services, which can keep encryption keys outside MongoDB’s direct control. Atlas also supports Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE) and Queryable Encryption (QE), which encrypt sensitive fields on the client side before data reaches the database. MongoDB cannot access plaintext for those protected fields during supported query operations.

BYOK, CSFLE, and Queryable Encryption (QE) can materially reduce data-layer disclosure risks by preventing unauthorized or platform-level access to plaintext data. However, the effective protection boundary depends on the key-management model, query capabilities, and whether sensitive metadata remains exposed.

Certified DBaaS and Enterprise Advanced are alternative deployment models to evaluate for workloads where data sovereignty and encryption considerations are material. The appropriate choice depends on the organization’s technical, contractual, operational, and legal requirements.

Role three: MongoDB Enterprise Advanced for maximum jurisdictional control

MongoDB Enterprise Advanced (EA) is a commercial subscription that grants organizations the right to run MongoDB on their own infrastructure: on-premises, in a private cloud, on a sovereign provider’s dedicated environment, or in an air-gapped facility. MongoDB does not operate the customer’s clusters and, in this model, does not have operational custody of customer data at rest.

The infrastructure operator remains responsible for the environment in which the clusters run. How access to customer data and any legal or regulatory request would be handled depends on the applicable law, contractual arrangements, and the specific operating model; the relevant custody and control analysis therefore focuses on the entity operating that infrastructure rather than treating MongoDB as the infrastructure operator.

Enterprise Advanced preserves the same document model and core query semantics as MongoDB Atlas, supporting strong application-level portability across deployment models. Organizations can typically move regulated workloads from Atlas to EA while preserving the application data layer and most core query logic, which can reduce redesign effort and support portability, exit planning, and concentration-risk evaluation. The relevance of these capabilities to any particular regulatory framework depends on the organization’s specific requirements and legal and operational analysis.

Aligning the deployment model to your sovereignty requirements

The three MongoDB deployment models offer different combinations of deployment location, operational control, data access, encryption, and portability, which organizations can evaluate against their own data or technology sovereignty-related requirements.

For organizations evaluating technical, contractual, operational, or procurement requirements associated with SEAL-3-style sovereign infrastructure, the Certified Database as a Service (DBaaS) path provides MongoDB capability through a European provider, previously assessed at SEAL-3 in the Commission’s April 2026 procurement.

For organizations evaluating a US-operated managed cloud service with technical controls, MongoDB Atlas with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), Client-Side Field Level Encryption (CSFLE), and Queryable Encryption (QE) can provide data-layer protections relevant to that assessment.

For organizations evaluating greater direct jurisdictional control, air-gapped operation, or self-managed deployment on sovereign or private cloud infrastructure, Enterprise Advanced preserves the same core document model and query semantics as Atlas and supports application portability without requiring MongoDB to operate the customer’s clusters. Depending on the deployment environment, it can also support customer-managed infrastructure and avoid dependency on a public cloud service, with no MongoDB operational custody of customer data at rest.

A practical advantage is that these three models are not mutually exclusive. An enterprise may evaluate a mixed deployment approach, such as using Atlas for standard workloads in EU-approved regions, Certified DBaaS for higher-sensitivity workloads, and Enterprise Advanced for classified or air-gapped workloads, while application-layer portability and governance requirements may vary by tier.

Final thoughts

Europe’s sovereign cloud ecosystem now includes an example of a formal assessment used in the European Commission’s procurement, four Commission-selected reference providers, and other national frameworks applicable in specific member states. These developments may be relevant to how regulated organizations evaluate cloud infrastructure over the coming years.

MongoDB is present at the database tier through Certified DBaaS partnerships with providers that have been assessed at SEAL-3 in the Commission’s April 2026 procurement, available with technical controls on managed cloud through MongoDB Atlas, and deployable in customer-managed environments through Enterprise Advanced. Each deployment model presents different technical, contractual, and operational characteristics for organizations to evaluate against their own requirements. Each preserves the same core document model and query semantics, which may help reduce redesign effort when moving workloads across deployment models.

*Within the CSF, the SEAL levels range from SEAL-0 to SEAL-4 and describe varying degrees of EU jurisdiction and control over legal, operational, and supply-chain dependencies. At SEAL-2 (Data Sovereignty), EU law is enforceable, though some material non-EU dependencies persist. SEAL-3 (Digital Resilience), assesses whether relevant non-EU dependencies have been reduced to marginal levels under the CSF. SEAL-4 (Full Digital Sovereignty), represents the theoretical goal of complete EU control without critical dependencies on non-EU entities, a standard no provider has reached so far. These descriptions refer to the CSF framework and the assessment made in the Commission’s procurement context; they do not prescribe what any particular organization must do.

Disclaimer

This content is for informational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. Regulatory requirements vary by jurisdiction and industry. Organizations should consult qualified legal counsel and their internal compliance teams to understand their specific obligations.

event_model_payload.headline: 대AI시대에 일하는 방식의 변화에 대한 고찰
event_model_payload.summary:
1인 1작업에서 1인 N작업으로, 병목이 코딩에서 판단으로 옮겨간 시대에 일하는 방식은 어떻게 달라지는가

들어가며

무신사 물류플랫폼팀에서 백엔드를 개발하고 있습니다.

먼저 밝혀두자면, 무언가를 가르치거나 교훈을 전하려는 목적은 없습니다.
AI 코딩 에이전트와 본격적으로 일하기 시작한 뒤 제 일하는 방식이 어떻게 바뀌었고 어디에서 넘어졌는지, 그래서 지금은 어떤 방식으로 일하는지를 돌아보는 글에 가깝습니다.

저도 아직 이 방식이 맞는지 의심하는 중입니다.

요즘 제 모니터에는 터미널 창이 여러 개 떠 있습니다.
각 창에서는 서로 다른 작업을 맡은 에이전트가 돌고 있고, 저는 그 사이를 오가며 결과를 읽고, 승인하고, 다음 지시를 내립니다.
몇 년 전의 저라면 이 화면을 보고 “저렇게 하면 하나도 제대로 못 끝낸다”고 했을 겁니다.

실제로 그때는 그 말이 맞았습니다.

이 글은 세 가지 질문을 따라갑니다.
왜 예전에는 한 번에 하나만 했는가.
무엇이 바뀌어서 지금은 여러 개를 동시에 굴리게 됐는가.
그리고 사람은 어디까지 따라갈 수 있는가.

왜 우리는 한 번에 하나만 했을까

돌이켜보면 1인 1작업은 규칙이라기보다 물리 법칙에 가까웠습니다.

첫째, 코딩 자체가 병목이었습니다.
설계하고, 코드를 작성하고, 테스트를 돌리고, 리뷰를 받는 흐름의 속도는 결국 제가 직접 작업하는 속도에 묶여 있었습니다.
두 작업을 동시에 잡으면 둘 다 눈에 띄게 느려졌습니다.

둘째, 컨텍스트 스위칭 비용이 컸습니다.
브랜치를 옮기면 머릿속도 같이 리셋됐습니다.
어디까지 봤는지, 왜 이렇게 고치려 했는지를 다시 떠올리는 데 시간이 들었습니다.
그래서 IDE 하나, 워킹 트리 하나, 브랜치 하나가 자연스러운 상태였습니다.
스프린트에서도 티켓을 하나 잡아 끝낸 뒤 다음으로 넘어갔습니다.

한 번에 하나에 집중하는 것이 미덕이었던 이유는 간단합니다.
제가 직접 생산해야 했기 때문입니다.
생산자가 한 명이면 생산 라인도 사실상 하나였습니다.

무엇이 바뀌었나: 기다림이 병렬을 불렀다

계기는 거창하지 않았습니다.
에이전트에게 작업을 맡기면 몇 분씩 돌아갑니다.
그동안 저는 화면을 멍하니 보고 있었고, 그 시간이 아까웠습니다.
그래서 다른 터미널을 열고 다른 작업을 시켰습니다.
마침 동시에 처리해야 할 요청이 몰리던 시기였고, 어차피 밀린 일은 많았습니다.

그게 굳어져 지금의 형태가 됐습니다.
요즘 제 아침은 대개 이렇게 시작합니다.
git worktree로 갈라둔 작업 디렉터리마다 tmux 창을 하나씩 열고, 각 창의 Claude Code 세션에 서로 다른 기능을 맡깁니다.
한 세션에서는 조사와 구현을 서브에이전트로 나눠 동시에 돌립니다.
변경이 끝난 세션의 테스트와 자동 코드 리뷰는 백그라운드로 넘기고, 저는 다른 창으로 옮겨갑니다.
코드 창 옆에는 인프라 설정을 만지는 창과 위키나 티켓을 정리하는 창이 나란히 떠 있는 날이 많습니다.

이 그림에서 제 역할의 중심은 생산 라인 위의 작성자에서 여러 라인을 조율하는 관제사로 옮겨갑니다.
두 방식을 표로 놓고 보면 이렇습니다.

이 표에서 가장 중요한 줄은 “병목”입니다.
코딩 속도가 병목이던 시절에는 손이 하나라서 작업이 하나였습니다.
지금은 코딩 속도가 병목이 아닙니다.
그래서 처음에는 작업 수를 얼마든지 늘릴 수 있을 줄 알았습니다.
실제로는 다른 한계가 금방 나타났습니다.

그런데 사람이 따라가지 못했다

항공 관제사를 떠올리게 됐습니다.
관제사는 비행기를 직접 조종하지 않습니다.
대신 여러 대의 움직임을 동시에 살피며 충돌하지 않게 순서를 정하고 착륙을 허가합니다.
비행기가 아무리 좋아져도 관제사가 동시에 교신할 수 있는 비행기 수에는 한계가 있고, 그 한계를 넘기면 비행기 성능과 무관하게 사고가 납니다.

제 경우 그 한계는 세 개였습니다.
동시에 관리할 수 있는 작업이 세 개까지였다는 뜻입니다.
세 개까지는 창을 오가면서도 각 세션이 어디까지 왔는지, 내가 무엇을 시켰는지, 다음에 무엇을 확인해야 하는지가 머릿속에서 유지됐습니다.
네 번째 작업을 시작했을 때부터 무너졌습니다.
무너지는 방식은 대체로 네 가지였습니다.

네 가지 모두에 공통점이 있습니다.
적어도 이 네 사례는 에이전트의 실패라기보다 제 운영의 실패에 가까웠습니다.
시킨 사람이 무엇을 시켰는지 잊었고, 나온 결과를 읽지 않았고, 엉뚱한 창에 말을 걸었습니다.
생산은 늘었는데 그것을 소화하는 쪽이 따라가지 못한 것입니다.

수치가 아니라 체감입니다.
두 개까지는 분명히 나아진 느낌이었고, 세 개는 유지할 수 있었습니다.
네 개부터는 네 번째 작업만 느려지는 것이 아니라 잘 돌아가던 앞의 세 개까지 흔들렸습니다.
교신하는 비행기가 한 대 늘면 새 비행기만 위험해지는 것이 아니라 이미 관제하던 비행기까지 위험해지는 것과 같았습니다.

천장의 정체

이 글을 쓰는 지금도 터미널 창은 열 개입니다.
그런데 무너지지 않습니다.
에이전트가 실제로 코드를 만지고 있는 창은 셋뿐이고, 나머지 일곱은 배포를 기다리거나, 문제 정의를 적어두었거나, 문서를 쓰다 멈춘 채 조용히 열려 있기 때문입니다.

그러니 천장은 창의 수에 걸리는 것이 아니었습니다.
지금 내 판단을 기다리는 작업의 수에 걸립니다.

관제사 화면에 비행기가 열 대 떠 있어도 교신 중인 것은 세 대입니다.
순항 중인 나머지 일곱 대는 지금 볼 필요가 없습니다.

그렇다면 판단을 기다리는 작업이 넷이 될 때 정확히 무엇이 바닥나는 걸까요.
처음에는 단순히 기억력 문제라고 봤습니다.
동시에 머리에 올려둘 수 있는 맥락의 수 말입니다.
그런데 기억만의 문제라면 메모를 잘하면 해결됐어야 합니다.
그렇지 않았습니다.

지금은 세 가지가 얽혀 있다고 봅니다.

  • 기억: 어느 세션에서 무엇을 시켰고 어디까지 왔는지를 동시에 기억하는 용량입니다. 에이전트는 세션마다 컨텍스트를 갖지만, 그것을 순회하는 사람의 머릿속은 하나입니다.
  • 판단: 에이전트가 내놓는 결과를 읽고 옳은지 가리는 속도입니다. 결과는 세션 수만큼 쏟아지는데, 읽는 사람은 저 하나입니다.
  • 책임: 제가 승인한 변경은 제가 설명할 수 있어야 합니다. 이해하지 못한 채 승인한 것은 산출이 아니라 부채입니다.

이 셋은 따로 늘리기 어렵습니다.
메모로 기억을 보완해도 읽어야 할 양이 늘면 판단이 밀립니다.
판단이 밀리면 이해하지 못한 채 승인하게 되고, 그러면 책임을 다하기 어려워집니다.
어느 하나만 개선해서는 천장이 오르지 않았습니다.
병목은 코딩에서 사라진 것이 아니라 제 머릿속으로 옮겨온 것이었습니다.

그래서 무엇을 바꿨나

정답을 찾았다는 뜻은 아닙니다.
지금 시점의 타협안입니다.
앞에서 나눈 기억, 판단, 책임에 맞춰 적으면 이렇습니다.

판단: 판단이 필요한 작업을 세 개로 제한했습니다. 제한하는 것은 열린 창의 수가 아니라 제 판단을 기다리는 작업의 수입니다.
제 환경에서는 에이전트가 코드를 만지고 있는 창이 곧 그 작업이라, 실제로는 그 창을 셉니다.
네 번째 코드 작업은 큐에 넣고, 하나가 끝나기 전에는 시작하지 않습니다.
대신 문제 정의나 문서처럼 대기 상태로 둘 수 있는 일로 돌립니다.
에이전트를 기다리는 시간이 아까워 시작하는 작업인지, 필요해서 시작하는 작업인지를 구분하려고 합니다.
리뷰 적체가 이걸로 가장 먼저 줄었습니다.

기억: 컨텍스트를 머리 밖으로 꺼냈습니다.
반복되는 규칙, 한 번 내린 결정, 저장소마다 있는 함정 같은 것은 에이전트가 세션을 시작할 때 읽는 지침 문서와 메모리 파일에 적어둡니다.
대기 중인 창을 닫지 않는 것도 같은 원칙입니다.
그 창이 진행 중인 맥락을 대신 들고 있어서, 돌아갔을 때 제가 다시 떠올릴 필요가 없습니다.
제가 잊어도 밖에서 기억하도록 만드는 쪽이 제 기억력을 늘리는 것보다 현실적이었고, 지시 망각이 눈에 띄게 줄었습니다.

기억: 동시에 진행하는 작업의 종류를 분산했습니다. 코딩 세 개보다 코딩 하나, 문서 하나, 조사 하나가 훨씬 덜 힘들었습니다.
같은 종류의 맥락 세 개는 서로 섞이지만, 종류가 다르면 창을 옮길 때 머릿속에서도 자연스럽게 분리됐습니다.
세션 혼동은 이걸로 줄었습니다.

책임: 1차 검증을 자동화했습니다. 변경이 생기면 자동 코드 리뷰가 돌고, 테스트는 서브에이전트가 실행해서 결과만 보고합니다.
전부 읽을 수 없다면 읽어야 할 것만 남게 만드는 수밖에 없었습니다.
다만 자동화가 책임까지 대신하지는 않습니다.
핵심 변경은 여전히 제가 직접 읽고 승인합니다.
무검토 승인은 이 둘을 같이 하면서 줄었습니다.

체감상 사고는 줄었습니다.
그런데 천장은 여전히 세 개입니다.
대응책이 올린 것은 천장이 아니라 세 개 안에서의 안정성이었습니다.

그리고 이 천장은 제 것만이 아닙니다.
제가 내보낸 결과를 읽는 동료에게도 같은 천장이 있습니다.
제 리뷰 적체를 풀면 그 적체는 동료의 리뷰 큐로 옮겨갑니다.
이 이야기는 마지막에 다시 하겠습니다.

나 자신에게 던지는 질문

같은 실패를 반복하지 않도록, 판단이 필요한 작업을 하나 더 시작하고 싶어질 때 스스로에게 묻는 것들입니다.
독자를 점검하려는 목록이 아닙니다.

  • 지금 내 판단을 기다리는 세션마다 무엇을 지시했는지, 화면을 보지 않고 말할 수 있는가?
  • 마지막으로 승인한 변경을 동료에게 설명할 수 있는가?
  • 오늘 병렬로 한 일 중 다시 읽어야 했던 것이 있었는가?
  • 이 창은 지금 내 판단을 기다리고 있는가, 아니면 그냥 열려 있는가?
  • 이 작업은 에이전트를 기다리는 시간이 아까워서 시작하는 것인가, 필요해서 시작하는 것인가?
  • 오늘의 분주함이 실제 산출로 이어졌는가?

대답이 막히는 질문이 하나라도 있으면 새 작업을 시작하지 않습니다.
돌아보면 시작하지 않는 편이 대체로 옳았습니다.

마치며

제 경험은 여기까지입니다.
여기서부터는 확신이 아니라 짐작입니다.

우리는 지금 아무도 가보지 못한 곳을 가고 있습니다.
1인 1작업이 물리 법칙이던 시절의 프로세스, 습관, 직관은 대부분 사람이 생산자라는 전제 위에 있었습니다.
그 전제가 흔들리는데 무엇으로 대체해야 하는지는 아직 아무도 모릅니다.

저 역시 지금의 방식이 맞는지 계속 의심하고 있고, 이 글의 내용도 반년 뒤에는 달라져 있을 가능성이 큽니다.
다만 두 가지 질문은 계속 들고 있으려 합니다.

천장을 올리는 것이 목표인가? 더 많은 작업을 동시에 굴릴 수 있게 되는 것과 지금의 천장 안에서 판단의 질을 높이는 것 중 어느 쪽이 더 나은지 저는 아직 모르겠습니다.
동시 작업 수는 눈에 보이지만 판단의 질은 잘 보이지 않아서, 자꾸 전자를 쫓게 됩니다.

팀은 어떻게 바뀌어야 하는가? 개인이 여러 작업을 동시에 굴리게 되면, 1인 1작업을 전제로 설계된 스프린트, 리뷰, 회의 같은 팀의 프로세스도 다시 봐야 합니다.
리뷰어 한 명이 하루에 읽을 수 있는 양은 그대로인데 리뷰 요청은 그보다 빠르게 늘어나는 상황을 어떻게 해야 하는지, 저는 아직 답이 없습니다.

정답은 없습니다.
단지 이 대격변의 시대에 각자 조금 더 나은 방향을 고민하고 생각을 나누는 것뿐이라고 생각합니다.
이 글도 그 나눔의 하나로 읽어주시면 좋겠습니다.

사족

  • 이 글은 특정 도구를 권하는 글이 아닙니다. 도구 이름은 제 환경을 정확히 적기 위해 썼을 뿐이고, 다른 도구를 쓰는 분들도 비슷한 벽을 만날 수 있다고 생각합니다.
  • 1인 N작업이 1인 1작업보다 낫다는 주장도 아닙니다. 어떤 종류의 일은 여전히 하나에 온전히 집중하는 편이 맞고, 저도 그런 날에는 창을 하나만 엽니다.
  • 세 개는 제 경험에서 나온 기준일 뿐입니다. 그것도 창의 수가 아니라 동시에 판단해야 하는 작업의 수입니다. 다른 분의 천장은 다를 수 있고, 같은 사람이라도 작업 종류와 컨디션에 따라 달라집니다.

TEAM MUSINSA CAREER

무신사는 2001년 온라인 커뮤니티로 시작해 2005년 무신사 매거진, 2009년 무신사 스토어를 오픈하며 빠르게 성장하고 있는 국내 대표 온라인 패션 스토어입니다. ‘입점 브랜드와 동반성장’이라는 경영 철학을 바탕으로 브랜드가 안정적으로 사업을 전개할 수 있도록 무신사가 보유한 노하우와 인프라를 지원합니다. 고객에게는 풍성한 패션 콘텐츠와 패션에 특화된 차별화된 서비스로 최상의 온라인 쇼핑 경험을 제공하고 있습니다. 글로벌 №1 패션 기업으로 성장할 무신사와 함께 새로운 도전과 혁신을 만들 인재를 기다립니다.
29CM는 ‘고객의 더 나은 선택을 돕는다’라는 미션으로 출발했습니다. 우리는 우리만의 방식으로 콘텐츠를 제공하며, 브랜드와 고객 모두에게 대체 불가능한 커머스 플랫폼을 만들어가고 있습니다. 이 미션을 이루기 위해 우리는 흥미로우면서도 복잡한 문제들을 해결하고 있습니다. 만약 우리와 함께 이 문제들을 해결해 보고 싶다면, 주저하지 말고 29CM에 합류하세요!

event_model_payload.headline: Unlink a customer's identity provider subject with the GraphQL Admin API
event_model_payload.summary:
As of API version 2027-01, you can use the identityProviderSubjectDelete mutation to unlink a customer from a third-party identity provider.

Pass the customer's ID as customerId and the identity provider subject's ID as id. You can get subject IDs from Customer.identityProviderSubjects. Unlinking signs the customer out of all of their existing sessions. The next time they sign in through the identity provider, they're linked again.

The mutation requires the write_customers access scope.

event_model_payload.headline: Store and app install details in the Dev Dashboard
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now view your organization’s installed apps, collaborator access, earnings, and app activity in one place in the Dev Dashboard.

Use the store page to view apps, users, and earnings for a store:

  • Apps from your organization installed on the store.
  • Users in your organization who have collaborator access to the store.
  • Earnings from the store, including total app earnings, total theme earnings, and recurring revenue share.

You can also dig in by app, with app install details:

  • Gross lifetime earnings from that store for the selected app.
  • An activity feed of installation and billing events.
  • The app’s current subscription, with quick access to logs for that store.

To get started, select a store in Stores in the Dev Dashboard. For app install details, open your app’s Overview, select the install count in the Installs card, then select a store. Available details depend on your permissions and store access.

Learn more about store details and app install details, including available information and permissions.

event_model_payload.headline: Secure your app with network access rules in `shopify.app.toml`
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now declare your app's external hosts and servers in a new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml. Normally Shopify warns customers when they navigate to a URL ouside Shopify; declaring your external hosts skips this warning, letting you remove friction for trusted journeys. Declaring servers, meanwhile, helps Shopify spot suspicious activity and protect your app.

What changed

The new network_access section has two properties:

  • allowed_navigation_hosts: The external sites your app links to from the storefront, such as your own domain. Shopify normally warns customers before sending them to a site outside the storefront. Links to these hosts skip that warning. List each host exactly as it appears in your links, up to 20.
  • allowed_sources: Up to 20 HTTPS origins that your app's code loads from or sends requests to on storefront, checkout, and Shopify admin pages. This includes your extensions, app home, and app proxy pages. We use the list to protect your app and monitor storefronts for malicious requests.

Here's an example configuration:

[network_access]
allowed_navigation_hosts = ["app.example.com"]
allowed_sources = ["https://api.app.example.com"]

Who's affected

Any app whose code links to or contacts external servers from a storefront, checkout, or the Shopify admin can use the new section.

What to do

For all apps, we strongly recommend you:

  1. Add the hosts that your app links customers to, such as your app's own site, to allowed_navigation_hosts.
  2. Add the servers that your app's code loads from or sends requests to, such as your API or CDN, to allowed_sources.
  3. Run shopify app deploy and release the new version.

For examples, see Declare your app's network access.

event_model_payload.headline: Search brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API (beta)
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify when you search the beta Catalog API. Add the new sources parameter to search_catalog to include external products in the same response as products from Shopify merchants. If you omit sources, results stay limited to Shopify merchant products and you don't need to change any existing calls.

What changed

The Catalog API beta now supports a sources parameter on search_catalog that controls which products you return:

  • Shopify merchant products only: omit sources, or set ["shopify"]
  • Both Shopify merchant and external products: ["shopify", "external"]
  • Brands that don't sell on Shopify only: ["external"]

The sources parameter works on the existing search_catalog method, with no new endpoint to call. The get_product method returns an external product when you pass its ID, and lookup_catalog support is coming later.

External products always return eligible.native_checkout: false, so shoppers can't buy them through Shopify checkout and these products don't earn Promoted Placements commission. Each external product includes a description, an image, a price, and a link to the brand's product page so the shopper completes the purchase on the brand's own site.

Who’s affected

This change affects apps that use the Catalog API to power on-site search or recommendations and want to include products from brands that don't sell on Shopify.

During the beta, external product data comes from each brand's website, and external products only return when the shopper is in the United States. Searches for shoppers in other countries continue to return Shopify merchant products only.

What to do

No action is required if you only want to keep returning products from Shopify merchants. Your existing search_catalog calls work without changes.

If you want to include external products, update your search_catalog requests to set the sources parameter to ["shopify", "external"], or to ["external"] if you only want brands that don't sell on Shopify. If you surface links to product detail pages, make sure you handle external product URLs correctly so shoppers land on the brand’s own site when they select an external product.

Related docs

  • Learn how to return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog-extension#catalog-sources
  • Read more about Global Catalog MCP tools: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog

event_model_payload.headline: Restrict Admin API access with an IP allowlist
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now limit Admin API access tokens by IP address. When you add your servers' IP addresses to an IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard, Shopify rejects GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests that use your app's tokens from anywhere else.

What changed

Your app's Settings page has a new IP allowlist section. Enter your servers' addresses or CIDR ranges, test them against recent traffic, and enable enforcement. Requests from outside your ranges fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

We strongly recommend using an IP allowlist if your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses. For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

Note: Support for apps hosted on serverless platforms with dynamic IP addresses is coming soon.

event_model_payload.headline: Promoted Placements beta now includes Shop Campaigns
event_model_payload.summary:
Promoted Placements is now in beta, and it includes Shop Campaigns. When a search_catalog result comes from a merchant running Shop Campaigns, you earn the commission that merchant funds, added to Shopify's base rate. No action is required.

What changed

Merchants running Shop Campaigns with external platforms turned on now include the Catalog API as one of those platforms. On their products, placement.commission.percentage.value returns the total rate, combining the merchant's commission and Shopify's base rate. Buyers who click a product with merchant-funded commission land in Shop (shop.com).

Who is affected

Organizations in the Promoted Placements beta that have accepted the terms and turned on Earn commission for a saved catalog. Access is invite-led, and you can join the waitlist from the docs.

What to do

No action is required, because commission comes back in the same field you already read. Keep passing your enrolled catalog.catalog_id on search_catalog and send buyers to the variant URL exactly as Shopify returns it. If you show a commission rate in your own reporting, read it from placement.commission.percentage.value, since it now varies by product.

Earning applies to search_catalog only, and only to products from Shopify merchants.

Related docs

  • Catalog API

event_model_payload.headline: POS UI extensions now support reactive storage access
event_model_payload.summary:
The new shopify.storage.current API lets POS UI extension developers respond automatically when stored values change across extension targets on the same POS device. It’s now available in API version 2026-10. No changes are required for existing extensions.

What changed

shopify.storage.current exposes each storage key as a read-only reactive signal. You can read its current value or subscribe to changes made by other targets of the same extension on the same POS device. Writes and removals still use the existing Storage API methods.

For example, a background target can fetch and store a customer’s loyalty points, and a smart grid tile can react to those changes automatically. This keeps the displayed balance up to date without repeated storage reads or custom polling logic.

Stored values load asynchronously, so a signal’s value is initially undefined until its key finishes loading. Make sure you handle this initial state as well as missing keys.

Who’s affected

This addition is available to POS UI extensions that use API version 2026-10 or later. Extensions that use earlier API versions can’t use shopify.storage.current.

What to do

You don’t need to take action. Existing Storage API methods continue to work as before.

To adopt reactive storage, update your extension to use API version 2026-10 or later and read or subscribe to the keys your extension needs through shopify.storage.current.

Related docs

  • POS UI extensions Storage API reference

event_model_payload.headline: Migrate to expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027
event_model_payload.summary:
Public apps still using non-expiring offline access tokens must migrate to use expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027 to remain listed in the Shopify App Store and continue accepting new installs.

New client credentials access helps your backend recover access without waiting for a merchant to reopen your app. Using a request signed with your app's private key, your backend can obtain a fresh, short-lived access token without a refresh token.

The enforcement timeline has been updated with incremental penalties for non-compliant apps:

  • January 1, 2027: Non-compliant apps are delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installations can continue making affected API requests until April 1.
  • January 15, 2027: Merchants using non-compliant apps see warnings in Shopify admin about the risk of service interruption and the action they can take.
  • April 1, 2027: Affected Admin API requests using non-expiring offline access tokens return HTTP 403.

This schedule applies to existing public apps previously covered by the January 1, 2027 deadline. The requirement for public apps created on or after April 1, 2026 remains in effect. Custom apps and apps created by merchants are excluded.

Follow the migration guide to update token acquisition, migrate existing installations, and validate token storage and refresh handling.

event_model_payload.headline: Manage payouts, billing, and settings in Dev Dashboard
event_model_payload.summary:
You now manage your Partner business details, payouts, billing, and the remaining Partner Dashboard settings in Dev Dashboard's Organization settings. New Partners also complete business verification there during setup. Existing Partners don’t need to take action because your current payout and billing settings stay the same.

What changed

The Settings and Payouts links in Partner Dashboard and the Home payout widget have moved to Dev Dashboard. To reach the new pages, open Dev Dashboard, select your organization, and open Organization settings.

From Organization settings, you can manage:

  • Organization details: business and contact details, emergency contact, App Store registration, and Partner ID
  • Payouts: payout setup, history, transactions, and payout methods

To learn more about where Partner Dashboard features have moved in Dev Dashboard, see the migration guide. For more about Dev Dashboard in general, see the Overview.

event_model_payload.headline: Discover a merchant's retail stores with UCP location search and lookup
event_model_payload.summary:
Shopify storefronts now support the UCP location capability, dev.ucp.common.location.search and dev.ucp.common.location.lookup, starting with UCP 2026-08-25. When you negotiate these capabilities over the storefront MCP endpoint, your agent can find a merchant's physical stores, narrow them by name, city, or distance, and check which stores carry the items a buyer wants. This is an optional new capability and doesn't require changes if you don't use locations today.

What changed

Storefronts with at least one retail location now list both location capabilities in their discovery profiles at /.well-known/ucp. A retail location is an active, merchant-managed location that the merchant set up to sell in person and enabled as a Physical storefront.

If your agent profile negotiates these capabilities, the storefront MCP endpoint at https://{storedomain}/api/ucp/mcp exposes two tools:

  • search_locations lists the shop's retail locations. An empty location object returns the first page. You can narrow results with a query that matches store names and cities, a distance relation with an explicit center and a max radius in meters, and filters.items.
  • lookup_locations returns locations by ID, such as gid://shopify/Location/123. It processes the first 10 distinct IDs. If you send more, the response includes a batch_limit_applied message, and you can send the rest in another request.

Each location includes its id, name, address, and geo coordinates when the merchant has set them. Search returns 10 locations by default, and up to 250 when you set pagination.limit. To get the next page, pass the pagination.cursor from the response.

filters.items accepts up to 10 product variant IDs. A location matches only when every variant is available there. Availability follows Shopify's existing store availability rules. It isn't a stock count, a pickup promise, or a reservation.

Shopify doesn't support the hours and amenities filters, custom filters, or the serves relation. Requests that include them return an invalid_input error instead of ignoring them. Pickup checkout for a selected location isn't supported.

How to set it up

Platforms and agents that use Shopify's storefront MCP endpoint with UCP 2026-08-25 and negotiate either location capability are affected.

Shops without a retail location don't advertise these capabilities or tools. Integrations that don't declare them, or that negotiate an earlier UCP version, aren't affected.

What to do

  1. Declare dev.ucp.common.location.search and dev.ucp.common.location.lookup at version 2026-08-25 in your agent profile.
  2. Call the location tools only when the shop's profile lists them.
  3. Send distance.center only from a location that the buyer chose to share. Shopify never infers a center from context or IP address.
  4. Treat item matches as provisional. Confirm availability and fulfillment options in cart and checkout before you tell the buyer that an item is ready.

Related docs

  • Configure agent profiles and UCP negotiation
  • Review the UCP location specification

event_model_payload.headline: Security update: Offline token dates, new security features
event_model_payload.summary:
On October 20, we asked all app devs to secure their app, and told you we'd share more before any security change takes effect. Here's what's new, and what you need to do.

Offline access tokens

The migration timeline for offline access tokens remains the same: All public apps that call the Admin API must migrate to expiring offline access tokens by January 1, 2027. We're sharing an updated enforcement timeline if an app isn't migrated by then:

  • January 1, 2027: Delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • January 15, 2027: Merchants using the app see a warning in Shopify admin.
  • April 1, 2027: Admin API requests using non-expiring offline access tokens return HTTP 403.

January 1 is the migration deadline: The later dates give merchants time to prepare, and should not be treated as extra time to migrate. Custom apps, merchant-created apps and online access tokens are not affected. Follow the migration guide.

New security features

We've rolled out several new features this week to help secure your app:

  • Recover access with client credentials. If your app loses a refresh token, your backend can now request a new access token signed with your app's private key, without waiting for a merchant to reopen your app. Set up client credentials access.
  • Restrict API access to your own servers with an IP allowlist. List the IP addresses your servers use, and we'll reject Admin API requests from any other IP, even if it has a valid access token. Set up your IP allowlist.
  • Tell us which servers and sites your app uses. In the new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml, list the servers your app's code loads from or sends requests to, wherever it runs on a store. We use that list to spot requests your app didn't make. You can also list the sites you link customers to, so those links skip the warning customers normally see before leaving the store. Declare your app's network access.
  • We now verify your identity before installing apps on development and client-transfer stores. This helps keep apps in trusted hands.
  • Use the new app security hub as your checklist. Every app security practice now has its own page in the dev docs. Point your agent at the hub to check which practices apply to your app, and run shopify app security check before every release. Go to the app security hub.

Get help

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.

Questions about these updates? Ask in the App Security board in the developer community.

event_model_payload.headline: Analytics queryable capability is configurable in shopify.app.toml for metaobject definitions
event_model_payload.summary:
Apps can now set capabilities.analytics_queryable on metaobject definitions in shopify.app.toml. This makes compatible fields on those definitions queryable in Shopify analytics and ShopifyQL. It applies to apps that declare metaobject definitions in their app configuration. No action is required, because the capability stays off unless you add the key.

What changed

Metaobject definitions declared under [metaobjects.app.] in shopify.app.toml now accept capabilities.analytics_queryable. When you set it to true, any field on the definition with an analytics-compatible type, such as single_line_text_field, number_integer, date, or product_reference, becomes available as a dimension and filter in analytics reports and ShopifyQL. This works wherever a product, product variant, customer, or order metafield references the metaobject. Fields with other types are ignored.

Previously, an app could only set this capability through the GraphQL Admin API, and only on definitions it didn't manage in TOML. Declarative definitions are read-only through the API, so there was no way to make them queryable.

Who's affected

This applies to apps that declare metaobject definitions in shopify.app.toml. Existing definitions don't change. If a definition doesn't include the key, the capability stays off.

It doesn't apply to these:

  • Metaobject definitions that you create with the GraphQL Admin API. For those, set analyticsQueryable with the metaobjectDefinitionCreate or metaobjectDefinitionUpdate mutation in API version 2027-01 or later.
  • Metaobject definitions that merchants own. Merchants turn analytics on or off for those in the Shopify admin.

What to do

No action is required. To make a declared metaobject definition queryable in analytics:

  1. Add capabilities.analytics_queryable = true to the definition in shopify.app.toml, and make sure at least one of its fields has an analytics-compatible type.
  2. Deploy your app configuration to a development store.
  3. Confirm that the definition's capabilities.analyticsQueryable.enabled field is true in GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later, and that its fields appear in analytics reports for the product, variant, customer, or order metafield that references it.
[metaobjects.app.designer]
name = "Designer"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.designer.fields.country]
name = "Country"
type = "single_line_text_field"

This example makes the country field of the designer metaobject queryable. Replace the definition and fields with your own. If none of a definition's fields has a compatible type, the release fails validation, so add or change a field before you deploy.

Related docs

  • Make your metaobjects queryable in analytics

event_model_payload.headline: Fuzzers vs. AI: Comparing Fuzzilli and BigSleep on JavaScript Engines
event_model_payload.summary: Summary Project Zero compared two automated tools used by Google to find vulnerabilities in Chrome’s JavaScript engine, V8, on a regular basis. Fuzzilli is a generative JavaScript engine fuzzer and BigSleep is an LLM-based bug finding system. In the past six months, BigSleep found more vulnerabilities than Fuzzilli (45 versus 37) with a 25% overlap in the specific bugs reported. Since this comparison methodology has a tendency to underestimate overlap, we also performed dedicated experiments to test theoretical overlap in vulnerabilities reported since 2023. These experiments estimated overlap at roughly 60%. Regardless of which value is accurate, a substantial portion of vulnerabilities were discoverable by only LLMs or only fuzzing. While it is extremely promising that LLMs have become able to find so many vulnerabilities so quickly, fuzzing and LLMs are still complementary approaches. We recommend vendors perform both fuzzing and agentic analysis of their code to maximize the number of vulnerabilities that get reported before they impact users.

event_model_payload.headline: Single-tenant Titus: VM-level isolation on a multi-tenant container platform
event_model_payload.summary:
Samartha Chandrashekar & Nick Parker

You click play on a Friday night, and in the second that follows, dozens of services answer in milliseconds. Most of them run on Titus, our internal container platform. Titus is, in essence, a Kubernetes-based container hosting platform: we keep both the control plane and the data plane (the container hosts that actually run containers) patched and up to date, so application teams get a consistent and reliable container experience. They hand us a container, and we run it, with no host, cluster, or kernel to own. Titus launches millions of containers every week across tens of thousands of EC2 instances in multiple AWS regions. It is multi-tenant by default: many containers from many teams share each host. That density is what makes container compute efficient, and it is why Titus has been the default home for so much of Netflix’s compute for years.

For most workloads, sharing a host works well. For a few, it does not, and those few include some of the most demanding real-time systems we run. This post is about them, and about single-tenant Titus, a mode that gives a task its own virtual machine while keeping everything else about Titus the same: the API, the deployment path, and the managed experience where the Compute/Platform team, not the application team, owns the host.

We will walk through why shared-kernel isolation runs out of road for certain workloads, how we measure isolation rather than asserting it, the options we weighed (microVMs, gVisor, EC2, and more shared-kernel tuning) and why a dedicated VM inside Titus won, how the mode is built on the Titus federation layer and autoscaling, and what we have seen along three axes: isolation, fleet efficiency, and the operational cost of keeping the fleet patched.

The cost of good neighbors

Multi-tenancy is a tradeoff. Packing many containers onto a large bare-metal instance keeps utilization high, but it also means those containers share a single Linux kernel and the underlying hardware. Titus isolates them with the tools the kernel provides: cgroups cap CPU, memory, and disk; namespaces give each container its own view of the system; seccomp and AppArmor restrict the system calls a container can make; the Completely Fair Scheduler divides CPU time; the iocost controller meters disk IO; and traffic shaping meters each container’s slice of the network. Each container also gets its own identity, IAM role, and security groups, so tenants are isolated for security and resource management.

These mechanisms provide isolation for what the kernel can partition. They cannot fully partition what is shared in hardware. A group of cores shares a last-level cache and a path to memory, so a container that suddenly pulls a lot of data from RAM evicts a neighbor’s cache lines and slows it down, even when both stay inside their CPU limits. There is no cgroup for memory bandwidth or cache residency, as there is for CPU shares. The interference is real, it is hardware, and it does not show up as either container exceeding its quota.

A noisy neighbor and a co-located app each stay within their cgroup CPU and memory limits, but both draw on a shared last-level cache and memory bandwidth that lack cgroup fences. The noisy neighbor takes most of it, so the co-located app stalls and its tail latency rises even though no one exceeded a quota.

We have written about this before. Predictive CPU isolation of containers at Netflix moved some placement decisions out of the kernel and into a service that forecasts each container’s CPU demand and re-pins containers to cores to reduce cache interference, formulated as a combinatorial optimization solved every minute. Noisy Neighbor Detection with eBPF instruments the kernel scheduler to surface per-container run-queue latency, so we can see a victim being starved in close to real time. And Mount Mayhem traced container-startup slowness to a global kernel lock amplified by modern CPU cache topology. Each of these raised the floor for everyone on the platform, and we are continuing that work.

A decade of shared-kernel isolation, at Netflix and across the industry, has not made co-tenancy invisible, because a noisy neighbor is not one problem but a family of them. Almost every physical resource a host shares is its own axis of interference, and a cgroup can fence very few of them:

  • CPU performance indeterminacy. Co-located threads contend for the run queue, so scheduling latency rises even while a container remains within its CPU quota. Separately, a neighbor with a large working set evicts a tenant’s last-level cache lines and saturates memory bandwidth, neither of which a CPU share can partition.
  • Network bandwidth and packets per second. Per-container shaping competes for link bandwidth, and receives processing runs in softirq context, charging one container’s packet work to whatever CPU a neighbor is running on. A flood of small packets exhausts a core’s softirq budget long before any bandwidth cap is reached.
  • Storage bandwidth and IOPS. A neighbor saturating a device’s queue serializes everyone’s I/O, and on cloud block storage, the per-volume and per-instance throughput ceilings are a shared budget in their own right.
  • Long tail. Page-cache reclaim, NUMA and cross-socket interconnect traffic, TLB-shootdown interrupts, PCIe and GPU contention, package-level power and thermal throttling, and contention on kernel global locks (the class of problem behind Mount Mayhem) each degrade neighbors in their own way.

What unites them is that they are physical, shared, and below the level a quota can reach. A platform can cap how much CPU time or memory a container is granted; it cannot hand each tenant its own slice of the memory bus, its own softirq budget, or its own portion of the last-level cache.

Of these, the network dimension has bitten hardest in our experience. Per-container bandwidth shaping uses a hierarchical token bucket (HTB) queueing discipline that serializes traffic with a global lock to account for each container’s bytes and packets. Under a flood of small packets from a single container, contention for that lock can burn kernel CPU and starve co-located containers of the time they need to process their own traffic, resulting in TCP retransmits and tail-latency spikes on services that did nothing wrong. The mechanism meant to prevent noisy neighbors becomes one.

The workloads most exposed to this are stateful, high-throughput streaming jobs: real-time data pipelines and stream processors that continuously move large volumes of data and maintain in-memory state. When one of these is perturbed, recovery is not cheap. A stream processor that falls behind or loses its place may have to restore from a checkpoint and pause processing for many minutes to catch up. For these jobs, intermittent interference from a neighbor is not a small slowdown that averages out; it is a stop-the-world event that pages an on-call engineer. The same teams report, accurately, that they never saw this on a plain EC2 instance.

Why we kept coming back to the VM

Full VM isolation, where a workload gets its own host and kernel, is the standard our customers are already happy with. The question was not whether VM isolation works; it was how to offer it without giving up what makes Titus worth using. We weighed four paths.

  1. Keep improving shared-kernel isolation. This helps every workload on the platform, needs no opt-in, and we are still investing in it (more on the roadmap below). Its limitation is structural. Each round of tuning narrows the gap without closing it, because the underlying hardware remains shared. Cache, memory bandwidth, and the kernel’s own shaping and scheduling locks are not things a container boundary can fully contain. Shared-kernel isolation is the right default and the wrong promise for a workload that cannot tolerate a bad minute.
  2. microVMs (Firecracker, Kata Containers). Lightweight VMs boot in about 150 milliseconds by emulating far less hardware than traditional VMs, which is why they power serverless platforms. They were the most appealing alternative on paper, and we carefully reviewed them. Three things made the cost hard to justify. First, the hardware virtualization they rely on is available only on bare-metal instances or through nested virtualization, and nested virtualization was not ready on the instance types we run at Netflix at the time, so adopting microVMs broadly would have constrained us to a narrow slice of the fleet. Second, there is no managed microVM service we could build on, which means we would have to run and maintain a virtualization layer ourselves: patching the hypervisor, live-migrating guests, and qualifying emulated devices. That is exactly the kind of operational surface we prefer not to own when we can avoid it. Third, even setting those aside, microVMs add virtualization overhead on CPU- and IO-bound work and do not support GPUs. Excellent isolation, but at a price in flexibility and operational load we were not willing to pay.
  3. gVisor. A user-space kernel that intercepts system calls provides sandbox-grade isolation without a hypervisor, thereby avoiding the bare-metal constraint. The catch is performance and dependency. Intercepting syscalls in user space adds overhead on IO-heavy paths, which are precisely the workloads we most need to protect, and the open-source project lags behind its internal counterpart in fixes and is effectively maintained by a single vendor. The isolation we would gain came with a throughput tax on the exact jobs we were trying to help.
  4. Move the workload to EC2. It is possible to run containers directly on EC2 instances. The problem is that the application team takes back the operational load that Titus exists to carry: choosing instance types, patching hosts, and sizing and scaling the fleet.
