    따라서 AI를 문제에 대한 Silver bullet을 제시하는 해결 도구로 사용하기 보다는, 문제 해결에 소요되는 비용을 낮추는 조력자로 활용하는 것이 더 정확하고 효율적인 방법이라는 것을 깨달았습니다.

앞으로

이번 경험을 통해서 AI의 도움을 받아 기존과는 다른 방식으로 더 정확한 해결 방법을 찾을 수 있다는 교훈을 얻을 수 있었습니다. 하지만 AI는 도구일 뿐 이를 사용하는 것은 결국 사람이었습니다. 이는 AI가 급격하게 발전했음에도 불구하고 결국 사람의 생각과 고찰이 문제를 해결하는 데 가장 중요한 요소라는 것을 시사합니다.

이러한 교훈을 바탕으로 왓챠의 플랫폼 팀은 AI로 달라진 업무 환경을 최적화할 수 있도록 기존의 SDLC 프로세스와 업무 수행 방식을 개편할 예정입니다. 구현을 어떻게 할 것인가에 집중하기보다는 왜 이 문제를 해결해야 하며 구현된 뒤에는 의도한 결과가 나타났는지를 중점적으로 다룰 수 있는 방식으로 개선하고자 합니다. 이를 통해 이제는 AI로 인해 낮아진 구현 비용을 지렛대 삼아 사람은 문제를 정의하고 이를 검증하는데 집중할 수 있도록 할 것입니다.

감으로 맞추던 값을 식을 세워서 kubernetes 최적화하기 was originally published in WATCHA on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: 모델만 바꿨는데 LLM 비용이 3배가 된 이유
event_model_payload.summary:
안녕하세요, 당근 커뮤니티홈팀에서 백엔드를 개발하는 제이(Jay)예요. 당근 앱의 커뮤니티 탭에는 이웃이 알려 주는 동네 정보부터 소소한 일상과 취미까지 나누는 동네생활, 모임, 카페, 아파트가 모여 있어요. 커뮤니티홈팀은 이 서비스들의 글을 한데 모아 보여 주는 피드를 맡고 있어요.

피드를 맡으며 가장 고민하는 건 사용자에게 더 알맞은 글을 어떻게 보여 줄지예요. 그래서 기존 머신러닝 추천에 더해, LLM으로 글의 다양한 메타데이터를 뽑아 추천에 쓰고 있어요. 그중 하나가 LLM에 카테고리 목록과 글을 주고 어느 주제에 속하는지 고르게 하는 주제 분류예요. 추천은 보여 줄 글 후보를 모으는 단계와 그 순서를 정하는 단계로 나뉘는데, 글마다 주제가 붙어 있으면 첫 단계부터 사용자가 관심 있는 주제의 글을 골라 올 수 있어요.

주제 분류를 할 때 LLM에 보내는 요청을 열어 보면 대부분이 매번 똑같은 지시문과 카테고리 목록이고, 글 본문은 끝에 조금 붙어 있을 뿐이에요. 이 글에서는 요청마다 똑같은 이 부분을 고정부라고 부를게요.

2026년 8월, 이 작업의 모델을 Gemini에서 단가가 20% 낮은 OpenAI GPT-5.6으로 바꿨어요. 응답은 정상이었고 에러도 한 건 없었어요.

닷새 뒤 보니 단가는 내렸는데 요청당 비용은 3.2배가 돼 있었어요. 원인은 프롬프트 캐시였어요. 입력 중 캐시에서 읽어 온 비율인 캐시 히트율이 85.8%에서 2.3%로 떨어져 있었죠.

교체 전후의 응답을 나란히 놓으면 달라진 곳은 사용량 정보 안의 캐시 필드 하나뿐이었어요. 캐시가 깨져도 에러는 나지 않아요. 비용만 늘어요.

이 글은 그 일을 해결하며 알게 된 것을 정리한 기록이에요. 캐시가 무엇을 재사용하는지, 비용은 어떻게 매겨지는지, 언제 켜지고 어디까지 저장되는지, 캐시에서 읽었는지는 어떻게 확인하는지를 OpenAI, Anthropic, Google Gemini를 나란히 놓고 살펴봐요. 같은 지시문에 입력만 바꿔 LLM을 대량으로 부르거나, 챗봇이나 에이전트처럼 앞부분이 같은 요청을 되풀이해 보내는 분이라면 참고가 될 거예요.

프롬프트 캐시의 원리

신입 검수자에게 매번 규정집 20쪽과 오늘 볼 글 한 편을 함께 준다고 해 볼게요. 규정집은 늘 같고 글만 바뀌는데, 이 검수자는 기억을 못 해서 글마다 규정집을 처음부터 다시 읽어요. 하루 10만 편이면 규정집을 10만 번 읽는 셈이에요.

LLM도 똑같이 요청마다 프롬프트 전체를 처음부터 다시 읽어요. 이 낭비를 줄이는 게 프롬프트 캐시예요.

앞 토큰을 돌아보는 어텐션

LLM은 글을 토큰 단위로 하나씩 이어 써요. 다음 토큰을 고르기 전에는 앞 토큰들을 돌아보며 무엇을 참고할지 따지는데, 이 계산을 어텐션(attention)이라고 해요.

“어제 시장에서 산 사과를 깎아서” 다음에 올 토큰을 고른다고 해 볼게요. 사람은 바로 “먹었다”를 떠올려요. “사과”와 “깎아서”가 가장 관련 있고 “어제”나 “시장에서”는 덜 중요하다는 걸 알기 때문이에요. 모델은 이 판단을 마지막 토큰 “깎아서” 자리에서 숫자로 해요.

어텐션에는 토큰마다 세 가지 값이 쓰여요. 도서관에서 자료를 찾는 일에 비유해 볼게요.

  • Q(Query, 질문): 마지막 토큰이 다음 토큰을 고르려고 들고 있는 질문이에요. “무엇을 했는지 이어 쓰려면 어떤 정보가 필요하지?” 같은 것이에요.
  • K(Key, 분류표): 앞 토큰마다 붙은 꼬리표예요. 책의 분류표처럼 “먹을 수 있는 물건”, “때를 나타내는 말” 같은 정보를 담아요.
  • V(Value, 내용): 앞 토큰이 실제로 건네주는 정보예요. 책의 본문에 해당해요.

마지막 토큰 “깎아서”는 자기 Q를 앞 토큰들(자기 자신 포함)의 K와 하나씩 맞춰 보고 점수를 매겨요. “사과”와 “깎아서”는 높은 점수를, “어제”는 낮은 점수를 받아요. 그다음 점수 비율대로 V를 섞고 그 결과로 다음 토큰 “먹었다”를 골라요. 분류표(K)로 관련 있는 책을 고른 뒤, 그 책들의 본문(V)을 점수만큼 읽는 것과 같아요.

실제 Q, K, V는 사람이 읽을 수 있는 문장이 아니라 숫자 묶음(벡터)이고, 위 설명은 그 역할을 말로 푼 거예요.

한 번 만들면 계속 쓰는 K와 V

“먹었다”를 고른 뒤에는 “먹었다”가 Q를 들고 같은 일을 해요. 이때 “어제”부터 “깎아서”까지의 K와 V는 앞 단계에서 만든 것과 똑같아요. 뒤에 어떤 토큰이 붙어도 앞 토큰의 K와 V는 바뀌지 않거든요.

그래서 모델은 한 번 만든 K와 V를 캐시에 쌓아 두고 다시 꺼내 써요. 이 캐시를 KV 캐시라고 해요. 새로 계산하는 건 새 토큰의 Q, K, V뿐이고, Q는 그 토큰이 앞을 볼 때 한 번 쓰고 끝나서 쌓아 두지 않아요. 캐시가 없다면 토큰을 하나 쓸 때마다 앞 토큰 전부를 처음부터 다시 계산해야 해요.

입력도 마찬가지예요. 모델은 답을 쓰기 전에 입력 전체를 한꺼번에 읽으며 K와 V를 만들어 캐시를 채워요. 이 단계를 prefill이라고 하는데, 입력이 길수록 오래 걸려요.

KV 캐시를 다음 요청에 물려주는 프롬프트 캐시

KV 캐시는 원래 요청 하나가 끝나면 함께 사라져요. 프롬프트 캐시는 그 앞부분을 요청이 끝난 뒤에도 서버에 남겨 두는 기능이에요. 다음 요청의 앞부분이 같으면 prefill을 건너뛰고 남겨 둔 것을 그대로 꺼내 써요. 캐시에서 읽은 앞부분은 Q, K, V 어느 것도 다시 계산하지 않고 새로 들어온 토큰만 계산해요. 규정집을 읽으며 만든 메모를 다음 글에도 쓰는 셈이에요. 제공사는 아낀 계산만큼 값을 깎아 주는데, OpenAI는 캐시에서 읽은 입력 토큰을 최대 95%까지 할인해요.

헷갈리기 쉬운 것

  • 프롬프트 캐시는 응답 캐시가 아니에요. 응답 캐시는 같은 질문에 저장해 둔 답을 그대로 돌려줘요. 뜻이 비슷한 질문에도 답을 돌려주는 시맨틱 캐싱도 응답 캐시의 한 종류예요. 프롬프트 캐시는 입력을 읽는 계산만 재사용하고 출력은 매번 새로 만들어요.
  • 캐시를 켜도 답의 품질은 그대로예요. 답을 만드는 과정은 캐시가 없을 때와 똑같다고 OpenAI와 Anthropic 문서 모두 적어 두었어요.
  • 캐시는 입력 비용만 깎아요. 출력 토큰은 캐시와 상관없이 정가예요.
  • 응답도 빨리 시작돼요. 입력을 처리하는 시간이 줄어서예요. 다만 공식 문서에 일반적인 수치는 없어요.

앞부분이 글자 하나까지 같아야 하는 이유

모델 구조 때문이에요. 모델은 여러 층으로 되어 있고, 층마다 가중치가 달라서 같은 어텐션이라도 층마다 다른 질문을 던져요. 아래층의 결과는 위층의 입력이 돼요. 예를 들어 아래층에서 “깎아서”가 “사과를”과 묶이면, 위층의 “깎아서”는 이미 “사과를 깎아서”라는 뜻을 담고 다시 앞을 봐요. 이렇게 층을 지날수록 앞 문맥이 쌓이니, 위층의 K와 V는 그 토큰 하나가 아니라 앞 토큰 전체에 묶여 있어요. 앞에서 토큰 하나만 달라져도 그 뒤의 K와 V는 모두 달라져요.

위치도 따져요. K에는 “몇 번째 토큰인가”라는 정보가 섞여 있어서 같은 문장도 100번째와 200번째에서 K가 달라요.

그래서 프롬프트 캐시가 다시 쓸 수 있는 건 처음부터 똑같은 부분뿐이에요. 중간에 한 번이라도 다른 토큰이 나오면, 그 뒤가 아무리 똑같아도 다시 계산해요.

예를 들어 프롬프트 맨 앞의 시각 2026-09-04 09:00이 1분 뒤 09:01로 바뀌면, 토큰 하나 차이인데도 그 뒤 지시문 전체를 다시 계산해요. 시각을 맨 뒤로 옮기면 끝의 몇 토큰만 새로 계산해요.

앞부분을 흔드는 것들

OpenAI 문서에 따르면 캐시되는 앞부분에는 OpenAI가 자체로 넣는 지시문, 개발자 메시지, 도구 정의, 대화 이력까지 들어가요. 그래서 프롬프트 문구를 고치지 않아도, 요청마다 끼어드는 값이나 함께 보내는 설정이 바뀌면 앞부분이 달라져요.

  • 앞쪽에 넣은 시각과 날짜. OpenAI 문서도 캐시가 깨지는 예로 지시문 속 타임스탬프를 들어요.
  • 요청 ID, UUID, 난수. 추적용으로 프롬프트에 넣었다면 맨 뒤로 옮기세요.
  • 키 순서가 흔들리는 JSON. 같은 데이터라도 직렬화할 때마다 키 순서가 바뀌면 다른 글자가 돼요. Anthropic 문서는 도구의 input_schema JSON이 매번 다르게 직렬화되는 경우를 도구 변경 원인으로 들어요.
  • 도구 목록과 그 순서. 도구를 더하거나 빼거나 순서만 바꿔도 앞부분이 달라져요. OpenAI는 어떤 요청에서 도구를 쓰지 않게 하려면 정의를 지우지 말고 tool_choice를 "none"으로 두라고 권해요.
  • 출력 형식과 스키마. 구조화 출력 스키마는 입력에 함께 들어가요.
  • 추론 강도 같은 설정. OpenAI는 reasoning.effort와 text.verbosity를 앞부분을 바꿀 수 있는 설정으로, Anthropic은 thinking과 effort 설정 변경을 캐시가 깨지는 원인으로 꼽아요.

캐시를 켜면 오히려 비싸지는 경우

캐시에서 읽으면 싸지만, 캐시에 저장할 때 추가 비용을 받는 제공사도 있어요. 이걸 모르면 캐시는 켜 두기만 하면 무조건 이득이라고 착각하기 쉬워요.

읽기는 대부분 입력 정가의 0.1배예요. OpenAI GPT-6.1 Sol, Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5와 Sonnet 5.5는 0.05배, Claude Fable 5.1은 0.025배로 더 싸요. Gemini는 캐시에서 읽은 토큰을 90% 할인해요.

쓰기 요금은 제공사마다 달라요. 캐시에 저장할 때 발생하는 추가 비용을 이 글에서는 쓰기 할증이라고 할게요.

  • OpenAI: GPT-5.6 이후 모델은 정가의 1.25배예요. GPT-5.5 이하는 할증이 없어요.
  • Anthropic: 기본 5분짜리 캐시는 1.25배, 1시간짜리 캐시는 2배예요.
  • Gemini: 자동으로 거는 implicit 캐시는 할증이 없어요. 미리 올려 두는 explicit 캐시는 저장해 둔 시간만큼 저장료를 따로 내요.

쓰기 할증이 있으면 캐시를 켠 쪽이 더 비쌀 수도 있어요. 고정부 토큰 하나는 캐시에서 읽을 때 0.1배, 못 읽고 새로 저장할 때 1.25배를 내요. 고정부 토큰 가운데 캐시에서 읽는 비율을 h라고 하면 평균 배율은 아래와 같아요.

0.1 × h + 1.25 × (1 − h)

h가 약 22%보다 낮으면 이 값이 1을 넘어, 캐시가 없을 때보다 오히려 비싸져요. 프롬프트 길이와는 상관없고, 읽기가 0.05배인 모델도 약 21%로 거의 같아요. OpenAI 문서도 요청 열 번 중 처음 한 번만 저장하고 아홉 번을 읽으면 2.15배로, 캐시 없이 열 번 처리하는 10배보다 훨씬 싸다고 설명해요.

캐시 상태별 비용 비교

고정부가 요청의 95%인 작업에서, 쓰기 할증이 1.25배인 모델의 입력 비용을 캐시가 없을 때를 100으로 두고 계산했어요.

같은 요청인데도 캐시 상태에 따라 비용이 여섯 배 넘게 벌어져요. 비용을 견적할 때 단가표와 함께 예상 히트율이 필요한 이유예요. 쓰기 할증이 없는 모델이라면 못 읽어도 캐시 없음과 같은 100이에요.

캐시를 켜는 법과 구분점 위치

캐시는 구분점(breakpoint) 단위로 저장돼요. 구분점은 “처음부터 여기까지를 한 덩어리로 저장해 두라”는 표시이고, 다음 요청은 앞부분이 그 덩어리 전체와 같아야 읽어요. 캐시를 켜는 방법과 구분점을 누가 어디에 찍는지가 제공사마다 달라요.

OpenAI: 모델마다 다른 자동 구분점 위치

OpenAI는 캐시가 기본으로 켜져 있고 구분점도 자동으로 찍어요. 그런데 GPT-5.6에서 자동 구분점의 위치가 바뀌었어요.

  • GPT-5.5: 2,048토큰 간격으로 찍어요.
  • GPT-5.6 이후: 가장 최근 메시지의 끝에 하나 찍어요. GPT-6 계열도 같아요.

저희 비용이 3배가 된 원인

저희 요청은 고정된 지시문을 앞에, 글 본문을 뒤에 두고 메시지 하나로 보냈어요. Gemini를 쓸 때는 대부분의 요청이 같은 지시문 부분을 캐시에서 읽었어요. GPT-5.5처럼 2,048토큰 간격으로 구분점을 찍는 모델이었어도 긴 지시문 안에 구분점이 여러 개 생겨, 글이 달라도 지시문 쪽 덩어리는 다시 읽을 수 있었을 거예요. 하지만 GPT-5.6에서는 구분점이 글 본문 뒤에 하나만 찍혀서, 저장되는 덩어리는 “지시문 + 글 A” 전체예요. 다음 요청 “지시문 + 글 B”는 지시문까지는 같지만 글에서 갈라지니, 이 덩어리 전체와 같지 않아 읽지 못해요. “지시문까지”만 담은 덩어리는 한 번도 저장되지 않았고요. 거의 모든 요청이 1.25배를 내고 저장만 했어요. 앞의 비용 그림에서 본 125가 바로 이 상태예요.

OpenAI 문서도 이 함정을 주의할 점(Gotchas)의 첫 항목으로 적어 두었어요.

A shared prefix is not always a cached prefix. This is particularly prevalent when migrating from earlier models to GPT-5.6 or later due to the change in implicit caching behaviour.
(앞부분이 같다고 해서 그 앞부분이 캐시돼 있는 건 아니에요. 자동 캐시 동작이 바뀌어서 이전 모델에서 GPT-5.6 이후로 옮길 때 특히 자주 생겨요.)

고정부 끝에 찍는 명시 구분점

해결 방법도 문서에 있어요. GPT-5.6 이후로 옮길 때의 안내는 “자동 구분점에 요청마다 바뀌는 부분이 들어가면, 고정부 뒤에 명시 구분점을 더하라”고 써요. 고정부가 끝나고 바뀌는 부분이 시작되기 직전이 그 자리예요. OpenAI API로 직접 보낸다면 아래처럼 써요.

{
  "model": "gpt-6.1-sol",
  "prompt_cache_options": { "mode": "explicit" },
  "input": [
    {
      "role": "developer",
      "content": [
        {
          "type": "input_text",
          "text": "(매번 같은 지시문, 규칙, 예시)",
          "prompt_cache_breakpoint": { "mode": "explicit" }
        }
      ]
    },
    { "role": "user", "content": "(요청마다 바뀌는 입력)" }
  ]
}

prompt_cache_breakpoint가 붙은 블록까지가 한 덩어리로 저장되므로 입력이 바뀌어도 지시문 덩어리는 다시 읽혀요. prompt_cache_options.mode를 explicit으로 두면 자동 구분점이 꺼지고 직접 찍은 곳에서만 저장해서, 매번 바뀌는 입력에는 쓰기 할증이 붙지 않아요. 자동 구분점과 함께 쓸 수도 있고, 요청 하나가 만드는 캐시 쓰기는 최대 4개예요.

저희는 프롬프트를 사내 LLM 플랫폼의 템플릿으로 관리하고 코드는 변수 값만 넘겨요. 그래서 플랫폼이 템플릿의 첫 변수 앞에 구분점을 찍도록 고쳤어요. 고친 뒤 주제 분류의 히트율은 95% 안팎으로 올랐고, 요청당 비용은 약 5분의 1로 줄었어요.

Anthropic: 직접 켜야 하는 캐시

Anthropic은 캐시가 기본으로 켜져 있지 않아서 요청에 cache_control을 붙여야 해요. 붙이는 자리는 두 가지예요.

  • 요청 맨 바깥: model, messages와 같은 최상위 단계에 하나만 붙이면 마지막 블록 끝에 구분점이 찍혀요. 대화가 이어지면 구분점도 새 메시지 끝으로 옮겨 가고, 직전 요청까지 저장된 부분은 그대로 읽혀요. 이전 대화에 새 메시지만 덧붙이는 챗봇에 잘 맞아요. 반대로 지시문 뒤에 매번 다른 글을 붙이는 작업에서는 구분점이 바뀌는 글 끝에 찍혀 캐시를 읽지 못한다고 문서가 경고해요. GPT-5.6에서 격은 것과 같은 함정이에요.
  • 블록에 직접: 아래 예시처럼 고정부가 끝나는 블록 안에 붙여요. 4개까지 찍을 수 있어요.

앞부분은 도구 정의(tools), 시스템 프롬프트(system), 메시지(messages) 순서로 만들어지므로 system 끝에 붙이면 도구 정의와 지시문이 함께 저장돼요.

{
  "model": "claude-opus-5-5",
  "max_tokens": 1024,
  "system": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "(매번 같은 지시문, 규칙, 예시)",
      "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral" }
    }
  ],
  "messages": [
    { "role": "user", "content": "(요청마다 바뀌는 입력)" }
  ]
}

Gemini: 자동인 implicit과 미리 올려 두는 explicit

Gemini의 implicit 캐시는 기본으로 켜져 있어서 따로 할 일이 없어요. 다만 문서는 “캐시에서 읽었을 때(when cache hits occur)” 할인된다고만 써서 읽는다는 보장은 없어요. 구분점을 찍는 방법도 없어서 Google 문서는 대신 이렇게 권해요.

Place large and common contents at the beginning of your prompt. Send requests with a similar prefix in a short amount of time.
(크고 공통된 내용을 프롬프트 앞에 두세요. 앞부분이 비슷한 요청을 짧은 시간 안에 보내세요.)

explicit 캐시는 고정부를 미리 서버에 올려 두고 요청에서는 그 이름만 부르는 방식이에요. OpenAI의 explicit 모드와는 다른 기능이에요. 올려 둔 내용 전체가 구분점 하나와 같은 역할을 해요. 문서는 이 방식이 할인을 보장한다(ensures)고 쓰지만, 저장해 둔 시간만큼 저장료를 따로 내요. Gemini 4부터는 explicit 캐시를 쓸 수 없어요. Gemini API 문서에 그렇게 적혀 있고, Google Cloud 문서의 지원 모델 목록에도 Gemini 4는 없어요.

# 1) 고정부를 미리 올리기 (응답의 name이 캐시 이름)
POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/cachedContents
{
  "model": "projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/gemini-3.5-flash",
  "contents": [{ "role": "user", "parts": [{ "text": "(매번 같은 지시문, 규칙, 예시)" }] }],
  "ttl": "3600s"
}

# 2) 요청에서는 캐시 이름만 부르고 바뀌는 부분만 보내기
POST https://LOCATION-aiplatform.googleapis.com/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/locations/LOCATION/publishers/google/models/gemini-3.5-flash:generateContent
{
  "cachedContent": "projects/PROJECT_NUMBER/locations/LOCATION/cachedContents/CACHE_ID",
  "contents": [{ "role": "user", "parts": [{ "text": "(요청마다 바뀌는 입력)" }] }]
}

최소 길이와 유지 시간

캐시를 켜고 구분점을 맞게 찍어도, 고정부가 충분히 길고 같은 앞부분이 캐시가 사라지기 전에 다시 와야 캐시에서 읽어요.

최소 길이

  • OpenAI: GPT-5.6 이후는 1,024토큰이에요. 문서는 모델을 바꿀 때마다 고정부 길이를 새 모델 기준으로 다시 재 보라고 권해요.
  • Anthropic: 같은 세대라도 모델마다 달라요. 2026년 10월 문서 기준으로 512토큰(Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5, Fable 5.1, Haiku 5.5), 1,024토큰(Opus 4.8, Sonnet 5), 2,048토큰(Opus 4.7), 4,096토큰(Opus 4.6, Opus 4.5, Haiku 4.5)이에요. 3,000토큰짜리 프롬프트는 Opus 5에서는 캐시되고 Opus 4.6에서는 캐시되지 않아요. 최소 길이보다 짧으면 cache_control을 붙여도 캐시하지 않고 에러도 돌려주지 않아요.
  • Gemini: Gemini 2 계열은 2,048, Gemini 3과 4 계열은 4,096토큰이에요. 일부 모델은 문서마다 값이 달라요. Google Cloud 문서는 Gemini 3.7 Flash, 3.8 Flash 등의 implicit 최소를 6,144로, Gemini API 문서는 4,096으로 적어요. 쓰는 경로의 문서로 확인하세요.

유지 시간

  • OpenAI: GPT-5.6 이후는 마지막으로 쓰거나 읽은 뒤 최소 30분 유지돼요. prompt_cache_options.ttl로 정하는데, 지금 고를 수 있는 값은 기본값인 "30m" 하나예요.
  • Anthropic: 기본 5분이고 읽을 때마다 연장돼요. "cache_control": { "type": "ephemeral", "ttl": "1h" }로 1시간짜리를 쓸 수 있지만 쓰기가 2배라서, 요청 간격이 5분보다 길고 1시간보다 짧을 때 따져 볼 만해요.
  • Gemini: implicit은 Google Cloud 문서 기준으로 길어야 24시간이고, 대부분은 그 전에 사라진다고 해요. explicit은 기본 60분이고 늘릴 수 있지만 늘린 만큼 저장료도 늘어요.

같은 앞부분이 유지 시간보다 드물게 오면 캐시는 저장만 되고 읽히지 않아요. 쓰기 할증이 있는 모델이라면 저장할 때마다 할증만 내서, 캐시를 쓰지 않을 때보다 비싸질 수 있어요.

캐시에서 읽었는지 확인하기

응답의 캐시 필드

앞부분은 같고 끝의 입력만 다른 요청 두 개를 연달아 보내고, 두 번째 응답에서 캐시로 읽은 토큰이 0보다 큰지부터 보세요. 똑같은 요청을 두 번 보내면 구분점이 잘못 찍혀 있어도 캐시에서 읽은 것처럼 보여요. 필드 이름은 제공사마다 달라요. 숫자는 예시예요.

// OpenAI (Responses API)
"usage": {
  "input_tokens": 5000,                // 전체 입력
  "input_tokens_details": {
    "cached_tokens": 4800,             // 캐시에서 읽음
    "cache_write_tokens": 0            // 캐시에 새로 저장함 (쓰기 할증)
  }
}

// Anthropic
"usage": {
  "input_tokens": 200,                 // 캐시를 거치지 않은 나머지
  "cache_read_input_tokens": 4800,     // 캐시에서 읽음
  "cache_creation_input_tokens": 0     // 캐시에 새로 저장함 (쓰기 할증)
}
// Anthropic은 세 값을 더해야 전체 입력이에요

// Gemini
"usageMetadata": {
  "promptTokenCount": 5000,            // 전체 입력
  "cachedContentTokenCount": 4800      // 캐시에서 읽음
}

구분점을 직접 찍었는데도 읽기 필드가 계속 0이라면, 게이트웨이나 SDK 래퍼가 그 구분점을 제공사까지 그대로 전달하는지 확인하세요. 저희도 요청을 조립하는 중간 계층이 일부 요청에서 cache_control을 빠뜨려, 그 요청들은 캐시를 전혀 읽지 못한 적이 있어요.

히트율의 두 가지 기준

요청 기준 히트율은 캐시를 한 토큰이라도 읽은 요청의 비율이고, 토큰 기준 히트율은 캐시에서 읽은 토큰을 전체 입력 토큰으로 나눈 값이에요. 앞부분 6,000토큰 중 1,000토큰만 읽어도 요청 기준으로는 히트로 세서, 요청 기준이 대개 더 후하게 나와요. OpenAI 문서는 토큰 기준 히트율을 사용자나 날짜 단위로 묶어 보라고 권해요. 이 글에 나온 히트율도 모두 토큰 기준이에요.

제공사 진단 기능

OpenAI와 Anthropic은 이전 응답과 이번 요청을 비교해 캐시가 어디서 갈렸는지 알려 주는 진단 기능도 제공해요. 요청에 OpenAI는 prompt_cache_options.comparison_response_id를, Anthropic은 diagnostics를 넣으면 응답에 tools_changed(도구 정의가 바뀜) 같은 미스 사유가 와요. 쓰는 법은 OpenAI 문서와 Anthropic 문서에 있어요. Gemini에는 아직 이런 기능이 없어요.

캐시에서 못 읽을 때 보는 순서

캐시가 의심되면 위에서부터 차례로 확인하고 해당하는 단계에서 오른쪽에 적은 대로 고쳐요.

마치며

모델 하나를 바꿨을 뿐인데 에러 한 줄 없이 비용이 세 배가 됐어요. 원인은 모델이 바뀌면서 달라진 캐시 규칙이었고, 그 규칙은 문서에 적혀 있었어요.

앞부분이 매번 같은지, 그 길이가 내 모델의 최소 길이를 넘는지, 유지 시간 안에 같은 앞부분이 다시 오는지 물어보세요. 셋 다 “예”라면 캐시가 비용을 크게 바꿔요. 그때는 고정부를 앞에, 바뀌는 부분을 뒤에 두고 구분점이 그 경계에 찍히는지 확인하세요. 시각이나 요청 ID, JSON 키 순서, 도구 목록 순서처럼 앞부분을 몰래 흔드는 것들도 치우세요.

돌아보면 Gemini에서 히트율이 높았던 건 저희가 요청을 잘 짜서가 아니었어요. 끝이 달라도 같은 앞부분까지는 알아서 읽어 주던 제공사 동작 덕분이었는데, 저희는 거기에 기대고 있다는 걸 몰랐어요. 잘 돌아가던 이유를 모르면 그 이유가 사라져도 알아채기 어려워요.

그래서 모델 교체는 코드 한 줄이 아니라 운영 조건을 바꾸는 일로 다뤄야 해요. 응답이 맞게 나오는지에 더해 요청당 비용, 응답 시간, 캐시 히트율을 교체 전과 나란히 비교하세요. 이 비교는 몇 건으로는 할 수 없어요. 캐시는 앞선 요청이 데워 둬야 읽히고 요청이 얼마나 자주 오느냐에 따라 달라져서, 몇 건만 보내 보면 실제와 다른 숫자가 나와요. 운영 트래픽에서 하루 이상 잴 값으로 보고, 배포한 뒤에도 이 지표를 계속 지켜보세요. 저희도 배포 다음 날 히트율만 봤다면 닷새가 아니라 하루 만에 알아챘을 거예요.

이 경험은 한 모델의 캐시 정책에서 끝나지 않아요. LLM을 프로덕션에서 쓰면 모델이나 제공사 동작, 프롬프트 구조가 바뀔 때 에러 없이 비용과 품질이 달라지고, 그 변화는 운영 지표에서만 드러나요. 그래서 지켜야 할 규칙은 사람보다 시스템에 두고, 나머지는 지표로 지켜봐야 해요. 저희도 구분점은 플랫폼이 찍게 하고, 사람은 “바뀌는 부분은 템플릿 끝에 둔다” 하나만 지키게 했어요.

마지막으로 세 제공사의 차이를 한 장에 모았어요.

참고한 자료

이 글에 쓴 제공사 동작은 2026년 10월 공식 문서 기준이에요. 캐시 규칙은 모델 버전마다 바뀌니, 적용하기 전에 다시 확인해 보세요.

  • OpenAI: Prompt caching, Prompt cache diagnostics
  • Anthropic: Prompt caching, Cache diagnostics
  • Google: Context caching overview, Gemini API context caching

event_model_payload.headline: Announcing the Workload Conformance Working Group
event_model_payload.summary:
We are excited to announce that the Kubernetes community now has a Workload Conformance Working Group. The working group is writing a shared standard for how workloads behave at runtime on Kubernetes. To get it right, we need input from the people who build those workloads and from the people who run the clusters they're deployed on.

Why workloads need a shared standard

Certified Kubernetes tests the cluster, and Kubernetes AI Conformance tests whether a cluster can run AI and ML workloads. Nothing comparable exists for the workloads themselves, so cluster operators still check each application by hand before routine maintenance or a Kubernetes upgrade.

The problems they find are familiar. A routine node drain is often how you discover that an application can't tolerate disruption. An upgrade can break an application that still depends on a removed API version. Others show up in day-to-day operation: workloads that ask for privileges they don't need, or reserve resources they never use.

Kubernetes already documents much of this, including security and handling disruptions. Even so, every cluster operator ends up repeating the same assessment, and application maintainers get the same questions from each environment they support. A common specification with repeatable tests would give both groups the same baseline to start from.

What the working group will deliver

The charter sets out three deliverables:

  • A specification of workload behavior for each Kubernetes minor version.
  • A method for testing each requirement against a running workload.
  • Upstream conformance tooling that implements those tests.

The first step is deciding which workloads and behaviors the specification covers. The scope includes security, resilience during disruptions, resource use, networking, storage, API usage, and observability, but the group hasn't yet agreed on specific requirements or on how to test them. However, one rule is already set: every requirement needs an objective test that a test binary can run, so nothing subjective goes into the specification.

The specification covers how a workload runs, and importantly not what it does. Consequently, application logic is out of scope of workload conformance. The binary won't retest anything Certified Kubernetes already covers, and it won't require a particular workload packaging format, or vendor tool like policy engine, security scanner, etc.

How the work is organized

Two Special Interest Groups (SIGs) are sponsors for the working group.

  • SIG Architecture will own the specification and tooling through a subproject, which will be created once the first artifacts are proposed by the Working Group.
  • SIG Apps will bring the application perspective.

Whenever a requirement touches another Kubernetes SIG's area, such as node behavior or networking, the working group will initiate conversations with those SIGs as well.

The working group is a forum where SIGs can get involved and shape the direction of Workload Conformance while the specification is being written. We're aiming for a stable first specification and working tests within two to three Kubernetes release cycles.

Get involved

The specification will and needs to be built from real examples, so we want to hear your experiences. If you run clusters, tell us how you assess workloads today and what broke during your last upgrade or maintenance window. If you maintain an application, tell us what it needs from the cluster and where the existing guidance left you guessing.

  • Beyond examples, the work needs reviewers for proposed requirements and contributors to write the tests and tooling.
  • When early versions of the tests are ready, we also want early testers to run the binary against your own workloads and tell us where the results differ between runs or environments.
  • If a requirement touches your SIG's area, help us check its scope and the test behind it.
  • And because the subproject will outlive the working group, we're also looking for people who want to maintain it for the long term.

You can find us in #wg-workload-conformance on Kubernetes Slack (visit slack.k8s.io for an invitation) and on the mailing list. The working group meets every other Wednesday at 15:00 UTC. The Zoom link and the agenda are in the meeting notes. If you want to raise a topic, add it to the agenda. Joining the mailing list usually adds the meeting invite to your calendar.

Thanks to everyone who reviewed and supported the working group proposal.

event_model_payload.headline: Spend less time on operational busywork and resolve incidents faster with Grafana Workflows
event_model_payload.summary:
You're investigating checkout errors when someone asks who's coordinating the incident. Support needs an update, and another responder is looking for the runbook. You stop what you're doing to get everyone pointed in the same direction.

They're all reasonable requests, but each one takes your attention away from understanding the problem. Yes, your team has a process for handling incidents, but carrying it out is another job for someone who's already busy.

Grafana Workflows, available in public preview, turns your team’s processes into automated steps across Grafana Cloud and your other tools. You can even include Grafana Assistant in those steps to investigate an issue, summarize findings, or draft an update. For example, a workflow can create an incident channel, page support according to your team’s rules, and ask Assistant to prepare a briefing from the available evidence.

The same approach works with your typical day-to-day operations. Once you define the workflow, Grafana Cloud can prepare the next engineer's handoff or gather the findings for your weekly service review. You decide what should happen consistently and where AI can help make sense of changing information.

Get the incident response moving

To illustrate how your team can benefit from Workflows, let's walk through a major incident response process.

For starters, your team needs a place to collaborate and someone to coordinate the response. A runbook helps, but someone still has to find the on-call commander, open the channel, and share the right links.

Workflows include blueprints, prebuilt templates you can adapt to your team's process. For this type of project, you'd start with the major incident kickoff blueprint, which can automatically respond to an active critical incident in Grafana Cloud IRM, including an incident that has just been escalated to critical.

It creates a linked Slack channel, looks up your incident commander schedule, and assigns an on-call commander. It also posts your response instructions, bookmarks the runbook and incident page, and records the kickoff on the timeline. If nobody is on call, it leaves a note so the team knows to assign a commander.

Now responders have the incident record and runbook at hand, and the commander can start coordinating the investigation. The setup follows the process you've configured. 

From there, you can build on that foundation. Suppose your policy is to involve support in every critical incident. Simply add a step that pages your support team in IRM and another that shares the incident link in their Slack channel. Support can get involved while engineers investigate, without waiting for someone to remember another handoff.

Note: Workflows is currently available under "More apps" in your Grafana Cloud navigation menu.

Put AI findings where people need them

Getting everyone together is just the beginning. The next person to join will need to know what's happening, what you've checked, and where to look next.

Extend the kickoff workflow with an ask Assistant step. Give Workflows the incident link, the affected service, and a specific task:

Review this incident and the available error and latency signals around its start time. Summarize the observed symptoms, link to the evidence, and suggest the next checks. Separate observations from hypotheses and flag missing information.

Assistant investigates using the available observability context and returns a briefing. Subsequent workflow steps post the briefing to the incident channel and add it to the incident timeline. The team can follow the evidence and ask better questions, and those who join later have a starting point for catching up.

At the same time, support has a different need. They have to turn technical findings into clear, customer-facing updates. An incident status update could trigger a workflow that asks Assistant to draft that explanation from the confirmed facts. A post message to Slack channel step sends the draft to the internal support channel, where the team reviews and edits it before sharing it externally.

This is where combining rules and AI becomes useful. You define the trigger, the task, and the destination. Assistant interprets the supplied context and returns a result that the next step can use. An engineer doesn't have to copy the answer out of a chat and put it in the right place.

You can also use AI to answer a specific question that determines the next step in your response. For example, when an alert fires, a workflow could ask Assistant to assess whether customers are affected and estimate how many. If the result exceeds a threshold you define, the workflow can declare an incident and page the SRE on-call. This focused assessment can run alongside a broader investigation into the root cause.

Give the next on-call engineer a head start

Soon after, the rotation changes, and the incoming engineer asks, "Anything I should know?"

Answering that question sufficiently can take some work. You remember the incident that's still open and fresh on your mind, but the incoming engineer also needs to know which alerts deserve another look. Gathering that context becomes one more task to finish before you can hand over the shift.

The on-call handoff report blueprint makes preparing that context part of the rotation change. It watches your selected IRM schedule and asks Assistant to review the team's recent incidents and alert groups. By default, it looks back over the past week, then posts a briefing to Slack with links to the relevant records.

The prompt asks Assistant to lead with what needs attention now: active incidents, recurring alerts, and follow-up work. You can adjust the time window and the report's focus to match your rotation.

The outgoing engineer can add anything that hasn't made it into the records. The incoming engineer gets a briefing to check and build on as they take over. That makes the handoff easier for both people, especially after a busy shift.

Come to the service review with the findings ready

The incident is now resolved, but the work doesn't stop there. Routine service reviews have their own preparation burden. For example, you may want to discuss whether latency is getting worse or error budgets need attention. First, someone has to open the dashboards, compare the numbers, and assemble an update for everyone else.

The weekly service health summary blueprint can have that first assessment waiting in Slack. Set it to run before the meeting for the services your team owns.

Assistant reviews the previous week's SLO status, error-budget consumption, and error and latency trends, along with relevant incidents and alerts. It produces a health assessment for each service and calls out risks for the coming week. The next workflow step posts the summary to Slack.

Your team comes to the review with an assessment to discuss, so you can spend the time deciding what needs attention. 

Start with one process your team already repeats

Ready to get started with Workflows? Pick the part of your week that keeps requiring someone to gather context or coordinate the next step. Choose a starting point from the blueprints library, or describe your process to Grafana Assistant and ask it to build a workflow for you.

The workflow opens disabled, so you can review and test it before turning it on. The visual editor shows how the steps fit together. Run history lets you inspect their inputs, outputs, and errors, helping you check both the actions taken and the information passed between them.

For example, click on the button below to create your first workflow using an Assistant prompt to build a daily summary of incidents and firing alerts.

Grafana Workflows is available now in public preview. Use the getting started guide to try your first blueprint and learn more about this new feature in Grafana Cloud. Start with the incident setup you keep repeating, the handoff that always takes too long, or the service review you wish you had time to prepare. Make that one process easier, then build from there.

event_model_payload.headline: Agent Observability FAQ: Understand the value of monitoring, evaluating, and improving your AI agents
event_model_payload.summary:
Agents have quickly become part of the tech landscape as organizations embrace AI across their businesses. But embracing agents also means embracing the monitoring best practices that have long been part of engineers' workflows: tracking performance, catching errors, and responding to incidents 

But it doesn't stop there. Agents also introduce new challenges. They can give different answers to the same question, be confidently wrong without throwing an error, and turn one request into a long chain of model and tool calls that’s hard to debug. A small prompt change can shift behavior as much as a code deploy. And because agents act on what they read, they open the door to new risks like prompt injection and leaked sensitive data.

It's a lot to learn, but that's why we built Agent Observability, now generally available, as part of our growing set of AI-enabled features in Grafana Cloud. It improves your agents by helping your teams:

  • Monitor performance and cost: Track latency, errors, token usage, and costs, and drill into individual conversations when something goes wrong.

  • Evaluate agent quality: Use built-in or custom evaluators to measure quality and detect issues like PII or prompt injection.

  • Test changes before you ship: Compare models, prompts, and other changes with offline experiments to catch regressions.

  • Build evaluations into CI/CD: Use experiments as deployment gates and track agent versions as you iterate.

Agent Observability was born out of our own challenges managing agents at scale, and it's the same tool we use internally today. In this blog, I'll address some of the common questions we get from customers.

Everything you want to know about Agent Observability

Monitoring, evaluating, and improving agents

Q: Why use Agent Observability to monitor my agents?

Agents are production workloads, and they need the same visibility as the services they touch. Agent Observability runs in Grafana Cloud alongside your metrics, logs, traces, and profiles, so you can tell whether a bad answer came from the model, the prompt, or a service the agent called. Monitoring, evaluations, guards, and experiments all live in one place, so you don’t need a separate tool.

Q: Can I monitor coding agents?

Yes. Integrations for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, Pi, and more send sessions to a dedicated Coding agents view, where you can track cost, tokens, and tool usage by user, repository, or branch. Want to try it outside of Grafana Cloud first? The open source local app keeps sessions on your machine, no Grafana account needed. See how to set up and monitor coding agents for more details.

Q: How do I know if a prompt or model change made my agent better or worse?

Agent Observability tracks agent versions automatically from changes to your system prompt, so you can compare quality, cost, and latency across versions. To catch regressions before you ship, run experiments against a baseline and use them as a CI gate.

Q: Do evaluations require an LLM judge?

No. You can use deterministic checks like regex or JSON schema validation alongside LLM judges, and mix both in the same evaluation.

Q: Can I see how multiple agents work together? 

Yes. Each conversation shows a map of how your agents hand work to each other, even across services. If one agent’s output fails an evaluation, you can see which steps downstream were affected. See our docs on instrumenting agent dependencies and workflows to set it up.

Working with your existing stack

Q: Can I use my existing OpenTelemetry instrumentation?

Yes. Agent Observability accepts spans that follow the OpenTelemetry generative AI semantic conventions, so you don’t need the Agent Observability SDK. Keep exporting through Grafana Alloy or your OpenTelemetry Collector, and opt in your spans in with a single resource attribute. See our docs on instrumenting agents with OpenTelemetry to get started.

Q: Can I build my own dashboards or get alerted automatically if something goes wrong?

Yes. Agent Observability metrics land in Prometheus, so beyond the built-in views. You can also build custom dashboards and run ad hoc queries, plus set up your own alerts for cost spikes, latency SLO breaches, and more.

Cost and pricing

Q: Can I see what’s driving my agent costs, and where to cut them?

Yes. Cost and token usage are tracked per agent, model, and conversation, and you can tag spend by team, project, or environment. Coding agents can also break it down by user, repository, or branch. From there, you can spot calls that are using a pricier model than they need, track cache hit rates, and compare cost across agent versions. See our guide to optimizing cost and performance for more information.

Q: How is Agent Observability priced?

Agent Observability bills on three separate meters: generations (each model call your agent makes), tokens used by LLM-based evaluations and guards, and the standard metrics and traces your SDKs send. Free and Pro plans include 30,000 generations and 25 million evaluation and guard tokens each month. That token allowance is shared with other Grafana Cloud AI features. See Agent Observability pricing for current rates.

Security, privacy, and access

Q: Can Agent Observability block bad behavior, not just flag it?

Yes. You can create guards that sit on the request path before each LLM call, using regex patterns and PII detection to catch or redact sensitive data before the model ever sees it. You can also block risky tool calls.

Q: What data gets captured, and can I keep sensitive content out of it?

Agent Observability captures what your agent sends, including prompts, responses, tool calls, and token usage. The SDK can redact secrets before any data is exported, and guards catch PII before the model sees it. Coding agents send only metadata unless you opt in to full content.

Q: Can I control who sees conversation content?

Yes. Built-in roles let you separate access. For example, the Data Reader role shows analytics, traces, and evaluation results without access to conversations. Each Grafana Cloud stack is fully isolated, so use separate stacks when you need hard boundaries, such as dev versus production.

Q: Is Agent Observability available outside Grafana Cloud?

Agent Observability for agents you build runs in Grafana Cloud. For coding agents, there’s also a free, open source local app that keeps sessions on your machine with no Grafana account needed. When you want to observe coding agent usage across your team, connect it to Grafana Cloud.

Get started with Agent Observability

Agent Observability is available today in Grafana Cloud, including on the free tier, which comes with 30,000 generations and 25 million evaluation and guard tokens each month. To get started, create a free account and follow our guide to setting up Agent Observability.

Want to build a new agent? The open source Grafana AI SDK for Go gives you one interface across model providers, and connects to Agent Observability from the first call. Have a question we didn’t cover? Ask us in the Grafana community forums.

event_model_payload.headline: How to fund Rust contributors
event_model_payload.summary:
TLDR:

  • To fund general maintenance, donate to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or sponsor the RustNL Maintainers Team
  • To fund specific features and improvements, sponsor fundable Rust Project Goals
  • To fund individual contributors, donate to their GitHub Sponsors accounts

There is always so much to do in the Rust Project! New features to implement, bugs to fix, performance optimizations to make, issues to triage… It takes a lot of work to keep our high bar of quality while also shipping new features and improvements. And the workload keeps increasing with the continuous growth of Rust adoption.

As is unfortunately common in open source projects, a large fraction of that work is currently done by volunteers. That causes various issues, such as people burning out or complex features taking many years to ship.

Unsurprisingly, one of the best ways to help improve that is to get more people who work on Rust funded! This year, several funding initiatives started ramping up, and we already experience many positive effects. They helped us improve the maintenance status of critical Rust projects and make significant progress on several long-awaited features, such as allocators, the never type, the next trait solver or the Polonius borrow checker. However, only a fraction of people working on Rust are currently funded for their work.

We know that there are Rust users, both individuals and companies, who would like to help improve Rust by funding it, but it might not always be obvious how exactly to do that. This post thus provides suggestions on how you can support the development of Rust in three ways.

If you're unsure which option fits, or would like to discuss funding on behalf of your company, please contact the Funding team.

Fund general maintenance

Maintenance is a continuous process required to keep Rust (or any software project for that matter) working. It consists of two main activities. The first is general housekeeping, such as ensuring that Continuous Integration works, dependencies are kept up-to-date and issues, bugs and security incidents are promptly triaged and resolved. The second is performing refactorings and code reviews, which ensures that the codebase will be able to evolve and continuously ship new features, without accruing extensive technical debt.

Having quality maintenance is crucial for the long-term health of Rust, yet it is typically very difficult to find funding for it; funders often want to sponsor specific new features, rather than just "keeping the lights on". However, without sufficient maintenance, it becomes much more difficult, and much slower, to ship new features. Improving the maintenance of Rust thus also helps us ship features and improvements faster, though the effects are sometimes only observable over longer periods of time.

Funding maintenance is a great choice if you want to let us decide how best to improve Rust. The Rust Funding team continuously looks for Rust teams and projects that require help with their maintenance efforts, and allocates available funds to Rust maintainers who could help improve the situation.

To fund Rust maintainers, consider donating to the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or sponsoring the RustNL Maintainers Team.

Fund specific features and improvements

There are always many Rust improvements and new features that are in progress. We track some of those initiatives through Rust Project Goals. Each Goal describes a specific improvement to Rust: what it is, who is going to develop and drive it forward and which Rust teams are willing to help reviewing and maintaining it.

Some of those Goals are looking for funding. Either to help their owner dedicate time and focus to push the given feature forward, or to fund maintainers who will perform refactorings necessary to unblock that feature and review its implementation. Often funding is required for both. When a Goal is properly funded, the probability that it will achieve its milestones is much higher, which then translates in the given improvement being shipped sooner to Rust users.

Funding Project Goals is a great choice if you want to help push forward specific Rust features or Rust toolchain improvements that will benefit you or your company.

To fund contributors working on Project Goals, consider taking a look at Goals that need funding and reaching out to their funding contact. If in doubt how to proceed, reach out to the Rust Funding team.

Fund individual contributors

There are hundreds of people in the Rust Project who continuously work on improving Rust. Some of them have personal fundraising profiles (e.g. on GitHub Sponsors), which allows you to support them directly.

There might be various reasons for supporting a specific person. Maybe they are maintaining a crate that you love to use, maybe you like reading their blog posts, or maybe you are simply a fan of the work that they do. Whatever the reason, we are sure that they would appreciate your support!

Funding individual contributors is a great choice if you want to directly support Rust contributors whose work you appreciate.

To fund individual Rust contributors, check out their GitHub profile or personal website to see what options there are for supporting them. You can also examine our list of Rust Project members who can be supported through GitHub Sponsors[1].

Conclusion

We hope that this post is useful to anyone who would potentially like to invest funds into making Rust better. You can also find a shortened version of the "how to fund Rust guide" at the Funding page of the Rust website, or check out a RustConf 2026 talk by Niko Matsakis about how Project Goals and their funding works.

If you are a company looking to fund the development of Rust, consider joining the Rust Commercial Network. Joining the network is free, and Rust Foundation membership is not required. It can help you find opportunities for funding improvements in specific areas related to Rust usage (e.g. user interfaces, language interop, supply chain security, etc.) and collaborate on funding Rust development with other companies.

There are of course other ways of helping Rust other than donating funds. For example, you can check out Project Goals that are looking for contributors or more generally check our contributor onboarding guide. Companies can also help by giving employees paid time to contribute upstream, or by hiring Rust contributors to do that work. One possible model is the Engineer in Residence role, that was recently established in the Rust Foundation.

  1. Note that this list is not exhaustive; there are some Project members who accept donations through GitHub Sponsors (or another fundraising platform), but did not opt into being listed on this page. ↩

event_model_payload.headline: What happens when vulnerabilities are discovered faster than you can fix them?
event_model_payload.summary:
We're entering a new era of application security. Frontier AI models are uncovering complex flaws that traditional tools overlooked, and attackers are using the same models to exploit them faster. Remediation isn't keeping pace: Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report (DBIR) measures the median time to fully remediate a known-exploited vulnerability at 43 days, up from 32 in 2025.

Security teams are already stretched across growing application portfolios, third-party dependencies, and a steady stream of new disclosures. And while agents that find vulnerabilities and write fixes are becoming more accessible, integrating them into how enterprises actually build and ship software remains difficult.

A generated patch still needs to be tested. Security policies need to be enforced. Changes need to be reviewed and approved. And eventually, the fix needs to reach production safely.

This is where I believe the next major shift in application security will happen. We need to put autonomous agents to work inside the software factory. That's why we've brought Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1 into GitLab, and why we're connecting discovery, remediation, and prevention in one trusted workflow.

When critical vulnerabilities emerge, the clock starts ticking

Critical vulnerabilities like PHP2Shell send security teams scrambling to understand exposure. For a large organization, that means assessing impact across hundreds or thousands of repositories, applications, and dependencies.

Identifying exposure is only the first step. Teams then need to assess exploitability, prioritize affected applications, coordinate fixes, run tests, and get changes into production. Every handoff takes time, and speed is vital: 31% of breaches now start with vulnerability exploitation, the top initial access vector for the first time in the DBIR's 19 years.

As more critical vulnerabilities emerge, the traditional model of manually investigating findings, assigning tickets, and waiting for developers to write fixes becomes harder to sustain.

The time between vulnerability discovery and verified remediation needs to shrink dramatically. That requires security workflows capable of operating at machine speed, while preserving the controls organizations depend on to ship reliable software.

Bring agentic remediation into the software factory

AI agents can do impressive work in vulnerability discovery and remediation. The challenge is making that work reliable and repeatable across an enterprise.

An agent can generate a patch in seconds. Whether it understood the application, whether it validated the change against the real build, and whether it followed your security policies are separate questions. They get harder to answer, and more expensive to get wrong, as you deploy agents across thousands of projects.

At GitLab, we're bringing agentic security workflows into the environment where teams develop, test, and ship software.

Everything an agent does rests on how well it understands your system, and that understanding extends beyond the repository. GitLab Orbit, a live context graph of your software lifecycle, connects findings to the changes that introduced them, the pipelines that shipped them, and the teams who own the fix. It's also how you answer the questions that follow a disclosure like PHP2Shell: Are we exposed? Is it reachable? How far does it spread, and how do we fix it without breaking production?

GitLab Duo Agent Platform investigates findings in the context of your software and how it's built, filtering out likely false positives and prioritizing by exploitability and reachability.

For the findings that matter, Duo writes a fix and puts it through your pipeline to check for regressions and rerun security scans. In a single merge request, developers review the change, Duo's explanation, and the pipeline results.

Security teams move from understanding exposure to initiating remediation in one pass, and developers shift from chasing findings to reviewing fixes. Because these workflows run inside the software factory, agents operate within the same processes and controls that organizations already use to deliver software.

That's how we turn agentic security from an isolated capability into something an enterprise can trust and operate across thousands of projects, at machine speed.

Put frontier AI to work on the most critical vulnerabilities

Some of the most dangerous application vulnerabilities require a deep understanding of how software is intended to work: missing authorization checks, broken ownership logic, and business logic flaws that expose customer data or let users take actions they shouldn't.

Traditional scanners struggle with these issues because finding them requires reasoning about the application's behavior and the relationships between components.

Our new Business Logic Security Analyzer, the first GitLab capability to support Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, examines how your application enforces its rules: it reads the whole repository and incoming merge requests, infers what each endpoint should enforce, and flags the gaps that pattern-based scanners often miss.

But the real opportunity comes from connecting those discoveries to the workflows teams already use. When a critical flaw is found, teams need to understand its impact, initiate remediation, validate the proposed fix, and ship it safely. Integrating frontier AI into the software factory creates a path to run that entire process at machine speed.

The intelligence of the model is only as valuable as your ability to act on it.

Prevent risky code from reaching production

Finding vulnerabilities earlier is valuable, and keeping vulnerable code and unsafe packages out of production altogether is even better. These protections become even more important as agents gain autonomy.

Security controls need to be embedded throughout the software factory and enforced independently of the people and agents making changes, with every change clearing the same gates before it moves forward.

GitLab Ultimate brings static analysis, dependency and container scanning, secret detection, policy enforcement, and approval gates directly into the software delivery process. Those policies are set centrally and apply consistently across projects and pipelines, so the author of a change, human or agent, cannot change or waive the controls evaluating its work.

The same scrutiny needs to extend to third-party software. Modern applications rely heavily on open source dependencies, and a vulnerable or malicious package can introduce serious risk before developers write a single line of code.

GitLab's Dependency Firewall blocks policy-violating packages before they enter your build. GitLab Secrets Manager lets each job access only the credentials it requests and is authorized to use, so a compromised dependency can reach only the secrets of the job it runs in.

Agents need the freedom to work quickly, within boundaries they can't cross. GitLab Duo Agent Platform gives each agent a composite identity that limits it to the permissions it shares with the requesting user, a sandbox that's destroyed when the task ends, and a record of every action. These boundaries are part of the GitLab Security Standard, under which agents earn more autonomy only as the controls at each stage are proven to hold.

The controls that make a change trustworthy need to hold at every step, even when the work happens at machine speed.

The next chapter of security will be defined by trusted execution

Frontier models will keep improving, security agents will get more capable, and vulnerabilities that were once difficult to discover will become easier to find. That progress will put enormous pressure on how organizations respond.

A security team can deploy the most advanced models available, but its ability to reduce risk will still depend on how quickly and safely it can turn findings into production-ready fixes.

This is why the software factory matters. It's where agents get the context needed to understand applications, where changes are validated against real builds and tests, where security policies are enforced, and where human oversight applies without slowing every step of the process.

At GitLab, we're bringing these capabilities together so you can automate remediation, uncover complex flaws, and prevent unsafe changes from shipping, all inside the workflows you already use.

The next security advantage will come from how quickly organizations can turn a critical discovery into a verified, trusted fix.

We invite you to run your next security sprint on us. Qualifying teams can request access to GitLab Ultimate, GitLab Duo Agent Platform, GitLab Orbit, and GitLab Secrets Manager, with free credits. Request access to the security sprint offer.

event_model_payload.headline: PHP2Shell: GitLab helps find and remediate critical PHP flaws
event_model_payload.summary:
GitLab is not affected by PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The GitLab application is not written in PHP and does not run it to serve web requests, and our Security team has found no evidence of impact to GitLab-managed infrastructure. GitLab.com, GitLab Self-Managed, and GitLab Dedicated are not impacted.

PHP is a widely used programming language that runs on web servers and powers popular platforms like WordPress, Drupal, and Magento, so a flaw in PHP itself can affect many websites and applications. On October 21, 2026, the PHP project fixed two critical remote code execution flaws in PHP, together known as PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). PHP rates both 9.2 on CVSS v4.0. The flaws are in the PHP engine, not in any framework, library, or application code, so there is no application-level fix. Any web server that runs PHP is affected, including NGINX and Apache. The PHP project confirmed the vulnerability on Apache with mod_php, where an unauthenticated request can achieve remote code execution before any application code runs.

Upgrade every server and container that runs PHP to serve web requests to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, or to your distribution’s patched package now.

This guide is for security and platform teams with PHP projects on GitLab. It covers the fixed version for each PHP branch and distribution, how to use GitLab features to locate PHP projects across your groups, how to track remediation, and how to check for signs of compromise.

Upgrade PHP to a fixed version now

Upgrade the PHP runtime on every host and in every container image to a fixed version. Framework updates, Composer updates, input validation, and authentication don’t help, because PHP handles the request before application code runs.

BranchFixed in
PHP 8.5.x8.5.12
PHP 8.4.x8.4.27
PHP 8.3.x8.3.36
PHP 8.2.x8.2.35 (end of life December 31, 2026)
PHP 8.6 release candidates8.6.0RC4. The official php:8.6-rc image was still on RC3 on October 21, and RC3 does not have the fix.
PHP 8.1 and olderNo official release. PHP published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1, and some distributions ship patched packages.

If your PHP comes from a distribution package, upgrade that package. Fixed package versions as of October 22:

DistributionFixed package
Ubuntu 26.04php8.5 8.5.4-0ubuntu1.5
Ubuntu 24.04php8.3 8.3.6-0ubuntu0.24.04.13
Ubuntu 22.04php8.1 8.1.2-1ubuntu2.28
Debian 13php8.4 8.4.27-1~deb13u1
Debian 12php8.2 8.2.35-1~deb12u1
Alpine 3.24php83 8.3.36, php84 8.4.27, php85 8.5.12
RHEL 10php 8.3.36-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87070), php8.4 8.4.27-1.el10_2 (RHSA-2026:87071)
RHEL 9php 8.0.30-8.el9_8.1 (RHSA-2026:87151), php:8.2 8.2.35-1 (RHSA-2026:87072), php:8.3 8.3.36-1 (RHSA-2026:87079); php:8.4 had no fix yet on October 22
RHEL 8php:7.4 7.4.33-8 (RHSA-2026:87080); check Red Hat’s CVE pages for php:8.2. Retired streams (7.2, 7.3, 8.0) get no fix

Sources: Ubuntu, Debian, Alpine, and Red Hat security trackers, as of October 22, 2026.

Ubuntu, and Red Hat for its 7.4 and 8.0 packages, keep the old upstream version number and backport the fix. Compare the package versions rather than php -v. Restart every process that runs PHP after upgrading.

Rebuild your container images. If your image uses a floating tag of the official php image, such as php:8, php:8.3, php:8.3-apache or php:latest, rebuild it with docker build --pull and redeploy it. Images that pin a patch version, such as php:8.3.35-apache, need the tag changed to the fixed version first. Images built on derivatives such as wordpress or drupal get the fix only after their maintainers publish an updated image, so check the upstream image before you rebuild.

Locate PHP projects across your GitLab groups

Any project that runs PHP to serve web requests needs a fixed version, including the ones that are easy to forget, such as an internal dashboard, a marketing site, or a CI job image. Finding them takes two views: a static search of what your repositories declare and your images contain, and a runtime inventory of what actually runs. GitLab covers the static view with three features. Use them in this order.

1. Container scanning

Container scanning reports vulnerabilities in operating system packages, so it finds PHP installed with apt, apk, or dnf, and it reports the two CVEs once they reach the scanner's vulnerability database. To turn it on for a project, add the template to .gitlab-ci.yml:

include:
  - template: Security/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml

container_scanning:
  variables:
    # Experimental, Ultimate only: also reports runtimes not installed by a package manager
    CS_BINARY_SCAN: "true"

You can also use a group-level scan execution policy to turn container scanning on for every project in a group at once. When a policy is enabled, the next time a pipeline is run, it will be run with container scanning. Container scanning results for the default branch can be reviewed in the Vulnerability Report after the scanner completes.

Additionally, you can set up Merge Request Approval policies with container scanning. With merge request approvals in play, if a code change contains PHP2Shell, the policy will block a merge without approval from the selected parties.

By default, container scanning detects only PHP installed as a package. The official images compile it from source, leaving no package record, so a project can pass container scanning and still run a vulnerable version.

Container scanning analyzer 8.7.0, released on October 29, adds an experimental binary scan that reports runtimes installed without a package manager, which closes that gap. It is available on Ultimate and off by default: set CS_BINARY_SCAN to "true" to turn it on. If you leave it off, Orbit and code search below cover it.

2. GitLab Orbit

GitLab Orbit indexes your projects, pipelines, security findings, and source code, including PHP, into a queryable graph, so you can ask an agent to review an entire group. With Orbit enabled on the top-level group, an agent can list every project that contains PHP code, including the projects that compile PHP or use the official php images, which container scanning misses. Orbit doesn't yet parse Dockerfiles (feature proposal issue #1416), so use that list to scope the code search in the next step, which confirms the base image and version in each project. You can also ask Orbit which projects have open findings for CVE-2026-109618 or CVE-2026-109619 once scans have run. Orbit indexes the default branch only and is in beta for Premium and Ultimate on GitLab.com and GitLab Self-Managed.

3. Code search

Exact code search can find the two types of files that indicate a PHP project. Run these at the top-level group with regular expression mode enabled (the .* toggle at the right of the search box):

  • Container base images: This query searches for every file GitLab detects as a Dockerfile. The pattern matches any image whose name or tag contains php, so it also finds derivatives such as wordpress, frankenphp, or bitnami/php-fpm. Expect a few false positives that you can rule out by reading the result: lang:Dockerfile ^FROM.*php
  • Composer projects: This query finds projects that use PHP even when they have no Dockerfile, or when the Dockerfile takes its image from a build argument such as FROM $BASE_IMAGE:
file:composer\.json$

Exact code search covers the default branch only. On GitLab.com it is on by default for paid plans. On GitLab Self-Managed instances an administrator must install Zoekt first. GitLab Dedicated doesn't support exact code search.

For each result, confirm the version. You can check the FROM php: line, or run php -v in the running container, and compare it with the table above. The group dependency list shows Composer packages and framework versions but not the PHP runtime version.

4. Compare with your runtime inventory

Container scanning and code search show what your projects declare and build, not what runs. PHP can run outside your GitLab projects, for example on web servers with mod_php or PHP-FPM enabled only in their configuration, on hosts configured by hand, or in containers that still run in clusters without an active pipeline. Compare the static results with an inventory of your running workloads from your configuration management (Ansible, Puppet, Chef, etc.), cloud, or VM inventory tools. For Kubernetes, operational container scanning scans the images that run in your clusters, with the same package-only detection as container scanning. Treat every PHP runtime that appears in only one of the two views as a gap to investigate.

Remediate at scale with GitLab Duo Agent Platform

GitLab Duo can run the discovery steps above for you, across all your projects, through Orbit and code search. From there, let agents do the repetitive work and keep people on review and merge.

Automate the fix. Use Agentic Chat to create an epic with one issue per affected project and assign the Developer Flow to each. The flow opens a merge request that updates the base image tag or package to a fixed version. A flow trigger on the Assign event starts it the moment the issue is assigned. Turn on automatic reviews with the Code Review Flow to get a first review that follows your custom review instructions. Review and merge each merge request, then close the issue once the fixed version is deployed.

Enforce with policies. The merge request approval policy from Step 1 blocks any change that reintroduces a vulnerable PHP version without approval, and the scan execution policy keeps container scanning on in every project so a regression appears in the vulnerability report.

Searches find candidates, but a security or platform engineer still has to review each match, resolve CI includes, and tell what the code declares apart from what actually runs. An example agent skill from the GitLab Developer Advocacy team handles this work. It runs on GitLab Duo Agent Platform and with agents that use GitLab MCP server or the glab CLI, such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

The skill checks container images, CI jobs, OS packages, configuration management variables, Composer pins, and environments. It returns a cited findings table with deployment evidence, and open gaps. The skill is read-only: It makes no changes, and remediation merge requests remain a separate, reviewed step. It cannot confirm what is running on hosts it cannot access, so verify those directly. Adapt the skill to your own environment before you use it.

Check for compromise

Reports of exploitation differ. Security researchers reported an exploit attempt on October 17, 2026, before public disclosure, and further reports of exploitation followed the release. The PHP project identified no functional exploits at the time of release. If an internet-facing server ran a vulnerable PHP version, review its logs from October 17, 2026, onward for:

  • Multipart requests followed by memory-limit errors or repeated HTTP 500 responses
  • Unusually large or malformed PHPSESSID response cookies
  • Unexplained PHP worker restarts, or shell processes started by PHP workers
  • Unexpected files on the PHP web server, outbound connections from PHP workers, or unexpected cron entries

A successful exploit can return HTTP 200 and leave the worker running, so an absence of errors doesn’t rule out compromise. If you find signs of exploitation, isolate the server and start an incident investigation. Where possible, capture memory, disk, and logs before patching and restarting. Restarting PHP workers may erase evidence. CVE-2026-109619 can also expose process memory, even when an attacker doesn’t achieve code execution. Rotate any credentials, tokens, or keys the PHP process could read.

Note: Scanners may flag the Gemnasium dependency scanning image (gemnasium:6), deprecated since GitLab 17.9, for its bundled PHP. It is used only as a command-line tool and never handles HTTP requests, so it is not exploitable, and a fixed version has already shipped under the same tag.

DateWhat happened
August 1Calif discovers the first flaw during an AI-assisted PHP audit and reports it to PHP on August 11; Wiz Research independently finds and reports the flaws on August 24.
October 17Amazon’s honeypots record the first known exploit attempt, while the flaws are still under embargo.
October 20PHP announces that a security release fixing two critical vulnerabilities will ship on October 21.
October 20Vulnerability details leak before coordinated disclosure. (Huntress)

event_model_payload.headline: Virtual models now available on AI Gateway
event_model_payload.summary:
Virtual models are now available on AI Gateway.

A virtual model is a saved configuration that tells AI Gateway which model and settings to use. Your apps and agents call it with a custom model ID, such as vmc/coding-agent. You can change the model or settings centrally in AI Gateway without redeploying your apps or reconfiguring your agents.

Use virtual models to:

  • Configure coding agents: Set reasoning effort, fast mode, prompt caching, and other options even when your agent doesn’t expose them.

  • Control routing and compliance: Choose providers, configure fallback models, and enforce requirements such as Zero Data Retention.

  • Attribute spend: Attach custom reporting tags to every request that uses the virtual model.

To create a virtual model, open the Virtual Models page and click Create Virtual Model. Enter a slug, choose the underlying model, configure the settings you want requests to use, and save.

Or create one with the Vercel CLI:

To use a virtual model, replace the provider model ID in your AI SDK or compatible API requests with vmc/, such as vmc/coding-agent.

For coding agents, connect to AI Gateway with vercel ai-gateway setup if needed, then select your virtual model in the agent’s model picker or configuration.

Virtual models work with every model type on AI Gateway. Read the launch post for examples or learn more in the virtual models documentation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

event_model_payload.headline: Introducing Vercel CI
event_model_payload.summary:
Coding agents are opening more pull requests than ever, and each one waits on CI before anyone can review or merge it. Most CI systems run the entire workflow on every push, even a one-line change. The more your agents push, the more time you spend waiting on CI.

Today, we're announcing Vercel CI in Beta. It runs only the tasks affected by your code change, and spins up only the compute those checks need, the same way Fluid compute scales with your traffic.

At Vercel, our CI now keeps up with our coding agents. Time from git push to "CI passed" is 2-6x faster than it was before.

How it works

Vercel CI uses Turborepo to understand your tasks and which ones depend on each other. It reads turbo.json, so if you're already using Turborepo, there's no separate CI config to write.

If you're not on Turborepo yet, add turbo.json and the turbo package. It works in single-package repos too.

Then tag the tasks you want Vercel CI to run.

"tags": ["ci"] is all you need to get started. No workflow YAML to maintain, no drift between your CI config and turbo.json, and Remote Cache is on by default.

When you or your agent push code, Vercel CI determines which tasks need to run based on the change. Tasks whose inputs haven't changed come from cache. The remaining tasks each run on their own machine, powered by Hive, Vercel's compute layer, and start as soon as their dependencies finish.

Vercel CI gives each task the compute it needs and nothing more.

Running your CI on Vercel

To get started, follow the documentation or prompt your agent from your repo:

Once set up, you or your agent can watch and inspect CI through the Vercel dashboard, Vercel CLI, or Vercel MCP. When something fails, go straight to the failing task, see what's blocked behind it, and open its logs, or search across recent runs to see whether a test has been flaky all week.

Vercel CI posts a check to your pull request on GitHub, so your existing branch protection rules can block merges on failure, the same way they do today.

Closing the loop

Vercel CI has already completed nearly 8 million tasks across our own repositories and the private beta, and we're just getting started. We're working to keep shrinking the time between writing code and running it in production.

As we work toward general availability, we plan to add:

  • Advanced observability

  • A vc ci CLI command for distributed execution before pushing code

  • More granular test selection

Vercel CI is available in Beta today on all plans. Read the docs and try it on your repository.
