event_model_payload.headline: Uncover the business logic vulnerabilities SAST scanners miss
event_model_payload.summary:
Broken object-level authorization ranks first on the OWASP API Security Top 10, and OWASP says that traditional static application security testing (SAST) tools struggle to find access control flaws. A missing authorization check is an absence of code, so a scanner that matches patterns has nothing to match. You can find the gap only if you already know what the endpoint is meant to enforce.

We're building Business Logic Security Analyzer in GitLab Duo Agent Platform to catch business logic vulnerabilities that pattern-based scanners miss. It is now in early access for GitLab Ultimate customers on GitLab.com.

Valid code, wrong intent

Any application security team will recognize these three findings:

  1. An endpoint takes an order ID from the request and returns the order without checking who owns it.
  2. A role field on a user profile accepts whatever JSON the client sends.
  3. A user ID is a sequential integer.

Each one is valid code that slips past most taint and pattern rules in a conventional SAST engine, because no untrusted data reaches a dangerous sink, and no known-bad signature appears. Chained together, they hand an attacker every customer's order and an administrator role.

Across GitLab's customer base, codebase size has grown as much as 500% as agents write code. CVE disclosures through April ran 46% above the February forecast from the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams. The same AI models that generate code also make existing weaknesses less expensive to discover and chain. Authorization logic is where that pressure lands: Developers and agents write a check in a line or two, but when one is missing, the gap often goes unnoticed. As Omer Azaria, vice president of Product Management at GitLab, put it at GitLab Transcend, "We're caught in the middle: more code, faster attacks, same teams."

Why whole-repository scanning starts here

GitLab Duo Security Review looks for authorization flaws in merge requests, but many business logic flaws aren't visible in a diff. Whether an endpoint should check ownership depends on the data model, the roles the application defines, and how other endpoints treat the same records. Judging one handler means reading the application around it.

That is why Business Logic Security Analyzer scans the whole repository, and why GitLab is the platform to do it on. The source code, the pipelines that build it, the security findings attached to it, and the policies that gate it all live in one system. An agent that scans here sees the full application and writes its findings where the security team already works.

At Transcend, we introduced the GitLab Security Standard: five stages each agent must clear to earn more autonomy, built on the premise that code is now abundant and trust is scarce. Its Verify stage requires every change, whether written by a person or agent, to pass controls the author cannot touch. Business Logic Security Analyzer runs outside the author's hands, and its findings persist in the same report and dashboards that govern the rest of the codebase.

How the analyzer works

Business Logic Security Analyzer is a foundational flow on GitLab Duo Agent Platform that targets business logic flaws, starting with broken object-level authorization, missing or improper authorization, and mass assignment. A practitioner can run a whole-repository scan, and scan each merge request automatically after its pipeline passes.

Detecting any of these flaws requires a model of what the application is meant to do. Pattern scanners have none, but an agent that reads the repository can build one. The analyzer starts by enumerating the application’s entry points and mapping who should be allowed to do what: which records belong to which user, and which actions are administrative. It then reads each handler in scope and checks whether the handler enforces that rule before touching the record. Findings land in the Vulnerability Report and the merge request security widget as first-class SAST results, to support triage, remediation, and auditing.

In the demo application below, refund_order accepts an order_id from the request and sets refunded=1 without checking that the caller owns the order or is an administrator. Taint rules stay silent because the query is parameterized. The analyzer reports it as CWE-639, Critical, at app/orders.py:17, and its explanation names the missing ownership check.

The models behind the analyzer

Business Logic Security Analyzer is the first GitLab capability supporting Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5.1, and is available in early access to customers in approved environments. The model sees only GitLab's prompts and the customer's repository, which holds the context the analyzer needs: the data model, roles, and rules each endpoint enforces. As Rajat Pandit, Head of Applied AI, Anthropic India, said at Transcend, "When defenders have more context than attackers, advanced models change the math in their favor."

Alongside Mythos, the analyzer supports Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6, with more models planned for future releases. All of them run as GitLab-managed models through GitLab’s AI gateway, under the same data handling terms as the rest of GitLab Duo Agent Platform.

Request early access

Business Logic Security Analyzer is in early access for a small group of GitLab Ultimate customers on GitLab.com. Participants run the analyzer on their codebases to find true positives their security teams didn’t already know about. We will work with each team to learn where the analyzer is correct, wrong, or silent. Each scan consumes GitLab Credits, and cost scales with the size of the application's attack surface.

To be considered, contact your account team, or, if you are not yet a GitLab customer, contact our sales team. Once your group is enabled, start a whole-repository scan from GitLab Duo Chat or through the API, and attach the Business Logic scan profile to a project to scan its merge requests. The Business Logic Security Analyzer documentation covers prerequisites and setup.

event_model_payload.headline: AI Governance: One view of agent activity
event_model_payload.summary:
AI coding agents are writing and changing code, from GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents to externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex. You are accountable for what those agents do, yet most of their activity stays invisible: which agents ran, who used them, and what they touched. Teams often struggle with understanding whether a developer used a tool or model that is approved or not.

The AI Governance Dashboard, now in beta, gives you one place to see agent activity across your top-level group. It brings GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and the external agents your developers connect into one view, showing which agents ran, who used them, and which projects they touched. The dashboard also shows the tools and sessions associated with each agent.

With that audit trail in place, you can answer the questions auditors and risk owners ask: who ran this agent, what did it do, and who is accountable for it. Every agent action gets recorded in one audit trail, detailing the model it used, the tools it called, and the project it ran in. You can now investigate a session or hand an auditor evidence without stitching together multiple sources of data.

Watch a demo of the AI Governance Dashboard:

Gain visibility into AI agent activity

More AI agents are running across your organization than you can track by hand. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents run inside GitLab, while externally connected agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex run on developers' own machines.

The result is the shadow AI problem: real work happening in your projects, from many tools, that no one accountable can see in one place or tie to a team member.

The AI Governance Dashboard brings that activity into view and connects each agent to the developer behind it. To turn it on in your top-level group, go to AI > Governance. GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and externally connected agents appear together, and you can toggle between the views to see all agents, just Duo Agent Platform Agents or just externally connected agents. Three tiles at the top give you a baseline: how many agents ran, how many sessions they started, and how many tool calls they made over the past seven or 30 days. Each tile shows the daily trend and the change from the previous period, so a spike, like a new tool your team started using last week, stands out. The cards below tell you where to act. You can check whether the agents your developers rely on match the ones you approved, see which projects carry the most agent activity and need closer review, and know who to talk to when usage shifts.

Prove what every agent did

Managing AI risk starts with knowing what every agent did and who prompted it. Traditional audit trails were built for human changes, so that record is often scattered across tools or missing. GitLab records every agent action as an audit event, so you can investigate an incident or answer an auditor from one place.

Open any GitLab Duo Agent Platform session to see the prompt the developer sent, the tools the agent called, the MCP servers it used, the model that ran, and the project it changed. From there, you can download an immutable copy of the session as evidence, or stream the events to your security information and event management (SIEM) system.

Set up your dashboard today

It only takes a few steps to set up the AI Governance Dashboard:

  1. Check access. The dashboard needs the Owner role on the top-level group, or a custom role with the read_agent_artifacts ability. If the people who should watch agent activity don’t have Owner access, create that custom role first.
  2. Turn on AI audit event storage. Storage is off by default, and events are only recorded after you turn it on. In your top-level group, go to Settings > GitLab Duo, select Change configuration, and then Store AI audit events in the Data and privacy section. You need to have an Owner or Security Manager role to have access.
  3. Open the dashboard. In your top-level group, go to AI > Governance, and select the Dashboard tab to see your GitLab Duo Agent Platform activity.
  4. Connect your externally connected agents. Sign in with GitLab CLI (glab) 1.122.0 or later on macOS or Linux. To capture Claude Code sessions, run glab govern setup, which installs the Claude Code hooks. To also capture Cursor and Codex sessions, run glab govern setup --agents codex,cursor, which adds a background job that sends those sessions every 30 minutes. Run glab govern doctor to confirm the setup works.

The AI Governance Dashboard is in beta for GitLab Premium and Ultimate customers. Turn it on for your top-level group to keep oversight of AI usage as fast as your teams adopt it.

Not on GitLab yet? Try GitLab Ultimate for free and use the AI Governance Dashboard to get started.

event_model_payload.headline: Three developer tasks worth handing to an agent
event_model_payload.summary:
You already have an AI assistant. It completes your code, explains code you didn’t write, and maybe even drafts a whole feature while you sip your coffee. An agent on GitLab picks up where your editor stops.

The AI in your editor only knows what's open in your editor. It doesn't know that your merge request has been sitting in the queue for two days, or that your pipeline failed for the third time this week. Without your pipeline logs, it can’t offer a fix.

GitLab Duo Agent Platform works within the project and across your software delivery workflow, taking into account merge requests, issues, pipelines, and repositories your whole team shares. This context makes all the difference.

Here are three ways to try out GitLab’s agentic features today, and you don't need a paid GitLab plan to do it.

Set up your group

On GitLab.com, a group Owner sets up your top-level group:

  • Purchase GitLab Credits.
    • Go to Settings > Billing and select Purchase credits.
  • Turn on GitLab Duo Agent Platform.
  • Turn on foundational flows.
    • Go to Settings > GitLab Duo.
      • Select Change configuration.
      • Under Flow execution, select Allow flow execution and Allow foundational flows.
      • Select Code Review and Fix CI/CD Pipeline.
      • Select Save changes.

1. Hand off the first pass on reviews

Code Review Flow reads a merge request's diff, description, and related files (like tests and dependencies), then posts detailed review comments directly on the merge request. The flow catches small issues, missed edge cases, and inconsistent patterns on your merge requests, so you can save your judgment for the critical details.

Try it on your project:

  1. On a merge request, assign @GitLabDuo as a reviewer, or comment /assign_reviewer @GitLabDuo.
  2. Watch the review comments appear on the merge request itself, the same place your teammates will see them. Code Review Flow checks the diff, the description, and related files like tests and dependencies before it comments.

To hand off the first pass on every new merge request, turn on automatic reviews.

Watch how merge requests can speed up with Code Review Flow:

2. Send a failed pipeline to an agent to investigate

Have Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow diagnose your failed pipeline and propose a fix, so you spend your time applying it instead of hunting for the cause.

This flow investigates logs, error messages, the merge request changes that likely caused it, and the repository contents. Depending on the failure, it either proposes an inline code suggestion on your merge request or opens a new merge request with a fix.

Try it on your project:

  1. On a merge request with a failing pipeline, select Fix pipeline with Duo from the Overview or Pipelines tab. The flow reads the pipeline logs and your merge request changes to find the cause.
  2. Select AI > Sessions to follow along, then review the result on your merge request. Depending on the failure, you get inline code suggestions you can apply, a new merge request if the fix touches files outside your diff, or a comment with next steps when a failure needs a person.

For pipelines that aren't tied to a merge request, you can trigger the same flow: go to Build > Pipelines, select the failing pipeline, and select Fix pipeline with Duo. You get a new merge request with the fix.

Follow along with this demo:

3. Get answers from across your project

Ask Agentic Chat what changed in a merge request or why last night's pipeline failed, and get one answer that pulls from your project's merge requests, issues, and pipelines. This is where most editor-based AI assistants fall short. Your IDE's assistant can tell you what a function does, but it can't tell you which issue introduced it or why last night's pipeline failed.

Try it on your project:

  1. In the GitLab UI, open your project. In the GitLab Duo sidebar, select Add new chat, then select an agent. You can also use Agentic Chat in VS Code, JetBrains IDEs, and Visual Studio.
  2. Make sure the Agentic toggle is turned on.
  3. Ask what you'd normally dig for by hand. Agentic Chat searches your project's issues and merge requests by keyword and retrieves pipelines to build its answer. For ready-made prompts, browse the AI Resource Library, for example Summarize Recent Changes to MR/Issue or Debug Failing Pipeline.

You can also ask Agentic Chat to run either flow above on a merge request. Each chat message you send uses GitLab Credits.

Watch the demo:

What these agentic features cost

On GitLab Free, you can use a set of GitLab Duo Agent Platform agents and flows, including all three above, without upgrading to Premium or Ultimate. Your group buys a monthly commitment pool of GitLab Credits that every group member draws from, so you pay for the work agents and flows do instead of paying per seat. The pool refreshes each month on an annual term. You can increase it at any time and decrease it at renewal.

Each feature uses credits at its own rate. For Agentic Chat and Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow, usage depends on the model and on how much back-and-forth a request needs. The credit multiplier tables list current rates. Buying the pool also turns on on-demand billing for usage beyond it, so set usage caps to control spend.

Where to start

If you only try one this week, make it the Code Review Flow. Assign @GitLabDuo as a reviewer on your next merge request and see what it comes up with. From there, Agentic Chat and Fix CI/CD Pipeline Flow are ready to be deployed when you are.

Ready to get started? You can purchase GitLab Credits for your monthly commitment pool in your Customer Portal.

event_model_payload.headline: Building AI security in the open
event_model_payload.summary:
When code becomes abundant trust becomes scarce.

That is the argument GitLab CEO Bill Staples made in his recent essay: AI is collapsing the cost of producing software, and everything around production, including context, verification, governance, and evidence, becomes proportionally more important. Both security and collaboration are key elements to producing trust. AI widens what has to be trusted to include the agents that now write software along with the software that gets written.

That is why GitLab is joining the Open Secure AI Alliance, which brings together organizations to develop and share open technologies, techniques, and tools that help safeguard software and agents in the age of AI. We joined because we believe AI security is strongest when it can be inspected, tested, adapted, and improved by a broad community of defenders.

This is an extension of work GitLab is already doing in the open.

GitLab’s AI Gateway is a standalone service that provides access to AI features across GitLab.com, GitLab Dedicated, and self-managed instances. Its source code is public, and so are the agent workflow configurations running on AI Gateway, including configurations for code creation, code review, secrets false-positive detection, and security review.

  • Developer Flow configuration
  • Code Review Flow configuration
  • Security Review Flow

These examples reflect an important principle: An AI system is more than the model behind it. Trust depends on the surrounding harness, workflows, controls, context, and evaluation. Open tooling makes it easier for defenders to understand how those pieces work, test them against real risks, and improve them over time.

We also believe enterprises need choice. Organizations should be able to use proprietary and secure open weight models, select the right model for the job, and make decisions about where and how AI systems operate. Model and cloud agnosticism helps preserve that flexibility, while an open ecosystem gives customers more options for building, governing, and securing AI.

Transparency also has to cover the risks. Our documentation on security threats in agentic systems sets out the attack paths that apply to our own agents and the controls that apply in each environment. We treat our agents as privileged actors: Each one runs with an explicit identity, constrained tools and permissions, and actions that can be audited. We share how this works through our documentation for composite identity, sandboxed execution, per-flow tool restrictions, and agent tool governance.

Through our participation in the Open Secure AI Alliance, GitLab has an opportunity to share practical work already underway across our AI and security teams and learn from the broader community. Our goal is not to position open weight and closed models as opposites. It is to help ensure that defenders have the transparency, control, and flexibility they need to build trustworthy AI systems.

AI security should be built in the open. Learn more about the Open Secure AI Alliance.

event_model_payload.headline: Vercel Sandbox commands now support stdin
event_model_payload.summary:
Vercel Sandbox now lets you send input to running commands through standard input (stdin). Use it to exchange messages with stdio MCP servers such as agent-browser, or send data to other command-line programs while they run.

In the TypeScript SDK, set stdin: true and detached: true in runCommand(). Use writeStdin() to send input and closeStdin() when you’re done:

You can also set stdin to a Node.js readable stream, such as process.stdin. The SDK forwards the stream’s data and closes the command’s standard input when the stream ends.

In the Python SDK, set stdin=subprocess.PIPE and send input with server.stdin.send(). Call communicate() to close stdin, collect remaining output, and wait for the process to exit:

For commands that receive all their input at once, you can pass input directly to Python’s run_process().

Read the Sandbox documentation to get started.

여기어때 오피스는 평소와 다르게 매우 한적했답니다.
바로 여기어때 전사 임직원이 다 함께 가을 운동회에 참석했기 때문인데요.

이날만큼은 모니터 대신 높고 파란 하늘을 바라보며, 회의 대신 응원을, 구글챗과 슬랙 대신 시원한 함성으로 운동장을 가득 채웠는데요. 활기 넘치고 따뜻했던 그날의 현장으로 여러분을 안내해 드릴게요! 🏃‍♀️🏃‍♂️

☀️ 디테일에 진심인 Culture TF의 세심한 준비

운동장에 도착하자마자 가장 먼저 눈에 띄었던 건 알록달록 무지갯빛 운동장이었어요. ‘여/기/어/때/컴/퍼/니/🖤’ 총 8개 팀의 부스가 운동장을 둘러싸고 있었는데요. 각 부스 안에는 웰컴 패키지가 동료들을 맞이했습니다.

자리마다 놓인 팀 컬러 조끼와 함께, 각자의 이름이 적힌 네임 스티커를 직접 조끼에 붙이며 서로의 닉네임을 확인할 수 있도록 했어요. 처음 만나는 타 부서 동료들과도 어색함 없이 “안녕하세요!” 하고 반갑게 인사를 건넬 수 있도록요!

여기에 가을 햇살 아래 열심히 뛰고 응원할 동료들을 위해 세심한 아이템들도 함께 준비해 두었답니다.

  • 뜨거운 가을 햇살을 대비한 쿨링 세트: 햇볕을 피할 수 있는 귀여운 종이모자와 그늘막 천막, 경기 후 땀방울을 시원하게 닦아낼 전용 손수건과 부스를 시원하게 식혀줄 대형 선풍기까지 완벽 구비!
  • 출출함을 달래줄 추억의 간식 꾸러미: 이른 아침부터 오느라 배고팠을 동료들을 위해 레트로 운동회 컨셉에 맞춰 정성스레 준비한 주전부리 세트!
  • 신나는 응원을 위한 팀 컬러 응원봉: 목청껏 소리 지르지 않아도 팀워크와 현장 열기를 북돋아 줄 응원 도구!

Culture TF의 세심한 배려로 모두가 시작부터 든든하고 기분 좋게 운동회를 시작할 수 있었어요. 🫶

📣 1988 레트로 감성과 함께 열린 오프닝 & 오전 경기

그냥 운동회라면 재미 없겠죠~ 여기어때의 전사 가을 운동회는 학창시절 ‘추억의 운동회’를 모티브로 준비되었어요. 말로만 추억의 운동회가 아닙니다! 스태프 복장부터 종목 선정, 간식 하나까지 모두 그 시절 추억의 운동회를 컨셉을 꾹꾹 눌러 담았어요.

레트로 착장을 멋지게 소화한 사회자와 응원단장들의 오프닝 무대 덕분에, 현장은 시작부터 즐거운 에너지와 웃음으로 가득했어요.

운동회의 첫 시작은 평소 마주치기 어려웠던 다른 팀 구성원들과도 자연스럽게 어우러질 수 있도록 아이스브레이크 코너를 진행했는데요.

음악에 맞춰 몸을 흔들다가 호각 소리와 함께 불리는 숫자대로 빠르게 뭉쳐야 하는 ‘둥글게 둥글게’ 게임, 다들 해보셨죠? 외쳐지는 숫자마다 서로 손을 잡아 끌며 “여기 한 명 더”를 외치다보니, 경쟁도 잊은채 웃음이 터져 나오더라구요.

특히 ‘칙칙폭폭 기차놀이’가 친밀감을 높이는 데 큰 역할을 했던 것 같습니다. 조별 기차가 마주칠 때마다 서로 눈을 맞추며 하이파이브와 반가운 인사를 나누다 보니, 어색했던 기류가 순식간에 사라졌습니다. 😝

이렇게 한껏 풀린 분위기 속에서 본격적인 경기를 시작했는데요. 운동회의 클래식 종목인 박 터트리기를 시작으로 큰공 굴리기와 줄다리기까지! 팀 단체전 경기를 진행했어요. 특히 줄다리기는 각 팀별의 재치 있고 기발한 응원전이 더해져 보는 재미가 매우 쏠쏠했답니다!

📻 맛있는 점심 식사와 마음이 따뜻해지는 라디오 부스

열심히 뛰었으니 이제 든든히 배를 채울 차례! 하지만 점심 식사만 하고 끝낸다면 여기어때가 아니죠.

소중한 휴식 시간 지루할 틈 없이 알차게 리프레시할 수 있도록 추억의 미니게임 부스와 라디오 부스도 준비했답니다. 🎪📻

점심 시간 동안 동료들이 직접 적어 보낸 신청곡 BGM과 함께, 평소 쑥스러워 건네지 못했던 고마움, 각 팀을 향한 유쾌한 응원이 담긴 사연들이 운동장을 채웠어요.

또, 한편에서는 학창시절처럼 잔디밭에 옹기종기 모여 공기놀이나 미니게임을 즐기며 승부욕을 불태우기도 하고, 팀원들끼리 단체사진을 남기며, 오후 경기를 위한 에너지를 기분 좋게 100% 충전했습니다. ☕✨

🔥 열정과 승부욕으로 가득 찼던 오후 경기

배를 든든히 채운 뒤 시작된 오후 경기에서는 그야말로 승부욕의 정점을 엿볼 수 있었는데요. 사실… 여기어때 구성원들이 이렇게나 승부욕이 강할 줄 몰랐어요.

모니터 앞에서는 세상 쿨하고 차분해보였던 동료들이, 호각 소리가 울리자마자 숨겨둔 승부사 기질을 뽐내시더라구요.

특히 운동장의 열기를 최고조로 끌어올린 하이라이트 종목이 있었는데, 바로 풋살입니다.

흡사 챔피언스리그 결승전처럼 팽팽한 긴장감과 열기가 대단했는데요.

풋살복과 풋살화를 챙기라는 공지는 어디에도 없었는데, 당일날 여기저기 자신만의 장비를 꺼내 준비하고 있는 모습을 보고는… 여기어때 구성원들 풋살에 진심이구나 알 수 있었어요.⚽

특히, 당일날 예정에 없던 여성 풋살 매치도 깜짝 진행될만큼 열기가 뜨거웠던 종목이었어요.

그 외에도 다섯 명이 한 몸처럼 발을 맞춰 미션을 수행하는 5인 6각 경기도 진행했고요.

마지막엔 역시 운동회의 꽃이라고 할 수 있는 이어달리기 경기도 진행했어요. 중간에 넘어지는 아찔한 순간도 있었지만, 툭툭 털고 일어나 끝까지 바통을 넘기며 완주하는 모습이 정말 뭉클했습니다. 👏

🏆 승패보다 소중한 추억을 선물받은 하루

너무 재밌었던 모든 경기가 끝난 뒤에는 기다리던 대망의 시상식과 럭키드로우 추첨이 이어졌어요. 최고 인기 상품이었던 금 한 돈을 포함해 아주 빵빵한 경품들이 쏟아졌는데요. 우리 팀과 동료들의 이름이 호명될 때마다 아낌없이 축하해 주는 모습을 보며, 승패를 넘어선 원팀 문화를 다시 한번 느낄 수 있었답니다. :)

아마, 시간이 지나면 경기 결과나 순위는 기억 속 저편으로 아득해질지도 몰라요.

하지만 같은 색 조끼를 입고 한 방향을 바라보며 목청껏 응원하고, 함께 웃으며 뛰었던 이 하루의 온기만큼은 앞으로 우리가 함께 일하는 과정에서도 커다란 에너지가 되어줄 거라 믿어요.

보이지 않는 곳에서 정성을 다해 준비한 Culture TF와 그라운드를 열정으로 가득 채워준 동료들이 있었기에, 2026 여기어때 가을운동회는 그 어느 때보다 반짝이는 하루로 완성될 수 있었습니다.

일할 때는 치열하게 몰입하고, 함께할 때는 유쾌하게 하나 되는 여기어때의 긍정적인 에너지가 글 너머 여러분께도 기분 좋게 닿았기를 바라요. 🥰

여기어때와 함께 몰입해서 일하고, 유쾌하게 땀 흘릴 줄 아는 동료가 되고 싶다면 언제든 문을 두드려주세요. 오피스에서 반갑게 맞아드릴게요! 😊

회의실을 벗어나 잔디밭으로! 여기어때 전사 가을 운동회 현장 was originally published in 여기어때 기술블로그 on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: Securing your app, together
event_model_payload.summary:
Merchants install your app because they trust it, and because they trust the Shopify App Store. There are bad actors out there who are motivated to exploit that trust. Alongside the rest of the industry, we are seeing the number of attacks increasing across the app ecosystem as AI gets better at finding vulnerabilities.

Security is the most important thing you can work on right now. We’re asking every app developer to act on the steps below this week.

  • Scan your app with our new security check. A single prompt with AI Toolkit checks for Shopify-specific vulnerabilities, such as unauthenticated routes, cross-shop data access and unverified webhooks. In early access, most partners found something they didn’t know about.
  • Move to expiring access tokens. Short-lived tokens limit the damage if a token leaks. This will soon be required for all public apps, so start your migration now.
  • Use vulnerability scanners to ensure all endpoints of your app are secured.
  • Treat all rendered data, whether pulled from metafields or your own servers, as untrusted, ensuring inputs are thoroughly escaped and sanitized.
  • Check your Dev Dashboard to look at your API requests and ensure you do not see any suspicious activity. To get started, filter your logs by client IP to look at traffic patterns and find suspicious sources.
  • Protect every account that touches your app. Turn on two-step authentication for your Partner account, hosting, CDN, code repositories and email. Remove access for anyone who no longer needs it.
  • Keep your emergency contact current. Make sure your emergency developer email in the Partner Dashboard reaches someone who can act quickly.
  • Review and apply the security best practices in Shopify Dev Docs.

What we’re doing alongside you

We’re tightening the boundaries for storefront app code, adding IP address restrictions so your keys only work from your servers, and raising App Store security requirements. We’ll share details and timelines with you before any change takes effect, so you have time to prepare. We’ll keep investing in platform protections, developer tools and guidance that make secure development the default.

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we’ll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.

event_model_payload.headline: Metaobject analytics queryable capability available in the Admin API
event_model_payload.summary:
Starting with GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, you can read and configure the analyticsQueryable capability on metaobject definitions. This applies to apps that create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions. No action is required unless you want your app to control whether a metaobject definition can be queried in analytics.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API now exposes the analytics queryable capability for metaobject definitions.

You can read MetaobjectCapabilities.analyticsQueryable, which includes:

  • eligible: whether the metaobject definition can use the capability. A definition is eligible if at least one of its fields uses an analytics-compatible type.
  • enabled: whether the capability is currently enabled.

You can also set the capability when you create or update a metaobject definition by using:

  • MetaobjectCapabilityCreateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityUpdateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityAnalyticsQueryableInput.enabled

The MetaobjectCapabilityType enum now includes ANALYTICS_QUERYABLE, and MetaobjectUserErrorCode includes CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE for definitions that can’t enable the capability.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later to create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions.

Apps that use earlier versions don’t see the analyticsQueryable field, input, enum value, or error code. Existing apps don’t need to make changes unless they want to support analytics queryability for metaobject definitions.

Why this matters

You can now determine whether a metaobject definition is eligible to be queried in analytics and enable that capability through the public GraphQL Admin API. This brings metaobject definitions in line with metafield definitions, and you get consistent control over which custom data types appear in analytics.

What to do

No action is required.

If you want to use this capability:

  1. Update your app to use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later.
  2. Update your metaobject definition queries or mutations to include analyticsQueryable.

For example, to read a metaobject definition’s capabilities, include:

capabilities {
  analyticsQueryable {
    eligible
    enabled
  }
}

When you create or update a metaobject definition, set analyticsQueryable.enabled in the capability input. Check eligible first, and handle CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE in mutation user errors. Use this method to confirm whether a definition supports the capability and give clear feedback when it doesn't.

Related docs

  • GraphQL Admin API reference
  • Metaobjects in Shopify apps

event_model_payload.headline: Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
event_model_payload.summary:
Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-Silva

When Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.

This post is about that search for the needle.

The Four hours before a fix

Consider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?

As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.

The MELT Layer

“What caused the issue?”

Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.

The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:

The timeline of an investigation

So how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?

In our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.

The disagreement underneath

The instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.

It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.

Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.

The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.

What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.

The Ontology

This agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.

api-gateway   rdf:type       ops:Application .
api-gateway   ops:ownedBy    "Team Bedrock" .
api-gateway   ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .

INC-5377      rdf:type       ops:Incident .
INC-5377      ops:affects    api-gateway .
INC-5377      ops:severity   "SEV 2" .

In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.

“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.

We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.

We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.

The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).

Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.

Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:

There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.

The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.

The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:

Creating determinism from non-determinism

Building this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.

The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:

# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:
category  IN ["incident", "question", "discussion", "decision"]
sentiment IN ["positive", "neutral", "negative", "urgent"]

# Result — a deterministic triple:
thread:123  slack:category          "incident" .
thread:123  slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .

There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:

Enrichers: Agents as entropy reducers

We use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:

class Enricher:
    async def _enrich_async(self, ...):
        raw    = await self.fetch(...)      # 1. read noisy input
        result = self.analyze(raw)          # 2. process (may be stochastic)
        graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X))   # 3. emit TYPED triples
        graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value)))
        return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)

Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:

  • every entity carries an rdf:type,
  • every URI follows a single naming scheme, and
  • the catalog gates every ops:Application.

Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.

This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.

The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chains

The correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.

The role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.

A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.

The knowledge flywheel

Each harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.

Observe collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.

Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.

Putting the graph to work

On top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:

Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.

Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.

If you want to build one of these

A fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.

  • Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.
  • Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.
  • Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.
  • Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.
  • Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.
  • Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.
  • Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.
  • Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.

What comes next

The graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.

Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.

Acknowledgements

None of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.

Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

event_model_payload.headline: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
event_model_payload.summary:
An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve.

Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes.

The plan determines the permissions

For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision.

Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy:

Plan

Work

Requested scope

Investigate the failure

Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one

read:deployment

Redeploy the last known-good build

Create a deployment

read-write:deployment

A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically.

The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do:

  • Intent: The outcome the user asks for.

  • Work: The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it.

  • Access: The scopes those tasks require.

  • Enforcement: The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits.

Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan.

The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read:. Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless.

Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has

Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions, so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have.

The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits.

A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions.

Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions.

Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use

When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry.

The credential used depends on the work:

Work

Credential

Read-only investigation

A baseline token with read-only scopes

Approved Vercel changes

A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes

External actions

Credentials and permissions specific to that provider

The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task.

A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments. Opening a pull request there requires its own approval.

Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions

A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning.

At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages:

  • Plan validation: Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval.

  • Approval: The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access.

  • Token preparation: Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work.

For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access.

Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry.

Resuming work requires an active, approved plan

Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes.

Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry.

If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential.

If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. A replacement requesting elevated access needs its own approval, giving the user a chance to review the revised work and permissions together.

Where permissions need more precision

As Vercel Agent reached more of the platform, we had to correct access rules for actions that involve multiple resources or have different consequences. Attaching a domain can require both domain and project permissions, while staging a firewall rule and publishing it need different levels of access. Scopes need to capture these distinctions while keeping each plan’s access request manageable.

Matching those scopes to a proposed fix requires care throughout planning:

  • Choosing scopes: Vercel Agent chooses scopes with incomplete information, so it can request too little access and leave a task blocked, or too much and grant more authority than the work needs. Task-level guidance helps it choose, while validation catches invalid scope names. Even a valid scope can grant broader access than necessary.

  • Describing the work: “Redeploy the last successful build” gives the user a concrete action to assess, while scope names alone leave them to work out the consequences. The plan needs to explain the intended change and make clear which limits the token actually enforces.

  • Understanding denials: A denied operation could indicate a missing scope, an incorrect resource, or an operation that should remain blocked. Vercel Agent needs to distinguish those cases before requesting additional permissions.

Even with the right permissions, a redeploy requires judgment about whether the selected commit is safe to ship. That depends on the application, the failure, and the proposed fix. The user needs enough information to assess the choice, and Vercel Agent still has to execute it correctly.

Read-only investigation also needs controls for the information it retrieves, including sensitive project configuration and operational details. We chose a read-only baseline so Vercel Agent can investigate before asking for approval, and that choice needs continued review as scopes and the information they expose change. Other systems may need a narrower baseline. Separate controls must govern how retrieved information is handled and where it can go.

Vercel Agent can make a wrong decision or encounter malicious instructions in content it reads, such as build logs. Scoped credentials limit which operations it can perform in either case, but permitted operations can still cause harm. Plans therefore work alongside sandbox isolation, network policy, secret handling, rate limits, audit logs, and service authorization. Our work on security boundaries in agentic architectures explains the separation between an agent, its credentials, and the code it executes.

From investigation to approved action

Authority stays attached to the work that required it. The runtime selects the approved credential for an active plan, and its scopes define the operations Vercel Agent can perform. With the investigation already done, the user can assess a proposed fix and its requested access together.

Try Vercel Agent to investigate an issue in your project. Review what it finds and, if it proposes a change, assess the plan and requested access before approving it.

event_model_payload.headline: Enable the analytics queryable capability on metafield and metaobject definitions from your app's TOML
event_model_payload.summary:
You can now enable the analytics_queryable capability on metafield and metaobject definitions that you declare in shopify.app.toml. Merchants can then use those metafields and metaobjects as dimensions and filters in Shopify Analytics and ShopifyQL. Previously, you could set this capability only through the GraphQL Admin API.

What changed

Declarative definitions accept a new capability: capabilities.analytics_queryable. When it's true, the definition's values become queryable in analytics, the same as when you set analyticsQueryable with the metafieldDefinitionCreate ,metafieldDefinitionUpdate, metaobjectDefinitionCreate, and metaobjectDefinitionUpdate mutation. 

[customer.metafields.app.membership_level]
name = "Membership level"
type = "single_line_text_field"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.ingredient]
name = "Ingredient"
capabilities.analytics_queryable = true

[metaobjects.app.ingredient.fields.name]
type = "single_line_text_field"
name = "Name"

[metaobjects.app.ingredient.fields.calories]
type = "number_integer"
name = "Calories"

Release your app version with shopify app deploy, and Shopify distributes the definition to every shop where your app is installed.

What you need to know

  • The capability is available for customer, order, product, and product variant metafield definitions.
  • Not every metafield type can be queried in analytics. To confirm that a definition can use the capability, check the eligible field on its analyticsQueryable capability.
  • A metaobject definition can use the capability only if at least one of its fields has an analytics-compatible type.

For more information, refer to the following resources:

  • Use metafield capabilities
  • TOML reference for metafield definitions
  • Metaobject analytics queryable capability available in the Admin API.
